title: Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Family recipes are passed down through the generations and the film "Grandma's Hands" focuses on six Southern Maryland individuals who cherish those recipes.Historic Sotterley held a screening and panel discussion with the stars of the film along with writer, executive producer, director and narrator Craig Sewell on Nov. 13 at the museum in Hollywood.
"This was a passion project for me," said Sewell. "Kitchens are magic places, whether they're commercial kitchens or home kitchens, because it's about where everything happens. It's where smiles happen and tears happen and stories happen and the aromas happen. Kitchens are places where people come together."
The 58-minute film was funded through a Maryland Heritage Areas Authority grant and filmed by the Southern Maryland National Heritage Area.
"Ask someone about their grandmother and chances are the story will quickly end up in the kitchen. And once there, the real story begins," Sewell said to open the film. "Lives change, but the food will always be with us. Food is powerful. It nourishes our bodies, it excites our tastes, it is infused and marinated in emotion and it provides us with a solid connection to our past. For generations our grandma's hands have made memories, continued traditions and blessed us with the knowledge of who we are."
The film stars six individuals who recreate their grandmother's recipes: Lexington Park's Teandre Thompson (bread pudding), Waldorf's Mary Louise Booth Webb (crackling bread), Newburg's Tiffany Barber (tomato sauce with meatballs), Benedict's Franklin A. Robinson (chili sauce), Greenbelt's LaWann Stribling (macaroni and cheese) and Lothian's Kayla Griffith (sweet potato pancakes).
Thompson said her grandmother Theresa Young would create "a masterpiece dessert using a few ingredients and her hands. She didn't use measuring cups and spoons; she did it just by sight. I'm not that daring yet."
The 98-year-old Webb, who cooked the dish in her grandmother's farm kitchen located near Zekiah Swamp, said it was made as a way to use everything of the pig.
Robinson, who lives at Serenity Farm, said his grandmother would make the sauce at the end of the tobacco harvest.
"For me these recipes are a way of keeping all of these people I've known alive," Robinson said. "Every time I open the cookbook, I remember my grandmother at her wood stove and my other grandmother who lived on another farm. It's remembering them and honoring them."
Barber, who lives on Grace Haven Farm, said her grandmother would take Wonder bread, slather it with the sauce and layer it with Parmesan cheese.
"My grandmother's recipes were the center of my childhood," Barber, who still uses her grandmother's cast iron skillet, said in the film, "and it's something I carry forward with my kids."
Barber said dinner at her two-table dining room — which is essential for eight children and five grandchildren — "became that place where you learned to express yourself, having conversations about what matters to you and those connections. Dinner matters, meals matter. It's the connection you build around that meal."
Griffith, who lives on the family farm, said her grandmother Lillian would make pancakes with chocolate chips, whipped cream, sprinkles, "the whole nine yards"
"She could not sit down for more than a minute or two," she added. "She would get up, make sure everyone had something on their plate. To most of us she would say, 'You don't have enough,' but [to my grandfather it would be] 'Earl, you're eating too much.'"
The film viewing earlier this month was the season finale of Historic Sotterley's Common Ground series.
"Throughout the peninsula that is Southern Maryland, people have gathered, cooked for centuries," Sewell says in the opening minutes of the film. "The recipes are messengers from whence we came. Food and recipes can divide a family, a region, even a culture."
Maryland Public Television will air a 27-minute version of the film — focusing on three of the cooks — at 7 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23.
The hour-long version of the film will premiere on mpt.org, pbs.org and the PBS app starting on Sunday, Nov. 24.
Find out more about the film at destinationsouthernmaryland.com/discover/grandmas-hands.

title: Author takes to the seas with 'The Pirate Series'
content:
Author takes to the seas with 'The Pirate Series'

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 7A | Section: News 
 
 552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland author Elizabeth Gagné recently self-published her second book "Evangeline Shores Forever" in July through Amazon Kindle.The book is her second book, and first in The Pirate Series after "Shores of Forever Search for Blackbeard's Treasure" was rewritten and changed to "Evangeline Shores of Forever." The 60-year-old Gagné, who writes under the pen name Bitsey Gagné, graduated from Charles County Community College (now College of Southern Maryland) in 1982 from the licenses practical nurse and registered nurse programs in 1984.Gagné retired in May after a 40-plus year career as a retired nurse in Charles and St. Mary's counties, the last 33 years as a dialysis nurse.Gagné's third book, "Angie's Soulmate," which was released in book and eBook form Sept.21, is available along with the other books at www.amazon.com.How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?I started writing back in 2016 while I was recuperating after having surgery for breast cancer, but I had an idea for this book long before that.What inspires you to write?I visit the Outer Banks in North Carolina several times a year. I love the story about the mystery about what happened to the lost colonists of Roanoke Island. Hence, this is where the idea for my story transpired and blossomed, somehow into the novel that it is now.Do you consider writing to be a career?I consider it my career now after retiring from nursing.What kind of writing process do you use?I used Microsoft word/One Drive initially after I wrote out my document for my first two books but am now just using my laptop.Who are some of your favorite authors and why?Nora Roberts, Diana Gabaldon, Deborah Harkness are three of the authors that I like to read. I enjoy reading and writing romance, paranormal suspense novels.What are you working on now?"Angie's Soulmate" is the sequel to my first book. It's a romance, suspense and paranormal novel about a young country singer who moves to Ocracoke Island and is visited by her ancestor's spirit, Evangeline.Evangeline leaves her with the clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure and guides her to her soulmate.And to add a twist, have they stumbled upon what happened to the Lost Colonists of Roanoke Island?Please include a brief description of your book "Evangeline Shores Forever." Angie Harriott, an upcoming country singer/songwriter grew up in a small town called Ripley, Maryland. She spent her summers vacationing on Ocracoke Island listening to tales about Lost Loves and Blackbeard's treasure. After a difficult breakup with her boyfriend and sudden death of her father, she follows her dreams and moves to Ocracoke Island.Angie has always called the island the Shores of Forever, because of its rich and mystical history. She becomes entwined in a mystery and a romance as her new life begins. Evangeline, Angie's long ago ancestor's spirit, roams the shores looking for her lost love. She leaves Angie and her friends clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure map and guides Angie to her true love. Angie wonders if there is such a thing as soulmates that can pass from one lifetime to another.

title: National Museum of Asian Art presents 'Park Chan-kyong: Gathering'
content:
National Museum of Asian Art presents 'Park Chan-kyong: Gathering'

 August 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 931
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Seoul-based artist Park Chankyong has gained international recognition for his use of photography and film to examine the complex history of modern Korea."Park Chan-kyong: Gathering" will be the first solo presentation of his work in a major U.S. museum.The exhibition will feature a range of works that highlight Park's masterful use of the photographic medium to explore the enduring traces of tradition, history and disaster in contemporary society. It will be on view at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art Oct. 7 through Oct. 13, 2024.This will be the inaugural exhibition in the National Museum of Asian Art's modern and contemporary galleries, opening as the museum celebrates its centennial year. The galleries will become a space dedicated to engaging visitors in the myriad formats and media employed by artists to examine Asian society from the late-20th century to today, in context with Asian art dating from antiquity to the present that is on view throughout the museum.Park's multi-channel video, "Citizen's Forest," will anchor this exhibition of five recent works. A panoramic video presented in the format of a monumental landscape scroll painting, "Citizen's Forest" draws on the poetry of Kim Su-yeong (1921-68), Minjung painting and folk culture to reflect on major tragedies in South Korea's history from the late 19th century to the present. In "Belated Bosal" and "Fukushima: Autoradiography," inverted images and the natural landscape convey the inescapable sense of ecological disaster.Another installment in Park's study of the history of North and South Koreas, a series of still and moving image portraits titled "Child Soldier" reimagines the presence of a lonely North Korean soldier.In-gallery public programs with the artist and guest speakers will accompany the exhibition, including a screening of a short film by Park and an artist-led discussion Oct. 22 (details below).The exhibition is an important opportunity to introduce visitors to a major figure in contemporary Asian art and engage them in multisensorial experiences and insights into modern and contemporary Korea.Park studied fine arts at Seoul National University and earned a Master of Fine Arts at the California Institute of the Arts. Weaving together art historical and literary references, along with folk traditions and current events, he creates visually powerful works grounded in the enduring impact of rapid socioeconomic development and the Cold War on South Korean politics and society."As the National Museum of Asian Art enters its next 100 years at the dawn of what is fast becoming the Asian century, we are even more committed to telling complex stories about objects from a variety of perspectives," said the museum's director Chase F. Robinson. "We are also dedicated to engaging new audiences with Asian arts, cultures and societies and using our platform to address present-day issues.The rich dialogue and learning engendered by contemporary exhibitions like Park Chan-kyong's enable us to reach these goals." "I have followed Park Chan-kyong's work for years and am grateful to him for collaborating with us on this exciting project," said Carol Huh, associate curator of contemporary Asian art. "The opportunity to learn more about his use of the photographic medium and powerfully nuanced insights into Korean society today is an ideal way to usher in the next landmark chapter in the museum's groundbreaking contemporary Asian art program.As the museum embarks on its second century, this exhibition deepens our mission to examine evolving perspectives on the histories and cultures of Asia." Following "Park Chan-kyong: Gathering," the museum's new modern and contemporary galleries will feature an exhibition of works by contemporary artist Munem Wasif (Bangladesh), opening in late 2024. Both exhibitions will treat the artists' practices and relevant artistic and social context in greater depth, offering alternative viewpoints on their respective homelands.PROGRAMIn conjunction with "Gathering," Park will come to the National Museum of Asian Art to screen his short film Night Fishing and to discuss his work on Sunday, Oct. 22, at 2 p.m. in the Meyer Auditorium Shot entirely on an iPhone, this surreal short was co-directed by Park and his brother, Park Chanwook, and won the Golden Bear for Best Short Film at the 61st Berlin International Film Festival.In it, a fisherman feels a tug on his line, and much to his surprise, pulls a woman (K-pop star Lee Junghyun) out of the water. She comes alive and is revealed to be a shaman priestess who performs a ritual in honor of a drowned man. Like "Citizen's Forest," a video work on view in the exhibition, Night Fishing was inspired by Park's fascination with Korean shamanism.(Dir.: PARKING CHANCE [Park Chan-wook and Park Chankyong], Korea, Korea, 2011, 33 min., DCP, Korean with English subtitles) ABOUT THE NATIONAL MUSEUM OF ASIAN ARTThe Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art is committed to preserving, exhibiting, researching and interpreting art in ways that deepen our collective understanding of Asia and the world. Home to more than 46,000 objects, the museum stewards one of North America's largest and most comprehensive collections of Asian art, with works dating from antiquity to the present from China, Japan, Korea, South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Islamic world. Its rich holdings bring the arts of Asia into direct dialogue with an important collection of 19th-and early 20th-century American works, providing an essential platform for creative collaboration and cultural exchange between the United States, Asia and the Middle East.Its galleries, laboratories, archives and library are located on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. The museum is free and open to the public 364 days a year (closed Dec. 25). For more information, visit www.asia.si.edu. 
 
 Caption: PARK CHAN-KYONG/NATIONAL MUSEUM OF MODERN AND CONTEMPORARY ART, KOREAN
 
A still is shown from "Belated Bonsal" by Park Chan-kyong, a 2019 HD film.

title: Maryland man's 1963 Chevy II 400 convertible wins national competition
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Maryland man's 1963 Chevy II 400 convertible wins national competition

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 916
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Fran Bailey pays meticulous attention to detail when working on his antique cars, making sure that every part that he installs is historically accurate, that it is the correct shape and that it is exactly the right color.Bailey, 82, also puts in hard work to present a pristine-looking automobile when competing in car shows across the United States, something the Fair Hill, Maryland man has successfully done for several years.
So it's not surprising that Bailey's 1963 Chevrolet Chevy II 400 convertible recently received the top honor — the Louis Chevrolet Memorial Award — in a nationwide competition that started with a field of 2,400 automobiles that were exhibited in numerous car shows across the United States.
Then, a group of highly discerning superior judges narrowed that field to 59 hopefuls, before selecting the automobiles they believed deserved national awards in various classifications. In addition to the trophy, photos of Bailey and his Chevy II 400 appear in the Antique Automobile Club of America (AACA) magazine, along with a blurb about his special antique vehicle.
Bailey bought the Chevy II 400 about two years ago, after learning about it while attending the AACA Grand Nationals in Bettendorf, Iowa in 2022 and then arranging to take a look at it.
He acknowledged that a great deal of work already had been done on the car but, after he got the Chevy II 400 back to his private shop on the residential property he shares with longtime friend, Nancy Simpers, 81, the perfectionist immersed himself in the tasks of making the antique automobile historically accurate and making it gleam.
According to the magazine blurb, "Francis used a lot of elbow grease, along with replacing many parts and pieces that weren't correct. Amenities on the car include power steering, full wheel covers, white sidewall tires and rear radio antenna. Under the hood is the 194 cid/120 hp six-cylinder engine mated to an automatic transmission."
AACA judges are sticklers for historical accuracy, stressed Simpers, who regularly travels with Bailey when he is pulling his trailered automobiles to car shows in Iowa, South Carolina, Virginia, Kentucky, New York, West Virginia, North Carolina and few other states.
"These are not local car shows. Don't get me wrong, the local car shows are fun, but they are just that — shows, not competitions," Simpers said, before further explaining, "These are competitions, and the judges pay a lot of attention to detail. Period correctness is the big thing. Everything on the car has to be accurate."
To make her point, Simpers recalled a Kentucky car show a few years ago and how Bailey's other antique automobile — a 1967 Chevy II sports coupe — earned 1st Place. After winning the competition, Bailey offered the guy who garnered 2nd Place some advice.
"Fran told him, 'You have a round antennae and it is supposed to be oval'," Simpers remembered, emphasizing, "The car has to look good, but it also has to be period correct."
Bailey, who has been retired for 34 years after his career as an E.I. DuPont lab technician, has loved cars since childhood.
"I grew up in New Castle (Del.), and I've been interested in cars ever since I was a kid. I hung around gas stations, and I went to drag races at the Cecil County Dragway (north of North East)," Bailey outlined.
He bought his first car, a 1953 Dodge, in 1959 when he turned 16. "It was my granddad's, and I bought it from him after I got my driver's license. I had a job and I made payments," Bailey said.
Then in 1961, after he turned 18, Bailey started racing regularly at the Cecil County Dragway for the next 17 years and, competing with various vehicles he acquired along the way, he won quite often. Bailey recalls competing with a 1962 Chevrolet Impala that he also used as his everyday car.
"My best car was a '69 Chevelle," Bailey said, referring to his favorite drag-strip vehicle, which is a National Hot Rod Association record holder.
Over the decades, Bailey also dabbled in purchasing and restoring classic vehicles, showcasing them in car shows, often winning trophies, plaques and other prizes.
Bailey bought his 1967 Chevy II sports coupe in 1996, approximately 16 years before he purchased his 1963 Chevrolet Chevy II 400 convertible. Reflecting the detail-oriented restoration work that Bailey invested in those antique automobiles, the '67 Chevy II is insured for $52,000 and the 63 Chevy II 400 convertible is valued at about $30,000.
Simpers, a former teacher who still works as a real estate agent, shares Bailey's interest in antique automobiles. When she was a girl and then a young lady, she competed in thoroughbred racing, Simpers noted.
"I gave up horses for horsepower," she commented, chuckling.
Simpers is the proud owner of a sharp-looking, black 1937 LaSalle, the earliest form of the Cadillac, and it, too, has won local car-show competitions. Her grandfather purchased that LaSalle when it was new, some 88 years ago, and then Simpers bought it at his estate sale in 1967.
As for another one of her classic vehicles, a restored 1938 Chevrolet Street Rod, she gifted that one.
"I gave it to my godson for his 16th birthday. He always loved that car. I told him, 'When you are old enough to drive it, it's yours'," Simpers said.
It's perfect that Simpers and Bailey are antique car enthusiasts and, despite being in their early 80s, the couple is always rolling to pursue their hobby. This year, as in years past, they will travel to car shows in more than a dozen states.

title: Youth art show kicks off new year at DCA
author: DEBRA MESSICK Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Youth art show kicks off new year at DCA

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DEBRA MESSICK Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Life 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — It's fitting that while 2024 is still young, Dorchester Center for the Arts' first exhibit celebrates Youthful Minds, Big Ideas.It's the first-ever show for the multi-talented students of E.L. Haynes Public Charter School in Washington, D.C. On Saturday, Jan. 13, the gifted youngsters traveled by bus to DCA to attend a Second Saturday reception in their honor.
Instead of finger food hors d'oeuvres, the teens were treated to pizza, cake, and punch to enjoy in between strolling the galleries and savoring the unexpected, exciting sight of their art class creations on display.
Many of the dozens of pieces, hung throughout the Center's gallery areas, feature a unique optical illusion art form known as Agamograph, a visual kinetic energy method developed by Israeli artist Yaakov Agam in the early 1950s.
Using a technique called lenticular printing, several images are combined on one surface to create illusions of depth when a viewer moves, forming a visual picture that appears to shape shift.
Longtime educator and artist Kamala Subramanian, in her first semester at Haynes, inspired students to choose their own subject matter to create a unique Agamograph under the heading "Transformations".
"They each made two different paintings, using gridded paper, which were sliced up, then glued onto the background 'skeletons,' Subramanian explained.
A graduate of Temple University's Tyler School of Art, her professional focus has long been centered on printmaking, mixed media, and murals.
A multi-artist project she collaborated on with eight other women throughout the tumultuous year 2020, a series of miniature books, was recently acquired by the Library of Congress, titled "NINE ARTISTS/NINE MONTHS/NINE PERSPECTIVES" (https://pyramidatlanticcenter.org).
Currently, Subramanian is working on a piece dealing with the transatlantic slave trade, a topic she's passionate about, and which she's devoted considerable time to researching.

title: Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 682
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The son of a Kent Island waterman, Brent Lewis, has been around men and women who make their living on the Chesapeake Bay his entire life.Lewis said his mother early on shut down any thought that he might follow that path, but over the years, the local author and historian's appreciation for the demanding work and the characters who keep the industry alive has only increased.
It's why Lewis is so passionate about offering watermen a platform to share their stories.
"Living here for so long, I just had this idea that a lot of the people in our community don't really understand the watermen's life or what they do," said Lewis, who will host a Watermen's Story Swap on Thursday, Jan. 11 at 5:30 p.m. in the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's Van Lennep Auditorium.
Lewis has emceed a handful of similar events over the past decade, and he's realized the power of gathering watermen together to explain their shared experience through enlightening, funny and often profound tales.
At CBMM, Lewis will lead a panel that features both working and retired watermen hailing from around the Eastern Shore.
The suggested ticket price is $8 per participant, with both in-person and virtual options available at cbmm.org/WatermenStorySwap.
The event is funded through CBMM's Regional Folklife Center under the Maryland Traditions program of the Maryland State Arts Council.
Lewis has found certain themes - mentors, bad weather, and unexpected Bay adventures, to name a few - to be universal, but ultimately, it's the panelists' unique memories collected over years on the water and the free-flowing format that make these conversations equal parts entertaining and unpredictable.
"You never know where we're going to end up," Lewis said. "We don't have to stick to the topics as long as everyone's involved and having fun. It kind of runs the gamut between really hearty belly laughs to more emotional storytelling." The author of four books with a fifth underway, Lewis has long helmed an oral history project with the Kent Island Heritage Society, and at the first story swap in 2016, held before a standing-room crowd in Grasonville, he brought together eight watermen who he'd interviewed for that project.
There have been other iterations, including a couple at Chesapeake College's Chesapeake Storytelling Festival, but it's been more than five years since the last one.
Lewis found a partner in CBMM through its Folklife Center to launch the latest Watermen's Story Swap, this time with the focus expanding beyond Queen Anne's County.
He and videographer Josh Willis are recording an ongoing series of oral histories as part of the partnership.
The Jan. 11 Speaker Event, bringing together watermen from the mid and lower Eastern Shore, will be documented among that group.
Lewis said working with CBMM's Director of Curatorial Affairs & Exhibitions Jen Dolde and Vice President of Education & Interpretation Jill Ferris has breathed new life into the project by backing his belief in the importance of capturing these stories - both the ordinary and extraordinary.
"Working with CBMM, their enthusiasm for getting these stories down before they're gone has helped keep my enthusiasm up," Lewis said. "I can tell by talking to Jen and Jill that this is something that they feel is positive and beneficial to the community. If we don't take the opportunity to document these watermen's stories, once they're gone, they're gone." As much as anything, Lewis is excited to reach a new audience with this Story Swap. He's worked hard to assemble a panel that will represent different voices within the industry and bring together watermen from across the Chesapeake.
With the group spanning geography and generations all together on Jan. 11, Lewis will start the conversation and see where it goes.
"It's a lot of fun," Lewis said. "If it goes right - and knock on wood I've never had one go badly - it's very entertaining, it's very informative, and I don't think the audience members forget it very quickly."

title: Sweets And Treats For Everyone - Food
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Sweets And Treats For Everyone - Food

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 16 | Section: News 
 
 1452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Everyone loves homemade sweets, but especially at Christmas.From the young cook to the young mother to the grandmother to the older great-grandmother to the retiree and the men in the kitchen - we love baking cookies, making candy and frosting loaf cakes to give as Christmas gifts.
These treats are so appreciated by the teacher, the mail carrier, the delivery person, your co-workers, your elderly neighbor, those who are unable to perform baking chores due to disabilities, anyone working right up until Christmas Eve. Everyone loves baked goods no matter who they may be. So many of us just love watching the faces of the recipients also.
The first step and the most important is to have a list of the cookies, candies and cakes you want to make. The second step is to make a list of the ingredients you will need and the third is to get the correct amount of supplies.
Storage containers for the finished products are important. I save cookie tins throughout the year and purchase other types of paper or cardboard containers whenever they are on sale.
Finally, choose the day or two where you can bake all day undisturbed. Carry out pizza that evening for the family. Maybe you want to reserve a day or afternoon for the children or grandchildren to help.
MISS MARY'S CHOCOLATE FUDGE Mix together one bag of semi-sweet chocolate chips, one small can of sweetened condensed milk and 1 tsp vanilla. Microwave for one minute and stir this mixture and pour into a 8 x 8 inch pan. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Remove and cut into squares.
ROCKY ROAD CANDY Melt 1/4 cup butter or margarine and 4 cups miniature marshmallows together in a double boiler.
Stir in 6 cups of Rice Krispies.
Press in a buttered pan.
Chill and cut into desired size. You can press some candy into the squares before chilling - preferably soft candies.
HERSHEY'S THUMBPRINTS Cream 1 cup softened butter and mix in 1/2 cup sugar, 1 tsp almond extract, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 cups flour.
Chill overnight. Roll into balls and place on a lightly greased cookie sheet about 2 inches apart. Push your thumb into cookie balls.
Add a small amount of raspberry preserves into the center of each ball - use about 1/4 to 1/2 tsp. Bake at 400 degrees for 10 to 12 minutes or until brown on the bottom. Chill before serving. You can use any favorite preserves.
CHOCOLATE CHIP COOKIES Blend 2 cups of Crisco with 2 cups white sugar.
Add 4 beaten eggs with 4 tsps vanilla; mix well. Add one cup brown sugar, 8 cups flour, 2 tsps salt, 2 tsps baking soda and blend well. Stir in 2 cups of chocolate chips.
Drop a few tsps on a cookie sheet. Bake at 350 degrees until lightly browned.
OATMEAL COOKIES Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Beat together 3/4 cup shortening, 1 cup firmly packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1 egg, 1 tsp vanilla until creamy. Add 3 cups uncooked oats, 1 cup flour, 1 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp baking soda. Mix well and drop by rounded tsp onto greased cookie sheets. Bake at 350 degrees for 12 - 15 minutes.
You may add chopped nuts, raisins, chocolate chips, and coconut. Makes 5 dozen.
M & M COOKIES Cream together 1 cup shortening, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup white sugar, 2 beaten eggs, and 2 tsps vanilla. Gradually add 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 tsp baking soda, and 1 tsp salt. Mix well and add 1 1/2 cups M & M's and mix. Drop by tspfuls on ungreased cookie sheets. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes at 375 degrees.
Kids love these cookies and like to help make them.
1950'S HOLIDAY PUNCH 1/4 cup sugar, 1 small jar (8 ounces) maraschino cherries,3 cups grapefruit juice, 1 large bottle club soda, 1 large bottle hi-spot lemon soda, 1 large bottle ginger ale, Citrus fruit slices.Combine first three ingredients; pour over ice into a large punch bowl.
Then add ice-cold hi-spot, club soda and ginger ale just before serving. Liquor if desired; stir gently. Makes about 30 punch cup servings.
TRIPLE TREAT HOLIDAY BARS 1 cup sliced natural almonds, finely chopped, 1 cup packed brown sugar,1 cup butter, softened, 1 egg,1 tsp vanilla (or 1/2 tsp vanilla extract and 1/2 tsp almond extract), 1/4 tsp salt, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 3 cups confectioners' sugar, 1/4 cup margarine softened, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 tbsps milk, 1/2 cup diced red candied cherries, 2 squares (2 ounces) unsweetened chocolate, melted and cooled, Whole almonds, for decorating.
Preheat your oven to 300°F. Set aside ¼ cup of the chopped almonds; add the remaining ¾ cup to a large mixing bowl with the brown sugar, butter, egg, vanilla and salt. Use a mixer to cream together until fluffy, then gradually mix in the flour on low speed. Press the cookie dough evenly into the bottom of a 9×13-inch baking pan. Bake for 20-25 minutes until the cookie base is light brown. (It will still be soft.) Remove to a wire rack and allow to cool completely.
Using a mixer, beat the softened butter, confectioners' sugar, vanilla and about 2 tbsps of milk together until fluffy, adding another spoonful or two of milk if the frosting is too thick to be spreadable. Spread the frosting over the crust, then lightly score the frosting into thirds. Sprinkle ¼ cup of finely chopped almonds over one section; in the center section, spread melted chocolate over the frosting.
Decorate the last third with candied cherries, pressing down lightly to make them stick. Chill for about 15 minutes, then cut into individual bars before the chocolate has fully set.
CANDY CANE SNOWBALLS 2 cups butter, softened,1 cup confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 3-1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup chopped pecans, 8 ounces white candy coating (melted), 1/3 to 1/2 cup crushed peppermint candies.
Cream butter and confectioners' sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes.
Beat in vanilla. Gradually beat in flour. Stir in pecans.
Refrigerate, covered, until firm enough to shape, 3-4 hours. Preheat the oven to 350°. Shape dough into 1-in. balls. Place 2 in. apart on ungreased baking sheets.
Bake until lightly browned, about 15 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; cool completely. Dip tops of cookies into candy coating, allowing excess to drip off; dip into crushed candies.
Let stand until set.
HOMEMADE PEPPERMINT PATTIES ½ cup sweetened condensed milk, 1½ tsp peppermint extract, 3 cups powdered sugar, 8 ounces dark chocolate chopped, 2 tsp oil. In a medium size bowl mix the sweetened condensed milk, peppermint extract, and powdered sugar together until thick dough forms. Sprinkle some powdered sugar on a flat clean work surface and place the peppermint dough on the sugar.
Using a rolling pin, roll out the dough to about 1/4 inch thickness. Using a medicine cup or other round object, cut out 1 inch circles from the dough. Place onto a wax paper covered baking sheet.
Place the peppermint patties into the fridge to allow to cool for about 30 minutes.
Place the chocolate in a heat safe bowl. Add the oil. Heat the chocolate in the microwave in 15 second intervals until the chocolate is fully melted. Stir until smooth. Using a fork, dip the peppermint patties into the melted chocolate and place back on the wax paper covered baking sheet. Once all patties have been coated, place the tray back in the fridge and allow the chocolate to set for another 30 minutes. Store the peppermint patties in the fridge until ready to be served!
NO COOK CHRISTMAS CANDY 1 box Betty Crocker Home Style Fluffy White Frosting Mix 7.2 oz. box, 1/3 cup light corn syrup, 1/2 cup boiling water, 1 lb. confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract or seeds from 1/2 vanilla bean, Assorted holiday sprinkles.
Cover two or more large baking sheets with parchment paper or waxed paper.
In the bowl of a standing mixer fitted with the whip attachment, combine the frosting mix (dry mix), the corn syrup, and the boiling water. Beat on high speed until stiff peaks form, about 5 minutes. With the mixer still running on medium, slowly add in confectioners' sugar a little at a time; mix until just combined. Don't over mix or you'll deflate the batter. Add the vanilla and mix briefly. The finished mixture should be billowy and light, and a little bit stretchy like classic divinity. Drop candy mixture by the heaping tsp onto the prepared pans. Immediately cover with sprinkles, if desired. Let candies stand, uncovered, until dry to the touch, about 6-8 hours. When the outside of the candies feel firm, turn over. Dry 6 more hours, or overnight. Store candies in an airtight container.

title: New virtual museum displays artifacts from home of Harriet Tubman’s father
author: Konner Metz
content:
New virtual museum displays artifacts from home of Harriet Tubman’s father

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new virtual collection of historic artifacts is shedding light on the early life of abolitionist Harriet Tubman and her father, Ben Ross.Archaeologists for the Maryland Department of Transportation led efforts in uncovering many items, such as plates, bowls and pitchers, in work done at Ross' home deep in the Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge in Dorchester County.
Experts spent the last four years finding and identifying hundreds of artifacts. Julie Schablitsky, MDOT's chief of cultural resources, said it all began when they found an 1808 half-dollar coin on the site.
"That coin gave us inspiration to keep on digging and keep on working," Schablitsky said.
Earlier this week, the department announced the artifacts and unveiled The Ben Ross Homeplace, an online museum since the physical site isn't open to the public.
Some of the artifacts provide insight into Ross' life as an enslaved person in the 19th century, as well as Tubman's early years, during which she learned how to live off the land.
Archaeologists found a lock to a door, which Schablitsky says may indicate Ross had some form of independence from his enslaver, Anthony Thompson.
"That's a bit of negotiated independence that not everybody would have had who was enslaved," she said.
Schablitsky pointed out a tobacco pipe with a bald eagle. While many may assume it's a patriotic symbol, she says it could be a "subtle signature" of defiance.
"I wondered that, in his hand or the hand of Harriet Tubman and her mother, … if that was somehow a way of resistance — (if) that symbol was there for freedom rather than allegiance to the United States," Schablitsky said.
Schablitsky and MDOT media relations manager David Broughton say the process of working in the wetlands of Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge was demanding due to weather conditions, mosquitos, snakes and more.
While the team knows the approximate area Ross' home was in, it didn't locate the exact markings or corners of the home. The exact location is "lost to time," Schablitsky said, but the online museum preserves as much as possible.
"It could be a valuable tool … for teachers and their children," Broughton said.
'RUSH AGAINST TIME'
Archaeologists aren't just battling the elements. They're working on a limited clock.
"Climate change, sea level rise made digging very, very difficult," Schablitsky said. "Within the next decade, I know that I'm not going to be able to return there."
Schablitsky said even when work began back in 2021, environmental conditions impacted their work. Holes already dug would fill up with water after just a lunch break, Schablitsky said.
Sea level rise makes the preservation and historical work even more pressing, experts say.
"We're definitely in a rush against time," Schablitsky said. "The waters are coming up, they're percolating up through the ground."
Amid the challenges, descendants of Tubman and Ross were able to join archaeologists at the wetlands of Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge. Schablitsky said the humility and gratitude they expressed to be able to dig at the historical site was impactful.
"The most meaningful part of the process was to have the descendants of Harriet Tubman and Ben Ross down on the site, walking where they walked, in her footsteps, in his footsteps," she said.

title: Museum celebrates oysters at OysterFest
content:
Museum celebrates oysters at OysterFest

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum will celebrate the Bay's favorite bivalve at OysterFest on Saturday, Oct. 28, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.CBMM's OysterFest features oysters served a variety of ways, along with other local fare, craft beer, and spirits, plus live music on two stages, an oyster stew competition, a full schedule of demonstrations and presentations, children's activities, and more.Guests can savor Chesapeake Bay oysters, with both raw and cooked options available, from the Talbot Watermen Association and other local oyster farms.There will also be a variety of Chesapeake delicacies and other food offerings via local vendors available for purchase, plus a beverage selection that includes specialty cocktails and an array of local craft beer options.For OysterFest, guests will enter campus through CBMM's new Welcome Center, getting a first look at the new building overlooking Fogg's Cove and the chance to shop in the new Museum Store inside. (Please note that the exhibition spaces within the Welcome Center are not yet open to the public.)Purchase your tickets in advance now for this rain-or-shine event and learn more at cbmm.org/oysterfest.The always-popular oyster stew competition invites guests to sample offerings from various local restaurants and then vote for their favorite to decide which chefs will claim the coveted title.There will be live music on both sides of campus all day long, with stages on both the Tolchester Beach Bandstand and Fogg's Landing. Swamp Donkey Newgrass will be playing the historic bandstand, bringing its unique "newgrass" sound with a combination of genre-spanning original songs and covers to OysterFest for the fifth time.Guests can head to Van Lennep Auditorium throughout the day to hear from a variety of guest speakers sponsored by the Upper Shore Regional Folklife Center through the Maryland Traditions Program of the Maryland State Arts Council. The offerings include a series of panels related to CBMM's special exhibition The Changing Chesapeake and a history presentation from Dr. Clara Small.The American Chesapeake Club will be on hand to discuss Maryland's official dog, the Chesapeake Bay retriever, and showcase its retrieving ability, while the 100 Hundred Shores Project will offer the opportunity for guests to dye their own shirts using water from the Miles River.There's also an oyster slurp-off contest to add to the friendly competition, plus a wide range of Chesapeake-themed children's activities, including games, model boat building, and story time.Guests can get in the festive spirit by purchasing OysterFest gear in the new Museum Store, showcasing this year's featured historic oyster tin from CBMM's collection. The one-gallon tin, packed in the 1940s by W.E. Rigging & Co., out of Crisfield, Md., is emblazoned on shirts and stickers, as well as the commemorative mugs that will be used for the oyster stew competition.This year, OysterFest is generously sponsored by M&T Bank with support from Eastern Shore Tents & Events, Kelly Distributors, and What's Up Media.OysterFest admission is $7 for museum member adults and active and retired members of the military (with ID); $19 for non-member adults; $16 for seniors (ages 65 and up) and college students (with ID); $7 for non-member children ages 6-17; and free for member children 6-17, and all children 5 and under. CBMM members at the Family & Friends level and above can also receive the $7 discounted admission for two adult guests.Tickets can be purchased online in advance or at the gate the day of the festival. Additional free event parking will be available at St. Michaels Middle/High School, with a complimentary shuttle service to and from CBMM running throughout the day.Food and drinks are available for an additional cost, with carry-on alcohol prohibited. For safety reasons, non-service dogs need to be kept home during museum festivals, including OysterFest.

title: Waterfowl Festival names Al Barker as 2025 featured artist
author: Staff Writer
content:
Waterfowl Festival names Al Barker as 2025 featured artist

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Al Barker has been named as the Waterfowl Festival's 2025 Featured Artist."Barker has displayed his work at every festival since its inception in 1971. His quintessential scenes of hunting, the outdoor lifestyle, and nature flawlessly capture a quiet and breathtaking beauty, bringing the viewer intimately into the scene without disrupting the magical and private moments his subjects are experiencing," the festival group said in an announcement.
The 54th Waterfowl Festival will be held November 14-16, 2025 in Easton.
"The Waterfowl Festival is about tradition — preserving our heritage and sharing it with the new generation," said Deena Kilmon, executive director of Waterfowl Inc, which puts on the popular Eastern Shore event. "Al's works are the perfect way to seduce anyone who is viewing them to fall in love with the romance of the outdoors. His works are generally not large which makes them the perfect size and price point for the new collector -a key element of the festival that is very important- making sure art is accessible to everyone."
Barker specializes in smaller sized paintings, completing works in both oil and watercolor, as well as rendering many small editions of etchings, the festival said in its announcement.
"Al Barker is the only professional artist that has exhibited continuously at the Easton Waterfowl Festival in Easton, Maryland, since its inception over fifty years ago. Al has won over fifty major awards in premier art competitions and principal exhibitions such as the Grand National American Artists Professional League, New York; Greenwich Workshop Galleries, Connecticut and California; Settlers West, Arizona; Gallery One, Ohio; and the prestigious Salmagundi Club in New York City in which he's been a member and on exhibit for more than 50 years. Al's work is displayed in many National Miniature Exhibitions in the continental United States. Notably, Al's work has been purchased by Museums for permanent collections, many private collections, as well as The White House fine arts collection," the announcement continued.
Barker's Featured Art piece for the 2025 festival will be released this summer and will be featured on posters.
Pre-orders are available by calling the Waterfowl Festival office 410-822-4567 or find the link online later in the summer in the Waterfowl store. Previous year's prints on for sale now at this site: https://waterfowlfestival.org/festival-posters/

title: Country Cooking: Fresh baked bread on a cool fall day
author: MARIE SAVAGE
content:
Country Cooking: Fresh baked bread on a cool fall day

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE | Section: Life 
 
 1772
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The temperatures are dropping slowly. What a great time to begin making fresh bread.The family will love the warm kitchen with great smell of fresh baked bread. Have plenty of whipped butter on hand with jam, jelly or honey to smear on top.
In the winter, I will feature my favorite biscuit recipes. Contact me to feature your family favorites to share.
Here are six tips to consider when baking your breads.
Place a small ovenproof dish with water in the oven when baking to help prevent the crust from getting too hard or brown.Use margarine or oil shortening to grease the pans as margarine and oil absorb more readily into the dough or batter.To make self-rising flour, mix 4 cups flour, 2 teaspoons salt, and 2 tbsps baking powder.Hot water kills yeast. One way to tell the correct temperature is to pour the water over your forearm. If you do not feel hot or cold, then it's just perfect.When making nut bread, they are better stored 24 hours after baking and before serving.Use an empty and clean salt shaker to store flour to be used for shaking when recipes call for it.
BASIC WHITE BREAD
When I began making bread, this was the recipe I used until I felt more confident. Give this a try if this is your first attempt.
2 envelopes yeast, 4 cups water (90-100 degrees), 2 cups sugar, 2 tbsps shortening, 2 tbsps vinegar, 2 tsps salt, 12 cups flour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Place all ingredients except the flour into the liquid in a large mixing bowl. Stir slightly until dissolved. Add 6 cups of the flour and beat. slowly stir in the remaining 6 cups of flour and let rest for 10 minutes. Place on a lightly floured board and knead for 2 minutes. Let rise until doubled in size. Punch down and let rise again. Shape into four loaves, place into loaf pans and bake in a preheated oven for 40 to 45 minutes. Enjoy.
SOURDOUGH BREAD
4 ¾ cups bread flour (or more as needed), 3 tbsps white sugar, 2 ½ tsps salt, 1 package active dry yeast, 1 cup warm milk, 2 tbsps margarine (softened), 1 ½ cups sourdough starter, 1 extra large egg, 1 tbsp water, ¼ cup chopped onion.
Combine 1 cup flour, sugar, salt and yeast in a large bowl. Add warm milk and margarine. Add in the starter mix. Mix in the remaining 3 3/4 cups of flour gradually; you may need to add more flour depending on the climate. Turn dough out onto a floured surface and knead for 8 to 10 minutes. Place dough into a greased bowl, turn once to the oil surface, and cover. Allow to rise until doubled in volume, about 1 hour. Punch down dough; cover and rest for 15 minutes. Divide dough in half and shape into two loaves. Place loaves on a greased baking pan. Allow to rise until doubled in volume, about 1 hour. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Stir together egg and water in a small bowl until well combined. Brush over the tops of loaves, then sprinkle with onion. Bake in the preheated oven until the loaves are golden brown and cooked through, about 30 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of a loaf should read 190 degrees.
HOMEMADE ARTISAN BREAD
3 1/4 cups bread flour (plus more for hands and pan), 2 tsps instant yeast, 2 tsps coarse salt, 1 1/2 cups water (close to room temperature at about 70 degrees).
In a large, ungreased mixing bowl, whisk the flour, yeast and salt together. Pour in the water and gently mix with a silicone spatula or wooden spoon. The dough will seem dry and shaggy, but keep working until all the flour is moistened. If needed, use your hands to work the dough ingredients together. The dough will be sticky. Shape into a ball in the bowl as best you can. Keeping the dough in the bowl, cover the dough tightly with plastic wrap or aluminum foil and set on the counter at room temperature. Allow to rise for 2-3 hours. The dough will just double in size, stick to the sides of the bowl, and have a lot of air bubbles. You can continue with step 4 immediately, but for the absolute best flavor and texture, I strongly recommend letting this risen dough rest in the refrigerator for at least 12 hours and up to 3 days. Place covered dough in the refrigerator for 12 hours — 3 days. I usually let it rest in the refrigerator for about 18 hours. The dough will puff up during this time but may begin to deflate after 2 days. That's fine and normal, nothing to worry about. Lightly dust a large nonstick baking sheet with flour and/or cornmeal. Turn the cold dough out onto a floured work surface. Using a sharp knife or bench scraper, cut dough in half. Some air bubbles will deflate as you work with it. Place dough halves on prepared baking sheet. Using floured hands, shape into 2 long loaves about 9-by-3 inches each about 3 inches apart. Loosely cover and allow to rest for 45 minutes. You will bake the dough on this prepared baking sheet. During these 45 minutes, preheat the oven to 475 degrees. When ready to bake, using a very sharp knife score the bread loaves with 3 slashes, about 1/2 inch deep. If the shaped loaves flattened out during the 45 minutes, use floured hands to narrow them out along the sides again. Place the shaped and scored dough on the flour dusted pan in the preheated oven on the center rack. Bake for 20-25 minutes or until the crust is golden brown. Gently tap the loaves—if they sound hollow, the bread is done. For a more accurate test of doneness, the bread is done when an instant read thermometer inserted in the center reads 195 degrees. Remove the bread from the oven and allow it to cool for at least 20 minutes before slicing and serving. Store leftovers loosely covered at room temperature for up to 5 days or in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
HONEY SPICE BREAD
2/3 cup packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup 2% milk, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 1/2 tsps baking powder, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/8 tsp ground cloves, 2 large eggs (room temperature), 1/2 cup honey, 1/3 cup canola oil. GLAZE: 1/3 cup confectioners' sugar, 2 tesps 2% milk.
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. In a small saucepan, combine brown sugar and milk. Cook and stir over low heat until sugar is dissolved. Remove from heat. In a large bowl, whisk flour, baking powder, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. In another bowl, whisk eggs, honey, oil and brown sugar mixture until blended. Add to flour mixture; stir just until moistened. Transfer the batter to a greased 8-by-4-inch loaf pan. Bake for 50-60 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean (cover top loosely with foil if needed to prevent over-browning). Cool in pan for 10 minutes before removing to a wire rack to cool completely. In a small bowl, stir glaze ingredients until smooth, drizzle over bread.
AMISH WHITE BREAD
2 cups of warm water (110 degrees), ⅔ cup white sugar, 1 ½ tbsps active dry yeast, ¼ cup vegetable oil,1 ½ tsps salt, 6 cups bread flour.
Dissolve sugar in warm water in a large bowl and then stir in yeast. Allow to proof until the yeast resembles a creamy foam, 5 to 10 minutes. Mix oil and salt into the yeast. Mix in flour one cup at a time. Knead dough on a lightly floured surface until it is smooth. Place it in a well-oiled bowl and turn dough to coat. Cover with a damp cloth. Allow to rise until doubled in bulk, about 1 hour. Punch dough down. Knead for a few minutes and divide in half. Shape into loaves and place into two well-oiled 9-by-5-inch loaf pans. Allow it to rise until dough has topped the pans by one inch, about 30 minutes. Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bake the risen loaves in the preheated oven until golden brown for 30 minutes.
COUNTY WHOLE WHEAT BREAD
2 1/2 cup warm buttermilk (body temperature is good), 2 tbsps honey, 1 tbsp dry active yeast, 5 1/2 cups fine grind whole wheat flour, 1 cup unbleached bread flour (plus more as needed), 1 tbsp kosher salt, 1 egg, 3 tbsps unsalted butter (soft), 2 tbsps poppy seeds, 1 egg white mixed with a tablespoon of water.
Warm the buttermilk to body temperature. In other words when you stick a finger into it you shouldn't feel it. Place the buttermilk in a large bowl. Add a tablespoon of yeast and honey to it. Let the yeast dissolve either by whisking it or letting it bloom. Add the whole wheat flour, 1 cup of bread flour, egg and salt. Using a thick handled wooden spoon mix the dough in a circular fashion adding the softened butter once the dough has started to form. Once the dough has formed remove it from the bowl to a clean countertop and knead the dough until it is smooth, elastic and the gluten has formed. Consider this your workout for the day. Roll the dough into a tight ball. Place the dough back into the bowl, cover it with a damp warm towel and set it in a warm place. Set a timer for 1 hour. At the end of the hour punch down the dough and set the timer for another hour. At the end of this hour the dough should be doubled in size. Punch down the dough and divide it in half. Roll it into a ball and either divide it into thirds so you can roll it into logs and braid it or roll it into two big logs. Place the loaves into prepared pans. I always oil and then shake flour into my pans. The thin coating of flour lets the baked bread easily release from the pan. Cover with a warm damp towel and let the dough rise for 40 minutes to an hour. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Once the loaves have doubled, brush them with the egg wash and sprinkle with poppy seeds or sesame seeds. You can also dust the tops with flour but if you do this don't use the egg wash. Bake the loaves in the oven for 45 to 50 minutes, rotating them halfway through baking. Remove the loaves from the oven and remove them from the bread pans to a rack and let them cool.

title: Centuries of legacy celebrated in Wye Mills
author: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Centuries of legacy celebrated in Wye Mills

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — A hint of beautiful autumn days set the stage for the Wye Mills Fall Cooking Festival last Saturday, where visitors soaked up 70-degree weather until rain dampened the final hours.Visitors arrived throughout the day at the historic Old Wye Mill, where millers demonstrated the centuries-old process of grinding organically grown buckwheat, grits and other grains. Established in 1682, the mill is the oldest continuously water-powered gristmill in the U.S. and played a vital role in the American Revolution, supplying flour to the Continental Army.
Modernized during the Industrial Revolution, the mill operated continuously until the state acquired it in 1953. The mill was restored in the 1950s, and the Friends of Wye Mill now manage the site, milling twice a month from May through October.
The atmosphere Saturday was lively, with families and history enthusiasts strolling through the grounds, learning about the mill's history and enjoying Dutch oven-made foods and local vendors.
2022 national Dutch oven champions Carolyn Graf and D'Nise Hefner brought flavor as they prepared recipes from the "Wye Miller's Grind Cookbook."
"Once you get used to it, it really is no different than turning on your oven, preheating it, and putting food in," Hefner said as she raised a Dutch oven lid, revealing an enticing brownie dish—perhaps the favorite of the day. Visitors savored molasses bread, ginger scones, apple pie and more.
Augustine Herman, a cartographer who owned land in Cecil County in the 1700s, was brought back to life by a reenactor, who displayed maps, surveying tools and history books. A trader and ambassador for New Netherland, Herrman recognized the need for a detailed map of the Chesapeake Bay region after engaging in boundary discussions with Virginia and Maryland, resulting in the map titled "Virginia and Maryland As it is Planted and Inhabited this present Year 1670" published in 1673.
Mason's Heritage Family Farm of Queen Anne's County offered fresh produce to passersby, and Easton author Timothy Young signed copies of his latest book, "Mac and the Millstone of Time," sharing insights about its characters and the mill's history.
Festival volunteers considered the day a success, noting the number of attendees and the enthusiasm from visitors, many of whom shopped at the Old Wye Mill store and perused through the downstairs museum.
Despite the rain, the event continued to showcase the charm of Old Wye Mill and the community's appreciation for local history and food traditions.

title: 'Black Panther' author discusses ins and outs of writing
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
'Black Panther' author discusses ins and outs of writing

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 657
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Nnedi Okorafor is an award-winning author who has garnered international acclaim for her work on Marvel's "Black Panther" comic book series, but her writing career unexpectedly took off following a life-altering event while in college.Okorafor, who writes African-based science fiction and fantasy novels for children and adults, stopped by Leonardtown High School Oct. 11 to talk about her career. St. Mary's College of Maryland Community Affairs Liaison Kelsey Bush served as moderator.
Building on the work of Stan Lee and Ta-Nehisi Coates — whose "Black Panther" comics were adapted into a blockbuster movie in 2018 — Okorafor authored several issues of "Black Panther — Long Live the King," a continuation of the series and earned Hugo nominee for best novella.
In addition, she authored "Wakanda Forever," which was adapted into a global hit movie, as well as its spin-off, "Shuri."
"I had a problem with Wakanda in general because the concept of it just didn't make any sense to me," she said. But during her early years, the two things that she loved more than anything was track and field, tennis and bugs.
"I loved sports and then bugs," Okorafor said, adding her mom was a Nigerian Olympic javelin thrower while her dad was a nationally known hurdler. "I thought I was going to be an entomologist. I didn't grow up wanting to write at all."
She later excelled at tennis — she said she had a 114 mph serve and she and her sister were "like Venus and Serena before Venus and Serena" — but at the age of 13 was diagnosed with scoliosis.
After playing singles her freshman year at the University of Champagne in Illinois, she was told the disease had compressed her spine and needed surgery. Following the operation, she was paralyzed from the waist down.
"You take an athlete that could do all that and you paralyze them?" she said. "That was my identity."
She sought solace in an Isaac Asimov book and eventually regained feeling in her lower body.
"It was in that moment of pure darkness descending on me that my mind just turned to storytelling," she said. "And as soon as I started doing it, it was like a light switched on and that light pushed all that darkness that was descending on me and went away."
She later took a creative writing class on the advice of a friend, whom she had a crush on, and "it opened up my world."
Okorafor — who moved with her parents to America in 1969 — said the hardest novel she's written was "Death of an Author," which is scheduled to be released in January, though she declined to say why.
She said a close second was "Who Fears Death," which she said she started writing on the night of her father's wake.
"I was very, very close to my father and it's literally autobiographical," she said. "The pain I was going through I just poured it all into that novel and still is the darkest novel I've written."
Marvel contacted her and asked her to write "Spiderman," though she declined.
"It was too much," she said. "I'm not jumping in the deep end when I don't know how to swim. Plus I just can't relate to that [story]. I like to start small. A lot of people would have jumped at that, but for me I like to build my way there and be comfortable and feel natural."
She said working with Marvel was quite stressful.
"The thing about Marvel is that once you agree and say, 'Yeah, I'll do that,' you have days to come up with a summary, which is scary because you have these beloved characters and if you come up with something wrong you'll hear about it in many ways," she said of the three-issue series she authored.
Among Okorafor's other works are the "Binti" trilogy, the "Akata Witch" books — both of which are optioned for the screen — and her latest, "She Who Knows."
To watch the whole interview, go to www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKv-8LS9RC0.

title: Kent County man wins first prize in world decoy competition
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent County man wins first prize in world decoy competition

 May 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 747
 Words 

 Read News Document

 MILLINGTON — On April 25, 26, and 27, several thousand people competed in the 53rd Ward World Championship Wildfowl Carving Competition and Art Festival at the Roland E. Powell Convention Center in Ocean City, Maryland.To those who are heavily invested in wildfowl decoys, it's like the Super Bowl of wood carving.
In the 50 years it's been held in Ocean City, there hasn't been a native-born Marylander who ever took first place.
Until this year.
Mali Vujanic, a native of Kent County, captured first place beating out 19-time World Champion Pat Godin and successful author and five-time champion, Tom Matus.
Godin came in second this year; Matus took third.
At age 56, Vujanic, born in Massey, Maryland, won a championship ring, $3000 cash prize and a plaque declaring him "Best in World," the Rich Smoker Heritage Award for Single Gunner.
Impressive as it is to take down former reigning champions, he also beat out 33 entries from four different countries in that category: Single Gunner.
The award winning painted decoy of a ringtail duck took him about 12 hours to carve.
There was no jealousy among the competitors either. When Vujanic was announced the winner, he was congratulated by his friends and peers to uproarious applause.
Not only is winning good for his business, Mill Creek Decoys, he also said it's great for the Eastern Shore.
"There was only one other guy from Maryland who ever won, and he was not native-born," Vujanic said.
For Vujanic, growing up on the Chester River, he sees his victory as coming full circle, dating back to Maryland's early wood carving roots.
He pointed out the late Stephen and Lemuel Ward, the Ward Foundation's originators, who were considered the godfathers of carving, were also native Marylanders, out of Crisfield.
He sees his winning as carrying on the Maryland tradition.
And he did indeed represent Maryland well. As all entries this year, he submitted a carving of a ringneck duck into the competition that was judged in three categories: form, function and ability to resemble the species."
The decoys were tested in Assawoman Bay behind the convention center and one of the judges was an ornithologist who scrutinized the decoy's appearance, how close it resembled the species.
Vujanic had many to thank for this achievement.
His ninth grade art teacher in Kent County High School Ben Dize was instrumental in his progress, a mentor from 1981 to present day. Dize, ironically also a native of Crisfield, helped his eager students by opening up the vocational wing of the shop, Thursday evenings.
Vujanic also practiced on his own, even avoiding partying with his friends to work on his craft, he quipped. As talent happens from dedication and practice, he began to get more efficient. Then after he graduated in 1985, clients began to take notice of his work.
He continued his passion of wood carving throughout his marriage and his career in land management. He kept his passion going, returning to that time when he first became enamored with the craft, in his middle school years.
He desired to get away from his work environment, and so three or four years ago he went into carving full time.
"That was a great decision," he said.
Since doing it full-time he's sold carvings to Mike Trout, the All-Star Centerfielder for the Los Angeles Angels, and also a former U.S. president in Texas, to name just a few. He said because of this craft, he has connections with people all around the world.
And as successful as he is, he's also accessible.
He teaches carving/painting classes at his workshop in Massey for beginners and advanced learners. He's also a published children's book author who's finishing up his latest, a series of how-to-books that will be available in the next year or two.
And with all this going, he fully plans to compete again next year, under the same category. Next years goal under World Single Gunner's is Blue Goose.
Vujanic stopped to reflect about his business and where he wants it to go and how to expand it.
Right now he works in the exact same spot he first started carving in middle school, in his mother's house two doors down from the home he shares with his wife, Brenda, his son Victor, graduating Kent County High School next week and his daughter, Sarah.
His mother was extremely pleased when she found out he won first place... but was not surprised.
"She always said I was a World Champion," he said with a smile.
Check out Vujanic at Mill Creek Studios for more of his work or to drop him a line, visit facebook.com/MillCreekDecoys/.

title: Olmert returns to lecture at Talbot Historical Society
content:
Olmert returns to lecture at Talbot Historical Society

 August 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A10 | Section: News

 EASTON - Michael Olmert will present a lecture at 1 p.m. Thursday, Aug. 24, at the Talbot Historical Society based on his forthcoming book, "Ink, Paint, Bricks: Intention & Ambiguity in the Arts." This illustrated talk will cover two short poems, one painting, and one architectural building shape, the octagon. The poetry will be by W.H Auden: "Musee des Beaux Arts" (1938) and "If I Could Tell You, I Would Let You Know" (1940). The picture will be Pieter Bruegel the Elder's genre painting, "The Fall of Icarus" (1560); and the architectural part will cover the all-important symbolism of the octagon in architecture, religion and literature.Overall, the book is to do with intention, interpretation and meaning in writing, painting, and buildings.The book will have 10 chapters, each covering one building, one novel, play, or poem and one painting.Olmert has been teaching Shakespeare and drama at the University of Maryland English Department for 37 years. This is his second Talbot Historical Society lecture based on the new book.He has also spoken at the THS on "The Invention of Colonial Williamsburg." He's written "The Smithsonian Book of Books" (1992), "Milton's Teeth & Ovid's Umbrella" (1996), and "Kitchens, Smokehouses & Privies" (2009). His television writing has won three Primetime Emmys.He has written 80 TV documentaries, as well as five books, seven plays, three feature films, an IMAX film, and over 200 articles, essays, and reviews.In 2005, he was inducted into the University of Maryland Alumni Hall of Fame.The lecture will take place at the Talbot Historical Society at 25 S. Washington Street, Easton. Reservations are required. The lecture is free for THS members and $5 for non-members.For more information or to sign-up, contact the Talbot Historical Society at 410-822-0773 or email kaylaw@talbothistory.org.

title: Music for the soul - Church choirs come together for special compline service Oct. 5.
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Music for the soul - Church choirs come together for special compline service Oct. 5.

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 356
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE - With the busyness of the fall season already in full swing, the choirs of Christ Church Kent Island and St. Margaret's Church in Annapolis will join in providing an evening of quiet music and prayer to promote spiritual peace.The compline service will be held at 7:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 5, at Christ Church Parish, Kent Island."Compline" takes its name from the Latin word com-pletorium, meaning completion, as it marks the completion of the working day through its focus on prepar-ing the body for temporal rest. Those taking part, both the musicians and guests, are led to still the body, mind, and spirit."It's an Episcopal service not offered in most places and is very different from the regular Sunday morning services we lead each week," said St. Margaret's music director and Stevensville resident Jim Douglas. "The church is lit only by candles and [the service] is mostly sung, not spoken."When Christ Church's music director Gary Van Essen asked Douglas if he wanted to do some sort of combined choir event, Douglas suggested joining together for a service of evening Compline, offering one at St. Margaret's and a second one at Christ Church.The varied music selections range from the works of Thomas Tallis, who served as a composer and performer for Henry VIII and Elizabeth I, to Bernadette Farrell, contemporary composer widely known for her gift of writing richly meaningful lyrics and comforting, prayerful melodies.The service will also commemorate the life of St Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals and the environment."This program is giving the choir members a chance to collaborate and work with singers from another congregation while at the same time providing a beautiful, ancient worship experience for those who attend the service," said Christ Church Music Director Gary Van Essen. "Compline is quiet, peaceful, and set in twilight, something very different from most people's daily experiences. The service is a meaningful. way to disconnect and end the day on a contemplative note."

author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com

Bigger and brighter - Lights shine through fog at Cambridge Christmas parade

 December 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Shrouded in fog, lights twinkled, blinked and glowed at the 74th annual Cambridge Dorchester County Christmas Parade Saturday evening.Although there was no snow for the "Snowflakes on Parade" theme this year, mild weather and a hazy atmosphere made for perfect parade watching conditions.Linda Bramble, who attended the parade with her nine-year-old granddaughter, Emily, said it was a good night for the parade."The wind's not blowing," she said, adding that the fog was a neat addition to the parade.Parade Co-chairman Bruce McWilliams thanked mother nature for stopping rain from pouring down Saturday evening."The fog made for some really nice pictures," he said.There were 105 floats registered in the parade this year, a few of which McWilliams said he knew didn't show.From bright red firetrucks to trucks decked out in wreaths and colorful lights to trailer beds covered in fake snow, residents and visitors watching the parade had a lot to keep them captivated. Floats embarked from Long Wharf Park, traveling down High, Poplar and Race streets before ending on Washington Street.A variety of performances, from marching bands to dance groups were interspersed throughout the parade.Ruby Kreiser, 10, said her favorite part, along with all the lights, was seeing the Eastern Shore Dance Academy, who danced to "The Nutcracker" at different spots along the parade route.Kreiser, who also attends the Eastern Shore Dance Academy said she was able to say hello to her friends dancing in the parade.The Dance Academy took home the judge's choice award in the parade.The National Judges Association out of Pennsylvania judged both the marching bands and floats at the parade. The 10 division winners included Dorchester Emergency Medical Services for best noncommercial adult float, Girl Scout Troop 131 for the best noncommercial youth float, Dorchester Dumpin' for the best commercial float and New Creation Marching Unit for the best marching unit on foot.When it came to marching bands, Snow Hill High School won the best band overall category.For best high school band, North Dorchester High School placed first, Mardela Middle and High School placed second and Crisfield High School placed third.For best middle school band, Salisbury Middle School placed first and North Dorchester Middle School placed second.Since the parade, McWilliams said they have received a lot of "super positive comments." "Everybody has said what a great time, what a great parade," he said.McWilliams said they are "extremely thankful" to the community for their donations as well as the participants for showing up."It was definitely a labor of love for the community," he said.And plans for next year's parade are already underway."Yesterday," McWilliams said laughing during an interview Monday about when plans had begun.For the next year's 75th parade, diamonds will be a major focus."Because it's the 75th annual," McWilliams said."We've got a lot of plans to make the 75th really shine."

title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 484
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said. "Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it."
"The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises."
"My tenure at the museum was wonderful,"
Hooker said. "Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me."
Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering."
"I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said. "And we really want to downsize our housing situation."
"It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."
