title: Heritage Area awards $25,000 in mini-grants
content:
Heritage Area awards $25,000 in mini-grants

 August 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 617
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - The Heart of Chesapeake Country Heritage Area has awarded mini-grants totaling $25,000 to 11 non-profit organizations and local municipalities to assist with projects that enrich heritage resources and events in Dorchester County.The mini-grants support the efforts of local museums, organizations and municipalities that advance the mission and goals of the Heritage Area. All the projects serve to preserve Dorchester County's heritage, to market local heritage to visitors and residents, or to improve the economic health of the area.The HCCHA Board of Directors said they are pleased to be able to promote these innovative and creative opportunities with mini-grants grants and collaborate with their heritage partners who are making a difference throughout Dorchester County. The mini-grants are just one way that the HCCHA provides support for projects and events that will encourage or improve heritage tourism.According to HCCHA, this year's grant round was especially competitive with application requests totaling nearly double the available funding.The awardees and projects approved for FY2024 at the Heritage Board's July 18 meeting are: Cambridge Main Street - Taste of Cambridge. Funds will also be used to hire local entertainment and for related expenses for performances during the festival on Oct. 7 in downtown Cambridge. ($2,925) Dorchester County Historical Society - Fresh Faces: Brochures to Benefit Our Museum & Society. Funding will support the creation of two new brochures, the first for general audiences and visitors to the museum campus and the second to attract volunteers. ($810) Friends of Blackwater Wildlife Refuge - Eagle Festival. Funding will help with programming fees associated with presentations, displays and exhibits at the annual festival in March 2024 at Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge. ($2,500) Groove City Black Heritage & Culture Group - Groove City Culture Fest. Funds will support new heritage banners, as well students participating in a six-week African Drum dance/drum program, all part of the annual event on Aug. 19. ($3,500) Harris Malone Cemetery Maintenance Fund - Harris Malone Church. Funds will assist in making the church secure, as well as support a new website and a May 2024 event. ($2,500) Maryland House and Garden Pilgrimage - Dorchester County Tour. Funding will support marketing and promotions for the event, which will benefit the Nanticoke Historic Preservation Alliance. ($1,500) Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians - Nause-Waiwash Annual Native American Festival. Funding will be used for stipends and related expenses for Native American performers and presentations at the annual event in September.($4,200) Pride of Baltimore - Pride of Baltimore II Visits Historic Cambridge.Funds will support a stop in Cambridge in 2024, which will feature free interpretive programming for visitors, free deck tours and two-hour day sails. ($2,500) Spocott Windmill - Displays and Newsletter. Funds will support new signage detailing the life of Jim Richardson, builder of the current windmill, and Arthur and Sophie Jones, both closely aligned with the windmill, as well as a newsletter. ($1,815) Town of East New Market - East New Market Heritage Tourism Brochure. Funding will support an updated walking tour brochure that highlights a number of historic homes. ($1,500) Town of Vienna - Relocation of Chesapeake Country Mural.Funds will support the removal and relocation of the acclaimed Chesapeake Country Byway Mural because the building where it was originally installed is scheduled to be partially demolished. ($1,250) The mini-grants are made possible through a Maryland Heritage Areas Association Block Grant to the Heart of Chesapeake Country Heritage Area. The heritage-tourism related project grants are available for up to $5,000 and require a one-to-one match. Mini-grant application forms for FY2025 are expected to be available on the visitdorchester.org website in the spring.

title: Art is full of shards, fragments — and it's alive
author: ROBERT C. KOEHLER
content:
Art is full of shards, fragments — and it's alive

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ROBERT C. KOEHLER | Section: Columns 
 
 897
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As I trek toward the Great Unknown, as life's struggles seem to intensify, some odd questions keep recurring.Art — what is it again? Why does it matter? How does it matter? What does it mean to be "good" at it?
That last question, in particular, can cut like barbed wire — especially if you've been swimming all your life in a sense of mediocrity, having learned that the Temple of Art is the home of the blessed elite. There's Mona Lisa, then there are scribbles and doodles: baby stuff. End of discussion. Your grade is C-minus. Welcome to consumer culture.
So why do I care about art? Indeed, why now? As I grow older (by which I mean "old"), I refuse, refuse, refuse to retire: to quit writing, to quit believing I'm doing something that matters . . . to quit believing that humanity is collective and, at the deepest levels of our being, we all participate in this collective.
This is what I call art, even though I don't know what I mean by that. Or at least I don't mean something that's simple and certain, or even particularly serious — at least not in an academic sense. Serious can be fun.
Yeah, really. This is a relatively new bit of awareness for me, for which I thank a number of friends, who have, you might say, pulled me out of a trance of certainty. In particular I thank Dawi, a poet who showed us some of the recent drawings he's been doing. They woke me up. I remembered the feel of a drafting pen in my hand. I loved to draw, once upon a time — to scratch and scrape a fine penpoint across paper, to let the lines wiggle and squirm and dance. Yet somehow they were mixed with precision. Sometimes a face would emerge. What mattered was that my childhood emerged.
Was it any good? I felt it was as I drew, but it never was good enough — not for a drawing career of any sort to emerge. And eventually I set the pen aside, or mostly aside. I stopped drawing on a regular basis. I knew I wouldn't find fame. I wouldn't make money. I needed a serious career and this wouldn't be it.
But after Dawi's art woke me up, and I thought about all the time I waste in the present moment, I started scribbling again, because why not?
Take my time. Enjoy. I started splotching random colors on the page, mixed with wiggling lines and black and white checks. I found myself immersed once more in childhood wonder. A mantra popped into my head: If it's fun, it means it's alive.
And it struck me that this is art. This is how it should be defined. This is how it should be taught.
But there's more: Art, or the effort to create art, is always aiming at something, though usually not something obvious. There's ache and awe in the creative process, quietly present with the fun. When I begin a project, when I feel it start to matter, I think of it as a reach into humanity's collective, evolving whole.
Careful! This gets quickly dangerous. Here's where I want it to be good — you know, objectively good/ Unique, original, special. That wanting can quickly kill the art, yet somehow — paradoxically — it's part of the process.
And then Alison came for a visit: my daughter, the stained-glass artist, who lives in Paris — who designs, creates and installs stained-glass windows for people. She also writes poetry. She came to Chicago to see her dad, to connect with lifelong friends and more. She has a connection with a man who has worked in stained glass all his life, who's ready to retire. He has an enormous collection of stained-glass pieces that he accumulated over the years, including church-window fragments. Some of them are stunningly beautiful. They can't simply be left to gather dust. Maybe a new home is possible.
And after Alison spent a day at his studio, she and I — can you believe it? — talked about the nature of art, the nature of creativity. She made an interesting distinction as she talked about her stained-glass work: the difference between shards and fragments.
Shards are pieces of broken glass — perhaps violently broken. She feels freer to give them new life. Fragments, on the other hand, preserve a closer link to their original whole. They may be part of a broken church window or some other historic work. Both are often beautiful and radiant, but the less broken they are, the more they still communicate what they once were and the less free she feels to reshape them.
This got my mind spinning. I don't work with stained glass, but I couldn't stop thinking about fragments of a shattered church window, and imagining myself creating something with them— mixing art and God, you might say. Mixing fun and spirit. And it felt like the essence of creativity.
When I taught writing over the years — at elementary, high-school and college levels — the essence of my message to the students, regardless of their age, was: We are all writers. We all have our own voices. Learning to write means finding that voice.
And those voices, I now realize, are full of both shards and fragments: craft and spirit. This is art, regardless of genre. Art is fun. Art is alive.

title: Port Tobacco Players celebrate 75th anniversary
author: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Port Tobacco Players celebrate 75th anniversary

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com | Page: D8 | Section: News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As they make the transition from performers to co-directors for the next three weekends of the Port Tobacco Players 75th anniversary celebration "An Evening of Song," Becky Norris Kuhn and Tara Waters noted the collaboration of musical numbers deviates from the norm of scripted performances.In a production that commenced with three shows last weekend, the Port Tobacco Players anniversary celebration includes songs from past musicals such as "Singing In The Rain," "Guys and Dolls," "Beauty and the Beast," "Annie" and "Oklahoma," and several of them remind both Kuhns and Waters of their own performances on stage, although from a different perspective."This is so much different than anything that we did on stage," Kuhns said. "Normally everyone sticks to the script, but with this show we wanted to highlight a lot of the songs from musicals here and just blend them together. I remember doing 'Beauty and the Beast' here and now I get to lend my hand as a director to the performers."Waldorf resident Amanda Hastings, a 2018 St. Mary's College of Maryland graduate and current teacher at nearby Lackey High School, has the chance to display her talents in a solo number early - "You Can't Get a Man with a Gun" from "Annie Get Your Gun" - as well as in a duet with Melina Raynes later and in various numbers when the entire ensemble is on stage, including a pair of songs from "White Christmas" to close the show."This is only my first year with Port Tobacco Players, but I love being a pair of it," Hastings said. "I really only do musicals. This one is different because you don't have a set script. Usually most plays the actor fits the part, but in this one the songs fit the performers. I really enjoy my duet with Melina. She's so talented."Although not entirely a show with Christmas themes, there are more than a dozen songs in each act on both sides of the intermission and performers maintain a lively tempo throughout, aided by the musical accompany of a band that takes its spot elevated on stage rather than in the customary pit below."We wanted to make the show lively and entertaining for the whole audience," Waters said."There are so many songs that remind me of being a performer.Now I get to see what it's like being a co-director with Becky and it's really fun for the cast and for the whole audience."IF YOU GOThe Port Tobacco Players production of "An Evening of Song" will feature songs from more than a dozen musicals and will run every Friday, Saturday and Sunday through Dec. 17. Friday and Saturday offer evening performances beginning at 7:30 p.m. while the Sunday shows begin at 3 p.m.Co-directed by Becky Norris Kuhn and Tara Waters, "An Evening of Song" highlights many of the memorable songs from past musicals offered at the Port Tobacco theater over the past 75 years and includes feature songs from "White Christmas" that are designed to bring holiday cheer to the occasion.For more information, visit www.ptplayers.com or call the box office at 301-932-6819 for ticket availability and prices.

title: Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 355
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Leaders in maritime heritage, arts and social justice gathered at Washington College for the annual Frederick Douglass Day of Acknowledgement, celebrating African American contributions to the Chesapeake Bay region.The ceremony, co-hosted by Washington College and Bayside H.O.Y.A.S (Helping Our Youth Achieve Success) at the Decker Theatre on campus, opened with Maryland Public Television's Emmy-winning documentary "Water's Edge: Black Watermen of the Chesapeake".
Film Director Alexis Aggrey joined a panel discussion alongside Salisbury University Professor Emerita Clara Small, Minorities in Aquaculture CEO Imani Black, and fifth-generation fisherman Capt. Tyrone Meredith. Artist Marc Castelli and Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Chief Historian Pete Lesher rounded out the panel examining the bay's role as an economic and cultural cornerstone for African Americans.
Composer Marlon Saunders performed selections from "ISAAC: A Musical Journey," commissioned by the Kent Cultural Alliance. The work chronicles Isaac Mason's escape from slavery in Chestertown and his emergence as a community leader.
This year's Frederick Douglass awards recognized Rev. James Jones, convener of Caucus of African American Leaders on the Eastern Shore; Vincent Leggett, author and founder of Blacks of the Chesapeake Foundation; and Saunders, founder of The Seamless Voice.
Social media influencer Tyshawn "YVNG SWAG" Johnson received the Bayside H.O.Y.A.S Shooting Star award. The 25-year-old entertainer, known for his role on Nick Cannon's Wild 'N Out and various brand partnerships, represents a modern parallel to Douglass's own mastery of public image.
Johnson's family, including two sisters and one brother, are all from the Chestertown area and attended schools here. Even before signing a record deal, (he signed with Atlantic Records as a high school senior) Johnson had an active Facebook and Instagram account with thousands of followers. A video of him dancing reached 1 million views on Instagram over the summer of 2016.
The honorees reflect Douglass's diverse legacy, from his early exposure to maritime life near Wye Mills to his later emergence as a prominent public figure who skillfully managed his public persona.
"This was the best event yet," said John Queen, H.O.Y.A.S. president. "The documentary and panel were greatly received. People absolutely loved the Marlon Saunders performance, and the award recipients are always top-tier community leaders and class acts."

title: Local artists win Poe awards
author: Staff Writer
content:
Local artists win Poe awards

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 214
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Local student artists from Kent Island High School captured all four finalist spots in the visual art category of the esteemed Saturday 'Visiter' Awards, presented by Poe Baltimore.The competition celebrates a new generation of artists inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's life and works, honoring creativity in media, art, performance, and writing.
The awards ceremony took place at Westminster Hall & Burying Ground in Baltimore — an iconic "Poe Place." The evening included a catacomb tour and a murder mystery event to commemorate what would have been Poe's 216th birthday.
Student finalists, are senior Brooke Register, junior Alexis Detamore, junior Grace Hartlove, and senior Mark Monroe, who claimed the top honor with a mixed media piece, "No Pain; I Am Done," inspired by Poe's tale "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar."
KIHS Art Department Chair Andrea Schulte said, "Mark was awarded $1,879 and a commemorative plaque in recognition of this achievement."
The Saturday 'Visiter' Awards are named for the periodical that famously launched Edgar Allan Poe's literary career. Poe won the original award for his short story "MS Found in a Bottle" while living in Baltimore. Today, the awards recognize works that adapt Poe's life or writings and original works inspired by his legacy, continuing to celebrate his profound influence on the arts and literature worldwide.

title: Ayreheart opens National Music Festival’s resonance season in Chestertown
author: Staff Writer
content:
Ayreheart opens National Music Festival’s resonance season in Chestertown

 October 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The National Music Festival will open its 2025-26 Resonance concert series with a performance by Ayreheart, a Renaissance and folk music ensemble, at 3 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 26, in the Parish Hall at St. Paul's, Kent.Founded by Grammy-nominated lutenist and composer Ronn McFarlane, Ayreheart performs Renaissance music from the time of Shakespeare, along with traditional folk and original pieces. The ensemble's instrumentation includes lute, vocals, colascione (a bass lute), violin, guitar and percussion.
"Ayreheart was an audience favorite when they performed here in 2019," said National Music Festival Artistic Director Richard Rosenberg. "We're thrilled that they're returning to Chestertown to open our concert season."
The program will feature works by Renaissance composers John Dowland and William Byrd, as well as traditional ballads and folk songs from England, Scotland and Wales. McFarlane said his goal is to connect audiences to the enduring vitality of the lute.
"I want 21st-century listeners to hear the lute as a vibrant, modern musical instrument, able to reach their hearts and their feet, too," he said.
McFarlane, who founded Ayreheart in 2010, will be joined by vocalist and guitarist Heather Aubrey Lloyd, bass, violin and colascione player Willard Morris, and percussionist Mattias Rucht.
The Resonance concert series brings five intimate performances to Chestertown each year, from October through April. Concerts are held Sundays at 3 p.m. in St. Paul's Parish Hall, where a fireplace adds to the cozy atmosphere in colder months.
Upcoming Resonance concerts:
Oct. 26, 2025: Ayreheart
Nov. 16, 2025: Francesca Anderegg, violin, and Joy Cline Phinney, piano
Feb. 22, 2026: Matchstick Percussion
March 15, 2026: Jennifer Parker-Harley, flute, and Camilo Carrara, guitar
April 12, 2026: Manuel Barrueco, guitar
Tickets for Ayreheart's concert are $25 for adults and $5 for students with ID and children ages 5 to 14. Tickets may be purchased online or at the door beginning one hour before the concert.
Season and combo passes for the 2025-26 Resonance and National Music Festival performances are now available. Combo passes include admission to all Resonance concerts and ticketed events during the 2026 National Music Festival, May 31–June 13.
The National Music Festival is supported in part by the Maryland State Arts Council, Kent Cultural Alliance, Mid-Shore Community Foundation, The Peoples Bank, and donations from music lovers. For more information, email info@nationalmusic.us or call 443-480-0221.

title: Caroline County Council of Arts hires new executive director
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County Council of Arts hires new executive director

 May 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Business 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County Council of Arts has a new executive director.George Karos has a passion for the arts, especially music, and is making the rounds to get to know the community.
His CV is a quilt of education and administration.
"I just re-arrived in this region from central Florida. I headed a chamber of commerce for six years. Earlier in 2011, I was communications director for Monteverde Academy. They are a huge basketball school. It is an international boarding school. I also lived in DC for 20 years and worked in the arts. I was a public information officer for a school district in Florida," Karos said.
One of his goals is to reach out into other parts of the county, bringing funding for the arts to places like Ridgely, Federalsburg and Preston.
If he can bring more money in, he wants to bring more staff in because there is only so much he and Megan Krizovensky, program coordinator, can do, he said.
He also wants to embrace more arts disciplines outside on the green, like dance. They are already planning a Christmas program called "Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfit Toys."
"The idea is that it is a nice Denton event to add to the holiday Season. It is in response to a wonderful event like Christmas in Ridgely," Krizovensky said.
But the CCCA has a host of other things in the works as well.
"We have programming in the Foundry and outside of the Foundry, which goes with Caroline County. We sponsor a lot like Caroline Pride or the Christmas in Ridgely or Summerfest. In the arts and entertainment district we are hosting the banner programming for the second year in a row. And the artist is residence," Krizovensky said. "We just got done with our student art show. We are trying to get more involved with students like the teen writers club is a new thing."
She pointed out that the vibrant and eclectic gallery invites artists of all walks. They have leveraged their mailing list to promote artists. And by using Constant Comment they get lots of feedback about an artist or show's success.
"That has been important for us to determine where we want to go next year. We have been intensely attending to that and that has been important for us as we have submitted to other new grants for the possibility of growing the organization with funding to hire a gallery assistant. To hire a social media manager," Karos said.
To grow CCCA, he wants to get more grants and more donors. That is how he will proceed as executive director, he said.
He also believes growth will come more from the small gesture of reaching out rather than some big email blast. He wants to build relationships.
"I have decades of experience with 501(c)(3)s and 501(c)(6)s. I have a keen understanding of how to keep organizations afloat in terms of budgets, grants and proposal writing," Karos said. "More importantly, I have a passion for the arts. Between volunteers, board members and actual artists that are associate teaching instructors here with our program, getting all those tools in the toolbox is what fires me up."

title: Washington College leads effort for African American art project
author: Staff Writer
content:
Washington College leads effort for African American art project

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 745
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Earlier this spring, the Washington College Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience was awarded a $10,000 Public Art Across Maryland grant from the Maryland State Arts Council to begin planning for a major artwork of national significance that engages African American history and culture in the Chesapeake Tidewater region.The planning grant will fund a wide array of activities open to the public, including regional bus tours, public presentations by experts in art and African American history and community forums. These events will ensure that all interested members of the local community will have the opportunity to contribute meaningfully to the process of commissioning the artwork. The artwork will be installed outside the historic Custom House in Chestertown, near the bank of the Chester River.
The project grows out of Chesapeake Heartland: An African American Humanities Project, a restorative community curation initiative launched by the Starr Center in 2020 that chronicles the region's Black history in collaboration with the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History & Culture and a coalition of community groups.
Situating the Chesapeake Bay watershed as a national heartland of African American history and culture, Chesapeake Heartland has digitized more than 5,000 documents, images, artifacts and recordings spanning almost 400 years; provided grants and internships to dozens of artists, researchers and writers; and hosted over 200 public programs. The archives are free to view online.
In addition to the initial Public Art Across Maryland planning support, the Town of Chestertown has awarded $5,000 to the effort and Washington College's Department of Art & Art History has given $3,000 — totaling $18,000 toward stakeholder engagement for the initial planning effort.
This project will continue to strengthen Chestertown's commitment to public art. Starting with a National Endowment for the Arts-funded master plan adopted by the Town Council in 2014, Chestertown has increased its public art through commissioned artworks and the donation of the Woicke Collection, a group of 24 contemporary sculptures.
A public artwork along Chestertown's waterfront is envisioned by both the Master Plan and the Chestertown Unites Against Racism framework adopted in 2020, which called specifically for a work along the Chester River addressing African American history.
"An artwork of remembrance such as this needs to be pursued with great care and wide community engagement from its inception. We are developing a highly inclusive planning process working with stakeholders across the Upper Shore, the Delmarva Peninsula and the college to identify and articulate the scope and goals of the effort," said Jaelon T. Moaney, deputy director of the Starr Center and project lead. "The African diasporic history and culture unique to the Chesapeake region is sacred, and it is our intention to engage these enduring legacies with respect."
Beginning in fall 2024, regional bus tours will engage with aligned works of public art from Philadelphia to Annapolis and across Maryland's Eastern Shore to build community with the visionaries involved in their creation and continuing use. Registration will be required to join due to space limitations.
Additionally, during winter 2024 and early 2025, the Starr Center will host a series of public presentations and discussions with experts in contemporary public art, art history and the stewardship of cultural heritage and historic resources to provide space for a deeper understanding of the full range of possibilities for the project.
Brent Leggs, African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund executive director and senior vice president of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, will launch the series on Monday, November 4. Time and location to be announced. Those interested in joining the bus tours and public meetings should sign up for the Starr Center's newsletter to receive notifications and sign up for more details before each event.
Next spring, the Starr Center will host community forums to provide space for facilitated public discussion, exploring the current understanding of the regional African American experience and how a public artwork might address intergenerational memory making.
Focal to the process has been convening a 10-person planning committee with diverse disciplinary and geographic representation to inform each phase. Members of the planning committee include: Jana Carter, Charles Sumner Post 25, Grand Army of the Republic; professor Arlisha Norwood, University of Maryland Eastern Shore; Kate Dowd, Chestertown Public Arts Committee; Christalyn Grandison; professor Ada Pinkston, Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture; Vince Leggett, Blacks of the Chesapeake Foundation Inc.; Matt Kenyatta, University of Pennsylvania Stuart Weitzman School of Design; Ashley Chenault, Maryland Tourism Development Board; DeLia Shoge, Kent County Public Schools; and Jason Patterson, Washington College.

title: Fourth free gospel concert in Denton marks the halfway point for series
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Fourth free gospel concert in Denton marks the halfway point for series

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 311
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The fourth free gospel concert of the eight-concert series is set to take place at Calvary Baptist Church in Denton on Friday, July 11, at 6:30 p.m. Russ Yates, vice president of Holiday Park, hopes the series can reach people and teach them about Jesus."Well, hopefully it reaches a lot of people that need to know about Jesus," Yates said. It certainly gives the Christian community an outlet to do something, that's basically free."
The free concert will feature groups Port City Quartet, from North Carolina, and The Hyssongs from Rockport, Maine.
Holiday Park campground hosted concerts and events before COVID-19, after COVID, Yates closed the park, but recently with the direction from God, he was led to continue events but at a different venue.
"We did 30 years from 1989 to 2019 here at the campground. And then when COVID hit we had to shut down everything," Yates said. "Then we lost all of our people that volunteered to help because we needed about 50 people to put on the concerts. I really thought that was the end of it. Then last year during the winter, I started getting the feeling the Lord wanted us to start this up again, and I called the church and asked them what about us doing it there.
"Pastor Don Reynold said 'Russ, I've been praying you would start this up again,' and I was like, 'Well, looks like that's what we're going to try to do.' So the church was all behind it and have been real supportive."
Yates said events like this are good for the community because it's free, and it gives believers fun activities to enjoy.
"We just hope the outreach reaches a number of people that need it," Yates said. "I hear all the time from Christian people there's nothing for Christians to do. We certainly are trying to do our best."

content:
Return engagements - Gabriela Montero bringing second season of global concerts to Ebenezer Theater

 August 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 2A | Section: News 
 
 671
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Renowned pianist and composer Gabriela Montero is bringing a second season of acclaimed, global concert artists for a second season of "Gabriela Montero at Prager" - a concert series featuring a wide range of international musicians held the Ebenezer Theater in Easton.The Venezuelan-born Montero made her piano concerto debut at age eight.She's also a graduate ad fellow of the Royal Academy of Music in London.She hosted a first season of concerts in 2022 at the Ebenezer (which is part of the Prager Family Center for the Arts) in downtown Easton.According to announcement from Bluepoint Hospitality Group and the arts center:· Season II opens with a gala performance on August 19th, 2023. Gabriela Montero at Prager will feature one of today's leading opera stars, American soprano Nadine Sierra, acclaimed for her mesmerizing portrayals at the Metropolitan Opera.· Sierra's concert leads to a September recital, Chopin's Salon, celebrating the 19th Century's relationship between music and painting. Gabriela Montero is joined by Time Magazine cover artist Allen Hirsch.· October brings an evening commemorating the 150th Anniversary of iconic Russian composer Rachmaninoff, performed by leading interpreter Sergei Babayan - acclaimed Armenian pianist and Deutsche Grammophon artist.· November showcases Norwegian violinist and Hardanger Fiddle virtuoso Eldbjørg Hemsing, who will travel from Oslo to share the music of her homeland. Hemsing's Nordic Fire evening starts with a talk by Theodore Brun, British author of The Wanderer Chronicles - a work of epic Scandinavian fiction.· December rings in the holidays with An American Christmas gala concert featuring 2022 Grammy Winner Morris Robinson, the All-American college footballer turned opera star.· Season II continues in April 2024 at the Ebenezer Theater with an Italian mystery guest - a star of the piano world whose identity cannot yet be disclosed for exclusivity reasons.· The spotlight on top talent extends in May with Mozart by the Met, an evening with a Metropolitan Opera Horn & String Sextet. The performance unmasks Costa Rican French horn Hugo Valverde, the youngest musician ever appointed to the legendary MET Orchestra.· In June 2024, Season II's final concert is with the famed, Anthony Kearns - founding member of the Irish Tenors - who returns to the series for The Last Rose of Summer, an evening of Irish song.Nadine Sierra's show on Saturday, Aug. 19, features the Metropolitan Opera soprano bring her vocals to the Eastern Shore in a show with Montero entitled "Made for Opera." Tickets are $150 and the show starts at 7:30 p.m.For concert details and tickets, please visit Montero-Prager.com or www.pragerarts.com/event-details/nadine-sierra-made-for-operaCOMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT & EDUCATIONThroughout the second series of Montero's concert series, "up to 20 seats at each performance are provided at no cost to underserved community members through the Access to Excellence ticket program," the announcement said.The Ebenezer Theater and Prager arts group will also host a "Next Generation" showcase in November featuring On the education front, the Ebenezer Theater hosts a Next Generation showcase in November 2023 featuring emerging global talents from the Gabriela Montero Piano Lab, a mentorship initiative of OAcademy Music Conservatory by The Orchestra of the Americas Group.Gabriela Montero at Prager continues to add global color and international excellence to the cultural landscape of Easton, MD, as the most acclaimed artists of our time gather to bring intimate music-making to the Ebenezer Theater and provide the community with unique experiences.The Ebenezer Theater was originally constructed in 1856 and housed the Ebenezer Methodist Episcopal Church. It was acquired by local businessman and Bluepoint Hospitality principal Paul Prager who has purchased, redeveloped and repurposed a number of Easton properties.For more: bluepointhospitality.com.

title: 'Urban Landscapes' exhibit at AAM
author: Staff report
content:
'Urban Landscapes' exhibit at AAM

 April 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff report | Section: Entertainment 
 
 400
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum is hosting a new exhibit "Richard Estes: Urban Landscapes", featuring cityscapes from Richard Estes.Estes is "one of the founding figures of photorealism," according to announcement from the Easton art museum.
The exhibit kicks off May 1 with an opening reception at AAM from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. and runs through Aug. 3.
"With twenty-five meticulously rendered paintings and prints spanning the 1980s through the early 2000s, this exhibition captures Estes' lifelong fascination with reflective surfaces, architectural symmetry, and the fleeting beauty of the everyday urban environment," AAM said in the announcement.
"Rendered with astonishing technical precision, Estes' images transport viewers into gleaming storefronts, glassy façades, and layered streetscapes—most often set in New York City—that are at once familiar and surreal. His work challenges traditional notions of landscape, offering instead a vision of place that fuses photography, memory, and hyper-observation. Though far from the Eastern Shore, Estes' worlds reflect back on our own, inviting fresh ways of seeing the places we inhabit," the announcement continues.
The exhibition is organized by the Portland Museum of Art in Maine and is supported by Art Bridges.
AAM is also hosting a number of other events including its Spring Gala on May 3. Here is rundown of the events from the Easton museum.
Spring Gala: Reflections & ConnectionsSaturday, May 3, 6 p.m.
Inspired by the sharp realism of Richard Estes: Urban Landscapes, this year's Spring Gala transforms an industrial warehouse just north of Easton into a sleek, city-loft experience. Guests will enjoy immersive projections, an original soundscape by local talent Kentavius Jones, bold cuisine by Gourmet by the Bay, and a special announcement about the Museum's upcoming Freeman Annex and Hormel Research Center. Join us for an unforgettable night where art ignites conversation, where every ticket fuels the Academy Art Museum's future, ensuring that the doors stay open, the lights stay on, and the museum remains free for all.
Reflections/Connections: Public Recording SessionsJune 28 & 29, 1–4 p.m.
Musician Kentavius Jones and his band will record original music and ambient sounds inspired by Estes' work and the streets of Easton in open studio-style sessions.
Reflections/Connections: Outdoor ConcertAugust 2, Time TBD
The exhibition culminates in an immersive outdoor concert where Kentavius Jones performs a score inspired by Estes, accompanied by projected images and community-generated art.
ArtReach Field TripsMay 1–August 1 | By request
Free K–12 field trips offer guided exhibition tours, hands-on activities, transportation, and take-home materials for local schools and youth organizations.

title: Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist
author: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life
content:
Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life | Section: News 
 
 1158
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chocolate-covered strawberries and hazelnut cream-filled truffles are classics, but why play it safe this Valentine's Day? There's a world of unconventional pairings that bring out chocolate's rich complexity in unexpected ways. Soy sauce, blue cheese or Kalamata olives may sound like strange partners for sweet chocolate, but that's the point — these daring pairings are bold and delicious, giving standard Valentine's Day offerings an exciting new twist.Why unusual chocolate pairings workThe magic behind these unconventional combinations lies in chocolate's unique chemical makeup. Cocoa contains both bitter compounds, like theobromine, and fats that mellow those sharp edges. When paired with salty, savory or even spicy flavors, chocolate's sweetness becomes more pronounced, and its richness shines through.
Scientists call this effect "taste contrast enhancement," where opposing flavors make each other more vibrant. According to a study in Flavour Journal, the interplay between sweet and savory flavors can enhance our taste experience. For instance, when you combine savory, meaty umami with sweetness, it creates a more complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and cheese: A match worth melting forCheese boards and chocolate trays rarely mingle at the same table, but they should. Chocolate, especially dark chocolate with a hint of bitterness, pairs beautifully with creamy, tangy and even funky cheeses.
Take blue cheese, for instance. Its saltiness and pungent flavors contrast perfectly with the deep cocoa notes of dark chocolate. It's the same principle that makes salted caramel irresistible — sweetness tempered by salty and savory undertones.
For a milder approach, try rich brie with milk chocolate. These two creamy ingredients melt together into something unexpectedly lush. Add dried figs or almonds for texture, and you've got a dessert that could replace the standard cheese plate.
Chocolate and soy sauce: Sweet, salty and savorySoy sauce's salty umami highlights cocoa's natural sweetness without overpowering it. There's even a Japanese company that makes chocolate-flavored soy sauce, combining two fermented ingredients — cacao beans and soybeans — into one umami-rich seasoning.
A sprinkle of soy sauce over dark chocolate ice cream — or even just a square of good-quality dark chocolate — is transformative. The umami kicks in just as the chocolate dissolves, adding depth without excess salt. If you're feeling adventurous, a dash of soy sauce in a cup of hot chocolate lends a richer, more rounded flavor profile.
Chocolate and olive oil: A Mediterranean revelationOlive oil is celebrated as a base for salad dressings and marinades, but its potential in desserts is usually overlooked. Paired with dark chocolate, a fruity extra-virgin olive oil adds silky texture and subtle bitterness that enhance the chocolate's depth.
Drizzle olive oil over a slice of flourless chocolate cake, sprinkle with flaky sea salt, and you'll wonder why you haven't done it sooner. For an easy experiment, try dipping pieces of dark chocolate into a small dish of olive oil and topping with a pinch of salt. The combination is addictive.
Chocolate and chili: A kick of traditionWhile chili and chocolate might seem like a modern trend, the combination has ancient roots. The Aztecs and Mayans famously combined cacao with chili peppers to create a bitter, spicy drink known as "xocolatl." It's a powerhouse pairing, with chili enhancing chocolate's bitterness while adding a lingering heat that begs for another bite.
Spicy chili peppers pair best with dark chocolate that contains a high percentage of cocoa. A pinch of cayenne in a cup of hot chocolate is an easy way to test the waters, or you can try chili-dusted truffles for a fiery twist. Other spicy additions include ginger, pink peppercorns and cinnamon.
Chocolate and black garlic: The umami powerhouseBlack garlic might not be a pantry staple, but it deserves a spot on your experimental dessert list. It starts as fresh garlic — sharp and aromatic — and as it ages and ferments, develops a mellow, caramelized flavor.
"The sweet molasses and balsamic undertones in black garlic make it a great flavor addition to many desserts," according to Black Garlic North America, the continent's largest black garlic processor. It's sweet and sticky, similar to a raisin or date, making it a perfect complement to chocolate.
"One of the remarkable things about black garlic is just how many layers of flavor it has," says Katy Heath, founder of Balsajo, a black garlic producer in the United Kingdom. Try black garlic in chocolate ganache or as a secret addition to rich, fudgy brownies. It adds complexity without overwhelming the dish.
Chocolate and Kalamata olivesIf you're an olive lover, don't sleep on this combo. Dark chocolate has fruity notes that complement the saltiness of the olives, and the result is kind of mind-blowing.
"We all know how a pinch of sea salt can enhance dark chocolate, but just wait until you experience what black olives can do," says Food52 writer Cathleen Clarity, who uses Kalamata olives in her molten dark chocolate and black olive cake. "Their brininess and slightly bitter taste are the perfect complement to the molten dark chocolate."
Chocolate and matcha: An earthy fusionCombining chocolate with matcha, finely ground green tea powder, creates an intriguing flavor profile. The earthy bitterness of matcha complements the sweetness of chocolate, creating a delightful balance.
Matcha works especially well with white chocolate, known for its pronounced sweetness and creamy texture. Matcha's bitterness tempers the sweetness of white chocolate, while the chocolate's creaminess softens the tea's intensity, creating a smooth, complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and wasabi: An unexpected heatPairing chocolate with wasabi, the Japanese horseradish commonly served with sushi, creates a surprising blend of sweet and spicy flavors. Wasabi's heat differs from that of chili peppers, hitting more in the nasal passages than on the tongue, and it dissipates more quickly. Wasabi cuts through the richness of the chocolate, exemplifying how contrasting flavors can both balance and accentuate each other.
White chocolate-coated wasabi peas capitalize on the addictive quality of the sweet-spicy, creamy-crunchy snack phenomenon. In Japan, you can even find wasabi and white chocolate KitKat bars made with wasabi from the Shizuoka prefecture, famous for its production of the spicy root.
To explore this combination at home, add a dollop of wasabi paste to chocolate ganache, hot fudge sauce or hot chocolate. Wasabi's heat sneaks up on you and can be quite potent, so start with a modest amount and adjust to taste.
The takeaway: Make bold moves this Valentine's DayWhen selecting a Valentine's gift this year, don't default to the same boring heart-shaped box of chocolates everyone goes for. Instead, surprise and delight your Valentine with unexpected chocolate pairings. If nothing else, these adventurous combinations are great conversation starters, and if they strike a chord with your sweetheart, they'll make the gesture — and you — unforgettable.
Robin Donovan is the author of more than 40 cookbooks and the founder and creator of All Ways Delicious, a food site loaded with easy recipes for the best dishes from around the world. Her writing and recipes have been featured in major media outlets including Huffington Post, MSN, Associated Press, Buzzfeed, Cooking Light, PopSugar, Chicago Sun-Times, Fitness, Parade, Mercury News and many others.

 Why would anyone from another planet even with to visit Earth?Puerile still, we wickedly, blunderingly, with self-aggrandizement, and from fear, choose war, without ever pausing to imagine another course, pausing to truly acknowledge a situation — too deeply to see, to consider anew, clearly and comprehensively to acknowledge the foremost reality of humankind's imperishable sisterhood and brotherhood.

 EASTON - Talbot Humane has introduced their inaugural holiday ornament.The idea was brought to Patty Quimby, Talbot Humane's executive director, and the TH Board, by the coordinating committee of the TH holiday "Pawsitively Fabulous Pet Boutique." The team presented the concept of establishing a shelter-animal-themed art contest across the community each year, with the winning selection becoming the annual ornament.In the late spring, TH launched the first contest and received a variety of fantastic submissions.While it was a tough decision, Quimby and the board ultimately selected Nicholas Casale's holiday pup design.Kristy Casale, Nicholas' mother, brought her very excited 9 year-old son into the front office of Talbot Humane just minutes before the contest was over.He had seen the contest and excitedly embraced the idea. title: Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: D3 | Section: News 
 
 1171
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For most of his life, Maryland filmmaker Samuel White has been focused on captivating audiences through the thought-provoking narratives and community-building aspects of his films, a drive that recently brought him recognition at the 2023 Cecil County Independent Film Festival."Through creating art, my hope is to get people wanting to talk about the art," said White. "Even if they disagree, I want people to communicate, talk about ideas and get to know each other and I think that's the reason I make films."White, 33, of Elkton, developed an interest in filmmaking after he saw the 1960 film 'Psycho' when he was 11 years old. White recalls seeing certain shots within the film the artistic intention of which peaked his interest.From that point forward, White took his enjoyment for writing stories and began to think of them as films until he began playing with his grandfather's camcorder to bring his ideas to life. Now, White says filmmaking is his favorite form of storytelling."I can not picture a time in my life where I didn't think cinematically," said White. "I don't know if I showed any talent as a filmmaker when I was a kid but at that time, I learned that the camera is an important storytelling tool."In high school, White was homeschooled under an umbrella program that granted him the opportunity to meet fellow students who were also interested in filmmaking. Based on their shared love of film, White and his friends created the "Cinematography Club," where they would get together and practice different filmmaking techniques.From 2004 to 2008, when White was in high school, video production technology was rapidly evolving with the introduction of HD video and video cameras. After White's senior year of high school, Digital Single Lens Reflection (DSLR) cameras took over the market."With the DSLRs, it was like a 'oh my god, we could actually do this,' moment for me with filmmaking because of how video friendly and available DSLRs became," said White.DSLR cameras often have interchangeable lenses, shoot on compact flash or SD cards and are capable of both still photography and shooting high quality video. To learn more about video technology, White attended Cecil College where he majored in Video Production."When I was at Cecil College, I didn't have an interest in the actual degree, I wanted to get as much hand on tech experience as I could and I did," said White. "It was fantastic because they gave me the tools and opportunities to work and learn with the technology and techniques."White said that his favorite course at Cecil College was called 'Gorilla Filmmaking,' where he had the opportunity to to work with top of the line filmmaking equipment while receiving guidance and criticism on his work from professional photographer and videographer Floyd Dean.During that class, White created his first short film that documented a female character suffering from an unknown problem that was slowly destroying her body. The horror film utilized only music - no dialogue - which White says was intentional, as it left much of the film up for interpretation."For me, the girl running around with her face falling off asking for help and being ignored was kind of like personal feelings I have had throughout my life relating to personal things," said White. "I enjoy films that are abstract that invite you to feel and interpret what you want."White graduated from Cecil College in 2012 and has gone on to build himself a filmmaking portfolio of 14 independent films; six of which he wrote and directed on his own.His most recent film, 'Safewords,' follows a soon-to-be bride and her adventure into an alternative lifestyle.The film won Best Full Length Feature and Best Scriptwriting.Safewords took three weekends for White and his crew of three to create, which he said took about 10 years off of his life expectancy due to stress."I didn't give myself enough time and it was a massive learning experience because of the amount of stuff I didn't know about while making an hour and a half long feature film," said White. "I am proud of the film and I am glad it turned out the way it did."White often holds his new films up against his 2020 film 'The Day Bingo Died,' as he said it is his favorite film that he has made to date.The film follows a brother and a sister who return to their childhood home to euthanize their family dog. Both siblings grieve the loss and decide to go to a bar after burying the dog. The siblings later end up intoxicated and arguing over who loved the dog more, which White said is the "weirdest mix between two adults acting like spoiled drunk children."Odd mix aside, White considers 'The Day Bingo Died' to be his favorite film because it presents viewers with an uncomfortable, yet relatable, view of grief and family."It plays on the power behind words and the expression of grief and how the differences between the two speak to human nature," said White."I love putting people in that uncomfortable space where they don't know if they should laugh or not because the uncomfortable feelings come from situations being relatable."Much of White's inspiration comes from directors Alfred Hitchcock, Lars Von Trier and David Zucker, as well as his personal competitive streak to build and improve film ideas using metaphor.White explained that he often views everything in his life as a scene in a movie, which helps him grow as a filmmaker because it allows him to connect metaphors to true meaning."When something emotional or interesting happens to me, I ask what it would look like visually and how would that fit into a story," said White. "If it's a fear of commitment, my metaphor would be a wedding ring stuck on a finger that irritates the skin - stuff like that."White's consistent hunt for metaphors to add into his films is what he says is the base of traditional filmmaking and is what makes his films art. But to keep the sense of traditional filmmaking alive, White said film festivals are essential as art on the big scene is slowly fading into the background."If you want to be a filmmaker, from now throughout the future, there will be less chances to get your film on an actual big screen, which is why I go to local film festivals - to keep the traditional art form of filmmaking alive because of streaming," said White.Looking to the future, White is working to grow his production company, Outsider Film Company, to a point where it can help independent filmmakers produce their work. The film company currently offers a variety of professional video services and can be found on Instagram or Facebook."I will be making art for the rest of my life," said White. "If you're considering making movies, Cecil County is a great place and you're in a great time period. Get out and give it a try."

title: Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum celebrates 60 years
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum celebrates 60 years

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST.MICHAELS — A staple of St. Michaels, the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is celebrating 60 years.Volunteers spearheaded the creation of the museum, which opened in 1965 at Navy Point and was accredited in 1978.
"The museum really started out by a community effort," said Pete Lesher, chief historian and ambassador at large at the museum. "The collections were built with an outpouring from the community over the idea that the place is changing and we need to establish a museum to remember the way it was."
Lesher, came to the museum in 1991 as a curator. He said the museum was created in a "series of themes" to represent the Bay and people around the it.
MUSEUM HISTORY
The museum started in May 1965 with two buildings that had been on the grounds since 1850 the Higgins house and the Dodson house. The eagle house building arrived in 1870. The three buildings now serve as administrative buildings after serving as exhibit buildings for nine years in the early days.
According to Lesher, the land where the museum's lighthouse and other exhibits now sit was reclaimed from the Bay.
"This was just a shallow part of the park," Lesher said. "You would have been standing probably knee deep sinking into mud about 150 years ago.
"This area started with actually a sawmill and grist mill but moved beyond that to seafood packing houses, and by the height here in the 1930s and 1940s, there were four different seafood packing houses out on this point. Every time they wanted to expand, they simply discarded more oyster shells, which they end up on themselves, pushing them into the harbor and built more land."
William Coulbourne and Frederick Jewett were two African American business owners who owned one of the four businesses on the land.
"They were early 20th century Black entrepreneurs from Crisfield, Maryland, who moved up here," Lesher said. "They learned the business and managed to get somebody to sell them land and managed to get somebody to give them a bank loan — a remarkable success story."
The museum plans to honor Coulbourne and Jewitt by renaming its education building after the two entrepreneurs.
The lighthouse, which is featured in the museum's logo, is the first historical structure the museum collected. It was acquired in 1966 when the Coast Guard was demolishing lighthouses "left and right" because of vandalism, according to Lesher.
The museum bought the lighthouse from the demolition company and moved it 50 miles north to the museum site.
"It was so early in our history, it became our logo," Lesher said. "The lighthouse is sort of what identifies the museum."
One of the new changing exhibits at the museum is the Sailing to Freedom exhibit, which highlights the Underground Railroad on the water.
"So we think of the Underground Railroad like the Harriet Tubman story of running up the Delmarva Peninsula to get to Philadelphia and freedom," Lesher said.
"Well, a lot of people made it by boat, whether they got a ticket on a steamboat, got away that way or stowed away on a coast-wise schooner, so many of them on the Chesapeake Bay, while the Chesapeake Bay forms a natural watery highway to the north. This was a route to freedom for many of those freedom seekers," he said. "That's what we try to show with this exhibit."
HELPING THE COMMUNITY
In addition to exhibits for museum-goers, the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum uses some exhibits to help with the curriculum in Talbot County schools.
An exhibit displaying the Maryland Crab Meat Company sits where the museum holds the Chesapeake's Best Crab Cakes program, in which third and fifth graders receive math, reading and social studies credits in the curriculum.
"The Chesapeake's Best Crab Cakes program meets learning goals for for math, for reading and for social studies in the Maryland curriculum," Lesher said. "Every Talbot County third grader and fifth grader has an experience tied to their curriculum, tied to their learning goals right here in the museum."
The museum also conducts an apprenticeship program where museum staff work with an apprentice for two years, ultimately leading to a state credential.
According to Lesher, the museum has hired some of these apprentices as permanent shipyard crew.
The museum has partnered with the St. Michaels Community Center on multiple occasions.
"We're working to do more community collaborations with them because both our missions align, and we want to enrich the lives of people who live in St. Michaels," said Amy Horne, executive director of the community center.

title: One Book One Maryland presents “Kin: Rooted in Hope” author talk at Chesapeake College
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
One Book One Maryland presents “Kin: Rooted in Hope” author talk at Chesapeake College

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 840
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — Exploring family and freedom, 2025 One Maryland One Book author Carole Boston Weatherford and illustrator Jeffery Boston Weatherford presented a discussion on "Kin: Rooted in Hope" as part of the state's largest annual reading and discussion program at Chesapeake College on Oct. 7.Originally published in 2023, "Kin: Rooted in Hope" is an illustrated verse novel that serves as a work of art, history and personal genealogy through the authors' search into their family tree.
Conjuring ancestors and tracing historical roots from the Maryland plantation where Frederick Douglass was also enslaved to Civil War battlefields and to the founding of a black, Reconstruction-era village, "Kin" interweaves rhythmic poetic imagery verse and stunning visuals to give voices through multiple perspectives.
Author of 80 children's books, Carole considered poetry her "first literary language," which lends itself to a different flow of words to convey emotions for her than traditional prose.
Carole is no stranger to addressing tough topics for young people in verse, including her 2021 picture book "Unspeakable: The Tulsa Race Massacre."
Carole said it is important not to shy away from telling children the truth and to ensure critical thinking and socially responsible civic contribution.
A pin drop could be heard in the Todd Performing Arts Center auditorium as Carole recounted tracing her ancestor's lineage back to the Wye House plantation in Easton.
Visiting the Wye House for research, Carole noted moving moments and powerful connections, including holding the enormous iron antique key to the home, something her ancestor must have held as well.
Carole recounted visiting the plantation's burial ground, now hallowed with a plaque marking where the enslaved people of the house were laid to rest.
"I knelt down and cried and it was almost as if my ancestors had said, 'We have been waiting for you,'" Carole said.
Carole learned of an ancestor, Isaac Copper, mentioned in Frederick Douglass' autobiography, who was enslaved at the Wye House at the same time.
The Weatherfords' ancestors went on to fight for the Union in the American Civil War and helped found the historically black communities of Unionville and Copperville.
In creating the book, the Weatherfords came to discover, "Knowing your history is generational wealth," Carole said.
The mother-son duo were proud to collaborate, and Carole said it was a dream come true to experience it all with her son.
In reconnecting with ancestral roots, the two's travels included the Door of No Return at Gorée Island, noted as the last thing Africans of the area saw before they were enslaved and shipped away from their home.
Jeffery utilized a scratchboard medium to "bring people out of darkness into the light" and often used his own family as character models.
Jeffery said working on the book gave him a greater appreciation and understanding for the work his mother has been doing since he was a child.
One of the biggest challenges faced while working on the book was connecting the dots, Carole said.
Comprehensive research brought Carole's nose into captain ship ledgers and the meticulous records kept by the Lloyd family, owners of the Wye House plantation.
Carole noted the emotions in seeing the names of ancestors inscribed in estate inventory alongside bought and sold goods.
Some information remained out of reach, like the exact ship names that brought her enslaved ancestors over, she said. Along with the tremendous amount of research that went into every page also came a certain amount of artistic license to create stories, she said.
For those piecing together their own family tree, Carole gave permission for imagination as long as it fit the narrative historically.
"Informed by facts, it is up to you to fill in the gaps," she said.
Carole encouraged everyone to know their own history and seek out their own family stories regardless of ethnicity to inspire future generations.
Amateur genealogy hunting doesn't have to break the bank, she said, with public libraries a wealth of information and often having access to ancestry data resources.
"When you are the only one who knows, you tell somebody," she said.
Stories are essential to know exactly what ancestors went through. "Without stories, a family tree is just a map," Carole said.
"All of our histories are intertwined," Jeffery said, and by connecting with history, warts and all, we will find we have more in common than different.
"Names, dates and places are the branches of a family tree," according to Carole. "But stories are the leaves that bring the family's past to life."
"Kin: Rooted in Hope" is the winner of a Coretta Scott King Honor, the Claudia Lewis Award from Bank Street College of Education and the Boston Globe/Horn Book Award.
The Weatherfords have toured across Maryland to discuss the book as part of the One Maryland One Book program to encourage a love of reading and develop a deeper sense of community through connecting events.
The event at Chesapeake College was made possible in partnership with Eastern Shore Regional Library, Washington College, Caroline County Public Library, Kent County Public Library, Dorchester County Public Library, Queen Anne's County Public Library, ShoreLit, Talbot County Public Schools and The Needle's Eye Academy.
More information about the Weatherfords can be found at cbweatherford.com.

title: The Digital Renaissance - Re-Imagining classic artistry in The age of Technology
author: Melanie Allen; Wealth of Geeks
content:
The Digital Renaissance - Re-Imagining classic artistry in The age of Technology

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Melanie Allen; Wealth of Geeks | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 1260
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The idyllic image of a painter, easel bathed in sunlight, is giving way to a new form. Today's art ist hunches over his laptop, frantically clicking his mouse to form perfect lines.Computers drastically changed art in form and function, forcing modern artists to adapt. Many yearn for the simplicity of ink on canvas while others love the ease o use and instant connectivity modern programs provide.Artists must find ways to bridge the gap to thrive in this ever-changing industry.TECHNOLOGY'S IMPACT ON ARTISTIC EXPRESSIONTechnology has a massive impact on the arts. Novice photographers can take professional quality shots in seconds with their phones, then edit them immediately with an app. Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) allow companies to create logos and images for branding with the click of a button, limiting job opportunities for artists who bought into digital trends. Fakers and hacks flood internet marketing channels with low-quality works, drowning out the talent.It's not all bad news for artists, though. They no longer depend on galleries and wealthy patrons, but can now set up online shops and connect directly with customers. Livia Ochmann, artist and founde of how-to-art.com, uses modern technology to share her passion for the arts with others. She says contemporary artists have numerous ways to earn a living from thei work, including print-on-demand shops, courses, tutorial websites, affiliate programs, and sponsorships. None of these income avenues existed 30 years ago.Technology has also changed what we consider to be art. Data scientist Kat Campbell, an expert on digital technology, says modern tools have allowed artists to create immersive experiences, making art interactive and multidimensional, and offering a host of new mediums to explore, from digital painting to 3D models.THE CASE AGAINST DIGITAL ARTSome traditionalists, however, view digital creations as imposters not worthy of the "art" designation "I have seen digital artists being sometimes unfairly judged," Ochmann says, adding the common refrains include statements such as "digital art isn't real art," "people working in this medium are lazy," and "anyone can do what they do."Critics also lament the ease of entry into the market that digital tools create. When anyone can be an artist, everyone becomes an artist, crowding the marketplace."While technology makes art more accessible, it also floods the market," explains Campbell. "Standing out amidst this digital noise becomes a challenge."ART AND AIArtists also express concern ove AI and its potential impact on their work.Illustrator Aimee Cozza explains, "Professional artists are losing their jobs already to LLMs [Large Language Models, commonly called generative AI]," she says. "Many long-time artists are feeling quite uneasy about the gen eral attitude of the Internet agains artists, including the fragmentation of social media and the introduction of LLMs."Noting the impact generative AI models are already having on artists, Cozza adds, "I have watched many of my professional artist friends making less money on projects and at conventions throughout the declining economy, with closures due to the pandemic wreaking havoc for many of them. Many friends have turned to picking up side jobs or have qui doing art as a full-time job entirelyALL FORMS OF EXPRESSION HAVE THEIR PLACEHowever, most artists say the judgment is unjust. "Digital artists like us traditional artists, require a deep understanding of anatomy, perspective, and various artis tic principles to create good art. The skills they employ are no less valid, and their dedication to their craft is just as genuine," Ochmann points out.Joseph Taveras, an American roboticist-turned artist, agrees. "Drawing a line between artists who use computers/graphic design and those who stick with traditional mediums isn't necessarily productive - it's all art, just differ ent forms of expression," he says.Despite the stigma, most artists, even those who produce work in traditional media, use modern technology in some fashion.Mikhail Belanovich, lead designer with CoinsPaid Media, thinks it's silly not to take advantage of technology. "Surely it would be ridiculous to ignore tech nology as a phenomenon in 2023, he says; adding that every artist should use social media to share their work.However, connecting with an audience is only a small part of how artists embrace modern technology.ARTISTS COMBINE DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES WITH TRADITIONAL MEDIUMSMany use a combination of traditional and digital mediums to complete their work.Drawing tablets provide an easy way to bridge the gap. Artists can use their natural drawing ability to produce images directly on the screen, which they can then retouch or enhance as needed.Sarajean C, an artist with leading drawing tablet manufacturer Wacom, says, "Traditional art-ists value being hands-on and intimate with their art. Wacom tablet allow traditional artists to maintain the quality of their work in digital form, may it be transitioning into digital art, or retouching their scanned-in pieces."She adds that drawing tablets enhance features in software appli cations that mimic traditional mediums, making these applications more accessible to classical artists.Drawing tablets aren't the only way to transform classical forms of expression into digital media. Ingenious artists use numerous methods of combining the two competing forms.Terena Bell, visual artist and writer, hand draws her work and then combines the drawing with printed photos to make a collage, using the original drawings as an underpainting. Next, she photographs the collage and uses the basic Apple Photos app to refine the lines and colors.Taveras uses digital resources to enhance, not replace his creativity. "I use the programs Sketch, Adob Premiere, Adobe After Effects, and Logic Pro X in my practice to help me with conceptual research and aesthetic studies, but a majority of my artworks (98%) are physical paintings. I also use holo-grams, robots, and projectors to assist with the process," he says.Some use older technology to bridge the gap. Ochmann works with traditional mediums like pen cils, colored pencils, and watercolor on paper, then uses an old scanner to turn them digital. Once there, she uses Adobe Photoshop to remove dust or blemishes before uploading them to her website.TRADITIONAL MEDIUMS WILL ALWAYS HAVE A PLACEDespite the rapidly changing landscape, classical forms of expression will always remain relevant, though how we interact with art may vary.Cozza points to the most famous painting in the world as an example. "Many people do not have the means to visit the Mona Lisa in person, but with the assistance of technology converting this legendary artwork into pixels, they can enjoy the artwork from anywhere in the world," she explains.Belanovich says traditional artworks are just as popular as ever. "Sotheby's hasn't closed, and museums are up and running too. Art academies keep recruiting talented people every year."Taveras explains further, "There is an irreplaceable, tactile quality to physical artworks that digital forms, as of now, cannot replicate. The weight of a brush stroke, the texture of paint on canvas - these are sacred elements that collectors, enthusiasts, and artists alike hold in high esteem."AS TECHNOLOGY EVOLVES, SO WILL ARTISTIC EXPRESSIONAs humanity advances in science and technology, artists will adapt to the new forms. Artistic expression will never disappear, but new generations of artists will find innovative ways to combine technology with creativity, unveiling works that today's patrons can't even fathom.However, traditional mediums will always have their place. The best artists of the future will find ways to walk between both worlds, using modern technology to enhance classical forms while expressing the essence of the human condition.This article was produced by Media Decision and syndicated by Wealth of Geeks. 
 
 Caption: WEALTH OF GEEKS
 
What is the future of art and digital art?
 
WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/DAVID S. SORIANO

title: Easton Music Academy up for national award
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Easton Music Academy up for national award

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — From classical to rock, the Easton Music Academy on Creamery Lane is dedicated to helping students improve, said Owner and Director Victoria Weaver.Those efforts are attracting national attention.
The 10-teacher and 150-student operation has been recognized to compete as one of the country's best music schools. Weaver is going to Las Vegas to compete against nine other music programs in April.
"We are nominated for a national award. It is called the National Music School of the Year," said Weaver, who trained at Berklee College of Music. "I am going in two weeks to Las Vegas... We have to present what we have done, who we are and what we have done for our communities, and maybe win."
"I am excited to go and represent our community," she said.
The Easton Music School's nomination comes from the Music Academy Success System, a national trade association for music academies from all over North America.
The academy was selected from a group of more than 500 coaching schools. There will be over 600 people at the conference. Weaver will have to deliver a 15 minute presentation to that audience to make the case of why her academy is the best.
"You have to be doing a lot and growing by leaps and bounds to even be considered," Weaver said.
The highlights of a Powerpoint presentation she will give during the two-day conference include Easton Music Academy's humble origin story.
"I started the business with absolutely nothing six years ago. I was gigging, and people would always ask me to teach them how to do that. So I started saying 'yes.' I was driving to students' houses. Then I converted a spare bedroom into a studio. I had like 20 students," she said.
Then Weaver decided to make a bigger commitment. The first week of March 2020, she signed a lease.
"I was literally freaking out. I thought I had made the worst decision ever, because everything was shutting down, and I was starting a business. We met virtual and some were done with masks. My space was 400 square feet behind Walmart. Just me. I was there a year before the opportunity to move here (Creamery Lane)," she said.
Weaver has a knack for attracting more students.
The academy teaches piano, voice, guitar, ukulele, drums, violin, cello, brass, woodwinds, viola, saxophone, flute and trumpet to students of all ages and ability levels.
And Weaver said she gives everything to the effort of being an entrepreneur.
"Your life is your business. My brain is easily 96% of the time on the academy and my clients making sure they have the best experience. We have the best teachers," she said.
Part of that effort is offering a variety of options to Easton Music Academy's students.
"We have group classes, private lessons, baby and toddler classes. We have an ensemble that is basically an orchestra. We are also starting up a rockstar program. We have six teaching rooms," she said.
But no matter her students' ages, skill levels or interests, Weaver has one goal that she sets for everyone who walks through the Easton Music Academy's doors.
"A big one for me is to watch the confidence. The moments when they get it. It is so good for them," she said.
