title: Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot Historical Society strives to keep the 360-year history of Easton alive with free historic walking tours held on the third Saturday of each month. Two tours are offered, one at 11 a.m. and another at noon, each providing a unique perspective on the town's history.The 11 a.m. tour takes participants on a walk through central Easton, highlighting important buildings and sharing stories about the town's rich history. The noon tour focuses on the architecture of the six buildings that make up the historical society's campus.
The historical society began offering these tours around 10 years ago. Archivist Patti Rockwell joined the society around that time and is now one of several tour guides.
"The people that live here are just blown away by the history," Rockwell said. "They said 'I had no idea.'"
The tours attract both tourists and locals, who often bring their visiting guests. They are free and open to the public, but registration is required.
The tours start at 25 South Washington St., in front of the historical society, and continue through downtown Easton, looping back to the starting point. The main tour features about 15 stops.
"I think what's really important is finding out how we've evolved to where we are today," Rockwell said.
The tours focus on the impact of the Revolutionary War and the Civil War on the town, as well as fires that brought destruction to several areas. One surprising fact, Rockwell said, is that the town of Easton took an early stand against British control — something many visitors are unaware of.
"You always hear about Boston, but this community took a stand at one time prior to the war starting too," Rockwell said.
Each tour is unique since tour guides create their own scripts. Rockwell said her favorite story to tell involves a hidden armory that stored weapons during the Revolutionary War. That site is now a parking lot partially used by the Easton Farmers Market.
Along with their information cards, tour guides carry a collection of photographs showing what Easton's buildings looked like a century ago. Some include drawings of Easton from before photography existed.
Rockwell said she hopes participants leave with greater awareness of the town's past.
"This town has done a remarkable job of preserving the past, keeping the same buildings here, if we can, without tearing them down so that people can see what it was like at least 100 years ago," Rockwell said.
"These buildings are still downtown, waiting for people to find out a little clue as to what was going on."
More information can be found at talbothistory.org.

 DENTON —The bloody fingerprint on the program of Fond Farewell says a lot. There is a contested will at stake that is worth millions, but with every passing moment, there are more people claiming the dough.This launches the hijinks for "Fond Farewell," a murder mystery dinner theater that played to a packed house at the Caroline Country Club on Friday and Saturday nights. According to Debby Bennett, chair of the murder mystery committee, "people kept calling asking to purchase tickets after our deadline. We sadly had to say no to them."
There was a bombshell vamp and a scheming personal assistant, and there was a cowgirl cop trying to figure it all out.
And the audience was laughing while trying to figure out who is the rightful heir to Ben Fullman's fortune. It was an audience participation show. Black "funeral" bands were given out to audience members at the door, and those who wore them opted to be included as part of the play. The actors were in character before the play started and even stayed in character during the dinner that followed their performance.
Kendall Teague, a planning committee member for the event, called the fundraiser "an exceptional success."
"The unexpected plot twists, hilarious dialogue and high-level audience participation brought on roars of laughter that filled the room all evening," Teague said. "In fact, several attendees shared with us that they hadn't laughed that hard in a very long time."
This was a successful fundraiser for the Caroline County Arts Council, which was a co-presenter with the Caroline County Public Library. There were several sponsors, including Simpkins Roofing and Siding, Foam Works, Big Bass USA, the Foundry, Shore United Bank, Hillside Coffee Roasters and On Your Mark.
All the actors volunteered their time, as did Director Keith L. Shaffer.
"I thought both nights were fabulous. It was so fun," Bennett said. "The food was great. The Culinary Center always does such a terrific job."

title: Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — When he moved to Washington, D.C., Wayman Pinder often traveled back to his Eastern Shore hometown down the unassuming Oxford Road.On the way, he saw a dilapidated building that he almost couldn't recognize. It was the John Wesley Methodist Episcopal Church, no longer used for services and worsening in condition by the year.
"I had to ride by this church where I used to be the organist, where I went all my life," Pinder said.
Following the church's closure in the mid-1970s, its exterior deteriorated, with roof problems, an unkempt cemetery and outhouse, and a lack of what once was a thriving group of community residents to look after the church. Pinder, now back in Oxford, felt it was ready to fall down at any moment.
"And to see it look like that, it hurt," Pinder said.
Pinder and his sister, Virginia Gibson, are just two of the many community members who have poured endless hours into renovating and rededicating the John Wesley Church. Earlier this month, the church celebrated a formal ribbon-cutting for its renovation — which has been an ongoing effort since 2003.
Renovations have included extensive roof repairs, a new wheelchair-accessible ramp, chimney and siding replacements and significant archaeological work on the cemetery that surrounds the building.
In the 2000s, the church was lifted to repair the foundation. Gibson notes that archaeological surveying found buried bodies beneath the church, which are now memorialized with gravestones in an expanded cemetery.
Upon walking in today, the church is welcoming and clean, with names of restoration donors and volunteers on the pews and window panes. It doesn't host services anymore, but it has hosted weddings and funerals.
"The inside of that church is just wonderful compared to what (it was)," Pinder said.
The restoration process wasn't always smooth sailing. Former John Wesley Preservation Society Vice President James Hollis founded the restoration efforts in 2003, Gibson said.
"We were spinning wheels for about five or six years," she said. Gibson attributed much of the credit to former Oxford Commissioner Kathleen Radcliffe, the preservation society's former president.
"She really mended (it) together," Gibson said. "She really was the person."
Through weekly and monthly meetings, board members rallied community support, hosted fundraisers and gathered the needed permits to fix up the semi-abandoned piece of history.
The preservation society gained official nonprofit status in 2014. Restoration took off thereafter, with major repairs performed by local contractors both outside and inside of the church.
Adjacent to the church is the Nellie Brooks Leatherberry Cook Shop, which Gibson said acts as the society's meeting room. An original stove used in the building still remains today. Nellie Leatherberry, born in Oxford in 1908, provided meals to churchgoers.
"People would actually sit in here and eat the best food ever made," Pinder said.
The cook shop became Talbot County's first African American Museum site in 2015. The church next to it has just as much history. Originally bought in 1838 as Oxford Neck Church, documents show it was a mixed congregation, with 31 white members and 26 Black members.
In 1875, the church was rebuilt to the single-room white building it has been since, becoming a part of the Oxford community and the Eastern Shore Black community until its closure in the 20th century.
Though the church hasn't hosted weekly services for decades, it has remained a cornerstone of the Oxford community. It's been home to quilt shows and community gatherings, and even served as a water stop for local cycling races.
Many board members and community volunteers have memories associated with the church, Pinder and Gibson both said. Whether they were members or their parents or grandparents were, many Oxford residents seem to resonate with the small but chronicled building off of Oxford Road.
"For us, it's personal history, too," Pinder said. "We experienced it."

 On Friday, July 18, from 5 to 7 p.m., the Zebra Gallery will open two new shows featuring artists Gabriel Lehman and Evan Fitzgerald.Gabriel Lehman's show, "A Bird's Eye View," will feature his fanciful, dreamlike landscapes with a particular emphasis on clouds, imbuing a sense of joy and wonder into his art. Lehman is a self-taught artist who started painting in 2009 after a career in construction with a focus on flooring for 14 years. Despite not having any formal training, Lehman's unique perspective and whimsical style quickly gained him a following.
Lehman is also offering painting classes from July 14 to 19 to learn his secrets to gorgeous clouds and fantastic creatures. Classes offered include "Three-Color Clouds," where students will learn the secrets of capturing the softness, depth and movement of clouds while transforming three simple colors into breathtaking skyscapes.
The "Sunset Skies" class offers students an enchanting journey through the colors of dusk as they learn to paint breathtaking sunsets on 16-by-20-inch canvases. In this immersive class, students learn how to capture the delicate gradients, vibrant hues and ethereal beauty of the sky at its most magical moments.
The "Rays of Light" class guides students through techniques to achieve the perfect balance of light and shadow, subtle color blending and atmospheric perspective, making the clouds look like they could float right off the canvas. This class invites participants to explore the endless possibilities of acrylic paint while creating stunning skyscapes that will brighten any space. All skill levels are welcome to all of these classes.
Evan Fitzgerald's current work explores the ideas of persona. The word persona is rooted in the Latin word for a theatrical mask. Carl Jung described persona as a social mask that we all put on — something to embody, a different mask for a different setting. By obscuring the subject's face, their headdresses are the focal point. The individual is merely a pedestal for displaying these objects.
"Both of these artists bring such creative and whimsical works to the gallery. I hope visitors will be mesmerized by the details these painters bring to their paintings. We are thrilled to have them exhibiting here," said Susan Schauer John, owner of the Zebra Gallery.
For more information or to sign up for Gabriel Lehman's class, call 410-253-9131 or email thezebragallery@gmail.com. title: Dorchester Historical Society looks to past and future
author: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester Historical Society looks to past and future

 August 31, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 551
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - The Dorchester County Historical Society is in the midst of a year-long celebration of the organization's 70th anniversary.DCHS Executive Director Zoë Phillips said the 70th anniversary speaks to the hard work and robust involvement of those members from the past.In its heyday, the organization was one of the most active of its kind. Phillips said a recently uncovered newspaper article reported that DCHS was one of the largest and most active in the nation.The director said the society's mission is to preserve and protect local history."There are so many pieces of history here (in Dorchester) that are starting to deteriorate or fade away that we're not hearing about," Philips said."But the more that people come in here and bring us their own family records and tell us their own stories, they get to be able to pass them on through us." Phillips said the anniversary celebration began in May in observance of the society convening for the first time in the spring of 1953."From here, we're hoping to focus on expanding the organization, expanding our outreach," Phillips said, forecasting an ongoing rollout of events for a broad variety of audiences."We want to showcase all aspects of Dorchester history," she said.That local history and the stories that comprise it are what drew Phillips to the field and to participate as a volunteer at DCHS for four years.Phillips was appointed to the position of executive director earlier this year after the passing of Mitch Anderson.While earning her degree in history, Phillips studied history from around the world, but she was particularly drawn to local history."There's something about Dorchester County that always spoke to me," Phillips said, an inclination she attributes to her grandmother, who told her stories about growing up in Hoopers Island.The historical society's location on 1003 Greenway Drive was active on a weekday early in August, with multiple people congregating there to work on genealogical research.Douglas Mitchell of Seattle was one of the researchers that Tuesday, poring over a bound copy of a local newspaper from the 1850s. Mitchell, a relative of Harriet Tubman, has been on an extended visit to Cambridge as he completes research about his family's history and works on developing his understanding of how things were.Mitchell said Dorchester County Historical Society had been "very integral" in his research, as it is one of the main repositories of historical information about Dorchester. He said the genealogical records collected by DCHS have been useful in finding connections with the Harriet Tubman family with other families in the area."Researching and studying the documents at this particular repository has been hugely informative and helpful, particularly in me building a broad, comprehensive view of culture and politics that were happening here in Dorchester," Mitchell said.Mitchell said the context he is gleaning is helping him better understand the world of Tubman, his great-great-grand aunt, and her father, Mitchell's great-great-great-grandfather, Ben Ross. He was drawn to Dorchester as a way to understand himself, because "this is where the story begins." More information on the Dorchester County Historical Society can be found online at https://www.dorchesterhistory.com/.

title: Local musician shares latest album, 'Impermanence'
author: ADRIAN COTTON Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Local musician shares latest album, 'Impermanence'

 September 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ADRIAN COTTON Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In mid-August, local singer/songwriter Ashton Mooday and her band, Gerry Werner, Jeremy Blouch and Connor Stoehr, held a concert at the Chestertown Volunteer Fire Company to celebrate the release of her newest album, "Impermanence."This is Mooday's fourth album, and many of her family and friends came out to support her achievement.
With gold and green lighting, balloons scattered throughout the room and refreshments, Mooday took listeners on a journey through the creative processes that made up her new musical creation.
The audience was captivated the entire night as Mooday and company treated the audience to a total of 24 songs which included all 15 tracks from the Impermanence album and nine bonus songs from some of her previous albums.
The album covers three stages of a relationship: the joy of being in love; the pain of breaking up; and the triumph of overcoming heartbreak.
Mooday and her band were a delight to watch because of their "realness." You could tell these people weren't just co-workers/bandmates but a family who enjoyed being around each other.
Two special guests joined Mooday's band, the audience told they traveled two and a half hours to be a part of the show — AJ "A-Juice" Mason who appeared on the song "My Person" and OfficialMacMan who appeared on the song, "Sike." Both could be seen bopping their heads, smiling with pride at their friend's performance.
When asked how she felt about the show, Mooday said, "The concert was phenomenal from my perspective. I couldn't have asked for a better band to back me up or a better crowd to share the experience with. I am lucky to have so much support with my family, friends and this community."
The audience felt lucky to hear her perform.
These past few months have kept her on her toes.
Currently, she runs her music school, Mooday's Music, LLC, located at 151 Dixon Drive Suite 4 in Chestertown.
She's also preparing for a mission's trip to Costa Rica with her fellow church members at Hope Fellowship.
Learn more about Mooday's Music LLC by visiting her website, moodaysmusicllc.org, and be sure to check out all of her work, which includes albums, singles and EPs that date all the way back to 2017 on Spotify.

title: Catalysts and Collaborations: Galleries partnering in Easton - Local ART
content:
Catalysts and Collaborations: Galleries partnering in Easton - Local ART

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 448
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Two art galleries are teaming up as Contemporary Art Galleries at 5 N. Harrison Street in Easton.Spiralis Gallery - which is owned by Gail Patterson and features contemporary Afro-Caribbean art - is partnering with The Zebra Gallery, which is owned by Susan Schauer John, an award-winning local fiber artist.The Spiralis Gallery launched its opening with some of its artwork being featured at Out of the Fire Restaurant in Easton in the summer with the show, "Things Fall Together."Susan John's fabric art was recently featured at the Smithsonian Craft Show in Washington, and at the Oxford Fine Arts Fair in Oxford, Maryland."When I met Susan there was an instant connection. I think we both were searching for a way to bring a fresh perspective to the already wonderful art scene here in Easton. We believe collectors are inspired and informed by having a variety of art to experience, and the sophisticated collector enjoys the challenge of watching emerging artists unfold," said Patterson."I think of a gallery as not just a place to sell art but a physical space where we engage in relevant conversations, build community, and celebrate creativity."John agrees."We hope to bring fresh, contemporary art that showcases the talents of remarkable contemporary artists from the area and around the world. We will highlight Afro-Caribbean artists as well as fiber artists, and modern art that are catalysts for experiences and new perspectives," she said.The collaboration will include social justice components and work with local charitable organizations.The gallery space will have a new show every 10 weeks to keep the content fresh for collectors, the owners said."Afro-Caribbean art has always resonated with me, with its vibrant colors, exquisite patterns, and strong spiritual imagery. And I am drawn inexorably to outsider artists, whose creations come directly from their souls," Patterson said.Patterson previously operated the Art Basel Miami gallery and the Outsider Art Fair. John's work has been featured in galleries in San Francisco and Washington D.C. and has works featured in the permanent art collection of the White House."Art is how I see the world, and what I see continues to evolve. This medium puts everything together," saidThe gallery will be open for the first show, "Woman, Phenomenally," on Oct. 28, with a reception from 4:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. and an artist talk at 5 p.m. featuring Ernesto Beckford, a collage artist. title: Wheatley Methodist Church celebrates 240 years, new renovations
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Wheatley Methodist Church celebrates 240 years, new renovations

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RHODESDALE — A mix of church members and residents packed the Wheatley Methodist Church Sept. 15 to celebrate the church's 240th anniversary and see the newly-renovated building."I haven't seen the church that full in forever," Pastor Barbara McShain-Keyser said about the event.
Along with tours of the space, a dedication service was held. The service included prayer, a presentation of the building and a consecration of the church. After the service, attendees went next door to the Community Hall for food and drink before gathering outside to listen to a gospel concert featuring the Jones Boys.
Member Suellen Wheatley Wilkins said she printed 125 church bulletins for the event, and they were all gone by the end of the service.
For Wilkins, a church renovation had been in the back of her mind for years.
"I always wanted to see a wood floor back in here and that ugly brown paneling off the walls," she said. "And I wanted the aluminum siding off to expose the (clapboard) siding on the exterior."
The church was built in 1784 on land that was granted by King George II to William Wheatley around 1750, according to Wilkins. Since the church was built, it has continuously served the community as a church.
In the 1970s, the floor fell through, and it was replaced with carpet covering plywood. Paneling was placed along the walls to cover damage to Victorian-pressed tin panels, and aluminum siding was installed on the exterior of the building.
During a 2019 project to restore part of the church, the building's underlying structure was looked at, and the church was condemned. Members chose to salvage the church, and a plan to restore and preserve it was made.
Now the aluminum siding on the exterior is gone and the carpet covering plywood has been replaced with reclaimed hardwood. Most of the tin on the interior is gone, and wide boards, painted white, that run along the walls have been exposed.
Wilkins, who is a descendent of William Wheatley, said the church has stayed around all these years because God intended it to. She said that when she sits in the church, memories come back to her.
"I can see my grandparents in here," she said. "I see all the old people that I thought were ancient when I was little."
McShain-Keyser said many churches have closed, but God keeps the Wheatley Methodist Church going. She said the dedicated members, who have made her feel "part of the family," also work very hard to keep things going.
"It's amazing because you don't see many churches like this," she said.
Wilkins said that around 2010, there would be somewhere between three and six people at the church for Sunday service. Over the years, the number of members has increased. Wilkins said the church now has 15 or 16 members. She said about 28 people come on Sunday mornings.
Beverly Wheatley, who has been coming to the church since she was about 5 years old, said the church looks different, but very nice.
"I think it's just nice that they repaired this church and didn't let it fall down," she said.
Annette Henry called the newly-renovated church "inviting."
"I had been in it before they started working on it," she said. "So it's very obvious that its improvements have been fantastic."
When talking about the success of the dedication event, Wilkins mentioned a grant the church was awarded from the Bartus Trew Providence Preservation Fund. She said requirements of the grant award include making the place available for people with like interests to visit and for education.
"That has been met 10 times over today," she said.

title: Kent County finds music that moves them at fair
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent County finds music that moves them at fair

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TOLCHESTER — Wednesday night, at the Kent County Fair, beneath the stars, local line dancing instructor Minnie Maloney guided folks on how to shift their weight, stepping to the beat to country, rock and hip-hop songs.After a sweltering afternoon judging chickens, canines and hogs, from 7 to 9 p.m., at the main pavilion, 4-H'ers let their hair down to line dance, something Maloney has been doing for over 20 years.
Everyone had something to dance to from music like "Barsong" by Shaboozey, "I was on a Boat" by Old Dominion, "Boots on the Ground" by 803Fresh, and "Jacked Up" by Colt Ford.
"It was an honor to bring some line dancing joy to the Kent County Fair," she said. "Even through the heat and sweat there were smiles and comments about how much fun it was."
At age 40, with fiery red hair and cowboy boots, she ain't stopping any time soon.
"I'm back dancing, it feels great," she said, recently recovering from plantar fasciitis, an inflammation along the bottom of the foot resulting in heel pain.
Yoga and proper stretching is getting her back to full strength, teaching Monterrey turns, (like 180 dance turns) rock steps and rock forwards.
Whether at the 4-H fair, teaching at the local VFW, or conducting classes in private parties, she loves seeing people having fun, memorizing the routines and producing all the positive results from line dancing.
For Maloney it is more than a hobby, it is a life choice that affects her on many levels and shares that joy she found early in life.
At age 12, she fondly remembers dancing with her father at the VFW in Fairlee learning her first line dance: "Baby Likes to Rock It" by the Tractors. The steps just made sense to her, clicking, connecting to her skill when dancing with her friends making up their own routines.
Past her teen years and 20s, dancing was not only fun but therapy for her. Maloney struggles with anxiety and depression, she acknowledges, and there is no better healing than scooting and scuttling past that.
"Dancing forces you to stay in the moment. You forget everything going on in your life."
While bartending for extra money at the American Legion in 2015, there was a push to draw more people. Maloney told them about her line dancing, and they gave her a shot instructing once a week, bringing joy to patrons.
Then she participated as a line dance instructor in the Wild Wild West fundraiser event for St. Martin's Ministry to help generate funds for those battling poverty.
Since then she has been teaching Mondays at the YMCA in Centreville under "Dancingontheshore," at the VFW, as well as private lessons, going off what she has seen from other instructors.
"It's a community builder. We're right beside you helping you. There is no race, age, no discrimination. We're here together."
She watches her students gain self esteem and confidence, relaxing and having fun.
"Some people come in having never danced in their life. They can be real self conscious at first, but I get them to lighten up."

title: Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON – Decoys have long been used in hunting communities, but to the crowd at the Waterfowl Festival, the wood carvings serve more than just a utilitarian purpose.According to Cooper Rossner, a Talbot County decoy carver, the imitation birds and mammals can also be used as historic art pieces for nature lovers.
As a teenager in south New Jersey, Rossner was mesmerized by a carving demonstration in a natural sciences high school class. Rossner said right before his eyes, a carver turned a piece of wood into a Canada Goose.
This demonstration would be the first step into his lifelong passion for carving decoys. The carver at his school would soon become his mentor, and the following weekend he met an additional mentor during a Ducks Unlimited event.
"I was probably 15 years old, and here I am turning 30 in a week, and I'm still obsessed with it, still carving every chance I get," Rossner said. "... carving is my world, and is my mind, and is my heart and soul. It puts everything that I love together: working with my hands, artwork, the history of it, the wildlife, the hunting aspect — it wraps it all up."
The hours of labor and craft artists like Rossner put into the carvings mean sometimes decoys come with a hefty price tag.
Jon Deeter, co-owner of Guyette and Deeter, a decoy auction firm, said his firm surpassed $200 million in total sales during 2020. In his experience, decoys at his firm would minimally be sold at $300. The most his firm had sold a single decoy for was $480,000.
According to Deeter, pricing on decoys depends on a variety of factors. Vintage decoys made between 1850-1950 tend to be more valuable than contemporary decoys made after 1962. Additionally, the history and ownership of a decoy also impacts its value, similar to how provenance affects the value of fine art.
Rarity and originality also play a large role in the pricing of a decoy. The decoys made by renowned carvers like the Ward Brothers from Crisfield, Maryland can fetch prices in the six-figure range. Limited production, unique design or age can often command premium prices at auction, with the record being $1.144 million for a pair of decoys.
Deeter emphasized that decoy collecting is an expensive hobby, but many collectors are not purchasing the high budget decoys and are there for the simple pleasure and admiration of skilly crafted decoys and the history behind them.
Tyler Bryan, an Eastern Shore collector and hunter, said he has around 75 decoys and enjoys the story and history associated with the decoys he purchases.
Bryan said he came to collecting naturally, influenced by his upbringing on the Eastern Shore and his fascination with nature. But one of the main reasons he continues to collect is the close community of decoy collectors.
"The decoy collecting community is really a fantastic group of people," Bryan said. "It's tight-knit. Everyone knows each other. Most people know what everyone collects, and they're very helpful."
Bryan recommends decoy newcomers seek out a mentor because there are facets to collecting that will be much easier to someone if they have a trusted mentor to guide them along the way. According to Bryan, plenty of people within the decoy collecting community are happy to take on a mentee.
Rossner said decoy collecting often gets associated with much older people and can be seen as a "dying craft," but in his eyes, it deserves more recognition for the layers of complexity it holds and the community that has welcomed him.
Rossner said he encourages anyone interested to spend time with other carvers and collectors and learn more about the shared love this community has for decoys.
"There's lots of people still doing it, but not as many as there once were," Rossner said. "So you are living history when you're carving a decoy or you're doing an art form … you're doing something that's been handed down generation by generation."

Mullaly learned a lot about running a Plein Air quick contest from her time at the Plein Air Easton.

For Mullaly the passion goes deeper than her creativity.
"I am deeply involved with the arboretum. I am a Maryland master naturalist and a trained docent there. I am there a lot and I just adore that place. I always feel so good when I am there. It is very healing and relaxing. Being able to paint there in that beautiful environment is such a treat," Mullaly said.
Beth Bathe was the judge and was generous with her time with all artists.
Bathe said, "Judging the works of over 50 artists this past Saturday at Adkins Aboretum was a true honor as each painting vividly showcased the rich colors and textures of the autumn season. There were collectors who have also attended the Plein Air Easton event. They came to see and purchase more great art.
The winners were Mullaly, second place winner Abby Ober and third place winner Maryellyn Lynott.
There were honorable mentions too. These included Lori Yates, Lynn Lewis, Ronaldo Dorado, Stephen Walker and Sheryl Southwick.
There was a tie for Artist's Choice — Nancy Fine and Toni Wolf.

title: Chancy title named state's 'One Book'
author: Staff Writer
content:
Chancy title named state's 'One Book'

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 431
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland Humanities recently announced it had selected the selection of Myriam J.A. Chancy's "What Storm, What Thunder" as its 2024 One Maryland One Book program.This marks the 17th year of Maryland Humanities' state-wide reading and discussion program.
The Haitian-Canadian-American author's novel follows a cast of characters during the 2010 earthquake that struck Haiti. They realize that everything they thought was certain suddenly isn't as they endure the chaos of a natural disaster.
Readers witness an NGO architect, a water-bottling executive, a drug trafficker, an immigrant cab driver, and others in scenes before, during and after during the earthquake.
"The novel takes its title in part from an epigraph by Frederick Douglass," Chancy said in a news release, "himself from the Baltimore area, writing in his essay, 'What to the Negro is the fourth of the July?' in 1852: 'For it is not light that is needed, but fire; it is not the gentle shower, but thunder. We need the storm, the whirlwind, and the earthquake.' Of course, Douglass was not calling for disaster, but for seismic change in America's social order in ways that I believe the reality of the earthquake called for in the Haitian context in more recent years."
"What Storm, What Thunder" made the shortlist for the Aspen Words Literary Prize and the long-list for the OCM Bocas Prize for Caribbean Literature. Chancy's 2010 novel "The Loneliness of Angels" also made the latter list.
Her next novel "Village Weavers" is scheduled to be released in April.
Maryland Humanities will announce details on the One Maryland One Book summer tour, a calendar of free events as well as an author tour will be released online within the next few months.
A selection committee of 18 Marylanders — including teachers, scholars, librarians, writers, booksellers, and community workers representing 10 counties and Baltimore — chose the novel.
A public call for books under the theme of "Restorative Futures" garnered nearly 250 titles, from which the committee made its selection.
"This year's One Maryland One Book theme feels important and timely," Maryland Humanities CEO Lindsey Baker said in the release. "I'm looking forward to seeing what resonates with Marylanders about 'What Storm, What Thunder' and the amazing programming I know our partners will come up with."
Through its Maryland Center for the Book program, Maryland Humanities created the One Maryland One Book program to bring together diverse people in communities across the state through the shared experience of reading the same book, and invites readers to participate in book-centered discussions and related programs at public libraries, high schools, colleges, museums, bookstores, and community and senior centers.
For more information, go to www.mdhumanities.org.

 EASTON — On Friday, The Waterfowl Building was full of pink art to be sold to raise money for The Clark Comprehensive Breast Center in Easton. Pretty in Pink, an awareness drive, and it is highlighting breast cancer awareness month, showcased over 60 framed pieces by Working Artists Forum artists.There were rows of paintings hung with bright lights. Many of the artists were breast cancer survivors. All of the artists wanted to give back.
There were pink tables set up with University of Maryland Shore Regional Health Clark Comprehensive Breast Center pamphlets. Half of this effort was to educate about breast cancer prevention for men and women. When men get breast cancer, it is usually worse because they don't check until it is too late.
Stacey Sass, chairwoman of Pretty in Pink, said, "The Clark Comprehensive Breast Center in Easton is doing amazing things for patients, men and women, who can't always afford everything. They do an incredible job with timely diagnosis."
She is a 27-year breast cancer survivor. She said that one in eight women will have a diagnosis in their lifetime.
"This is the first time Working Artist Forum has done a charity event. We are a group of about 120 artists who have been juried into this group. Everyone really stepped up. We had 48 members contribute work," Sass said.
A lot of the educational outreach was aimed at getting people to be checked early.
"Breast cancer is not something you should be a afraid of. There is help here. You can go to the Clark Center regardless of their status of insurance, of immigration, income and get diagnosed and learn about treatment options," Mary Ford said.
On her committee, Ford did all of the group's graphics and social media.
Mary Ellen Lynott said, "The younger generation tends to think, 'That is my mom's generation,' but the statistics is it is really hitting us younger."
Lori Yates was there with her work on display.
"That is the tricky part. Getting these women in for screenings," Yates said. "It is really miraculous where we are with breast cancer. There is so much that can be done. It can be caught like before it is really even cancer."
She recommended getting checked once a year.

title: 'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Showcasing a world of inspiration around us, Stevensville's newest gallery and art studio Abstract Truth held an official gallery opening Nov. 29.A retired architect, gallery artist Ray Moldenhauer, of Grasonville, focuses his attention on creating abstract paintings and sculptures with dimension, noting "art is a natural extension of architecture."
Outgrowing his previous space at My Little Studio, Moldenhauer remarked the new location is proving to be a blessing.
Leaning into layers in his art as well as in his gallery, Moldenhauer designed the space to take full advantage of the existing glass enclosed cubicles and provide natural light.
By staggering the paintings from one cubicle to another, the gallery visually takes on a special 3D experience from one space to another. Many of the paintings are mounted back to back on the glass to create an allusion of them floating in the space, according to Moldenhauer.
"At night, the extensive front glass wall of the building just glows and reflects the beautiful artwork within," he said.
"I love the idea of flowing paintings," he said.
Moldenhauer utilizes many different creative techniques for his work. From traditional brushes and sponges, to business cards to even finger painting, Moldenhauer isn't afraid to try something new with his inspiration. Moldenhauer also incorporates resin, cellophane, and even foam to create something completely new.
For Moldenhauer it is the inspiration behind each artwork that brings forth its beauty and meaning and makes it "more than just another landscape or sunset."
Moldenhauer's work typically starts with a Bible verse and lets his inspiration guide his hand, for instance, Moldenhauer sculptures based on the Pillars of Creation present an abstract look of the universe.
As an accomplished SCUBA diver, Moldenhauer also finds inspiration in the natural world of water, sunsets and sunrises.
Moldenhauer also takes inspiration from the surrounding Eastern Shore, has also incorporated his love of the Eastern Shore into his work.
His very first sculpture "Be Still" repurposed an old sailboat skeg and was selected for the Maryland Federation of Art's Off The Walls 2024 exhibition.
According to Moldenhauer Abstract Truths are works that, "in some way, reveal God," and each art piece has a corresponding Bible verse accompaniment for patrons to take to heart.
For artists just starting out, Moldenhauer encouraged finding inspiration around you in what you enjoy doing and where you enjoy being.
"There are so many sources of inspiration if we just look," he said.
Moldenhauer welcomes everyone to discover the work for themselves, noting the studio gallery isn't for the purpose of business or making money, "it's about sharing art," he said.
Moving forward, Moldenhauer looks to collaborate and connect with the surrounding art community and plans to eventually have rotating monthly artists featured and juried art exhibits.
Abstract Truths is located in the Stevensville Art and Entertainment District at 214 Island Plaza Court. and typically open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Special showings are available by appointment at 410-490-6302.
Moldenhauer is an award winning abstract artist and Maryland Federation of Art juried exhibitor. He is also a Christian author and music writer with a Youtube channel and Instagram account.

Christmas Cheer - Maryland Stories: Cabaret Carolers Warm Up The Winter With Song

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 During a busy month of performances for their talented, youthful group, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will continue their merry delivery of glad tidings throughout the area this weekend by hosting a pair of concerts at two Calvert County establishments.Comprised of nearly two dozen elementary and middle school students primarily from Calvert County with several from St. Mary's County added to the mix, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will perform on Saturday from 1 to 4 p.m. at Mrs.
Moo's in Prince Frederick then again on Sunday at the Bulrushes Cafe from 9 a.m. to noon.
"The carolers will perform three sets of six to eight songs at each location over those two days," said Southern Maryland Children's Theater public relations and social media manager Lara Reisman, who is slated to be the group's president for two years beginning next month. "Most of the group is from Calvert County, but we have a few from St.
Mary's County. They're a very talented, dedicated vocal group and they love to perform at area venues during the holidays."
In fact, the group's two performances this Saturday at Mrs. Moo's holiday open house and again the following morning at Bulrushes Cafe will put the finishing touches on a very busy month for the carolers.
Last Saturday, Dec. 9, the Cabaret Carolers performed for three hours at the Holidays Tree Lighting in Prince Frederick and several days earlier they performed at Asbury Solomons retirement community.
"The kids love to perform any time of year, but especially around the holidays," said Reisman, who has been associated with the group since its inception in 2001. "They enjoy rehearsing together and they can't wait to perform.
They usually do three sets of six to eight songs beginning at the top of each hour."
While most residents do not associate ice cream with the winter months and upcoming Christmas and New Year's Day holidays, Mrs. Moo's is going to sweeten the pot for the local group by unveiling an ice cream sundae named in their honor on Saturday.
Reisman admits that it is a fitting tribute to a youthful group that provides holiday cheer each winter.
Aly Cross, who has directed the group in "Newsies, Jr.," "A Christmas Story," "Beauty and the Beast" and "Once On This Island Jr." and will be directing "High School Musical" in the spring, also teaches all of the acting classes each semester.
In the spring, the acting classes will be held at the College of Southern Maryland's Prince Frederick campus.
"This group is very, very unique," Cross said.
"We have a great group of kids. There's no pressure on these kids to memorize things. It's a great chance for them all to sing Christmas carols together.
They're learning a little bit of choreography to go along with the songs.
When they performed at the Asbury Solomons they were overwhelmed by the response from the audience."

title: Country Cooking: Mom's recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Mom's recipes

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We are celebrating Mother's Day on Sunday, and this year I decided to gather favorite recipes from many moms around the countryside. I am constantly sharing my mom's cooking, and I appreciate the many wonderful comments I receive, but let's share your favorite mom recipes.As I made my calls, emails and text messages to my readers, it was amazing to find how alike our mom's recipes were.
Remember how moms dumped in, sprinkled, spread, eye measured and judged the size by holding the product? They held recipes by "memory instead of measurement."
Years ago, I asked my mom to write down some recipes and she replied, "I'll try."
When I speak of and recall Mother's Day, there are many definitions of a mom or mother. This person can be our birth mother, adopted mother, step mother, sister who replaced a mother, aunt, grandmother, close family friend who stepped in to help, father who served as both parents — it does not matter who they are.
But what does matter is they were, or still are, there to fill those shoes of a loving adult guiding your life forward.
My mom was a blessing, and her love and guidance will forever be treasured by all who knew her as Mom, Grandmother, Great Grandmother or Miss Laurie.
MRS. HOLLAND'S GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP
Mrs. Holland is now in her late 80s and remembers her mother making this soup any time of the year to help feed the family. They grew lima beans on the farm, and this soup fed many family members and farm hands cheaply.
In a large soup pot add 6 cups of water, 1 number 10 can whole tomatoes or 1 quart jar of home canned tomatoes, 1 piece of salt pork or ham, 3-4 cups green lima beans (fresh or frozen), 1 can yellow or white corn, 3-4 white potatoes (peeled and cubed), and 1 tbsp sugar. Cover and simmer until all ingredients are tender. During the first 30 minutes of cooking, taste soup for seasonings. Serve hot with fresh baked biscuits.
COLLINS FAMILY BISCUITS
My elementary school friend Fay makes some great homemade biscuits to go with the bean soup. Fay grew up in the country and had a large family also.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Cut one cup shortening or lard into 6 cups flour, 1 tbsp salt and 3 tbsps baking powder. Then add 2 cups of milk. Mix well and knead at least eight times. Form biscuits by rolling the desired amounts of dough with your hands and place them on a floured baking sheet. Bake for about 10-12 minutes. Serve warm.
PECAN PIE
My friend Joy's mom, the late Mrs. Eva Dixon of Greensboro, was well known by family and friends for her delicious pecan pie. This fresh baked pie appeared at all family functions.
Prepare or purchase an eight-inch pie shell, unbaked. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Beat 3 eggs until frothy and add 1 cup white or brown sugar, 1/2 cup light corn syrup, a dash of salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 1 cup chopped pecans. Mix well and pour into the pie shell. Place some halved pecans on top for decorative purposes. Bake for 10 minutes, then lower the temperature to 350 degrees and bake another 30 minutes. Cool before serving.
PEPPER RELISH
My niece, Jamie, often talks about her relative who makes pepper relish throughout the year and about how delicious it is. After convincing her to share this recipe for my special column today, let's make this relish.
Prepare 12 green sweet peppers and 12 sweet red peppers (remove the seeds and chop up fine). Clean and chop 12 onions, mix peppers and onions together and pour boiling water over this mixture and let it stand for 5 minutes. Drain well. In a small pot, add 3 cups vinegar, 1 tbsp salt, 2 cups sugar, 2 tbsps celery seed and 2 tbsps mustard seeds. Let stand for five minutes. Cook gently for 10 minutes. When mixture comes to boiling point, remove from heat and pack in pint jars. Makes 6 pints. Instead of hand chopping, you can use a blender to chop peppers and onions.
FRESH CATFISH
Let's go fishing together with Donna and her husband for some fresh catfish. Most weekends, weather permitting, this couple fish and share in the cleaning and cooking.
Combine 2/3 cup yellow cornmeal with 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 2 tsps salt and 1/2 tsp paprika. Dry the fresh fillets thoroughly and coat each side with cornmeal mixture. Fry in 1/2 cup vegetable oil for about 4 minutes on each side. Drain well on paper towels. This coating mixture can be used on any type of fish.
FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
These were submitted to me by three different ladies in honor of their mothers. So, since their recipes were almost identical, let's call this Rose, Marilyn and Edna's fried green tomatoes.
Use 3 large tomatoes (about 2 1/2 pounds), sliced crosswise about 1/3 inch thick. Arrange the tomatoes on paper towels and sprinkle with 1 tsp salt. Set aside for 30 minutes to draw out the moisture. In the meantime, make a dredging mixture consisting of 2 cups of yellow cornmeal and 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper. When tomatoes are ready to fry — place 1/4 cup solid vegetable oil in a fry pan. When the oil is hot, place a single layer of tomato slices in the pan and fry until golden on each side, turning once. Remove to paper towels for draining. serve immediately.
One note to be added — you can use green tomatoes, red tomatoes or pink tomatoes (partially green but not ripe yet). The green tomato may need a sprinkle of sugar on top at serving time.
SOUTHERN CORNBREAD
How about some Southern cornbread from a true Southern lady and mother — Ms. Bea? She's been living down in Tennessee for the past 15 years.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Sift together 1 cup white or yellow cornmeal with 1/2 tsp baking soda and 1/2 tsp salt. In another bowl, mix one beaten egg with 1 cup buttermilk and 1 tbsp melted shortening. Add wet and dry ingredients together, mix well and pour into a shallow greased pan. Bake for 18 minutes.
BISHOPVILLE BANANA PUDDING
Let's close with a few deserts for that special day, because one thing I know… Moms love desert.
This was always a favorite no matter what time of year in our house. Gather ⅓ cup all-purpose flour, a dash of salt, 2 ½ cups 1% low-fat milk, 1 (14-oz.) can fat-free sweetened condensed milk, 2 egg yolks (lightly beaten), 2 tsps vanilla extract, 3 cups sliced ripe bananas, 48 vanilla wafers, 4 egg whites and ¼ cup sugar. Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. Combine flour and salt in a medium saucepan. Gradually stir in 1% milk, sweetened condensed milk and yolks, and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes or until thickened. Remove from heat, stir in vanilla. Layer 3 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding and 3 vanilla wafers in each of 8 (1-cup) ramekins or ovenproof glass dishes. Top each with 6 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding, and 3 vanilla wafers. Beat egg whites at high speed with an electric mixer until foamy. Add sugar, 1 tbsp. at a time, beating until stiff peaks form and sugar dissolves (2 to 4 minutes). Spread about ½ cup meringue over each pudding. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes or until golden. Let cool for 30 minutes.
EASY PINEAPPLE UPSIDE DOWN CAKE
Gather 3 tbsps butter melted, 1/3 cup packed brown sugar, 9 canned unsweetened pineapple slices, 9 Maraschino cherry halves, 2/3 cup sugar, 2/3 cup fat-free milk and 3 tbsps canola oil. Pour butter into a nine-inch square baking pan; sprinkle with brown sugar. Arrange pineapple slices in a single layer in the pan; place cherry halves in the center of pineapple slices; set aside. In a large bowl, beat the sugar, milk, oil, egg and extracts until well blended. Combine the flour, baking powder and salt; gradually beat into sugar mixture until blended. Pour into the prepared pan. Bake at 350 degrees for 35-40 minutes or until a toothpick comes out clean. Immediately invert onto a serving plate. Serve warm.

title: A battle royal at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A battle royal at the library

 February 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 810
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I'm pretty sure I have William Shakespeare and Bernard Cornwell to thank for the fact the battle of Agincourt has long fascinated me, for it was after I read Cornwell's novel of the same title and saw Shakespeare's "Henry V" that I began to seriously ponder that battle's many imponderables. These are, in no particular order:In 1415, Henry V of England attacked France. His first goal, the seizure of the fortified town of Harfleur, took much longer than expected. By the time the city's garrison surrendered, Henry had lost a sizable number of his troops to disease, probably cholera.
Now, knowing that the king of France had sent a great host to drive the English from his realm, Henry's only hope—if he was to avoid the destruction of his army and his own capture and imprisonment—was to race all the way across northern France toward the safety of the English-held town of Calais.
But before he set off on this desperate march through miserable weather, he had to weaken his army even further by leaving enough men behind to defend Harfleur, the prize won at such great cost.
For a while the two armies played cat and mouse, but, eventually, near a village called Agincourt, the French managed to place their much larger force between the English and the road to Calais.
By this time the English force was on half-rations, so the soldiers that faced the French the next the morning (Oct. 25, 1415) were hungry, exhausted and riven by disease (it is believed that the dysentery was so bad among Henry's troops that some of them went into action that day sans culotte).
Looking at the odds—a well-fed, armor-clad French army of at least 15,000 men against an English force of, at best, 7,000, all of them half-starved and some half-naked—it's easy to see why everyone expected a great slaughter of Englishmen.
Yet the English not only carried the day, they killed so many Frenchmen that it took that country's nobility nearly a century to recover its numbers and sort out the property transfers necessitated by so great a mortality.
Authorities disagree on the precise numbers, but there is no doubt that thousands of Frenchmen died that day, while contemporaneous accounts claim only 30 English dead.
Thousands vs. 30. You would have thought Henry V had machine guns at his disposal, not bows and arrows.
And if such a lopsided English victory isn't enough to make you scratch your head in wonder, there's one final conundrum that never fails to intrigue me: despite numerous attempts to do so, no archaeological evidence of the battle has ever been found—no hastily dug graves, no broken sword hilts, no dented helmets, not even so much as a thrown horseshoe.
Despite the fact that, for centuries to come, the British would celebrate the victory and the French lament it, as far as professional archaeology is concerned, it never took place.
And so it was that, when I learned Michael Livingston, a professor at The Citadel, had written a new book about the battle, I immediately did two things: (1) I used the "Suggest a Title" option on the Talbot County Free Library's website to ask our acquisitions librarian to purchase a copy for Talbot's collection, and (2) using our inter-library loan system, I ordered a copy for myself from the Anne Arundel County Public Library.
I won't give away any of his conclusions, but I can tell you Livingston's exhaustive research has led him to propose a new site for the location of the battle (which, if he's correct, should solve the missing artifacts dilemma) and an English battle plan that helps explain Henry's improbable victory without making the French look like fools.
But Livingston's book does more than just solve the many mysteries surrounding Agincourt.
It ends up being an extended lesson in not just history but the making of history: how we study the past; how, in telling and retelling it, various biases inevitably slip into the narrative and how our view of the past is just as inevitably colored by our present, the intellectual paradigm that structures our study.
Perhaps just as interesting, and far more disturbing, the book—which spares none of the senses in describing close quarters combat between men wielding axes, hammers, halberds and flails—makes us wonder, yet again, how rational human beings can so willingly engage in war (it was the older men, the veterans who had already experienced such battles, who were the most eager that day to enter the fray).
Finally, Livingston's "Agincourt: Battle of the Scarred King" is a good story, well told. I brought the thing home from the library on a Friday and finished reading it before the fire on Sunday afternoon.
By the time this column is published, the Talbot County Free Library will own its own copy of Livingston's book. You should be able to find it on the New Books shelf at 944.0254 LIVI.

title: Portraits preserve Indigenous leaders' legacy
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespubcom
content:
Portraits preserve Indigenous leaders' legacy

 October 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespubcom | Section: News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — "Astonishing Portraits, Untold Stories: The World of Thomas L. McKenney" opened Oct. 4 at Wright's Chance, weaving together national and local history through portrait recreations of Native American leaders commissioned by 19th-century Marylander Thomas L. McKenney.At a time when policies of removal and displacement threatened Indigenous communities, Thomas Loraine McKenney (1785-1859) sought to preserve and immortalize the history of Indigenous leaders and their families through portraiture, Queen Anne's County Historical Society volunteer Barb Pivec said.
McKenney was born in 1785 in Somerset County to a Quaker family and attended Washington College in Chestertown.
In 1816 McKenney was appointed superintendent of Indian trade under the War Department by President James Madison, and in 1824, McKenney served as the first head of the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
McKenney traveled the country and published accounts of Indigenous nations, negotiations and the traditions.
"The councils and landscapes I witnessed revealed both the dignity of the Native nations and the urgency of their uncertain future," McKenney wrote in "Sketches of a Tour to the Lakes," recounting his 1826 journey to the Great Lakes.
In the early 19th century, Indigenous delegations traveled to Washington, D.C., to meet with government officials as sovereign nations and negotiate treaties to shape the future of land and people.
McKenney initiated the Indian Gallery to commission dignified portraits of visiting leaders as a "national project of preservation," between 1821 and 1830, Pivec said.
McKenney ensured each portrait was paired with a biography, recording personal histories, orations and family lineage.
Housed at the Smithsonian, nearly all of the original painted-from-life oil portraits of the Indian Gallery were lost in an 1865 fire.
Fortunately, Pivec said, McKenney's foresight in ensuring historic preservation continued with his insistence on lithograph reproductions published in the book "History of the Indian Tribes of North America (1836-1844)."
With these lithograph reproductions, dedicated contributing artists, historians and writers were able to recreate the portraits. Surviving against odds, the image copies on display at Wright's Chance stand as powerful reminders of resilience, diplomacy and cultural identity, Pivec said.
"Without him, we would not have these images. We would have none of this understanding of these people from this era if McKenney hadn't had the foresight to have portraits painted," she said.
Enhancing visitor immersion, the exhibit features the society's first guided audio tour, led by McKenney's "voice."
"The intent is to engage people with discussion," Pivec said.
The inspiration for the exhibit collection at Wright's Chance came about as Pivec became incredibly engaged reading "The McKenney-Hall Portrait Gallery of American Indians" by James D. Horan, and sought to share the important history, particularly with its local relevance.
McKenney's Eastern Shore roots also run deep, with family ties connected directly to Centreville and the Wright family of Wright's Chance, she said. The McKenney family were prominent business leaders in town, at one point owning close to 100 farms, she said.
A smaller exhibit also featured local heritage artifacts and materials discovered from around Queen Anne's County.
Weaving national history with local legacies, the Society aims to showcase how the work of one man connects the history of Native American policy in Washington with the heritage of Queen Anne's County.
"These genealogical links remind us that national history and local history are inseparable," Pivec said.
Artifacts and portraits were provided by the Queen Anne's Museum of Eastern Shore Life and the private collections of Stephen K. Wilson and James H. Barton III.
The exhibit was made possible through the Wright family of Queen Anne's County and an Inclusive History Grant from the Maryland 250 Commission.
The exhibit runs through mid-January.

title: Country Cooking: Canning day on the farm
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Canning day on the farm

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The fresh vegetables were picked, washed and ready to be processed for "canning day" on the farm.Canning day was decided by the ripeness of the vegetables. Let me tell you right now, canning involves a lot of work.
Outside in the storage building, there were baskets full of empty jars. The jars were made by Mason or Ball, and those jars, if handled correctly, could be used year after year.
Two washing tubs were set up outside, one with hot soapy water and the other with clear water for rinsing. The bushel baskets holding the canning jars from the previous year's canning day were carefully carried to the house and placed on the long counter tops in the old-fashioned country kitchen. On top of the kitchen stove would be two heavy duty kitchen pots filled with vegetables, and as soon as they were blanched, the veggies were placed in the canning jars, leaving about 1 inch space from the top. The jar lids were put on lightly and the jars placed in the canning pots — usually the big blue agate pots with inserts inside to hold the jars in place.
The canning pots started rolling on the fire, thus cooking the vegetables. Mom just seemed to know when it was time to turn off the heat, remove pots from the stove and wait for the heat to cool enough to remove the jars, tighten the lids and begin again. This scene lasted all day, or until the veggies were all used.
Let's do it the modern way.
CANNED PEACHES
4 lbs peaches, 1 1/2 cups granulated sugar, 8 cups water.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Fill a large bowl with ice water. Using a paring knife, cut a shallow "x" into the bottom of each peach. Add peaches to boiling water and let boil for 3 minutes. Remove peaches and place directly in a bowl of ice water. When peaches are cool enough to handle, peel peaches. Slice peaches and discard the pit. Divide peaches between four sterilized canning jars, being sure to leave about 1 inch of space from the top of the jar. Make simple syrup: In a medium pot over medium heat, add sugar and water and bring to a simmer. Stir until sugar is dissolved. Pour simple syrup over peaches, leaving about 1/4 inch of space from the top of the jar. Gently tap jars on the counter to settle peaches and syrup. Add more syrup as necessary to each jar. Tightly seal jars with lids. To seal, fill a large stock pot about halfway with water and bring to a boil over medium heat. Once water is close to a simmer, use tongs to carefully lower jars into hot water. Let water come to a gentle boil and boil for 25 minutes. Carefully remove jars from the stock pot and let sit at room temperature until completely cool. Press down on the lid of the jars to test if they are properly sealed. If the lid bounces back or pops the jar is not sealed. Repeat the sealing process or refrigerate and eat within a week. Once jars are properly sealed and cooled, store in a dry, dark space until ready to eat.
PICKLED BEETS
4-5 lbs small beets, 2 tsps pickling salt, 1 1/2 cups white sugar, 3 cups white vinegar, 2 tbsps mixed pickling spice tied in cheesecloth bag, 1 cup water.
Wash the beets and remove most of the tops, leaving about 1/2 inch of beet top remaining. In a large boiling pot of water, cook the beets until barely tender. Remove from the stove. Submerge the beets in a large bowl of ice water, I find this helps the skins come off with more ease. Cut off the tops and the roots completely, then remove the skin. Peel and slice beets into preferred size, I like larger chunks and not slices. Combine the vinegar, sugar, water, salt and pickling spice in a nonreactive pot and bring mixture to a boil; reduce the heat and simmer for 10 minutes. Add the beets to the pickling liquid and return to a boil. Remove the spice bag. Carefully ladle the beets and pickling liquid into hot sterilized pint jars, leaving 1/2 inch headspace. Remove any air bubbles with a non-metal utensil. Add additional pickling liquid, if needed, to keep the proper headspace. Wipe the jar rims thoroughly with a clean damp cloth. Seal the jars and process for 35 minutes in a boiling water bath.
PICKLE RELISH
2 1/2 lbs cucumbers (peeled, seeded and finely diced), 1 large yellow onion (finely diced), 1 small red bell pepper (finely diced), 1 small green bell pepper (finely diced), 3 cloves garlic (finely minced), ¼ cup kosher or pickling salt, 3 cups white vinegar, 1/2 cup sugar, 2 tsps dill seeds, 1 tbsp yellow mustard seeds, 2 tsps celery seeds, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 bay leaves.
Place the diced cucumbers, onion, bell pepper and garlic in a large mixing bowl. Combine with the salt and pour water over the mixture until covered. Let sit for at least six hours or overnight. Drain the cucumber mixture in a colander, rinse thoroughly with water, and drain again. In a large stock pot, add the sugar, vinegar, and spices and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer for five minutes. Add the drained cucumber mixture and return to a boil. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 10 minutes. Discard the bay leaves. Ladle the hot relish into hot sterile jars, leaving ¼ inch of headspace. Wipe the rims of the jars clean and seal tightly with the lids. Process the jars in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Sealed jars will store in a cool, dark place for a year. If the seal is broken, the relish will keep in the fridge for at least a month. Makes four pints (you can use pint-sized or half pint jars). Best eaten at least a week later after the flavors have had time to meld and the vinegar mellows out a bit.
STRAWBERRY JAM
5 cups crushed fresh strawberries, 4 16-oz containers, 7 cups granulated sugar, 1 packet original Sure-Jell Premium Fruit Pectin powder, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1/2 tsp butter.
Wash jars, lids and bands in hot soapy water, dry completely and set bands aside. Simmer lids in warm water in a saucepan until ready to place them on jars. Keep jars warm by simmering in hot water until ready to use. Do not boil. Fill a 20 quart stock pot or water bath canner with hot water, and place on the stove over medium-high heat. You'll need enough water to later cover your jars with at least 1 inch of water, crush strawberries in a large mixing bowl or shallow glass baking dish using hand masher until nice, smooth consistency. Small chunks are okay. Transfer crushed strawberries to 8-quart stock pot. Add pectin, lemon juice and butter to the pot, and stir constantly with a wooden spoon over high heat, while bringing to a rolling boil. Once boiling, add sugar, return to rolling boil, then boil for 1 minute while stirring constantly. After 1 minute, remove foam from top of jam by skimming it off with a metal spoon. One by one, remove a jar from hot water, transfer to a cookie sheet, place regular mouth canning funnel on jar, and ladle in strawberry jam mixture leaving 1/4 inch empty head space at top of the jar. Then wipe off the rim of the lid and threads of the jar with damp cloth. Continue until all jars have been filled. Remove warm lids from the saucepan and place one lid on each jar. Then screw one band on each jar just until snug but not overly tight. Place filled jars on a rack in a 20 quart stock pot or water bath canner, then lower down into hot water. Make sure there is enough water in the pot that there is at least 1 inch of water above the jars. Place the lid on your pot, and bring to a gentle boil. Once water is boiling, set your timer for processing and boil for 10 minutes, once jars have finished boiling, turn off heat, remove the lid from the pot and let jars sit for 5 minutes before removing. After 5 minutes, lift up the rack to an elevated resting position, then carefully remove jars one by one using a jar lifter, and transfer to a folded towel to cool. The lids on the jars will begin to 'pop' into the sealed position, signifying the jam has been preserved. Jars can be stored in your pantry, or a cool, dry cupboard for up to 1 year.

title: Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 857
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Over the years, Edinburgh University's Professor Celeste-Marie Bernier has taught me a great deal about Frederick Douglass, though her most important contribution to the study of the man may be, curiously, the research she has done not on Douglass but on Douglass' wife and children.Bernier's work has revealed just how important his family's support was to the Great Orator's success.
All of which has gotten me thinking about the other people that must have made the road Douglass trod a tad easier. Probably the most important of these would also be the least known: the people that helped him escape slavery.
We know that his wife Anna put the money together and sewed the clothing that would make her husband's flight possible, but we also know there would have been others, perhaps many others, involved as well: conductors on the Underground Railroad, people who took him in for the night along the way, and who knows, perhaps a boat owner or two, or even someone with a wagonload of hay.
We know that these people — however nameless now — existed because they are in Douglass' autobiography, though he alluded to them obscurely. Douglass always carefully avoided providing their names or any particulars that might aid those intent upon derailing their clandestine work. "The peculiar institution" was thriving when Douglass first penned his autobiography, and the last thing he wanted to do was reveal routes, methods and personnel still being used to funnel enslaved African Americans to freedom.
But there would have been others too, perhaps not as dramatic in their assistance, but important to Douglass's eventual success nonetheless.
Some of these are well known: Polly and Nathan Johnson, who sheltered Douglass and Anna in their home when the couple first arrived in New Bedford; William Lloyd Garrison, who brought Douglass to the attention of the abolitionist movement; and Abraham Lincoln, who befriended Douglass and wrote the pass that would allow him to travel unimpeded during the Civil War.
But what about the other people who must have made contributions, perhaps only small contributions, to Douglass's journey from property to prophet? We all depend upon people like this, the childhood friend who stuck up for us when we were bullied, the person who helped us with some difficult task, the passing stranger who gave us a smile when we were feeling down. Life is often obstructed, but then something gives, and, for a moment, there is an intoxicating sense of forward motion. How many now anonymous souls helped remove an obstacle from Douglass' path? Helped send him sailing toward us?
Perhaps more important still, how many would-be, could-be, Douglasses do we unknowingly lend a hand to today?
On Saturday, Sept. 27, the people of Talbot County will come together once again to honor the legacy of Frederick Douglass, their most famous native son. The parade this year will feature, among others, the Easton High School Junior ROTC Color Guard, the Easton Middle School and White Marsh Elementary School marching bands, Randy Welch on bagpipes, the Hispanic Dance Group, and, for the first time, engines from both the Easton and Oxford Volunteer Fire Companies.
At the Welcome Ceremony on the courthouse lawn, 15-year-old Javion Jones, a minister at Union Baptist Church, will give the opening invocation, county and city officials will offer their thoughts, Washington College fellow Darius Johnson will read a portion of a famous Douglass speech, the MidShore Community Band will play two pieces and Dana Bowser will sing a capella.
Afterward, at the Children's Village set up in front of the library, there will be story time with St. Michaels library branch manager Shauna Beulah, face-painting, the ever-popular portrait booth with Frederick Douglass, Frederick Douglass coloring books with sticker insert, a prize wheel with toy giveaways, and the opportunity for youngsters to sign up for the Frederick Douglass Reading Challenge (featuring six $50 Target gift certificates as prizes).
Within the library itself, the National Park Service will have an exhibit of Frederick Douglass artifacts on display, and, at 1 p.m., Nicholas Buccola — the Dr. Jules L. Whitehill Professor of Humanism and Ethics at Claremont-McKenna College — will lecture on his book, "The Essential Frederick Douglass," copies of which will be available for purchase and signing.
From noon to 3 p.m., the festival's entertainment stage will feature performances by the Bay Country Chorus, Sofia Fernandez, the New St. Johns Male Chorus, the St. Michaels Middle School Choir, Friends in Faith, Ruby Fisher, the Allegro Academy, Ayla Dennis and the Asbury United Methodist Church choir, as well as line dancing and block party music provided by Allan Butler.
Oh, and of course, once again, there will be food vendors on hand with delicious food to satisfy the most demanding hunger.
All in all, it's shaping up to be a fun day for people of all ages and interests. Moreover, it's a day where your attendance, your enthusiasm, could end up encouraging some youngster (think the BAAM kids who will be in attendance, or the recipient of one of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society's scholarships) to set his or her eyes on the prize.
Like so many before you, you could be clearing the path for America's next great freedom fighter.

title: Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints
author: Staff Writer
content:
Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 267
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new exhibit at the Academy Art Museum in Easton highlights sporting, waterfowl and bird prints from American artist Frank W. Benson.The prints are from AAM's collection and the exhibit runs through Dec. 8.
The exhibit is entitled "Sporting: Frank Benson's Waterfowl Prints."
Here are some details about the artist and his prints from AAM:
"Born and raised on the North Shore of Massachusetts, American artist Frank W. Benson (1862–1951), grew up sailing, fishing, hunting, and birdwatching. These interests persisted throughout his life, and he ultimately became one of the fore- most American practitioners of the genre of printmaking known as the sporting print.
In the early 20th century, Benson established a reputation as a painter of portraits and landscapes inspired by French Impressionism. He joined a group of Boston and New York painters known as "The Ten" who organized carefully curated annual exhibitions of paintings between 1898 and 1918. He was also interested in printmaking, particularly etching. Beginning in 1914, he returned to his early fascination with birds, ultimately creating more than 300 images of the many species of waterfowl native to the beaches and marshes of New England.
Sporting prints by Benson first entered the Academy's collection in 1987 when Berlin Voorhees included two of the artist's waterfowl etchings with a larger gift of late 19th and early 20th century works on paper. The collection grew to encompass more than 30 works by Benson, largely due to the generosity of the late Robert K. Keller, who began donating prints from his collection to the Museum in 2001 and continued with these gifts until his death in 2009."
For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/sporting-frank-bensons-waterfowl-prints/
