title: Welcome fresh spring vegetables
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Welcome fresh spring vegetables

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I recently moved some of the late fall frozen vegetables to the top rack in the freezer to be used before it is time to begin preserving, canning and freezing for the 2024-25 season. I usually make that mental list of what not to freeze or preserve too much of and what I need to increase the most.A lot depends on what is best and just how late it is to begin these procedures. Each year is different from the last because of availability, favorites and space to use for storage.
No matter the situation, let's enjoy some fresh early spring veggies and incorporate last year's leftover veggies.
CHICKEN & RICE WITH SPRING VEGETABLES
2 tsps extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tsps unsalted butter, 1 shallot (finely chopped), ½ cup finely diced red pepper, 1 tsp dry thyme, 1 pound boneless skinless chicken breast (cut into bite-sized cubes), 2 ½ cups reduced-sodium chicken broth or home-made chicken stock, 2 cups quick cooking brown rice, ½ tsp salt, 2 oz cream cheese, ½ bunch asparagus (trimmed and cut into small pieces), 1 cup shelled peas (or frozen and thawed), 1 cup snap peas (cut in half), ¼ cup shredded parmesan (plus more for serving), 2 tbsps chopped chives, 2 tesps chopped tarragon.
Heat oil and butter in a large skillet or straight-sided sauté pan over medium-high heat until the butter is melted but not browning. Add the shallot, red pepper and thyme and cook, stirring often until the vegetables start to soften, 1 to 3 minutes. Add chicken and cook, stirring occasionally until the chicken is no longer pink, 4 to 6 minutes. Add broth, brown rice and salt, and bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally. Cover, reduce heat to medium-low to maintain a simmer and cook until the rice has absorbed most of the broth, about 5 minutes. Remove lid and increase to high. Stir in cream cheese until melted. Add asparagus, peas and snap peas on top. Make sure the mixture comes back to a simmer, then cover, reduce heat to medium-low and let cook for 3 minutes. Remove from the heat, without removing the lid and let sit for 3 to 4 minutes or until the rice absorbs the liquid and fully softens. Before serving, stir the vegetables, ¼ cup parmesan, chives and tarragon (or chervil) into the rice to combine. Serve with additional Parmesan if needed for flavor.
ROASTED PARSNIPS
2 pounds parsnips, 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, 1 ½ tsp herbs of your choice, Italian seasoning, 1 tsp kosher salt, chopped parsley for extra flavor and garnish.
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Peel parsnips and cut into 1-inch chunks. Toss with oil, herbs and salt in a large bowl. Spread out on a large, rimmed baking sheet in a single layer. Roast, stirring once or twice, until the parsnips are tender in the center and browned in spots on the outside, 25 to 35 minutes. Transfer to a platter or plates and garnish with parsley.
GREEK ORZO SALAD
1 ½ cups dry orzo pasta (about 11 oz), 1/3 cup lemon juice, 1 clove garlic (finely minced), ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tbsp chopped fresh dill, 2 tbsp chopped fresh mint, 2 ½ tsp dried oregano, 1 ¼ tsp salt, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 pint cherry tomatoes (cut in half), 1 European or Mediterranean cucumber (peeled, seeded and diced), 1 cup crumbled feta cheese (preferably reduced fat), ½ cup pitted black Greek olives (roughly chopped), ½ cup minced red onion.
Bring a large pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Cook orzo according to package instructions. Drain through a fine mesh sieve and rinse with cold water. Drain thoroughly. Whisk lemon, garlic, olive oil, dill, mint, oregano, salt and pepper in a large bowl. Add the pasta and toss to coat. Add tomatoes, cucumber, feta, olives and red onion and toss to combine. Serve immediately or chill. You can make this a day ahead, but cut and add the cucumber and tomatoes just before serving for the best texture. You may need to add additional olive oil on the second day so taste it to see if it seems a little dry.
SPINACH QUICHE WITH ARTICHOKES AND ROASTED RED PEPPERS
Nine-inch baked pastry shell, 6 oz ricotta cheese, 1/2 cup cottage cheese, 5 green onions (chopped, include green tops), 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp dried basil, 1/2 tsp pepper, 1/4 tsp garlic salt, 5 eggs, 1/2 cup light cream, 2 cups baby spinach, 1/4 cup artichoke hearts (chopped, pat dry with paper towel), 1/4 cup roasted red peppers (chopped, pat dry with paper towel).
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. In a food processor, blend the ricotta cheese, cottage cheese, chopped green onions, olive oil, dried basil, pepper and garlic salt together until smooth. Add eggs and light cream; blend again until smooth. Layer your spinach at the bottom of the pastry shell, then add chopped artichoke hearts and roasted red peppers on top. Hold aside a little bit of roasted red peppers if you'd like to add a bit of color to the top. Pour egg mixture over the top of the vegetables. Bake for 35-40 minutes or until the toothpick inserts into the center cleanly. Let quiche sit for 10 minutes before cutting.
EASY ROASTED ARTICHOKES
3 large artichokes, 2 lemons, 2 tbsp olive oil (sub with butter), 6 cloves garlic (halved or quartered depending on size), 1 large sprig fresh thyme (broken into smaller pieces, sub with your favorite herbs), salt and pepper to taste.
Trim about 1/4 inch off the bottom and peel the tough outer peel with a vegetable peeler. Cut off the top 1/3 of the artichoke. Snip off the thorny tips off each petal. Cut in half and remove the fuzzy top of the artichokes. Rub cut sides with fresh lemon juice to reduce browning from oxidation. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Place the artichoke halves cut side up in a 13-by-9-inch baking dish or rimmed baking sheet. Coat each side with oil, season with salt and pepper to taste, and fill each cavity with the garlic and thyme. Cut the remaining lemon in half, then cut one half into small slices. Place one small lemon slice on top of the garlic and herbs in the artichoke and turn upside down (the lemon slice will help hold the garlic and herbs in the middle). Brush the artichoke leaves with the remaining oil in between the leaves and season with salt and pepper. Cover the artichokes with foil and roast for 30-40 minutes or until the artichokes are very tender. Remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly. Flip the artichokes and remove the garlic and herbs. From there, you can smash the garlic and add it to mayo for garlic aioli if desired. Serve with additional lemon if desired. Enjoy.
ANGEL FOOD CUPCAKES WITH WHIPPED CREAM AND BERRIES
1 1/2 cups sugar, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 cup cake flour (sifted), 12 egg whites (the closer to room temperature the better), 1/3 cup warm water, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 1 1/2 tsp cream of tartar, whipped cream, strawberries and raspberries (any sort of berry you want, those two are just the ones I prefer).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. If you have regular sugar: Blend the sugar for about 2 minutes until it is superfine. Sift half of the sugar with the salt and the cake flour in a medium bowl and set the remaining sugar aside. In a large bowl, use a whisk to thoroughly combine egg whites, water, vanilla extract and cream of tartar for two minutes. Then, using a hand blender, slowly sift the reserved sugar into the eggs, beating continuously at medium speed to achieve medium peaks, Once the eggs are whipped to medium peaks, sift the flour over the mixture, 1/4 a cup at a time. Repeat until all of the flour mixture is finished. Carefully spoon mixture into a lined cupcake tray and fill 3/4 of the way up. Bake until the tops of the cupcakes are turning slightly golden, and you can insert a toothpick between the liner and the cake and have it come out clean. Cool completely & top with whipped cream and berries.

title: 'Bringing life to a variety of women's experiences' - Denton's famed author Sophie Kerr celebrated with events Nov. 4
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'Bringing life to a variety of women's experiences' - Denton's famed author Sophie Kerr celebrated with events Nov. 4

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 659
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Interest in the talent and work of Denton native and prolific author Sophie Kerr attracted dozens of new fans and existing aficionados to two events Saturday, Nov. 4, just down the river from her beloved hometown.Kerr, who grew up in the Sophie Kerr House in Denton in the late 19th century and became a popular author in the early 20th century, was celebrated with both matinee and evening "literary visits" at the old Caroline Country Club on Pealiquor Road.Headlining the celebration of her work and colorful personality was Washington College alumna Brooke Schultz, who researched Kerr's life and created a presentation that included photographs, pages of handwritten story drafts, letters and newspaper articles.Schultz, a reporter for the Associated Press and a former reporter of APG Chesapeake's Newark Post, did extensive research on Kerr, who wrote 23 novels, over 500 short stories, several plays and articles during her career as managing editor of The Woman's Home Companion, a leading periodical during the first half of the 20th century.The event was organized by Caroline County Council for Arts and the Caroline County Public Library.The 3-hour program included a local readers theatre group sharing dialogue from about a dozen excerpts, cocktails and a luncheon catered by the Chesapeake Culinary Arts Center, displays of novels and magazines featuring her stories, several raffles, and a performance by Wayne Martin and members the North Caroline High School Band.Master of ceremonies was CCCA board member and local playwright Keith Shaffer."It is so much fun to put this together and get a chance to read a lot of stuff by Sophie Kerr that I had not had a chance to read otherwise," he said."I love 'The Blue Envelope' and a couple of the other books she wrote. They're a whole lot of fun," Shaffer said. "I think she got a bad rap from the critics after she passed." "The Blue Envelope" was also the first Kerr novel Schultz read.She told the audience the New York Times called Kerr's works "light amusing fiction" and the Kirkus Reviews deemed it "easy, flimsy feminine fare." However, because of her half-million dollar endowment, and being something of a "myth on the Washington College campus," Schultz was drawn to research Kerr.Born in 1880, Kerr earned degrees from Hood College and the University of Vermont, and pursued a journalism career. She later wrote fiction for the leading magazines of the day, often with biting humor and critiques of the mores of her day.Many of Kerr's settings were based on the Eastern Shore, including a thinly disguised Denton, as well as Long Island and New York City.Schultz quoted Kerr's own words about her writing style. "She says, 'I have no propaganda spirit; the story's the thing. Time and time have indignant readers berated me for beliefs expressed in the speeches of my characters - beliefs which were at wide variance of my own, but perfectly in keeping with the character who expressed them.'" "She was taking controversial figures that people were seeing and she was humanizing them through entertaining fiction," Schultz said."So while she can contend that she had no propaganda spirit, she was ultimately bringing to life a variety of women's experiences to huge blocks of readers." Kerr's bequest to Washington College in 1965 established the Sophie Kerr Prize, the nation's largest undergraduate writing prize, awarded to a graduating senior who shows promise in literary endeavors. Kerr is buried alongside her parents in Denton Cemetery."One of the things that amazed me from the get-go is how many people - natives to this area - drive by the Sophie Kerr House day after day after day and have no idea all the stuff she did," Shaffer said.

title: Maryland professor edits 'Good Eats' book
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Maryland professor edits 'Good Eats' book

 March 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 412
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While she is rapidly approaching her 25th year as a professor of English at the St. Mary's College of Maryland — where her students range from freshmen in her introduction to creative writing course to those in the more advanced creative writing courses — Jennifer Cognard-Black recently co-edited the book "Good Eats" that includes the work of 32 writers, including one of her former students.Cognard-Black, who was born and raised in Fort Worth, Texas, graduated college from Nebraska-Wesleyan then earned her masters degree at Iowa State and her doctorate from Ohio State University before she began teaching at St. Mary's College in 2000.
Along the way, Cognard-Black has written several books, including "Narrative in the Professional Age" (Routledge, 2004), "Kindred Hands" (Iowa University Press, 2006) and most recently "From Curlers to Chainsaws: Women and Their Machines" (Michigan State, 2016).
Earlier this year she co-edited, along with Melissa A. Goldthwaite, the book "Good Eats: 32 Writers on Eating Ethically" (New York University Press, 2024) which included a work from one of her former students, Will Becker, a 2020 St. Mary's College alumnus.
"Working with the University press companies, the process is a little slower than working with a national publisher," Cognard-Black said. "The process started in 2021 and then we finished the book in January. But it's a very interesting collection of works by award-winning writers, chefs, farmers, activists and educators who invite readers to inquire about what we eat and why we eat."
Cognard-Black, a two-time Fulbright Scholar and recipient of the Robert Poster Cherry Award for Great Teaching, bestowed upon her in 2020, has also produced two lecture series and is the process on working on another series for Audible.com, following her first venture in 2021 called "Books That Cook: Food & Fiction." A definite timeline for the next one in the series has not been solidified.
"One advice that I give all of my students is that you have to have a thick skin," Cognard-Black said. "It's a very tough market and not many people get paid for their work. You have to understand that rejections are part of the process. Not everything a writer submits is going to get published, so you occasionally have to expect some works to be rejected."
Cognard-Black's specialties include women novelists, Victorian adaptations, fiction writing and the literature of food. She has also published works under a pen name, J. Annie McLeod, and she has also been the recipient of Maryland State Arts Council and Mid-Atlantic Arts Council grants.

title: Storytelling in collage - Artist exploring her Eastern Shore Roots and the history of Caroline County during residency
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Storytelling in collage - Artist exploring her Eastern Shore Roots and the history of Caroline County during residency

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 758
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Yolanda Vanise Acree's medium to explore issues of identity, Afro-Christianity and family lineage is collage.Give her some scissors and a stack of magazines, and she explores what it means to have grown up Black in Caroline County.Acree is the new artist in residence at Caroline County Arts Council, and for her, art is an expression of history, both personal and of her community.Caroline County, located at the northern tip of the Confederacy during the Civil War, has a deep history of slavery, the underground railroad and the abolition movement."We are the northern South. We are the tippy top," Acree said. "The Eastern Shore tried to secede from Maryland a few times to become part of the Confederacy.To become its own state. I have a piece of my grandmother and her two friends standing in front of Mount Zion Church in Marydel. A lot of our family is buried there in the cemetery across the street. That is where the Mason Dixon Line is."Acree has studied some art, but her major at the University of Delaware was anthropology and Latin American studies."The African diaspora was my focus with my anthropology studies," she said. "I studied African Americans and Africans in other countries and how slavery impacted them.""How they combined their African culture remnants with the Catholic religion (in Central and South America), they used Catholic saints to disguise their African deities," she said. "Syncretism. That didn't happen as much here because the Protestants don't revere the saints the way Catholics do."The mixture of African and Protestant religions in the United States produced a different belief system, she said."Even though they didn't have any saints to disguise their deities, here in the US, they did develop their own religion called Hoodoo," Acree said. "The development of Black Christianity started with Hoodoo. It is a way for me to acknowledge and honor my ancestors.A central tenet of Hoodoo is you are because of your ancestors. Everything they are is carried on within you."As in traditional Christianity, not every soul who has gone before is considered an ancestor in Hoodoo. Acree said ancestors had to have lived a life worthy of being acknowledged."Living a right life is about living in community, supporting your community. Mutual aid, mutual support. It is also about being in the right relationship with the Earth," she said. "You can ask permission of herbs to help heal you and keep you alive and keep you alive and give messages and protect you."This history is central to Acree's collage, and she highlights many of stories of those who lived this history in her work.But she includes her personal history as well, learning to incorporate a mental health struggle into her work.After she gave birth, Acree developed generalized anxiety."I want to explore that during my residency," she said. "Not just the anxiety, but my transformation over the past few years going through the pandemic and becoming pregnant. After my experience at the hospital, I started experiencing panic attacks. I had never had that before, so I thought I was having a heart attack. I feel like this is going to be some art therapy, this process."Acree considers herself, like a novelist or a filmmaker, to be a storyteller."I am telling stories like the flight to freedom and also telling my own personal family history within these art pieces," she said. "I am highlighting narratives that aren't always prominent. Aren't always told."Among the works she plans to create during her residency, she highlighted several."One area I want to work on is my transformation and rebirth over the past several years," she said."I am working on a piece called, 'Flights of Freedom.' So I am imagining, interpreting escapes from Caroline County on the Underground Railroad," she said. " Another series is going to be scenes and dreams.It is all just paper and glue for now."Her residency lasts from Nov. 15 to Jan. 31, and her show will be in February. She plans to have at least 30 pieces created.Acree will be teaching a class at The Foundry on Jan. 12 and 26 on abstract landscape collage.

title: Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene
author: Staff Writer

Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life

 STILL POND — Just off Route 292, on a chilly Friday night, the star that church lay minister Justin Bitter created using welded scrap metal and an LED rope light, burned brightly in the trees. The Christmas hymns that were sung resonated with the 85 in attendance for the nativity scene beside the road.At the creche, maintained year-round by hardworking volunteers, local children dressed in robes and sandals. Telling the story of Jesus, Joseph, Mary, the wisemen, shepherds and animals, was Eddie Taylor, board member of Still Pond-Betterton Methodist Charge.
The reading of the gospel story followed by classic hymns with audience participation is a beloved tradition, now in the 10th year.
As night fell, seated atop bales of straw, attendees endured the cold sipping hot cocoa, enjoying Christmas cookies, and singing along as Taylor narrated the gospel scenes.
The story was told with Taylor's wit and affection, followed up by a hymn introducing the kid actors and actresses.
As Taylor read, "He is Christ the Lord. And, this is how you will know who he is….you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger," congregants sang the first verse of "Angels We Have Heard on High"; the angels of Still Pond were introduced, making their way to the manger.
During the production, Noel the donkey, Rosie and Annie the sheep, and Cookie Dough and Lollipop the goats were provided by Party Animals LLC., from Sudlersville, a company the church has relied on regularly during this event.
Owner of the company, Ashley Winterstein regretted she could not personally be there this year as this is her favorite holiday event. She was on a float with their 4-H club at Sudlersville's first annual Christmas Parade and Tree Lighting.
"Taylor is my favorite narrator," Winterstein added.
Pastor Greg Boege, replacing the late and greatly missed Pastor Bill Carroll, was pleased with how the event came together.
"Everybody did their part and we pulled it off," he said.
Boege said for those interested in a similar service, without the animals, in a more meditative, reflective atmosphere, they will hold their Christmas Eve service in Betterton at 5:30 p.m. followed by a service at the Still Pond location at 6:30 p.m.

title: Civil Rights Photographs come to Academy Art Museum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Civil Rights Photographs come to Academy Art Museum

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Arts 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There is a new photography exhibit about the Civil Rights era hanging at the Academy Art Museum, and to walk through it is to see decades unfold.It is called "A Fire That No Water Could Put Out" and comes from the High Museum of Art in Atlanta. It will be in Easton until March 10.
According to Sarah Jesse, the executive director of the Academy Art Museum, the show was hung chronologically on purpose.
"It makes it like a visual depiction of a history book that stirs your emotions more than just reading a book," she said. "It starts in the late 1950s — so pre Civil Rights movement — to the sanitation worker strikes where Martin Luther King was called in to help resolve the issue. That was his last public speech before he was assassinated. Then it is post Martin Luther King's funeral and what happened in the aftermath all the way to contemporary artists' responses."
These mostly black-and-white images were curated to thread the needle from the freedom riders on their buses to present day protests for Freddy Gray and the Black Lives Matter movement.
The visual iconography of protest used by the photographers was filled with newly integrated schools, white people taunting Black customers at lunch counters and firehoses trying to dissuade crowds from gaining ground.
Gordon Parks, who started as a photojournalist and moved on to direct movies including "Shaft," captured one of the few color images in the show. It depicts a Black family confronted with two seperate water fountains, one marked for use only by white people. It is called "At Segregated Drinking Fountain, Mobile, Alabama" and was taken in 1956.
One of the show's iconic images is "Daddy, I Want To Be Free Too," captured by Ernest Withers in 1961. This silver gelatin print shows a dad pushing his stroller with his daughter past a car of white police officers. Atop the stroller is the message "Daddy, I want to be free too" on a placard.
There are other photographic luminaries like Roy DeCarva, Bruce Davidson, and Danny Lyon, who all have striking images, featured in the exhibit. But when the exhibit leaves the past, it confronts the viewer with a continuation of the Civil Rights movement and Black Americans' struggle for equality into the current time.
One current artist, Dawoud Bey, came up with a time traveling portrait device. He takes a photo of a 10-year-old girl and another of a 70-year-old woman and makes a diptych.
In 60 years, how much has this time traveler seen? How much potential exists in the younger person living under oppression? What if there was no oppression and people could just grow gracefully old?
Jesse had a historically-grounded interpretation of the Bey diptychs that interpret four school girls killed in a Birmingham church for a modern viewer.
"The child is the age that the children, the four girls, were when they were murdered. And the adult is how old they would have been 55 years later," she said. "Loss of innocence and loss of life, loss of potential."
In the introduction to the show it said, "Following his death in Memphis, Dr. King's enormous funeral procession through Atlanta took over the city's streets with thousands of heartbroken Americans who gathered to celebrate his life and legacy. While his assassination is often described as the closing bookend on the Civil Rights movement, activism across the intervening years has proven that the movement for racial equality and justice in the United States is ongoing."

 1077
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Author Christine Trent recently published her book "St. Clements Bluff - Heart of St. Mary's" through her self-publishing company Twopence Press, LLC.The California resident has lived in St. Mary's for about 35 years and has worked at Naval Air Station Patuxent River and Webster Field.She also recently learned to pick crabs and admitted that she has "no idea what took me so long." "St. Clements Bluff" is her 13th book and the first in a new series set in St. Mary's County.The book is available at Amazon, Barnes & Noble, and other online sellers, as well as locally at Marie & Nash, Fenwick Street Books, Cecil's Country Store and the Patuxent River Naval Air Museum.For more information, go to www.ChristineTrent.com.How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?I've been writing since 2003. It really just started as a hobby. I loved reading - particularly historical fiction - and after reading a particular novel that I loved, it seemed like it would be fun to write my own story. Those early attempts are long dead and buried, thank goodness.As this new "hobby" seemed to be taking root in me, I realized I probably needed some more formal training [so] I began attending writer conferences and workshops, honing my skills and learning about the publishing world. A couple of years later, I was totally hooked on everything about writing.Do you consider writing to be a career?Yes. I have written both as a fulltime pursuit and also while managing a full-time outside job. Writing full-time is infinitely better.What kind of writing process do you use?1. Be struck by an unusual time period, person, location, or historical event that I'd like to tell.2. Research, research, research.Hands-on research if I can manage it. 3. Plot, plot, plot. In the writing world, authors refer to themselves as either "plotters" or "pantsers," meaning they write by the seat of their pants. I tend to be a heavy plotter. I've written at least a five-page synopsis of the book and I know exactly where my story is going before I write my opening lines. Then it's just a matter of sweating precious droplets of blood until I write "The End." How did you publish your book?I was traditionally published for many years, but in 2015, I started my own imprint, Twopence Press, LLC, for any self-published books, thus I am now what is considered a hybrid author, with books published both ways. Self-publishing also gives you a lot of freedom and control over the process.I think I will probably always be a hybrid-published author.Who are some of your favorite authors and why?Some favorites include Margaret George, Edward Rutherfurd, and Marie Benedict. This question reminds me of the backstory as to why I began writing as a hobby.I was visiting friends in Fredericksburg, Va. in 2003, and we went to a used bookstore. In the shop was a sad, tattered cardboard box of books for $1 each. A dust jacket caught my eye, as it was a stylized drawing of the French palace of Versailles and I had recently been reading about Marie Antoinette.Well, this sweeping historical romance, by an older British author named Rosalind Laker, moved me to tears. I sought out other books she had written and loved them all.Then one day I decided to try and contact her. I wrote to her agent in England, who passed my letter on [and] lo and behold, wrote back to me! This started a sweet friendship that lasted until her death in 2014.She always encouraged me to write when I told her of an idea knocking around in my head. I remember her telling me that I was sure to get published one day. I probably owe my writing career to that dear lady.What are you working on now?A follow-up to "St. Clements Bluff." It's loosely based on an unusual local farm and will be less serious.Please include a brief description of your book.Raleigh Bishop's perfect life in rural St. Mary's County, Maryland, has just come to a shattering end. Her naval test pilot husband, Grant, has been killed in a flight accident, and Raleigh is left to pick up the brittle shards of that life. She prefers to stay hidden away in her grief but is unwillingly dragged out of it by the contents of her husband's will, which contain a shocking bequest.Grant has left her St. Clements Bluff, an old Bishop family home with a noble background as a stop on the Underground Railroad. But serving as a safe house for escaping slaves in the 19th century is just the beginning of what Raleigh learns is a dark and winding history.It is a history that someone is willing to keep secret at any cost.Please include an excerpt from the book.Kip Hewitt shut off the single outboard engine of his small trawler as he consulted with his electronic fish finder to determine whether there were any swimmers below him. He didn't typically wander into St. Clements Bay since there was no commercial fishing permitted there, but today he was out just for himself."Nothing," he muttered to himself as he floated in the still waters of the bay. The frigid air didn't bother him after so many years as a waterman. In fact, Kip enjoyed having many parts of the area's rivers and bays to himself during the winter.Kip was about to switch the engine back on to trawl another part of the bay when his attention was caught by activity a couple of hundred feet away along the shoreline.Was that a woman wading into the water? Hard to tell at this distance but it sure did seem like a female form. "Damn," he said softly. While Kip didn't mind cold air, he sure as hell wasn't about to dive into this icy body of water.He tossed the fish finder into the boat's lock box, his attention now fully riveted on whatever it was the woman was doing. She would move forward a little, then stand there as if getting used to the cold, then step forward a little more.What was her purpose in this? Was the woman seriously planning to take a swim? In a winter coat?Trent will sign copies of her book on the following dates:· Sept. 21-24 at the St. Mary's County Fair· Sep 27-Oct. 1 at the Calvert County Fair· Oct 7 at Calvert Marine Museum's Patuxent River Appreciation Day· Oct 21-22 at the St. Mary's County Oyster Festival· Nov 18 at the St. Francis Xavier Church Bazaar, 21725 Newtowne Neck Road in Leonardtown· Nov. 25 at Fenwick Street Books, 41665 Fenwick St. in Leonardtown

title: A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GLEN ECHO — In 1974, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, then a Princeton student, wrote a letter of complaint to her university to call attention to the low Latino student numbers, the absence of Latino administrators and faculty members, and the lack of any courses dealing with Latino culture.That letter pushed the increase in Latino enrollment in Princeton University and was a critical moment in Sotomayor's life. This event is featured in the musical "She Persisted," a show centered on history's most famous women and how modern girls can take inspiration from their stories.
The musical is showing at Adventure Theatre in Glen Echo, Maryland. Victoria Gomez, a Talbot County resident, plays Sotomayor in the show.
Inspired by her character, Gomez decided to take a lesson from Sotomayor and wrote a letter to the justice.
"I admire your work and perseverance you have that led you to becoming the first Latina on the Supreme Court," Gomez wrote in her letter. "You are a role model for many people but especially for aspiring Latinas who dream big, like myself."
In the letter, Gomez shared her story of coming to the United States with her mother as a child. She wrote how honored she was to play Sotomayor in the musical.
Because of that letter, Sotomayor and her family sat in the front row of the Adventure Theatre Sunday.
Gomez said she is honored to be casted in this empowering musical. For Gomez, her passion for the theater began when she was a student at St. Michaels Elementary School when her class went on a field trip to see a musical.
For Gomez, the theater has opened a new world to explore and grow in. She has learned to advocate for herself and has developed a strong sense of her identity.
While on stage, Gomez jumped and sang with immense enthusiasm as she played a curious young Sotomayor in the Bronx with dreams of being a detective. Then later, as she played a college-aged Sotomayor, she comprised the emotional uncertainty of a young woman who sought to make change for her community.
Gomez said while studying for this role, she learned Sotomayor's strong connection to the women in her family. Like Sotomayor, Gomez was encouraged by her mother and grandmother, who taught her to be "proudly Latina" and to help those in her community.
"(Sotomayor's) mom was always someone who helped everyone in the community, which is something that I immediately related to in terms of my mom," Gomez said. "...She's already helping everyone, but even outside of that, she is such a wonderful role model for me to have. And I just really connected with (Sotomayor) in the way that she saw her mom as such an impactful role model."
"She Persisted," based on the children's book by Chelsea Clinton, follows the journey of Naomi, a fourth-grade girl struggling with perfectionism.
Play director Mary Hall Surface, said her hope for the play was to celebrate not only the historical figures and their stories but to really highlight the central character and her struggles.
"I think that is a pervasive feeling of young women and young boys as well, and not to mention grown women, all of us really, as we struggle to sort of measure ourselves against other people and find our own strengths and power and purpose," Hall Surface said.
After the final song of the play, Gomez's mother and Sotomayor, rose to their feet and gave her a standing ovation.

title: Historic Christ Church bell to be restored
author: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat
content:
Historic Christ Church bell to be restored

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The Historic Christ Church Bell Tower in Stevensville will be restored with proceeds from the May 3 Maryland House and Garden Tour of Queen Anne's County.On July 7, board members from the Queen Anne's County Historical Society presented a check for $9,010 to Nancy Cook of Friends of Historic Christ Church.
Cook gave a talk on the 1631 founding of Kent Fort on Kent Island, the third-oldest permanent English settlement established by William Claiborne.
He and settlers built the first Christ Church on the south tip of Kent Island. In 1680, a new town and Christ Church were moved to the new town of Broad Creek, where Bay City is now. Then, in 1880, Christ Church was moved to the new town of Stevensville.
The new Christ Church was built in 1880 in Queen Anne style. The bell tower is in the "lancet" chimney style. Wooden pegs and bricks were reused from the earlier Christ Churches. Historic Christ Church recently was designated as the Arts & Cultural Center of Historic Stevensville.
Mike Thomas has researched the church bell. The bell was made in 1880 by the McShane Bell Foundry of Baltimore, America's oldest bell company, established in 1856. The bell is bronze, rings in C sharp, and weighs 400 pounds including the mountings. In 1880, the bell was shipped to the Rev. Thompson, Christ Church, Stevensville. Church bells are rung for religious and ceremonial purposes such as Christmas and for significant events such as weddings.
Donations also are needed for Christ Church upkeep. Checks may be sent to: Nancy M. Cook, 124 Bryce Road, Queenstown, MD 21658. Historic Christ Church is nonprofit organization registered with the state of Maryland. Donations are tax-deductible to the fullest extent of the law.

title: A fisherman's nod to Noah: An ark makes it mark in Chesapeake Bay's history
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
A fisherman's nod to Noah: An ark makes it mark in Chesapeake Bay's history

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 994
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the tiny Chesapeake Bay town of Betterton, an ark rests on a hill. Unlike its famous biblical counterpart, this historic vessel carried only fishermen and their catch.An ark is the newest addition at the Betterton Heritage Museum, which also features exhibits of vintages postcards and waterfowl decoys created by carver Charlie "Speed" Joiner.
"The Betterton fishing ark is one of a handful of historic arks known to exist today. It was used as temporary overnight housing by watermen so they could stay in remote locations on the water. The authentically restored Betterton ark travels to special events around Kent County and is permanently on display at the Community Center Park by the museum," according to an announcement from the musuem.
Although flooding isn't uncommon in the Bay village, it's a unique relationship that Kent County has with the water, especially among watermen. Nothing portrays that better than a photograph from 1939, in lifelong Betterton resident Larry Crew's home near the park.
It's of Crew's grandfather Jim and his uncle Caldwell Crew. They're standing in what's best described as a camper on the water, pulled by a Howell Gilling skiff, a style of fishing boat used in that era.
The camper structure, Crew explained, is a fishing shanty, hearkening back to an era, before the modern conveniences of commercial fishing such as fish-finding radar.
On a bright Friday morning, the 79-year-old history buff presents another black and white photograph, angling it upwards to block the glare from his window. It's a scene portraying a series of these fishing shanties in a neat row, like a trailer park. But instead of resting on concrete, and steel, they are positioned along the water's edge.
In front of these "floating villages," fishers mend their nets.
"They followed the fish," Crew said. "Fish could be off Tolchester and in the spring migrate up the flats in Betterton. Wherever they went, the shanties followed."
These specific watermen didn't go home when they were done, Crew explained. They fished all day in the skiff, then came back to the shanties on the shore. During storms, they stayed in and played cards. At night after duty, they mended their nets. Inside many shanties were wood stoves necessary during those harsh winters.
One of these shanties was a regular sight for Crew growing up. It was on Ottawa Avenue in Betterton, sitting in the marsh for many years, first built by Winfield Scott Crowhart in 1885.
Crew recalled in his youth, his friend Charles "Speed" Joiner conversing with a hermit who lived in the shanty for a time.
Many years later, and when the hermit moved on presumably, in order to preserve the piece of history, the Betterton Community Development Corporation, consisting of Crew and Joiner and others sought to restore the fishing shanty to its former state.
Funds came from various places including from Joiner's sale of his handcrafted full-sized decoys, selling them over the internet.
Even with the money, moving it was easier said than done. When he and others got it loaded up in the trailer, predictable of a building exposed to the elements since 1885, it fell apart.
Crew laughed, "We had to bring it to Chestertown in pieces."
Once in Chestertown, Crew said, the boat builder of the Sultana, John Swain's expertise, was vital for its restoration. They aimed for 100% accuracy, measuring precisely while keeping all the original wood that fell off. They worked on the roof and the sides.
While Swain's workers labored on that, Crew scraped all the paint from the interior, getting it down to its natural color. On the outside he scraped the paint, taking a sample to Lowes where they duplicated the color precisely.
After a lot of work, it's restored, and has been deemed "the Ark," by Betterton residents.
Resting up the hill on Main Street in Betterton, the sight welcomes people to the Betterton Heritage Museum. The Ark also made a temporary appearance at Betterton Day, revealing to visitors and residents alike a fascinating aspect of the town's history.
Not only did Crew restore the Ark, but he's studied the background behind these little fishing shanties while delving into the tradition of Betterton as a place people flocked to, coming to the Sassafras River by way of ferry and steamboat.
He relives the magic of that bygone era, collecting postcards from Betterton, spending, in some cases, $100 for one.
"Each postcard is so unique. On the back of them people give a brief statement of what they've experienced," Crew said.
He desired to share this information, and chance had it he met Jack L. Shagena Jr., publisher. Shagena had stopped at the museum while working on a book on the Chesapeake and Delaware canal. After talking to Crew, he saw a book in Crew's life's work.
They combined forces to write the book, "Betterton: Jewel of the Chesapeake," a collection of about 364 of Crew's postcards. It's written where it's accessible enough for everyone to enjoy in a few sittings.
From steamboat transportation and trade to entertainment, all kinds of enriching factoids are found in the book.
Crew poured out a lifetime of research, taking pride that it can only be purchased by visiting the town of Betterton itself, in the museum and possibly soon to be at Marzella's by the Bay, the only restaurant in town.
He enjoys uncovering history, and was encouraged that the shanties weren't just a Betterton or a Kent County thing. They're found all over the world.
However, just southwest of the Sassafras, in Rock Hall, he's encouraged by three women restoring another fishing shanty, originally created by Stanley Van Zant with the intention of preserving that history. Built in the 70's, the work is ongoing.
Crew knows all about that, now retiring from the shanty-restoration business but keeping busy as a lifelong learner.
If you ever bump into Crew, he'd gladly tell you about these gems of history he's always discovering, while not taking himself too seriously.
When asked why focus on Betterton, his home, he might respond with a grin and chuckle, "Some people weren't smart enough to leave."
For more: https://www.bettertonheritage.org/

title: Chorus of Dorchester donates to local schools

Chorus of Dorchester donates to local schools

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Dorchester 
 
 294

 In 2025, led by its founding director, Virginia "Cookie" Brohawn, the all-volunteer Chorus of Dorchester is marking the 50th anniversary since its inception in 1975.Earlier this year, the chorus assembled its 70 members to develop and perform two concerts. Presented in late spring, these concerts were offered as a fundraiser for the Cambridge South Dorchester and North Dorchester High School choral departments. Audiences were wowed by stirring performances featuring the medleys of "Les Misérables" and "Phantom of the Opera" as well as the concert title song, "You Raise Me Up." Included in the show were a rousing arrangement of "Battle Hymn of the Republic" and a beautiful pairing of "Ave Maria" and " I Believe."
While the Chorus of Dorchester concerts are free and open to the public, on this occasion a love offering was taken and is being presented as a gift to the Dorchester County high school choral departments. Dividing a collection of $5,245 equally, on Oct. 7 the two schools each received checks for $2,622.50 from treasurer Marty Gray.
The Chorus of Dorchester is now back in full swing and has already begun rehearsals for two Christmas concerts. Featured will be well-known sacred and secular favorites as well as other numbers that range from soaring classical pieces to others that will tickle your funny-bone. Director Brohawn again wields the baton and is supported by the accompanist Laura Todd and the sparkling narrations of Steve Long.
The concerts will be held on Saturday, Dec. 13, at 4 p.m. at Christ Church on High Street in Cambridge, and again on Sunday, Dec. 14, at 4 p.m. at Immanuel United Church of Christ, 5401 White Hall Road, Cambridge. As always, the public is invited and admission is free. For further information, call Cookie Brohawn at 410-463-1778.

title: Delicious Thanksgiving sides
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Delicious Thanksgiving sides

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 4A | Section: News 
 
 1230
 Words 

 Read News Document

 That big juicy turkey that just came out of the oven and is waiting to be carved does not get all the attention!Side dishes share the spotlight at many Thanksgiving dinners. Everyone loves side dishes and looks forward to piling them on their plates!The first dish that comes to my memory is when I go back to the country Thanksgiving dinner my mom would prepare. Mom always had her menu planned ahead of time, and the morning before Thanksgiving, she would get a basket and sharp knife and walk to the field on the farm where the fresh collard greens were growing.Mom loved cooking big dinners for family members, who came from afar to share the bounty of food that was mostly homegrown.She would cut the greens and mash them down in the basket until it was full.Returning to the house, we would chop the stems off, place them in a tub, pour cold water over them and sprinkle with some coarse salt. to bring any bugs to the top.After at least three to four times, we changed the water and shook the greens to ensure they were pest-free.In the house already on the stove was her largest pot, filled 1/4 of the way with boiling water and with either a ham hock or fat meat cooking for flavor.In came the clean greens that were gently dropped into the hot water. The lid was placed on loosely, and the rolling boil continued until the greens were tender. with us checking to see if more water was needed every so often.We'd sprinkle some table salt or coarse salt on top, and, during the last few minutes of cooking, sprinkle a very light amount of baking soda (yellow box) over top greens that will cause greens to steam up and fall back down.Recently, my daughter in law, Shannon, visited a local farm in Pittsville called Ard Brac Acres.While there, she picked up some bags of collard greens already cleaned as well as some ham hocks.Shannon put a "modern" touch on this dish, and let me tell you, they were amazing!Look up Ard Brac Acres on social media, as we will definitely be visiting them again soon for more country style dishes. Also, today, Nov. 8, is Shannon's birthday, so I'd like to wish her a very happy birthday!SHANNON's HAM HOCKS AND TURNIP GREENSUse a bag of collard greens purchased from the store. or two bags according to your crock pot size. Place one large or medium ham hock in a crock pot. season with 2 tablespoons minced garlic, 2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar, and 2 tablespoons sugar. Fill the crock pot to the top with chopped greens and pour a 32-ounce container of chicken broth or broth of your choice over greens. sprinkle top with salt and pepper to taste.Cover pot with lid and cook for 7 to 10 hours. Shannon (my daughter-in-law) cooked this and shared it with me. it is delicious and so much easier to make. try it and you will agree.GREEN BEANS WITH BACONThis is tasty, quick and easy. In a large skillet, cook four diced bacon strips with 1/2 cup chopped onion until the bacon is crisp. Meanwhile place 8 cups of fresh green beans, trimmed, in a large saucepan and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, or until crisp-tender.Drain well and add the bacon mixture. Sprinkle top with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Serve immediately.This recipe is not the one grandmother or mom made, but it is great too.Give it a try.SWEET POTATON' MARSHMALLOWFor a Small casserole dish size. Mix together well with an electric mixer: 1 can sweet potatoes, 1 egg, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 1/4 teaspoons vanilla, 1/3 cup evaporated milk and 1/3 stick of margarine.Mix well and bake in a 350 degree oven for 30 to 40 minutes. Remove from the oven and top with one bag of large marshmallows and return to the oven just until the marshmallows turn golden brown. Remove from the oven and let set for a while before serving.CORNBREAD DRESSING WITH OYSTERS2 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more for greasing the dish, 1 diced yellow onion, 3 diced stalks celery, 5 minced cloves garlic, 8 cups crumbled cornbread, Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, 3 1/2 cups chicken stock, 6 large eggs, 1/2 cup chopped Italian parsley, 1 bunch fresh tarragon with leaves stripped and chopped, 2 cups shucked oysters with their juice. Heat the oven to 350 degrees. Butter a 9-by 13-inch baking dish.In a large skillet, melt the butter over medium heat.When the butter is foamy, add the onion and celery, and cook, stirring frequently, until softened, 6 to 8 minutes. Stir the garlic and cook until aromatic, about 1 minute.Stir in the crumbled cornbread and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, then remove from the heat. In a large bowl, beat the eggs until smooth. Whisk in the chicken stock, parsley and tarragon. Stir in the cornbread mixture and the oysters. Pour the dressing mixture into the prepared baking dish and bake until the dressing is set and golden brown, about 1 hour. (Alternatively, cover and refrigerate overnight before baking; see note.)Let rest for 5 minutes.GREEN BEAN CASSEROLEHeat oven to 350 degrees.In a large bowl, stir together 2 cans of green beans with 1 can of golden mushroom soup, half a can of water, and 1 cup grated cheddar cheese.Lightly mix and transfer to a 2 quart casserole dish. Sprinkle top with one can of fried onions. Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil and bake for another 15 minutes until bubbly.ASPARAGUS CASSEROLEGoes great with baked ham. In a buttered casserole dish place a layer of asparagus and then a layer of crumbled cheese nips crackers.Wet with cream of mushroom soup mixed with water according to directions on the can. Finish the casserole with a few more crushed cheese nips. Bake in a 350 degree oven until asparagus is tender.OLD FASHIONED BREAD DRESSINGIn a skillet, cook 1 1/2 cups finely chopped onion in 1/3 cup butter with 1 1/2 cups chopped celery until tender.Add this mixture to 8 cups of dry small bread cubes which have been placed in a large pan. Sprinkle with 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, 1/8 teaspoon black pepper, 1/2 teaspoon poultry seasoning, 1/2 teaspoon sage, and combine well. Add 1/4 cup water and 1 beaten egg. Toss together with a fork. Stuff a thawed bird immediately and bake according to directions on the turkey label.ITALIAN GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE6 ounces Parmesan cheese, grated (about 1 1/2 cups), 1. cups Italian-style breadcrumbs, 4 garlic cloves, minced, 1 teaspoon kosher salt,. teaspoon black pepper, divided, 3 (28-oz.) cans Italian-style green beans, drained, 2 (9-oz.) pkg. frozen artichoke hearts, thawed, drained well and chopped,. cup extra-virgin olive oil, chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley.Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Combine Parmesan, breadcrumbs, garlic, salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper in a large bowl. Reserve 1/3 cup of the breadcrumb mixture then set aside. Add green beans, artichoke hearts, and olive oil to bowl with remaining breadcrumb mixture, and fold to combine well. Pour green bean mixture into a lightly greased 13-x 9-inch baking dish. Sprinkle reserved breadcrumb mixture evenly over the casserole.Cover with aluminum foil, and bake until heated through, about 30 minutes. Uncover and bake until lightly golden and bubbly, about 10 minutes. Sprinkle with remaining 1/4 teaspoon pepper, and if desired, chopped parsley.

title: The Oxford Museum celebrates 60 years with '60s theme
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
The Oxford Museum celebrates 60 years with '60s theme

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 537
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Wanda Whedbee knows her father would have been so proud to witness The Oxford Museum's 60th birthday party on Saturday.Whedbee's father, Lee Willey founded the museum in 1964. Whedbee said that six years later, Willey died of a heart attack, and so he didn't get to see the museum's growth over the years.
"I think it's amazing how it's grown," she said. "And the reason it has grown like this is because of the people that moved (into) town. And so many of them have taken an interest in it and worked so hard to keep it going."
For many years, Whedbee was a docent at the museum. When people would come in, she said she would point to the museum's first pieces — glassware and pottery that her father excavated from the grounds of the old Maryland Military and Naval Academy in town — and tell them about the museum's humble beginnings.
"And I would say, 'Look around. And if you really work hard, that's what you can accomplish,'" she said.
Saturday afternoon, community members had the opportunity to celebrate that growth — and another year around the sun for the museum — with the museum's current exhibit, "Oxford 1964: The Times They Were A-Changin,'" and cake and ice cream.
Terrie and Barry Smale, who haven't been to the museum in a decade, were blown away when they returned Saturday. They said it has transformed since their last visit.
Terrie's favorite part of the current exhibit was the 1960s area in the back corner of the museum, which was complete with vinyl records, a TV from the '60s and a rotary dial phone hanging on the wall. Terrie said she remembered having the same TV when she was growing up.
At the event, LIza Ledford and John Tochko were named winners of the Doug Hanks Jr. Oxford Preservation Award, which recognizes the efforts of people or organizations to preserve Oxford's history and heritage.
Ledford, who is the executive director of the Oxford Community Center, said the award means everything to her.
"It means the world to me to feel recognized by the public and the town, and just to feel that people are appreciating the stuff we're putting out there," she said.
Ledford has been with the community center for seven years. She said she feels lucky that what she loves to do every day is getting appreciated by the community.
"Thank you to everyone who was part of making this happen," she said. "And I share it with everybody who's part of the Oxford Community Center."
Tochko, who could not be in attendance Saturday, has been chairman of the Museum Building Committee for the last few years. When the winners were announced, Tochko was praised for his "quiet" support of different local organizations over the years and his involvement with the community center.
Because of the high temperatures outside, the museum's birthday party was held inside the museum Saturday afternoon. The Oxford Museum Executive Director Julie Wells said she knew the event would be crowded if it was held inside the museum.
"But we like being with each other," she said, later adding, "This is such a happy event."
The Oxford Museum is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Fridays through Mondays. Admission is free.

title: It's going to be a great film, 'you know'
author: ANNIE HASSELGREN Special to the Kent County News
content:
It's going to be a great film, 'you know'

 April 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANNIE HASSELGREN Special to the Kent County News | Section: News 
 
 1309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — Jon and Sarah Ware are always on the hunt for the unexpected. As visual storytellers, they search for people, imagery, and themes that will resonate with viewers — and they rarely have to look beyond their Eastern Shore home.The Wares moved to Elkton 17 years ago and one of the first things they did was reach out to the Cecil County Arts Council. Since then, they have been working with director Anne Marie Hamilton and, with her assistance, the Wares have gotten connected with various artists working with all different types of media. They soon began production on a series titled "Artists in Elkton," composed of short film pieces on those making art and living in Cecil County. About a year ago, Hamilton introduced the Wares to J.P. Henry, a young man with autism who is well known in his community for his talent in photography.
Hamilton "showed us some of [J.P.'s] work, and told us about his neurodiversity and how prolific and talented he was," Sarah Ware said. "We met J.P. and his mom, Jane, and asked if they would be interested in allowing us to do a documentary on them."
The film duo soon began spending time with Jane and J.P., and learning more about him and his process as a photo artist. Though the original and current goal is to make a feature-length film, the Wares created a short film in the meantime entitled "A Clear Lens," which was a finalist in the 2024 New York International Film Awards. It also received Official Selection at the Five-Minute Film Festival.
"J.P. is very charismatic and extremely talented, and his photographs are stunning," said Sarah. "It's quite a talent to pick up a regular old cell phone, see something in the community, and figure out that it would be a good photograph."
J.P. has a strong following on social media, and his platform has become a place where community members can feel that they are a part of his creative process and see themselves and the Shore represented in his work.
"There are very few places we can go without J.P. being recognized," said Jane, J.P.'s mom, business manager, and number one fan. "Living part-time in Rock Hall has really opened him up."
Growing up on the family farm in Earleville, J.P.'s childhood was spent surrounded by animals and nature. As he grew older, however, Jane felt that farm life had become limiting and began to look for a second, smaller residence where J.P. could become more independent by walking to town unaccompanied and getting to know neighbors.
"Here in Rock Hall," Jane said, "J.P. can walk down to the water or to the post office to mail a letter. He has started to come out of his shell. He goes for daily walks and always stops to talk to people along the way."
Jane noticed J.P.'s creative talent when he was quite young. After he was diagnosed with autism at age two, Jane learned that children and adults with autism often possess an exceptional attention to detail. J.P. enjoyed drawing for many years and took off-campus arts classes while attending Elkton High School.
"His drawings were very linear, but with 3D elements to them," Jane said. "I have many portfolios of his work."
But, she says, like any pastime for many people with autism, their interest in them tends to be finite. "He feels that he's 'been there, done that,'" she said, "and it's in the past."
J.P. moved on to photography around 2018 when he became engrossed in the photo capabilities of smartphones. Jane uses a Google Pixel and J.P. quickly mastered the finetuning of settings to bring his perspective to life. He particularly enjoys shooting anything related to boats or the water.
"My favorite boat is 'The Nipper'," J.P. said of a craft docked in Rock Hall. Jane and J.P. have become friends with the boat's owner and J.P. has taken many photos of it. In fact, some of his most popular photos have been of boats. The Henrys' lovely Craftsman home is the hub for J.P.'s work, all in various stages of being framed, mounted, or shipped out to customers. With more than 1,600 followers on his Facebook page, J.P. has become a prolific artist on the Eastern Shore and beyond, shipping his photographs all over the country.
His talent was first put on display in a one-man show in 2019 at the Cecil County Arts Council, the same organization whose director brought him to the attention of filmmakers Jon and Sarah Ware. At his 2019 show, "Visual Embrace," J.P. displayed 170 photographs with subject matter ranging from the nautical to images from the wide-ranging travel he and Jane do together. One of his favorites is a scene from a worship service at a Black church in Clarksville, Mississippi, which depicts the church's pastor conducting a healing on a parishioner. The way J.P. was able to immortalize the emotion and energy of the moment is one of many reasons for his wide and loyal following.
J.P. loves to take in all the world has to offer, particularly through travel. He looks most forward to trips and will tell you that "if you don't take a plane, it's not a vacation." One of his favorites was a cruise to Central America that he and Jane took prior to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Since his 2019 show, J.P. has exhibited his work at the Cecil County Arts Council twice more, in 2021 and 2023. His 2021 show was titled "Happiness Behind the Mask" and contained primarily photos of sunsets and local Shore life. In 2023, "Happy for this #3: I Love Where I Live" included primarily watermen and their boats. And J.P. continues to shoot photos wherever he goes. Jon and Sarah Ware will soon be taking more footage for a longer film featuring J.P., including an upcoming motorcycle ride in which J.P. will be wired with a microphone for full commentary.
"J.P. has a special leather motorcycle jacket ready to go for the ride," Jane said. "It has a skull on the back and metal detailing on the front." Jane shares that J.P. has a proclivity for fancy jackets and enjoys attending events where getting dressed up is a must. Two of his favorites are adorned with gold sequins and were made by a tailor at the Peabody Hotel in Memphis. J.P.'s flair is just one of the many attributes of his personality that have resonated with fans of his photos and is a reason why Jon and Sarah Ware want to share his story.
And they have a good sense for storytelling. The Wares' production company, WareTech Studio, is based in Elkton and has received critical acclaim for many of their works. A 2013 film they produced, "The Nowtime of Peace," is a 10-minute short which received an Honorable Mention at the Ron Kovic "My Hero International Film Festival." WareTech went on to produce "40 Steps," a narrative drama short which was officially selected and subsequently screened at the 2014 Maryland International Film Festival in Hagerstown. Another of their films, entitled "Liz and Iris: A Love Story," won a Best Documentary award in 2022 at the Philadelphia Cinema Awards and was officially selected by several other festivals, including Exceptional Merit at the 2022 LGBTQ Unbordered International Film Festival. That documentary was also an Official Selection of the Love Story Film Festival in London and was screened online worldwide.
"We didn't start out with a short film [on J.P.] in mind," said Jon Ware. "The short was a result of the goal of producing a feature film."
And the Wares are excited to continue their production of it.
"I remember when we first saw a few of his photos," said Sarah Ware. "We looked at each other and said, 'Ok, this is definitely something we need to do.' We think it will be a really impactful story to share with the community."

title: Casting call: 'The Boys From Syracuse'
author: TRED AVON PLAYERS
content:
Casting call: 'The Boys From Syracuse'

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TRED AVON PLAYERS | Section: Arts

 OXFORD — Tred Avon Players will be hosting auditions for its upcoming musical production of "The Boys From Syracuse," which will be performed April 18 to 28 at the Oxford Community Center.AUDITION DATES
Auditions will be held at the Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road, on:
Tuesday, Jan. 30 from 6 to 8:30 p.m.
Wednesday, Jan. 31 from 6 to 8:30 p.m.
Saturday, Feb. 3 from 1 to 3:30 p.m.
PLAY SUMMARY
Filled with two sets of twins, mistaken identity, and women chased and chaste, "The Boys From Syracuse" was the first musical ever adapted from Shakespeare.
Identical twins Antipholus of Syracuse and Antipholus of Ephesus were separated as children in a shipwreck. Both have menservants, also twins, both named Dromio.
When the Syracuse set arrive in Ephesus, mishaps and mischief ensue as they are mistaken for their brothers by merchants, wives and mistresses. Perplexed partners, disgruntled courtesans and outraged policemen are left in the duo's wake before this show's tangled web is unraveled.
Based on Shakespeare's "The Comedy of Errors," "The Boys From Syracuse" is often considered the finest of all Rodgers and Hart. With big band, late 1930s swing numbers, familiar songs include "Falling in Love with Love," "Sing for Your Supper," and "This Can't Be Love."
CASTING NOTES
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE Male, age 20s-40s, baritone.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE Male, age 20-50s, baritone.

CITIZENS OF EPHESUS Male and Female, age 18-70s of all vocal ranges. Spoken roles include Merchant of Ephesus, Merchant of Syracuse, Sorcerer, Tailor, Apprentice, Fatima, Emilia, Maids and Courtesans.
Liz Clarke will direct "The Boys From Syracuse," with Sam Stenecker as music director and Cavin Moore as choreographer. They ask that you come prepared to:
Sing a song of your choosing with two copies (preferred), not to exceed 48 bars of music. Ideally, you will choose music that is in keeping with the character and vocal range of your preferred role.
Learn and dance a short movement sequence.
Read selected scenes from "The Boys From Syracuse" script that will be provided during the audition.
PRODUCTION CREW
"The Boys From Syracuse" will also need a production crew — sets, lights, sound, and stage crew. If you are interested, come to any audition to find out more information, or send an email to auditions@tredavonplayers.org.

Wolves arrive at Wilmer Park

 Wolves have arrived at Wilmer Park to art lovers and residents' anticipation. "The Wolves" created in 2000 by Sally Matthews is the 16th sculpture from the Peter and Hanna Woicke collection, and can be seen at Wilmer Park in front of Aunt Sarah's Playground.According to Elizabeth Healy of the Chestertown Public Arts Committee, they were installed in the afternoon of Nov. 13, overseen by Dave Hegland, acting chairman of the Committee, after being stored for minor stability repairs at the Woicke's property in St. Michaels.
Hegland pointed out, the sculpture was repaired and conserved by Howard Wellman of Wellman Conservation and his team, then were de-installed and palletized for transport by Howard Wellman and Ben Herr of Anthony's Flowers and Landscaping.
According to Hegland, the work was well worth it.
Back in early September, he told the Chestertown Council the wolves were one of the most highly anticipated of their pieces.
He later told the Kent News, "This has been our most anticipated sculpture and in the short time since its installation we have seen adults and children enjoy the thrill and mystery of these life size sculptures walking in the tree line at Wilmer Park."
There are five wolves, each weighing 350 lbs., rugged and lifelike from a distance; bronze snouts pointing towards the water, trekking through fallen leaves.
Up-close you see their craftsmanship and appeal.
And very shortly, the wolves will be joined by the next sculpture, Durbar. The sculpture weighs approximately 3500 lbs and is about 15 ft tall, to be installed in the South East corner in Bailey Park. The complex structure will be disassembled and reassembled by an art team.
Durbar will set on a concrete pad installed by the Chestertown Streets and Public Works Department, Hegland said.
The Peter and Hannah Woike Collection consists of 23 outdoor sculptures which are diverse in style, subject matter and origin. For more information about Chestertown Public Art go to chestertownpublicarts.com/.

title: The Zebra Gallery: a place for 'evolutionary' artists
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
The Zebra Gallery: a place for 'evolutionary' artists

 September 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — For Susa Schauer, art has stayed consistent in her life no matter her career. Whether it was being a professional woodturner or a neuroscientist, her heart has kept its love for creativity.Schauer's The Zebra Gallery has provided Easton with a collection of "evolutionary" art and artists.
Her journey to opening the business began during the COVID-19 pandemic, when she was diagnosed with cancer. She described her diagnoses as a wake-up call. It pushed her to make her dream gallery a reality.
"I thought if I'm ever going to open a gallery, maybe I should (now)," Schauer said. "Life is short. So this beautiful spot across in the Tidewater came open, and I kind of leapt into it."
Schauer's decision to not wait allowed her to create a place that would not only help her through the pandemic and her illness, but also helped her establish a community she loved.
Schauer said her choice in name for her gallery came as a bit of surprise to her. She did not have a particular connection with zebras growing up, but one day she received a text from her daughter-in-law saying her grandson, who was 3 years old at the time, had just been diagnosed at Johns Hopkins with Ehlers Danlos Syndrome, an illness that affects the skin, joints and blood vessels.
After some research, she learned the symbol for Ehlers Danlos Society is a zebra. The symbol called to her and she decided to name her gallery after the animal. Additionally, she made a commitment to give 10% of proceeds to Ehlers Danlos research.
"So I took the name Zebra Gallery, and thought it was destined to be," Schauer said. "It has made just perfect sense for me in terms of where I am in my life, making this more than just about me, selling other people's art, but in fact, also giving back to some degree. So it feels like a really nice circle."
Now, Schauer's gallery features local and international artists. Schauer said when looking for artists to feature in her gallery she seeks art that is evolving, risk-taking and intriguing. Though she has a love for traditional art, she said she wants to help foster high-end art with a contemporary spin.
In her own work, she has worked in a variety of media including portrait painting, woodturning and thread painting.
Ingrid Matuszewski, a featured artist at the Zebra Gallery, said she had been a long time admirer of Schauer's art and it has been a pleasure to work with Schauer in her gallery. Matuszewski, who got into portrait painting later in life, said working with Schauer has established a community of growth for her and her art.
"I think Easton has amazing galleries, so I think the Zebra Gallery complements the other ones in a way that maybe hasn't been there before and represented before because it's more of a contemporary take on art," Matuszewski said. "I think Susan tries to get in touch with artists who just kind of have different viewpoints on things."
Adam Himoff, a muralist at the Zebra Gallery, said Schauer's gallery is the first gallery he had been featured in. Her excitement for his work was magnetic, and her love for art in general drew him in.
"I met Susan, and she lights up a room and has some amazing energy," Himoff said. "And we talked about my art and her art, and I shared photos of my other work. She had seen the mural before. And she was amazing. She just lit up, and without a millisecond passing just expressed so much excitement and interest in the work. And so it just seems clear that energy was very convincing."
Schauer said she loves the people on the Eastern Shore, and the opportunity to have her gallery feature local talent, she said, has been wonderful.
"There really are so many spectacular people in this town and visiting this town, it's why I came here from grad school and never left 40 years ago," Schauer said. "It's a beautiful area, and we have a remarkable group of both artists and buyers, and they're all wonderful people who have great stories to tell. So every day is a kind of learning and creating."

title: Tradition continues with 77th annual National Outdoor Show
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Tradition continues with 77th annual National Outdoor Show

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 473
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — People packed the gym of South Dorchester School Friday night to see pageant contestants strut the stage, showing off talents from lyrical dancing to powerlifting to filleting a snakehead, and to see the fastest muskrat skinners compete for champion status.The 77th annual National Outdoor Show, held Friday and Saturday in Church Creek, brought Dorchester County residents together to celebrate the county's culture. The show's events included three different pageants, exhibits, demos and competitions, including trap setting, skinning and oyster shucking.
National Outdoor Foundation President Buddy Oberender said good attendance and good weather made it a great event this year. He said 515 people came Friday night and estimated that attendance was "well over 1,500" people on Saturday.
Oberender, who has been involved with the organization since 1994 and has been president since 2003, said tradition is what makes the National Outdoor Show so special.
"It's a tradition of the area," he said, adding that the muskrat skinning contest started in 1938.
Friday night, seven contestants competed for the title of 2024 Miss Outdoors. The women showed off their talents, walked the runway in different outfits and answered the question, "What does friendship mean to you?"
Laila Insley was crowned Miss Outdoors. During the competition, Insley demonstrated how to fillet a snakehead fish on stage, guiding the audience through each step.
"I found my love for snakehead fishing during COVID," she said on stage. "When the world was shut down and there was nothing to do. My family and I would spend countless hours fishing for snakehead."
Syndey Hughes, who demonstrated duck calls alongside her dog Smoke during the talent portion of the pageant, was named first runner up. Madison Schuyler, who deadlifted 185 pounds during the talent portion of the pageant, was named second runner up.
Hughes said the best part of her night was getting to be on stage with her dog.
"I love anything I can do with my dog," she said. "That dog is my ride or die."
Kate Price, who is from Woolford, said she has been coming to watch the pageant for at least 20 years.
"I still know most of the kids in the pageant," she said. "They're my kids' ages. And I just enjoy seeing everybody."
Saturday, contestants vied for the titles of Little Miss Outdoors and Little Mister Outdoors. Rose Bloodsworth was named Little Miss Outdoors. Edwin Bramble was named Little Mister Outdoors.
Following the pageant Friday night, once the stage was cleared, skilled skinners removed the pelts from muskrats faster than you can say, "It's the Senior World Champion Muskrat Skinning Semi-Finals."
It wasn't long after the competition began that the faint smell of dead, skinned muskrat wafted throughout the school gym.
The next day, those finalists vied for the titles of men's and women's International World Champion. Dakota Flowers took home the woman's title, and her husband Dusty Flowers took home the men's title.

 The wraps came off a unique art project last Friday at Calvert Marine Museum in Solomons.The effort by 13 young people was supervised by young adults and aided by experts. A modest national grant helped with funding. The results were priceless.
"Beneath the Bay," a mural depicting the many inhabitants of the Chesapeake and its tributaries, was a work of art accomplished through the Calvert County Youth Mentor Program, which was championed and supervised by county government's department of parks and recreation.
"We all need mentors," Nate Smith, recreation division chief, said April 25 before the modular mural was unveiled to a roomful of young project participants, parents and volunteers. County Commissioner Catherine M. Grasso (R) and Commissioner Todd Ireland (R) also attended and spoke at the unveiling ceremony.
"It's been a wonderful journey," Brenda DiCarlo, the youth mentor program coordinator, added.
According to information provided by parks and recreation, during the summer of 2023 the department "was one of 29 agencies nationwide to receive a $70,000 grant from the National Recreation and Park Association to establish a youth mentor program."
The program is designed to enrich the lives of children ages 10 to 14 in the community through fellowship, education and activities that include life skills, good citizenship, health and wellness, and more in fun and interactive programs.
Last fall, Calvert's parks and recreation department debuted its first youth mentor program with 10-week sessions offered at Northeast Community Center in Chesapeake Beach and Southern Community.
