title: Festival of Trees readies for 38th year of fundraising - November event benefits Talbot Hospice
content:
Festival of Trees readies for 38th year of fundraising - November event benefits Talbot Hospice

 September 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A12 | Section: News 
 
 318
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In 1986, when the Festival of Trees was a fledgling organization, Midge (Fuller) Menzies and Leslie Ware could hardly have dreamed that it would be going strong 38 years later.Festival of Trees has been so successful that Friends of Hospice has donated over $3.7 million to the Talbot Hospice Foundation, all generated from the annual Festival of Trees event.Each year the theme changes and events may vary, but the mission stays the same: to raise monies to benefit hospice patients and their families in Talbot County by hosting an annual fundraising event and to bring awareness to community members about Hospice Care.Today, Midge and Leslie continue to support the event they started, serving on the board of directors as well as on various committees.Leslie sums it up this way, "Never did Midge and I imagine that our community would embrace and support us to the extent that they did.(Festival of Trees) would not only become a part of our community for 38 years, but also raise almost $4 million that has provided compassionate care and support for the terminally ill and their families in our community." Presented by Friends of Hospice, the 38th Festival of Trees will take place in Easton on Nov. 25-28.This year's Victorian theme is "Caroling, Caroling Through the Town." Events include Festival of Trees, which is held in the Tidewater Inn, as well as Carols by Candlelight, Santa 5K Run, a Poinsettia Sale, a Santa's Workshop and more.Festival of Trees is the largest fundraiser for the Friends of Hospice to benefit Talbot Hospice. To get involved in any capacity, big or small, contact Festival of Trees Chairman Karla Wieland-Cherry at dkcherry4@aol.com or 410-310-8421.Prefer to help by way of a sponsorship? Visit festival-of-trees.org to learn more.

title: Oxford Day celebrates community with parade, events
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Oxford Day celebrates community with parade, events

 May 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Oxford Day serves a lot of purposes — it is a homecoming, a tourism draw, a marker of the start of the town's busy summer season. But above all else, event organizers said, Oxford Day is a celebration of community."The primary thing is community and giving people a reason to come out of their houses and connect," said Kathleen Case, the event chair of this year's Oxford Day, which took place on April 27.
Though exact numbers had not yet been calculated, volunteers said they thought this year's event had drawn a record crowd, citing overflowing parking lots and the large number of entries in the Oxford Day parade, which Case described as the "backbone" of the event.
Participants from dozens of different organizations marched down Morris Street shortly after 11 a.m. on Saturday, including five marching bands from local middle and high schools.
First responders and representatives from local nonprofits and businesses waved to hundreds of onlookers, who lined the street in downtown Oxford.
The grand marshal of this year's parade was Jennifer Stanley, who was honored for her decades of service to the Oxford Kids Camp, which Case said "probably 75% of those watching the parade had some connection to."
This year's Oxford Day featured events beginning shortly before 8 a.m., with Talbot Hospice's annual memorial walk, and lasting well into the afternoon. There was a dog show, free walk-on rides on the Oxford Bellevue Ferry, a marketplace of vendors in Town Park and a pickleball tournament, among other attractions.
"Everybody is involved in this, and it's really a good thing," said Julie Wells, a former Oxford Day event chair. Wells watched the events unfold from the Oxford Museum, which opened an exhibit celebrating its 60th anniversary just in time for Oxford Day.
A lot goes into coordinating an event of this scale, Case said.
"There are 13 chairs under me," she said. "... There are over 70 volunteers."
Case said Oxford Day would not be possible without the work of these volunteers and the support of the town. Looking forward, she said she felt encouraged by the success of this year's event.
"This year has been really an amazing joy and surprise," Case said. "Last year was kind of our first year back into the swing after COVID, and we felt we had pretty good turnout, pretty good participation. But this year we had much more, so it feels like people are really finally coming back out and connecting and wanting to be part of these community types of events."

title: Holiday gallery sale features local artists
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Holiday gallery sale features local artists

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Arts 
 
 800
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — A new show is in the works following the astounding success of the November-December annual Holiday Show at the Chestertown RiverArts Gallery. This season, there were plenty of traditional paintings and art pieces but also intricate jewelry, festive holiday crafts and woodworking.Styles ranged from folk, traditional, abstract and whimsical. Patrons could browse or purchase a one-of-a-kind piece over the holidays.
The top sellers this year, RiverArts Board member Carol Droge said, were items like Moravian stars, created by Kris Kelley, the Arts Education Coordinator.
One of Kelley's favorite pieces to make, the stars are made with Tiffany-style stained glass. Each one, Kelley said, takes about an hour to create.
And they made beautiful Christmas decorations.
The stars were placed beside the homemade wreaths, another seasonal best seller.
Like the stars, the design for them is straightforward but elegant. The crafter, Amos Rudderow said they sell as well as anything he's ever done.
Finding everything he needs in his yard, it takes him about 20 minutes to make. The side pieces are hard wood; the uprights are birch branches. The rest is decorative placing using skill Rudderow has honed over the years.
They were a success with the public, selling 22.
Rudderow's wreath-making is closely related to his membership with the All Seasons Garden Club in Chestertown. Since he's retired he's been working with the club on projects, offering scholarships to the science students at the high school since 2013. The club is always looking for new members, meeting on the second Monday of each month during the periods Sept.-Dec. and Feb.-June at the Sacred Heart Roman Catholic Church.
For those who enjoy blending their art with their fashion, Ronn Akins' custom jewelry was on display.
Akins works with semi precious metals, silver and gold filled. The whole process requires finding the items, organizing them on a bead board, fusing glass, cutting and then placing the items in a kiln. His work yielded alluring results, selling 17 of them. A piece of his jewelry takes at least three hours to create. "It's a lot of dedication involved," he said, "but I enjoy it."
For traditional art lovers there was plenty to see and purchase as well. There were impressive flower paintings from Amanda King. She enjoys making floral pieces between her job as a nail technician at "P Nails." Her style is mixed media, using traditional paints as well as pressed flowers.
Her piece, "Olivia," was inspired by the daughter of the owner of the "China House." With all of her art, she thinks about a person she likes when she creates. Relatively new to the Chestertown art scene, she was welcomed by RiverArts with open arms in May. Two pieces she submitted for December, one a painting of poinsettias, and another of pressed black sunflowers were both sold.
King thanked the people who encouraged her to move forward with her art, recalling how nervous she was when she first submitted her works to RiverArts. "They automatically called me an artist," King said. "They were all so welcoming and friendly to me."
She offered encouragement to anyone who wants to pursue art. "I think everybody, if they have a positive attitude, can do this. Don't let shut doors be an obstacle."
Patrons at the gallery could go from King's tapestry of organization and colors to the surreal beauty of an abstract painting by Sheila Exum. Born in Chestertown, Exum's been involved in art since she was a child and has been painting for eight years now. Although many of her pieces are sold, including the latest one in Chestertown entitled, "Misty Copeland," a famous ballerina, she also sees art as a chance to give back to the community. King recently donated art to a ballet company in Wilmington and some sports pieces at a silent auction.
Of all the arts, she enjoys painting the most, and hopes to make it a career one day.
She's taking strides because on Feb. 9, her artwork will be displayed courtesy of the Good Aesthetic Gallery presenting the "TIDAL WAVE" group exhibition at the Rehoboth Art League.
King said her pieces are getting bigger and she is currently working on another painting of a ballerina, acknowledging she appreciates the grace in the postures.
The talent all these artists demonstrated this year was commended by those running the gallery.
Droge said, "Everyone has been extremely helpful and it's been a wonderful turnout."
Right now, the gallery walls are bare while they prepare for the next show on March 1, a new idea featuring clay works.
Executive Director, Chris Sade announced the show will be called "Grounded." The instructor for the Studio, Manager Kris Neiman, will head it up and will feature the works of local clay artists.
Participants will hear from these potters and a little about the process as well, adding a workshop element.
"The community will be amazed at what they can do," Sade said. 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Auctioneer hopes momentum carries to St. Michaels
content:
Auctioneer hopes momentum carries to St. Michaels

 September 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A10 | Section: News 
 
 450
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - Local auction company Guyette & Deeter is hoping to build on their success at an out-of-state auction in the upcoming Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum auction to be held Sept. 11 and Sept. 12 in St. Michaels.The St. Michaelsbased company recently announced that their Portsmouth, New Hampshire, auction of fine and sporting art grossed a record-breaking $5.4 million.The auction held on Aug. 8 and Aug. 9 saw several important objects go on the block, including a 1930 pintail duck decoy made by the Ward Brothers, which fetched $120,000, and a late-career oil painting by American artist Mary Cassatt, which sold for $480,000.Guyette & Deeter credited their nationwide network of collectors and bidders, as well as diverse expertise, with help gathering significant examples of fine and folk art from acclaimed collections.A 19th-century walking stick, carved by the formerly-enslaved and now rediscovered woodworker Henry Gudgell, sold for $140,000.Guyette & Deeter prioritized the cataloging, research and presentation of the objects on offer, and published a 400-page catalogue highlighting the pieces' provenance and significance.In addition to rare examples of decoys by Al Weis, Elmer Crowell and John Dilley, the auction presented museum-quality works from the Betty and Kenneth Lay Collection, including a Winslow Homer watercolor depicting the artist's brother, an etching of Homer's famous Eight Bells painting, three works by Mary Cassatt, and a painting by George Bellows.Among the bidders for these pieces were museums, public institutions and private collectors.The event space quickly ran out of seating on both days of the auction, as bidders and watchers gathered for the first time after the pandemic to follow the race. Phone and online bidders showed overwhelming interest, quadrupling some estimates."Gathering to appreciate the artistic accomplishments of these carvers, artists and makers is central to our work. Every piece that passes through our auction house gives us renewed enthusiasm, and we look forward to seeing everyone at our next event on Sept. 11 and 12 at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum in St. Michaels," said the auction house's co-owner Zac Cote.Guyette & Deeter displays sporting and fine art pieces at its showroom and gallery at 1211 South Talbot Street prior to each major auction. The showroom is open to the public on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.More information can be found online guyetteanddeeter.com.

title: What to know about Hanukkah and how it's celebrated around the world
author: Giovanna Dell'Orto
content:
What to know about Hanukkah and how it's celebrated around the world

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Giovanna Dell'Orto | Page: D8 | Section: News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hanukkah - also spelled Chanukah or other transliterations from Hebrew - is Judaism's "festival of lights."On eight consecutive nightfalls, Jews gather with family and friends to light one additional candle in the menorah - a multibranched candelabra.In Hebrew, Hanukkah means "dedication," and the holiday marks the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the 2nd century BC, after a small group of Jewish fighters liberated it from occupying foreign forces.With the tiny supply of ritually pure oil that they found in the temple, they lit the menorah - and it stayed lit for eight days. The ritual of lighting a nightly candle, as well as the emphasis on cooking foods in oil such as potato pancakes called latkes, memorialize this miraculously long-lasting oil.WHEN IS HANUKKAH 2023?The dates of the holiday are based on Hebrew month of Kislev, which usually coincides with November-December in the Gregorian calendar.This year, Hanukkah will be celebrated from Dec. 7 through Dec. 15.DOES HANUKKAH OBSERVANCE VARY?Jews across the religious observance spectrum - from Reform to Conservative to Orthodox - focus on the same theme of bringing light into the darkness and emphasizing that even a small, againstthe-odds effort can have a transforming effect.For this reason, even though the Talmud reflects a dispute over the order of lighting, most start with one candle and increase the lighting by one more candle each night while reciting or chanting special blessings.The candles are added from right to left, but lit from left to right on the menorah, thus always starting with the newest light.The special menorah used for Hanukkah has eight branches, with a ninth place for the candle called shamash from which all others are lit.The tradition calls for candles with a real flame, though some also use electric ones in public displays, such as in hospitals, for safety reasons.HOW IS HANUKKAH CELEBRATED?A menorah is lit in each household and traditionally is placed where it can be seen from the outside, such as a doorway or windowsill, to symbolize the spreading of God's light to all nations.The lighting of menorahs in city streets and parks has become more prominent in recent years in countries around the world, including in front of public landmarks.In addition to menorah lightings, giving to charity and social works are also part of the celebration for many, reflecting the belief that the Jewish people are called by God to help make the world better for all.Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP's collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content.

title: Sept. 29 Concours event on Kent Island features rare autos
author: Staff Writer
content:
Sept. 29 Concours event on Kent Island features rare autos

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A rare 1906 Locomobile Vanderbilt Cup race car is heading to the waterfront Kent Island Yacht Club on Sunday, Sept. 29 as part of the 17th annual St. Michaels Concours d'Elegance on Chesapeake Bay, along with several other notable automobiles, including a 1931 Cadillac 370A V12 Roadster once owned by the actress Jean Harlow as a gift from Howard Hughes."This Locomobile may be the most historically significant race car entry we have ever had," says St. Michaels Concours d'Elegance Chair Luke L. Phipps. "It's a fantastic car with an outstanding history."
Phipps says the Locomobile Vanderbilt Cup race car is one of two purposely built by Locomobile for their race program at $20,000 each in 1906. The automobile ran at the 1906 and 1908 Vanderbilt Cup races, driven by Jim Florida and placing third in 1908. Its sister car, "Old 16" was driven by George Robertson and placed first in 1908, becoming the first American car ever to win an international competition.
Old 16 is now on permanent display at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan. Both cars have a 1,000 cubic inch F-Head 4-cylinder engine with a 7-1/4 inch bore and 6-inch stroke putting out 120 Horsepower. This car, along with Old 16, was purchased from the Peter Helck estate 30 years ago, with restoration finally completed last year.
This year's Concours also features a 1931 Cadillac 370A V12 Roadster once owned by actress Jean Harlow as a gift from Howard Hughes. With Fleetwood coachwork and Pilot Ray options, this automobile is one of 91 built and one of only 10 known in existence today.
After Harlow, the next owner was a coal baron from Kentucky named Claude Canada, the world's purportedly richest man at the time. It was then acquired by famed Texas real estate tycoon Jerry Moore, followed by Daniel Schmitt and Co. The automobile was museum-preserved for 40 years throughout these ownerships. Two other owners followed.
The Concours event features the debut of a special class of pre-1975 Porsche automobiles and the return of last year's world-famous Le Mans and Sebring-winning Corvettes. The Grand Marque of the show is in celebration of Chrysler's 100th anniversary, with a spotlight on Chesapeake Bay yachting. Additionally, three Pebble Beach award-winning pre-war motorcars will be competing in a single class at this year's show.
Proceeds from this year's St. Michaels Concours d'Elegance support the Queen Anne's County Mental Health Committee, a non-profit organization established to support community members in need of assistance coping with mental illness. The group was founded in 1986 by Lynette Nielson, who realized that local mental health programs needed access to additional funds to serve the needs of their patients.
Tickets for the event will be available to purchase at the event. Attendees are encouraged to arrive by boat, with dockage available at the Kent Island Yacht Club and Hyatt Place Marina. Limited slips are available, and advanced reservations can be made through www.docwa.com.
The event is presented by Bentley Motors and sponsored by Porsche Annapolis, with Porsche Annapolis also serving as the exclusive sponsor of this year's motoring tour and welcome reception.
More is at www.smcde.org.

title: 5th annual Fire & Ice Festival a success despite weather challenges
author: Konner Metz
content:
5th annual Fire & Ice Festival a success despite weather challenges

 February 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With ice sculptures positioned at restaurants, stores and downtown landmarks, many Easton residents and visitors enjoyed the fifth annual Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival last weekend.Friday brought clear skies for the event's opening night, while Saturday attendees endured rainy conditions. Despite the suboptimal weather Saturday, festival organizers say it was a success.
Holly DeKarske, executive director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation, said solid crowds made their way to the festival Saturday before the afternoon rain hit.
There were over 60 ice sculptures around town, including a firetruck and firefighter in front of Easton's Town Hall. Attendees watched the firetruck carving process happen Friday evening.
"We had more ice this year," DeKarske said. "And it was spread out from The Market at Dover Station down to Talbot Town (Shopping Center) all the way down to The Academy (Art Museum). So it was nice to get traffic walking and flowing all through town."
In the Waterfowl Festival building on South Harrison Street, children enjoyed crafts. Across the way, many gathered around fire pits for food, drinks and games. St. Michaels-based Lyon Rum served cocktails and Delmarva Craft offered local wines and beers.
DeKarske said the fire pavilion was a major addition to this year's festival, especially as people looked for cover from the rain.
"It worked out really well, and we'd like to do that again," DeKarske said. "People seemed to really enjoy that, and being able to have the music right there and have a beer garden. We had some snack food, but of course, we want you to go and eat at the restaurants."
With five years of Chesapeake Fire & Ice complete, DeKarske hopes it can grow in the future. She pointed out that she'd like to see not just more locals, but more out-of-town visitors in attendance.
"It's also great to have people from out of town who will spend the night in our hotels," DeKarske said. "And that brings in accommodations tax, which helps fund the county and our municipalities. It's great to bring those dollars in."
Adding a day onto the festival schedule is a possibility, she said.
"If we can find a way to maybe expand into Sunday a little bit to encourage sort of that two-night stay, it'd be great," DeKarske said. "And just help to sort of feed the tax base here, which would be nice."
Carlos Mir, known by his stage name of "Cascading Carlos," has performed at the festival since its inception. The skilled juggler and two-time Guinness World Record holder was at his usual spot last weekend, Thompson Park at the corner of Dover and Washington streets.
Mir performed for festivalgoers, including many families, spinning and juggling fire. Easton residents Sara Guest and Jude Spillman were the two of the first to watch Mir work his magic Friday evening.
Mir said the first annual Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival was a hit. He recalled crowds of people filling up the grass around Thompson Park and standing on the brick walls.
"The way they kicked it off, it was the first year, everything seemed to be like, it was a novelty," Mir said. " … The success of that one, I came back the next year. And I did Friday night and Saturday."
The skilled performer has been back every year since. Mir said it's an "awesome event" put on by organizers and the Town of Easton.
As evening turned to night Friday, more attendees gathered at Thompson Park to get a close look at Mir's performance.
Mir said his favorite part about the event is interacting with the audience, especially children.
"You just look at everyone playing with analog," Mir said. "They're playing with toys, they're not on the digital end of it. And you just see it. I just love that aspect of the juggling and what I can offer to people."

title: Temple B'nai Israel's Rabbi Hyman to retire in October
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Temple B'nai Israel's Rabbi Hyman to retire in October

 August 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 777
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On a narrow wall of Rabbi Peter Hyman's office in Temple B'nai Israel hangs a silk Ghom Persian rug that displays the 99 names of God in Arabic.The detailed green, orange, red and yellow rug that Hyman purchased in Israel 40 years ago for $3,200 using his parents' credit card (which he has since paid them back for in full), is more than a woven work of art that brightens his office. It's a bridge, connecting people of different faiths in the community.
Creating bridges between people and groups has been something of a priority in Hyman's more than four-decade career. Hyman — who is retiring in October after 18 years at Temple B'nai Israel — said that through demystifying and teaching people about a group or a person, you can "wipe out the bigotry and the stupidity."
"That's an important thing," he said. "That's how you build relationships."
Hyman remembers the first time the temple worked with the local Muslim community. He asked the president and vice president of the mosque if they could come in and translate the Arabic words on his rug.
"And they were just blown away that this was on the rabbi's wall," Hyman said.
Hyman said he loves the rug because it means something to him.
"People come in, especially Muslim folks come in, and they see this, and it creates a bridge," he said.
Throughout his career, Hyman has tried to build those bridges in multiple ways. He said he has established relationships with leaders from different groups and institutions, such as Father James Nash at Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church and Richard Potter with the NAACP.
"Building relationships that not only create friendships, but cement ties," he said.
A moment that Hyman is especially proud of, which highlights his efforts to build bridges, is his trip to Saudi Arabia. He went as the national Jewish chaplain for Scouting America. Hyman said it was the most amazing experience of his life because as a Jewish rabbi, he was welcomed and embraced in the Muslim country.
"This was a long time ago now, but I still maintain correspondence a few times a year," he said. "Like when it's Ramadan, I send all my Muslim friends 'Ramadan Mubarak.'"
Ben Schlesinger, who served as president of the temple from 2021 to 2023, said Hyman has a respect for and understanding of other religions. Schlesinger said Hyman leaves the door open for all people.
"If you want to talk to him, you can always talk to him, from any position or stance," Schlesinger said. "We have a lot of interfaith members in our temple. A husband and wife of different religions. ... He's very accepting of that."
In 2021, Hyman was awarded the Bronze Wolf Award, which is the Scouts' highest honor. According to Scouts' website, the award, which is presented by the World Scout Committee, recognizes the service, commitment and contributions of volunteers to the Scout movement. Hyman said he received the award for his interfaith activities and "building bridges between people and nations."
Schlesinger said that through Scouts, Hyman has participated in the broader community on a regular basis.
"In that role, he's built wonderful relationships within the community," Schlesinger said.
Although Hyman doesn't have any plans to leave Easton once he retires in October, he does have some travel plans in the works. He said he is planning to be a part of the clergy contingent on cruise ships for holidays like Hanukkah and Passover.
"Wherever they send me, I'll be glad to go," he said.
It is not yet known who will be taking Hyman's place as rabbi at Temple B'nai Israel. Hyman said a search committee has been tasked with this.
Looking back on his career, Hyman said Easton's Temple B'nai Israel has been his favorite of the four synagogues he served in.
"When I first came, I said I didn't care how big we are, I cared that we were seen as legitimate participants in the broader community," he said. "And that was always very important to me. And we've done that."
Elaine Friedman — who has been a member of the temple for 31 years and was president for six years — said Hyman has been "a breath of fresh air" for the synagogue. She talked about how the temple has grown since Hyman has been there.
"He, along with our active members, created a wonderful space for education, for religion, for socializing," she said. "He brought us all together for that."
Hyman said he thinks it's his time to retire and pass on the torch.
"I think it's important to leave and pass it on to somebody younger (who will) hopefully protect and maintain and preserve the foundation and build on what we've done," he said.

 Words

 CHESTERTOWN - Perfect weather, beautiful boats and tall ships, toe-tapping music, and a spectacular fireworks show made this year's Sultana Downrigging one of the best ever.The event, welcoming historical replicas of Colonial-era vessels and some of the most up-and-coming music bluegrass groups in the country, is the largest fundraiser for the Sultana Education Foundation located in Chestertown.Julia Knight, an event volunteer, was happy to see the crowds. "This is my third year volunteering, but we've been fans from the beginning," said Knight, "and it's so important what the foundation does here." Attendees young and old headed to the tall ships for tours and, for the lucky ticket holders, a ride on them.Sailing tickets were sold out before the event even happened.Crew members on the replica of the Kalmar Nickel, the tall ship of Delaware, provided information on the original vessel and its 1638 expedition that founded the colony of New Sweden, the first permanent European settlement in the Delaware Valley, now present-day Wilmington, Delaware.One of the present day 24-member crew gave instructions on how the boat was steered, as ship steering wheels were not invented yet at the time this ship was built. It took two people to steer, one man who was located in a lower deck with a whip staff in hand that rotated, and the mate up above who could see what was ahead and yell down directions below.Next up was the Maryland Dove, a replica from the Ark and Dove, one of two ships that first brought colonists to Maryland. Tale teller Michael Connor from the replica of the Dove told guests, "The Ark was a 400-ton capacity cargo ship hired by Cecil Calvert to transport about 140 colonists and their equipment and supplies to Maryland. The Dove was a much smaller 40-ton capacity cargo ship purchased by Cecil Calvert and investors so that the colonists would have their own ship to use once Ark had sailed for England." Attendees who appreciated restored classic boats were treated to a collection show put on by the Antique & Classic Boat Society, Chesapeake Bay chapter.Bob Wallace made his first 18' Gone Crab Skiff Krazy in 2016, proceeded to win seven competitions, and was named National Hard Crab Derby Champion. "Once I took it to the Crab Claw restaurant in St.Michaels," said Wallace. "The owner asked me to move it because all the customers wanted to come out and see it." Guy Beckley from Millington who brought his own boat to the pier said he came every year. "This is like Christmas for me," he said.Over in the Music Village tent, the crowds were enjoying some of the finest Bluegrass music in the region.The band Scraping Plates was first up and wowed the crowd with both old favorites and some of their new tunes. When asked how they got their unique name, guitarist and vocalist Andrew Jordan said the group began playing parties, and they never got time to eat. "We just went in the back kitchen and started scraping off what was left," he said.Miriam Satchell, owner of The Spicerie, and Chestertown Farmers Market vendor, said she was thankful for her hardworking staff. "The crowds are really enjoying it," she said."We're happy to be here." Oyster shucker order taker Sam Brahan said on Friday they shucked over 2,000 oysters. "Today will be more than that," she said on Saturday only an hour after opening.The Sultana Education Foundation provides hands-on educational opportunities that promote stewardship of the Chesapeake Bay's historic, cultural, and environmental resources. Over 200,000 students have taken courses so far, and the programming is always building.President and Founder Drew McMullen said this year's event was a big success, thanks to good weather, beautiful vessels, music diversity, the support of the community, and the large number of volunteers. "We are well into raising in the high, five-figures," he said.

title: 160-year-old Indigenous dog pelt studied in Smithsonian’s collection
author: Staff Writer
content:
160-year-old Indigenous dog pelt studied in Smithsonian’s collection

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 1079
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Researchers from the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History led a new analysis that sheds light on the ancestry and genetics of woolly dogs, a now extinct breed of dog that was a fixture of Indigenous Coast Salish communities in the Pacific Northwest for millennia.Anthropologist Logan Kistler and evolutionary molecular biologist Audrey Lin analyzed genetic clues preserved in the pelt of "Mutton," the only known woolly dog fleece in the world, to pinpoint the genes responsible for their highly sought-after woolly fur.
The study's findings, published Dec. 14, 2023, in the journal Science, include interviews contributed by several Coast Salish co-authors, including Elders, Knowledge Keepers and Master Weavers, who provided crucial context about the role woolly dogs played in Coast Salish society.
"Coast Salish traditional perspective was the entire context for understanding the study's findings," said Kistler, the museum's curator of archaeobotany and archaeogenomics.
Coast Salish tribal nations in Washington state and British Columbia bred and cared for woolly dogs for thousands of years. Prized for their thick undercoats, the dogs were sheared like sheep and often kept in pens or on islands to carefully manage their breeding and to care for the canines' health and vitality. Coast Salish weavers used the dogs' wool to craft blankets and other woven items that served a variety of ceremonial and spiritual purposes. Woolly dogs themselves possessed spiritual significance and were often treated as beloved family members. As emblems for many Coast Salish communities, woolly dogs adorned woven baskets and other art forms.
By the mid-19th century, this once thriving dog wool-weaving tradition was in decline. In the late 1850s, naturalist and ethnographer George Gibbs cared for a woolly dog named Mutton. When Mutton died in 1859, Gibbs sent his pelt to the nascent Smithsonian Institution, where the fleece has resided ever since. However, few were aware of the pelt's existence until it was rediscovered in the early 2000s.
Lin first learned about Mutton when she was a Peter Buck postdoctoral fellow at the museum in 2021.
"When I saw Mutton in person for the first time, I was just overcome with excitement," said Lin, who is now a postdoctoral researcher at the American Museum of Natural History. "I had heard from some other people that he was a bit scraggly, but I thought he was gorgeous."
She was surprised to find out that virtually no work had been done on the genetics of woolly dogs, which disappeared around the turn of the 20th century. She teamed up with Kistler and they reached out to several Coast Salish communities to gauge their interest in working together on a potential research project on woolly dogs.
Many in the Coast Salish communities were eager to share their knowledge.
"We were very excited to participate in a study that embraces the most sophisticated Western science with the most established Traditional Knowledge," said Michael Pavel, an Elder from the Skokomish/Twana Coast Salish community in Washington, who remembers hearing about woolly dogs early in his childhood. "It was incredibly rewarding to contribute to this effort to embrace and celebrate our understanding of the woolly dog."
To complement the perspectives they received from Pavel and other Coast Salish people from British Columbia and Washington state (the text from their interviews is available in the study's supplementary materials), Lin, Kistler and their colleagues began analyzing Mutton's genetic code. They sequenced the woolly dog genome and compared it with the genomes of ancient and modern breeds of dogs to determine what set woolly dogs apart. They also identified certain chemical signatures called isotopes in Mutton's pelt to determine the dog's diet and teamed up with noted natural history illustrator Karen Carr to create a life-like reconstruction of what Mutton looked like in the 1850s. Carr's work is the first in-depth reconstruction of a Coast Salish woolly dog in nearly three decades.
Based on the genetic data, the team estimated that woolly dogs diverged from other breeds up to 5,000 years ago — a date that lines up with archaeological remains from the region. They also discovered that Mutton was genetically similar to pre-colonial dogs from Newfoundland and British Columbia. The researchers estimate that nearly 85% of Mutton's ancestry can be linked to pre-colonial dogs. This ancient ancestry is surprising because Mutton lived decades after the introduction of European dog breeds. This makes it likely that Coast Salish communities continued to maintain woolly dogs' unique genetic makeup until right before the dogs were wiped out.
In total, the team analyzed more than 11,000 different genes in Mutton's genome to determine what gave woolly dogs their fluffy fleece and wool fibers that could be spun together to create yarn. They identified 28 genes that have links to hair growth and follicle regeneration. These included a gene that causes a woolly hair phenotype in humans, and another linked to curly hair in other dogs. Similar genes were even activated in the genomes of woolly mammoths.
However, Mutton's genetics could tell the researchers little about what caused the dogs to decline. Traditionally, scholars have speculated that the arrival of machine-made blankets to the region in the early 19th century made woolly dogs expendable. But insights from Pavel and other traditional experts revealed that it was improbable that such a central part of Coast Salish society could be replaced.
Instead, woolly dogs were likely doomed by numerous factors impacting the Coast Salish tribal nations after European settlers arrived. Due to disease and colonial policies of cultural genocide, displacement and forced assimilation, it likely became increasingly difficult or forbidden for Coast Salish communities to maintain their woolly dogs.
"It was thousands of years of very careful maintenance lost within a couple of generations," Lin said.
But despite their disappearance, the memory of woolly dogs is still embedded into Coast Salish society. And Pavel thinks their understanding of woolly dogs is only getting clearer thanks to the new research effort.
"All of our communities held a certain aspect of knowledge about the woolly dog," Pavel said. "But when woven together, as a result of participating in this study, we now have a much more complete understanding."
About the National Museum of Natural History
The National Museum of Natural History is connecting people everywhere with Earth's unfolding story. It is one of the most visited natural history museums in the world. Opened in 1910, the museum is dedicated to maintaining and preserving the world's most extensive collection of natural history specimens and human artifacts. The museum is open daily, except Dec. 25, from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Admission is free. For more information, visit https://naturalhistory.si.edu/.

title: Grave marking ceremony held for Revolutionary War patriot
author: Riley Dauber rdauber@somdnews.com
content:
Grave marking ceremony held for Revolutionary War patriot

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Riley Dauber rdauber@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It was an act of bravery nearly two and a half centuries ago, but it has not been forgotten.The Thomas Stone Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution, which includes members from Calvert, Charles and St. Mary's counties, dedicated a patriot grave marking to Hatch Dent, who fought in the 1776 Battle of Brooklyn, this past Saturday.
The ceremony took place behind the Dent Memorial Chapel at the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home, where Dent and his family are buried. The new patriot grave marking was installed in the center of the grass, right in front of Dent's grave, to remember his sacrifice on the battlefield.
According to Mike Morthland, president of the Thomas Stone Chapter, the idea for the grave marking came from the late George Owings, who spoke at Morthland's induction ceremony in 2022.
Owings was a member of the Thomas Stone Chapter and a former state delegate and secretary of Maryland Veterans Affair. He died in 2023 before the grave marking could be installed, so Saturday's ceremony honored both Dent's sacrifice and Owings' wish.
Members from other local organizations, including the Sons and Daughters of the American Revolution, greeted the crowd following Morthland's introduction.
"Events such as this remind us that our freedom was hard won, and it is our responsibility to keep alive the memory of those who made it," Stacey Park, regent of the Major William Thomas Chapter of the DAR, said.
Sandy Sterrett, Dent's fourth great-grandson and a member of the Society of the Cincinnati, read Dent's biography and introduced the crowd to Dent's other fourth great-grandchildren.
Dent was born in Charles County in 1751. At the age of 24, he joined the First Maryland Regiment as a third lieutenant before being promoted to second lieutenant.
He was one of the only survivors of the Battle of Brooklyn, which took place on Aug. 27, 1776. About 65% of the Maryland army died in battle, and their sacrifice earned them the name "Maryland 400."
During the battle, Dent was captured and held until April 1778. He later resigned in 1779 and gave back to his community through his roles as a reader and rector at Trinity Church and principal and professor of languages at the Charlotte Hall School.
"Our organization … is dedicated to keeping the history of this wonderful county alive and perpetuated so that others in the future can understand both why we're here in such a unique place and the people that made this county what it is," Peter LaPorte, the executive director of the St. Mary's County Historical Society, said.
After the marker was unveiled and the organization leaders delivered their wreath presentations, the Maryland Society SAR color guard performed a musket salute. U.S. Navy Veteran David Osborne played "Taps" while the crowd sang memorable renditions of "America the Beautiful" and "God Bless America" to remember Dent and his role in the Battle of Brooklyn.

title: COUNTRY COOKING: Hamburger favorite recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
COUNTRY COOKING: Hamburger favorite recipes

 March 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1226
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After a cold snowy winter, we are ready for that extra hour of daylight and warmer temperatures. Everyone is already talking about the yard work and clean-up that needs to be done. This brings back those memories of my childhood on the farm.We would go out on a spring Saturday morning to do yard and farm work for the day. My mother, my sister and I did the yard work around the house, and my dad and brothers did the barnyard and ditch banks close to the house and barn.
The fields were eventually spread with manure later during the week by the farmhands. Oh, what a lovely spring cleaning smell that was.
Since we lived out in the country, we were used to it, but boy, those town kids on that school bus that came to the country were not.
I decided to make the recipes this week using ground beef, and I remembered the farmer my father bought our beef from. We raised our own pork but bought our beef.
Raising beef began with a small herd of cows who gave birth once a year to calves. We had one milk cow, and that was enough to do with all the chickens, hogs, ducks and geese we had. The cattle needed lots of grazing fields, and we had a small pasture.
Ground beef was always popular with the cooks as you could make so many different dishes. When you are looking for the tastiest, cheapest, fastest meals, ground beef is number one.
It is very versatile, quick cooking and great for when you have a crowd to feed. Keep some burger on hand to make those classic dishes like meatloaf, burgers, barbecue meatballs, tater tot casserole, goulash, tacos and taco bake, stuffed peppers, chili, sloppy joe's, shepherd pie and much more. Let's get started.
STUFFED PEPPERS
6 medium green bell peppers (tops and seeds removed), 2 tbsps vegetable oil, 1 large onion (finely chopped), Kosher salt, 1 pound ground beef, 2 large cloves garlic (finely chopped), freshly ground black pepper, 1 28-oz can diced fire-roasted tomatoes, 2 cups cooked rice, 1 cup loosely packed fresh parsley leaves (roughly chopped), 1 1/2 cups shredded mozzarella, 1/2 cup plain dry breadcrumbs, 2 large eggs (lightly beaten), 4 tsps Worcestershire sauce.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Add about 2 inches of water to a large pot fitted with a steamer insert, and bring to a high simmer. Arrange the peppers in the steamer, cover the pot and cook, rotating the peppers as needed, until they are very tender and pliable, about 25 minutes. Remove the peppers with a slotted spoon and drain upside-down on paper towels. Put the oil, onions and a pinch of salt in a large skillet over medium heat, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions are soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the beef, garlic, 2 tsps salt and a few grinds of pepper, and cook, stirring and breaking the beef up, until browned and mostly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add the tomatoes, bring to a simmer, then remove from the heat. Let cool in the skillet for at least 10 minutes. Transfer to a large bowl, add the rice, parsley, 1 cup of the mozzarella, breadcrumbs, eggs and Worcestershire and mix to combine. Stand the peppers up in a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. If they fall over, cut away a little of the bottoms (without cutting through the pepper) to make a flat surface. Generously fill and pack the peppers with the meat-rice mixture. Top with the remaining 1/2 cup mozzarella. Add just enough water to the pan to cover the bottom to help steam the peppers. Loosely cover with foil, and bake until the peppers are tender and the filling is heated through, about 30 minutes. Remove the foil, and continue to bake for 10 minutes more. Traditionally people use green peppers, but you can use any of the colors available.
HAMBURGER STEAKS WITH GRAVY
Hamburger Steaks: 1/2 tsp ground mustard, 1/2 tsp smoked paprika, 1 large egg, 1 clove garlic (minced), salt and freshly ground black pepper, 1 pound ground beef (80/20 works the best), 2 tbsps breadcrumbs, 1 tbsp vegetable oil.
Onion and Mushroom Gravy: 10 ounces baby bella mushrooms (sliced), 2 sprigs thyme (leaves picked and stems discarded), 3 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 small onion (thinly sliced), 1 clove garlic (sliced), 3 tbsps all-purpose flour, 2 cups low-sodium beef broth (hot), 2 tsps Worcestershire sauce, 2 tbsps fresh parsley (roughly chopped).
For the hamburger steaks: Whisk together the mustard, smoked paprika, egg, garlic, 1 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp pepper in a medium mixing bowl. Mix in the ground beef and breadcrumbs by hand, then form into 4 oval patties, about 1/2 inch thick. Set a large nonstick pan over medium-high heat and add the oil. Add the patties and brown on both sides, about 3 minutes per side. Transfer the patties to a plate; set aside. For the onion and mushroom gravy: Turn the heat down to medium and add the mushrooms and thyme. Cook until the mushrooms release their liquid and are browned, about 8 minutes. (The mushrooms might seem dry at first, but will eventually release liquid and add moisture to the pan.) Transfer the mushrooms to a plate; set aside. Melt the butter in the pan, add the onions and garlic and cook until translucent and lightly golden, about 10 minutes. Sprinkle in the flour and cook, stirring, until the butter and liquid are absorbed, about 1 minute. Pour the broth and Worcestershire into the pan and stir until the flour is dissolved. Turn the heat to high and bring to a boil. Stir the mushrooms back into the pan and nestle in the beef patties. Cover with a lid and reduce the heat to medium low. Let simmer until the sauce has thickened and a thermometer inserted into the patties registers 165 degrees, about 10 minutes. Turn the patties over a few times to coat in the sauce. Season with salt and pepper and top with the parsley.
WESTLINE MEATLOAF
1 tsp dry mustard, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 1 pound ground beef, 1/2 onion (finely chopped), 1 egg, 2 tsps Worcestershire sauce, 1 cup breadcrumbs, 1 cup ketchup.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a small bowl, mix together the horseradish, mustard, salt and pepper. Set aside. In a large bowl, mix ground beef, onion, egg and Worcestershire sauce. Add the contents of a small bowl and mix thoroughly. Add the breadcrumbs and combine well. Place mixture into a 1-pound loaf pan. Pour ketchup over top and place in the oven. Bake uncovered for 45 to 60 minutes.
HAMBURGER or CHEESEBURGER
1 large egg,½ tsp salt, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 pound ground beef, ½ cup fine dry breadcrumbs.
Preheat an outdoor grill for high heat and lightly oil the grate. Whisk egg, salt, and pepper together in a medium bowl. Add ground beef and breadcrumbs; mix with your hands or a fork until well blended. Form into four 3/4-inch-thick patties. Place patties on the preheated grill. Cover and cook for 6 to 8 minutes per side, or to desired doneness. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read at least 160 degrees. If you are going to use cheese, this is the time you'd lay a slice on top so it starts to melt as the burger cooks.

title: Museum of the Rockies to open immersive multimedia exhibit on the legacy of Jane Goodall
author: MSU News Service
content:
Museum of the Rockies to open immersive multimedia exhibit on the legacy of Jane Goodall

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MSU News Service | Section: News 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Jane Goodall, founder of the Jane Goodall Institute and a United Nations Messenger of Peace, created an indelible legacy in the fields of science and conservation.That legacy is celebrated in "Becoming Jane: The Evolution of Dr. Jane Goodall," a new exhibit opening at Montana State University's Museum of the Rockies on Friday.
The museum will host a member-only opening at 5:30 p.m. It will feature a video that Goodall recorded exclusively for museum members. The evening will include family activities, a ribbon cutting and a discussion with primatologist Isabel Behncke.
Produced in partnership with the National Geographic Society and the Jane Goodall Institute, the exhibit explores Goodall's life, from her early years as a young woman with a dream to learn about animals in Africa and years establishing herself as a renowned scientist in Gombe, Tanzania, to her role as an activist, mentor and advocate for creating a better world. "Becoming Jane" will remain open through Jan. 18, 2026.
Goodall died Wednesday at age 91.
"We join the world in mourning the loss of a legend: a champion for conservation and the natural world," said Christopher Dobbs, the museum's executive director. "Her passing makes it all the more important to carry on her message. By hosting this traveling exhibit, we honor the remarkable legacy and memory of Dr. Jane Goodall, celebrating her life's work and the inspiration she continues to share with the world."
Highlights from the exhibit include:
A multiscreen experience where visitors are introduced to Goodall's work, alongside surprising encounters with virtually rendered chimpanzees.
A replica of Goodall's research tent where, in a hands-on experience, visitors can envision themselves as scientists.
A hologram-like projection of Goodall, who shares her memories in Gombe and recalls her thoughts, feelings, impressions and lessons learned while living among chimpanzees.
An immersive projection of Tanzania's Gombe Stream National Park.
Interactive augmented reality activities, including one in which visitors can test their skills at matching the pant-hoot vocalization of a chimpanzee.
Updates on the current state of Gombe Stream National Park and the chimpanzee range in Africa, along with the work of the scientists and conservationists who are following in Goodall's footsteps.
A call to action to visitors from Goodall to join the Jane Goodall Institute and National Geographic to ensure a more sustainable future.
A pledge station where visitors can share what actions they will take to help advance Goodall's mission and legacy.
Museum of the Rockies is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the "Becoming Jane" exhibit is included with admission. Learn more at museumoftherockies.org.

title: Easton's new Zach Gallery aims to curate relatable art
author: Tom McCall
content:
Easton's new Zach Gallery aims to curate relatable art

 September 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts 
 
 404
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The new Zach Gallery at 17 S. Washington St. has a current exhibit of watercolors by California artist Shana Frase.The works are bold and concentrated. Some of the work is representational, like of a flock of blue birds. Others shapes imply aqueous floating jellyfish or the strong lines of bamboo. This is process driven-work. Sometimes with big brush strokes and other forms are achieved by pouring paint onto the paper.
"You can tell she has been painting these forms for many, many years," said Aynsley Schopfer, manager of the Prager Family Center for the Arts. She is curator and manager at the new gallery.
Schopfer wants the work displayed in the new space to connect with people on the Eastern Shore.
"What is happening here is just bringing artists that are contemporary and fresh and relatable to the residents of the Eastern Shore," she said. "There is a lot of light and water inspiration."
Before Schopfer landed in Easton, she got a bachelor's degree in painting from Cornell University and has worked in galleries on Long Island and in Rhode Island.
"To me, curation is all about storytelling and relationships — bringing art that is perhaps new but relatable to residents of the Eastern Shore," she said.
Schopfer said Frase's work has a sense of the coast in it. Blues and greens are from an aquatic inspiration. Beneath the color, there is a deep physicality and movement to each piece.
Malachite, royal blue, gold — the colors are bold and exciting. All of her work is untitled, which leaves the door wide open as to "what it is."
"These are pieces of art that you can look at for years and years and find something new," Schopfer said.
The gallery has been divided into halves. One side is green and blue, and the other side is pink and yellow. It is located right next to the Ebenezer Theater, another Prager property showcasing world class music and a smart lineup of films.
"It to me is an eloquent way to complement what is happening at the Ebenezer Theater," Schopfer said. "We are bringing all this incredible music. It seemed nice to have a visual component. People can stop by the gallery here on their way to hear some music and just have a really soulful artistic evening in Easton."
Zach Gallery is open Wednesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. or by appointment. The Frase exhibit will run through Oct. 5.

 CHURCH HILL - Church Hill Theatre will host auditions for the time-honored musical "My Fair Lady" on Sunday afternoon, Jan. 21, at 3 p.m., followed by more auditions on Tuesday and Thursday, Jan. 23 and 25 at 6 p.m.This favorite Lerner and Lowe masterpiece is being directed by Sylvia Maloney, with Erin Bradley as music director and Cavin Moore as choreographer. title: Country Cooking: The recipe box
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The recipe box

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 877
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I decided to do some spring cleaning a few days ago — I should have known better.It never fails. I always come across something that three hours later I am still involved with. This time it was the recipe box with my collection of Mom's recipes that she wrote down for me.
These old simple cooking recipes from the '30s, '40s, '50s and '60s never fail to consume the rest of the day, just remembering her love of the kitchen and cooking. Some of the recipes are beginning to fade, but they are still precious to me.Mom had beautiful handwriting.
Let's explore some of these recipes.
QUICK & EASY BREAD PUDDING
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Break up 6 slices of bread and place in a mixing bowl. Add 2 tbsps of melted butter, 4 beaten eggs, 2 cups milk, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1 tsp vanilla and 1/2 cup raisins. Mix well and pour into a greased baking pan. Bake for 45 minutes or until the top springs up when touched. Serve warm.
LAURA'S CRAB CAKES
In a large mixing bowl, place 2 to 3 pounds of fresh lump crabmeat and add 1/3 cup mayonnaise, 1 1/2 tbsps mustard, 2 to 3 large eggs, 1 1/2 tsp Old Bay seasoning, 1/2 cup soft breadcrumbs, 1 pinch cayenne pepper, salt and pepper to taste. Mix into crab cakes and fry in hot oil or broil. Make sure they are golden brown on top, but watch closely so they do not burn.
GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP WITH DUMPLINGS
To a big soup pot, add either a big piece of salt pork or a ham bone with about 6 to 7 cups cold water and proceeded to let it cook until boiling began. At this point, add a quart of canned tomatoes from last year's canning or a size 10 can of store-bought tomatoes. Cover and let simmer for about an hour. Add about 4 to 5 cups of fresh green lima beans, one medium can of white or yellow corn, about a tbsp of sugar, 3 to 4 small peeled white potatoes (cut into chunks), salt and pepper to taste, cover and let cook while you make the dumplings.
DUMPLINGS — combine 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking powder, 2 tsps oil or lard, and water to moisten, Mix well adding enough water to make a stiff dough. Roll out on floured surface and cut into 2-inch squares and when bean soup is almost cooked add dumplings.
MOM'S BAKING POWDER BISCUITS
Heat oven to 450 degrees. Sift 2 cups of all-purpose flour, 3 tsps baking powder, and 1 tsp salt into a mixing bowl. Cut in 1/4 cup lard or shortening. Make a well in the center and add 3/4 cup milk. Stir quickly and lightly with a fork just until dough clings together in a ball. Do not over-handle. Turn dough out on a lightly floured surface. Knead gently 8 to 10 times. Flour your hands and pinch off the balls of dough about 1/2 in size and roll in your palm placing on an ungreased baking sheet or simply cut out with a cutter. Place biscuits on baking sheets about 1 inch apart . Bake for 12 to 15 minutes or until golden brown. Serve warm.
EASY ZUCCHINI BREAD
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large mixing bowl, place 1 1/2 cups peeled and shredded zucchini with 1/4 cup oil, 1 beaten egg, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1/2 cup white sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 1/2 cups flour, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1 tsp nutmeg, 1 tsp baking soda, and 1 tsp baking powder. Mix well and pour into a greased loaf pan and bake for 50 to 60 minutes or until done. This recipe card had a note that said it was given to Mom by one of her friends and that it was GOOD in capital letters.
MOM'S FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
Combine 2 large eggs with 1 cup buttermilk and set aside. Combine in a shallow bowl or pan two cups of all-purpose flour with 2 cups cornmeal, 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper. Wash the tomatoes and slice into 1/3-inch slices. Pour about 1/4 to 1/2 inch of vegetable oil or olive oil into a fry pan. Dredge the tomato slices through the egg mixture and then into the flour mixture and then place in the hot oil in a frying pan — cook about 2 minutes on each side (until lightly browned). Remove from pan to a flat dish with paper towels to absorb oil. Sprinkle the tops only with light sugar — serve warm.
All these recipes may seem to be so old fashioned to the younger cooks, but they were part of my teenage years and on into my early housewife years. When the more modern gadgets and appliances began to appear, I was right on board for change.
Funny how I still used some of the "old fashioned ways" to cook as I still do today! Right up until her death, Mom still cooked "her way" with her iron fry pans, baking pans, percolator coffee pot on the stove top, the hand beater, and hand washing the dishes.
However, one day a microwave appeared on the countertop, a gift from one of my brothers. Mom loved it.

title: Orchestra honors three for ongoing contributions
author: Staff Writer
content:
Orchestra honors three for ongoing contributions

 May 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 324
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra recently honored its 2024 Legacy Award recipients, honoring exceptional individuals who have significantly contributed to sustaining the orchestra and providing resources to support their continued success and growth.The first of the awards was presented to Mary Lou Tietz during the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra Gala on Saturday, May 4, at the Restaurant at Lighthouse Sound, just outside of Ocean City. Tietz, who has dedicated 15 years to the orchestra as a grant writer and fundraiser, was recognized for her contributions to securing essential funding and organizing fundraising activities for the orchestra. General Manager Dane Krich presented Tietz with the Legacy Award plaque, highlighting her critical role in sustaining the orchestra's mission and ensuring its continued excellence.
"Mary Lou Tietz's unwavering commitment and expertise in fundraising have been instrumental in the MSO's success. Her dedication has allowed us to continue bringing world-class music to our community," said Dane Krich during the award presentation.
On Sunday, May 19, following the Ensemble Series concert at the Academy Art Museum in Easton, the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra honored Jocelyn and George Eysymontt with the Legacy Award. The award recognized their ongoing support of the orchestra. The celebration included a special dinner in their honor at the Academy Art Museum, where the couple's contributions to the orchestra were warmly acknowledged.
"Jocelyn and George Eysymontt's generosity and support has been and continues to be vital to the MSO. Myself and the entire board of directors, our staff and the orchestra members are so very grateful for their unwavering commitment to classical music performance in our community," said board President Jeffrey Parker during the event.
The Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra is the only professional symphony orchestra serving southern Delaware and Maryland's Eastern Shore with a full season of programs. The orchestra is supported in part by the Maryland State Arts Council, the Talbot County Arts Council; the Worcester County Arts Council; the Sussex County Council; and the Community Foundation of the Eastern Shore.

title: German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through visually stunning paintings of zebras made from recycled cans collected in crisis zones to brightly colored paint portraits, Erdman Hummel is able to tell stories about the complexities of war and how to continue moving with hope.The Zebra Gallery hosted Hummel, a German artist and international journalist, last Friday evening. Hummel's paintings will be on display at the gallery through October.
According to Hummel, his path toward being an artist was a challenging one. Hummel, who was born under comunitst rule in East Germany when the Berlin Wall was still up, learned early on the importance of art.
Hummel said in the political context of Berlin, government approval was needed before any artist could practice their craft. At the age of 20, after a few of his artist friends were denied by the government, Hummel secretly opened his own gallery, which was forbidden at the time. Eventually, Hummel had an encounter with the Secret Service in East Germany, and it led to his imprisonment.
While in prison, Hummel read about zebras. To his surprise, zebras, over millennia, have never been domesticated. Hummel said he found inspiration from the animal and used it as a mantra during his time in prison.
"I decided these zebras are a symbol for me," Hummel said.
After spending over a year in prison, Hummel's release was negotiated by the West German government. After the Berlin Wall came down, Hummel decided to devote his life to sharing information and began his career in broadcast journalism. Over the years, Hummel has reported on war zones and crisis areas in Africa, Asia, Afghanistan, Iraq and Gaza.
And now Hummel has come back to art, focusing on the animal that kept his spirit going while he was in prison. His pieces are portraits of brightly colored zebras.
Gail Patterson, owner of the Spiralis Gallery, a separate gallery that occupies the same space as the Zebra Gallery in downtown Easton, said she has a strong appreciation for the uniqueness of the gallery's art, particularly with Hummel's work.
"This is just so unique compared to the waterfowl art and even open air art," Patterson said. "I mean, just everything about it is different for our town… I love (Hummel's) colors and the way there's some camouflaging."
Susan Fay Schauer, owner of the Zebra Gallery, said she was excited to include Hummel in her gallery.
"(Hummel) only paints zebras, and many of them he makes out of aluminum cans that he collects around the world," Schauer said. "He's a German war correspondent, so he collects unusual cans from war zones."
Hummel said he is excited to share his art with the Eastern Shore. According to his biography, the zebras changed the way he viewed his own liberty and the complexities of life.
"Zebras are a symbol of freedom for me," Hummel said. "I translate this freedom into joy of color. As a painter, their stripes give me an opportunity to put complementary colors against one another. Zebras are very individual. No animal is like another. Each has a unique stripe drawing."
This report has been updated from an earlier version to correct the name and title of the Spiralis Gallery's owner.

title: Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Pulling away from the local seafood store yesterday with a basket of fresh caught and fresh steamed crabs surely brings back memories of the 1950s and 1960s.Mom would set aside the designated weekday for crabbing. The other chores would be done. Mom would back the pickup out, and we would load the supplies, which included the baskets with inner tubes attached to help the baskets to float, the chicken necks for bait, the heavy string to tie the hook and sinker to, crab nets, towels, a picnic basket with sandwiches and a big jug of water with chunks of ice inside.
We loaded up and rode in the back of the truck so we could hoot and holler at our friends as we rode through town. Our friends would holler, "Take me" as we passed because they knew the fun we would have along with the work involved.
Our destination would be one of two country landings with docks for crabbing and areas for swimming. The first one was Mumford's Landing off St. Martin's Neck Road (now a development off the Route 90 bridge outside of Ocean City) and the second one was a little dock called Little Georgetown, just down the road from our farm on the Delaware side.
Upon arriving at the landing, Mom picked a spot to tie our strings on the dock poles. We took the lines and hung the nuts, bolts and sinkers on the bottom so the weight held the line down. Then we tied on the bait.
You had a choice — go swimming now or later, but you had to move down a good distance to stay away from the baited lines. Mom would get two baskets ready, grab a crab net and walk along the shoreline and crab. Someone stayed back with another net and basket to gradually pull up the lines, placing the net under the line to catch the falling crabs. Sitting on the dock would be one- or two-bushel baskets with lids to place the freshly caught crabs in.
If it was a slow catching day, the bushel basket would be set at the shoreline to partially filled with water to keep the crabs alive. Meanwhile, back on the farm, whoever stayed behind was pulling out one of the largest iron pots, used for winter hog killing and summer beet cooking. They placed stick-seasoned pieces of wood to start the fire to steam the crabs.
Upon arriving at home, the still kicking crabs were unloaded, the fire started and the Old Bay seasoning was put in. Once the crabs were bright orange/red in color, the fire was pulled away and the crabs pulled and placed on the picnic tables to be picked.
Of course, we ate the delicious meat until we were full, and then we put it in containers to be carried to the kitchen to be made into dishes such as crab cakes, crab soup and much more.
So let's explore what to make with our crabmeat.
CRAB CAKES
1 large egg, 1/4 cup mayonnaise, 1 tbsp chopped fresh parsley (or 2 tsps dried), 2 tsps Dijon mustard, 2 tsps Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp Old Bay or J.O seasoning, 1 tsp fresh lemon juice (plus more for serving), 1/8 tsp salt, 1 lb fresh lump crab meat, 2/3 cup saltine cracker crumbs (about 17 two-inch crackers).
Whisk the egg, mayonnaise, parsley, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, Old Bay, lemon juice and salt together in a large bowl. Place the crab meat on top, followed by the cracker crumbs. With a silicone spatula or large spoon, very gently and carefully fold together. You don't want to break up that crab meat. Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 1 day. Preheat oven to 450 degrees. Generously grease a rimmed baking sheet with butter or nonstick spray, or line with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat. Using a 1/2 cup measuring cup, portion the crab cake mixture into 6 mounds on the baking sheet. Don't flatten. Use your hands or a spoon to compact each individual mound so there aren't any lumps sticking out or falling apart. Bake for 12–14 minutes or until lightly browned around the edges and on top. Drizzle each with fresh lemon juice and serve warm. Cover leftover crab cakes tightly and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 3 months.
MARYLAND CRAB SOUP
1 28-oz can whole tomatoes (cut into small pieces), 3 cups water, 2 cups beef broth, 1 cup frozen lima beans, 1 cup frozen baby carrots, 1 cup frozen yellow sweet corn, 2 tbsps chopped onions, 1 tbsp Old Bay or JO seasoning, 1 lb lump crabmeat.
Place all ingredients, except crabmeat, in 4-quart saucepan, Bring to boil on medium heat. Reduce heat to low; cover and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in crabmeat; cover and simmer for 10 minutes.
CLAMS WITH GARLIC SAUCE
Clamming was also something we enjoyed doing. This meant a trip out into the water knee to waist deep with the clam rakes and innertubes. While we were there crabbing at the Isle of Wight Bay, my brothers would walk the edge of the marsh back towards Ocean City and clam near the rocks. It had to be low tide to get the best clams. Otherwise we'd buy them from the waterman who'd clam near Assateague.
3 dozen clams (scrubbed), ½ cup cornmeal, 1 tbsp salt, ¼ cup olive oil, 1 small onion (minced), 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 small dried red chili, 2 bay leaves, ¼ tsp hot paprika, pepper.
In bowl, cover the clams and cornmeal with water; add the salt and soak 45 minutes; drain and rinse. Heat the oil in a large non-reactive skillet. Add the onion; cook until soft. Add the clams, lemon juice, chili, bay leaves, paprika and pepper. Cover and cook over high heat, stirring constantly, removing the clams as they open. Garlic Sauce:4 garlic cloves minced,¼ cup parsley minced,½ cup fish stock or ¼ cup bottled clam juice diluted with ¼ cup water, In blender, puree garlic with 5 tbsps of the parsley, add the fish stock and garlic mixture to a skillet; cook until sauce is slightly thickened. Divide the clams among four soup plates. Spoon the garlic sauce on top and garnish with remaining parsley.
CLAMS LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 1 lb linguine, 6 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, ½ cup finely chopped shallots, 6 cloves garlic (coarsely chopped), ½ tsp red pepper flakes, 2 lbs Littleneck clams (scrubbed), ¼ cup plus 2 tbsps fresh flat-leaf parsley (finely chopped), 3 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 tsp lemon zest, 1 tbsp lemon juice.
In large pot over high heat, bring 4 quarts of water and 2 tbspss of kosher salt to a boil. Add the linguine and cook according to the package directions until just shy of al dente (the pasta should still be firm to the bite since it will cook another minute or two in the sauce). Drain in a colander (do not rinse), reserving ½ cup of the cooking water for the sauce. Meanwhile, in a very large sauté pan over medium-high heat, heat the olive oil until hot but not smoking. Add the shallots and garlic and sauté until just golden, about 30 seconds. Add the wine, red pepper flakes, ¾ tsp kosher salt, clams, and ¼ cup of the parsley; bring to a simmer and cook, covered, until the clams open, 6 to 8 minutes. Discard any unopened clams. Add the pasta to the sauté pan with the clams. (If you don't have room for everything in one pan, transfer the clams to a plate and cover to keep warm. When ready to serve, add them back to the pasta on a serving platter). Increase the heat to medium and cook the linguini with the clams, tossing occasionally, until the pasta absorbs most of the sauce and is just tender, 1 to 2 minutes. If necessary, add some of reserved cooking water to keep moist. Remove the pan from the heat. Add the butter, lemon zest, lemon juice, and the remaining 2 tbsps of parsley; toss to coat. Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt, lemon zest and/or lemon juice, if necessary. Transfer to a serving dish or bowls and serve.

title: Parade, performances and history mark Juneteenth at Kennard
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Parade, performances and history mark Juneteenth at Kennard

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 208
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — A celebration of freedom, unity and heritage brought the community together June 14 as the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center hosted its seventh annual Juneteenth festivities.The all-day event featured an expanded parade, live music, dancing, readings by prominent Black authors, a visit from the Mobile Library, a breakfast buffet, free haircuts, basketball clinics, vendors, food trucks and exhibits inviting the public to explore Kennard's museum and resource library.
Welcoming the crowd was newly appointed Executive Director Tara Coursey of the Kennard Alumni Association, who expressed appreciation for the participants and supporters.
Carole Boston Weatherford, author of this year's One Maryland, One Book selection Kin: Rooted in Hope, participated in the event with book signings and conversation. Weatherford, who has strong ties to the Eastern Shore, is also known for writing Juneteenth Jamboree in 1995 — the first children's book to highlight the Texas-rooted holiday.
"It is a great day to celebrate with the community," Weatherford said.
What began nearly 20 years ago as a grassroots initiative to revive and restore the historic Kennard High School has become a reality. The center now serves as a hub for African American history programs and events and is home to the Kennard African American History Museum.
More information is available at kennardheritage.com.

title: Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum
author: Contributed
content:
Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Nao Trinidad arrived in St. Michaels on Oct. 25, when it docked at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, where the replica historical boat will serve as a display of maritime heritage.The Nao Trinidad was the flagship of what was called Armada del Maluco (1519-1522), captained by Ferdinand Magellan.Five ships (naos) departed from Seville, but only two made it to the Spice Islands. Nao Trinidad was one of them.This beautiful replica weighs 150 tons, is 93 feet in length and has a 26-foot beam, three masts and a bowsprit. The height of the mainmast is more than 82 feet, with five sails and five decks, built with exquisite work in Iroko (an African hardwood) and pinewood.This ship has sailed to many different ports across the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic European Coast as a training vessel and floating museum.Naos have a unique and original design that made them the most advanced in naval engineering for their time, used first as cargo ships in Spain and then taking the lead as exploring vessels.The Nao Trinidad currently docked in Talbot County is a fullscale replica, faithful to the original's design and dimensions.More than a hundred artisans of the sea worked on its construction, including ship carpenters, rope masters and naval engineers.Visitors will be able to tour four decks to get a feel for how life was onboard during the ship's heyday and how it is to live today on an historical ship of these characteristics.They will be able to learn about the maneuvering and rigging of the boat and interact with the crew, who have the most amazing experiences from their long voyages.The boat will be available to visit at the maritime museum until Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.A ticket to enter the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum must be purchased to access the ship, except for museum members.IN addition to this ticket cost, the cost to board the ship is $12 for adults, $5 for children ages 6 to 17 and free for children 5 and under.
