title: 'Her voice is still heard ' - Shirley Jackson's legacy honored at Handsell tree dedication
author: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com
content:
'Her voice is still heard ' - Shirley Jackson's legacy honored at Handsell tree dedication

 August 31, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com | Page: A9 | Section: News 
 
 433
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA - A gathering of more than 70 family and other loved ones gathered to commemorate the life and work of the late Shirley Jackson on what would have been her 87th birthday.The commemoration was held on Friday at Handsell, where Jackson served as a trustee, one of the many places she invested her time, energy and love."Although Shirley is not physically present, her gentleness and wisdom still guides us on our journey," fellow Handsell trustee Midge Ingersoll said. "Her voice is still heard at our meetings as we plan programming and as we develop this beautiful site to be a home fore three cultures.Ingersoll shared the story of arriving at Handsell after Jackson's death to look for a spot to plant a memorial tree, a willow oak.As she approached Handsell's Memorial to the Enslaved, a 6.5 ton stone paying tribute to those that lived and labored on the grounds as slaves, she found a large feather. "Shirley, is this where you want us to plant the tree?" Ingersoll recalled saying out loud as she held up the feather she found that day.During the smudging ceremony, as Nanticoke Indian Tribe member Herman Johnson explained the fragrant items being burned and the meaning behind each, a bald eagle flew over Handsell, a symbol too powerful to be dismissed as a coincidence.Friends and family in turn stood and spoke, sharing stories about Jackson's involvement in the community and anecdotes about personal interactions with her.Bill Jarman told a story about being with Jackson when someone asked him for help with a new volunteer role. "You volunteer too much," she told. "YOU volunteer too much," Jarmon said he responded, before Jackson's next response: "Hush." The story, and the delivery, drew laughter, but the unspoken implication rang out - as much as she had done and was doing, Jackson never viewed it as too much.Shirley's sister, Lillian Jackson-Morris closed the ceremony with a song, its lyrics another poignant tribute to a woman who freely gave so much of herself: "The work that you've done, the service you gave and the life that you lived speaks for you."

title: Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps
author: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation
content:
Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1269
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Twenty years ago, in October 2003, 26-year-old Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie burst onto the North American publishing scene with her debut novel," Purple Hibiscus." Since then, Adichie's literary fame has only grown: She's published two more novels and a collection of short stories, while two of herTED talks have garnered tens of millions of views. In September 2023, she published her first children's book - a joyful celebration of mother-daughter love - under the nom de plume Nwa GraceJames.But the October 2003 publication of "Purple Hibiscus" didn't just signal the start of a single author's brilliant career. It also forged a path for a whole new generation of African novelists who had come to America as immigrants or students and who have been mining that experience in their writing.The struggles to get published by prior generations of African authors are almost legendary.Thirty years apart, Chinua Achebe and Tsitsi Dangarembga have both described how close their manuscripts of "Things Fall Apart" (1958) and "Nervous Conditions" (1988) came to being lost. Achebe's only copy of the manuscript was a handwritten draft. He sent it to a typing agency in London that nearly dismissed it as a joke. Dangarembga's manuscript sat unread in the basement of a British publishing house for years. Only when the writer stopped by the offices during a work trip to London did the editors agree to read it.Through attending American MFA programs, however, Adichie and her contemporaries were able to tap into the networks of agents and found their work snapped up by American publishers.Writers born in Africa who studied at American universities - Teju Cole, Yaa Gyasi, Uzodinma Iweala, NoViolet Bulawayo and Akwaeke Emezi, to name just a few - have followed in Adichie's footsteps."Purple Hibiscus" has been to these writers what Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (1967) was to aspiring Latin American writers during the Latin American literary boom of the 1960s and 1970s, and what Salman Rushdie's "Midnight's Children" (1981) was to the proliferation of Indian writers in English from the 1980s on.While it would be reassuring to think that the current surge of African novelists represents a wider American interest in all things African, the success of these novels may also have to do with the fact that so many are actually set in the U.S.The recurrent theme of immigration to the U.S. gives many of these works direct - and instructive - relevance to U.S. readers. As Black outsiders in the U.S., African immigrants have a particularly acute insight into the way race and racism affect daily life in this country.One of the common features of these novels is the way in which they explore the tension of racial solidarity and mutual misunderstanding between African immigrants and Black Americans.When I first started teaching African literature, I often had difficulty finding books in print. Now my problem is deciding who to leave out of my syllabus. Here is a very brief list of some of the books that I would consider must-reads.1. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, "Americanah" (2013) As its title suggests, Adichie's fourth novel, "Americanah," is arguably the definitive novel of contemporary African immigration to America.It tells the story of Ifemelu, a young Nigerian woman overstaying her student visa, and how she negotiates the new Black identity forced on her by the blunt instrument of American race-construction.In a brilliant metafictional move, Adichie has Ifemelu achieve internet fame by writing a blog dedicated to non-American Blacks: "Dear Non-American Black," Ifemelu writes, "when you make the choice to come to America, you become black. Stop arguing. Stop saying I'm Jamaican or I'm Ghanaian.America doesn't care. So what if you weren't 'black' in your country?You're in America now." Ifemelu's experience of racism is simultaneously hurtful and baffling to her. On the one hand, her illegal status makes her both psychologically and physically vulnerable. But at times American racism is almost comical; Ifemelu doesn't understand why an innocent reference to eating watermelon might be misconstrued, for instance, and she is totally bewildered by a shop assistant's attempt to avoid distinguishing between two shoppers by reference to their skin color.2. Yaa Gyasi, "Homegoing" (2016)Ghanaian-born Yaa Gyasi's debut novel takes the form of a series of skillfully interwoven stories set on either side of the Atlantic.Beginning with two half sisters, Effia and Esi, in the Gold Coast in the middle of the 18th century, the stories trace the two sets of the sisters' descendants through six subsequent generations in West Africa and the U.S. In the final two stories we meet the young teenager Marjorie, who, as the Americanborn daughter of Ghanaian parents, struggles to come to terms with her identity as one of Ifemelu's "Non-American Blacks." She finds herself ostracized by her Black classmates for "acting white" but is unable to enjoy a normal relationship with a white classmate. One of the only Black teachers at her high school tells her, "You're here now, and here black is black is black." 3. NoViolet Bulawayo, "We Need New Names" (2013)When "We Need New Names" appeared, Nigerian novelist Helon Habila accused NoViolet Bulawayo of peddling "poverty-porn" by pandering to American stereotypes of Africa.However, for Bulawayo's teenage protagonist Darling, it's American culture that is dangerously dysfunctional - and personally discombobulating. Darling finds American high school ridiculously easy, is horrified by the laxness of American parenting and is generally unimpressed by the urban blight she sees around her in the city she calls Destroyed, Michigan.Late in the novel, her mentally ill countryman Tshaka Zulu is shot to death by police when off his meds and ranting in his home language.You might think that such a violent, tragic event would be a major plot driver. Sadly, it seems to exemplify just one more random peril - little different from being hit by a car or struck down by cancer - that many Africans coming to America have to endure.4. Uzodinma Iweala, "Speak No Evil" (2018) Even wealth and class status offer no protection from such perils.In Uzodinma Iweala's "Speak No Evil," the main character, Niru, is the high-achieving son of high-achieving Nigerian parents in supposedly cosmopolitan Washington, D.C. The first three-quarters of the book appear to be exploring Niru's dilemma: how to come out as gay to his conservative parents.It turns out that Niru's gayness - an invisible characteristic, after all - is not the problem; his Blackness is. When he gets in a row outside a bar with his best friend, Meredith - an equally well-off, well-connected, high-flying white female classmate - someone calls the cops. In the space of a paragraph the inevitable has happened: Shots are fired. "You're safe," someone says to Meredith."He can't hurt you." By extraordinary coincidence, Adichie grew up in the very house that Chinua Achebe had lived in on the campus of the University of Nigeria in Nsukka.She, and the other writers of her generation, grew up in the house of fiction that Achebe and his generation established. The writers of that older generation were concerned with the material and cultural despoliation of colonialism. In Achebe's words, their task was to let their African readers know "where the rain began to beat" them.Today's African writers demand readers' attention by letting them know that for African and African-descended people in the U.S., although the winds may have shifted, the storm is far from over.Simon Lewis has been teaching African and Third World Literature at the College of Charleston since 1996. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article here: https://theconversation.com/20-years-after-the-publicationof-purple-hibiscusa-generation-of-africanwriters-have-followedin-chimamanda-ngoziadichies-footsteps-214052. 
 
 Caption: ROLF VENNENBERND/POOL PHOTO VIA AP
 
Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, sits on the stage while taking part in a panel discussion in Duesseldorf, Germany, Wednesday, Sept. 8, 2021. 

 © Copyright © 2023 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Chalk festival draws artists of all ages
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Chalk festival draws artists of all ages

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - People of all ages and skills got to show off their chalk abilities during the second annual Chalk Arts Festival in Cambridge last weekend.The event, which began Oct. 28 and ended Oct. 29, gave attendees the chance to listen to music, eat, see chalk artists from around the country do their thing and, of course, put chalk to the pavement.The festival was held in and outside of the Dorchester County Office Building.California artist Lori Antoinette led chalk art workshops for all ages on both days of the festival.Cambridge City Council Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said it was nice to have an event where kids could immediately have fun and express themselves without having to stand in a line."I think an event like this where it's open and free to the families and it inspires kids to pick up something with their hands and be expressive, it's a really nice event," she said.Atkiss herself drew a fish on the pavement outside the County Office Building."I just followed my heart because the rockfish tournament was just over the hill yesterday and just went with the nautical, fishy theme," she said of her creation.Hoopers Island Chalk Artist Ed Krell originally had the idea for the festival before pitching it to the Dorchester Center for the Arts.In its second year, the DCA is still hosting the event, which celebrates chalk arts and raises awareness for mental health. Krell said he wanted the festival to raise awareness for mental health to honor his friend, who passed away.Throughout the event, mental health information was presented on the music stage.This year, the festival garnered more community support, from Dorchester County Tourism to Dorchester County Public Schools.Chalk artists visited DCPS middle and high schools the day before the festival started, to give workshops and teach students about chalk art.North Dorchester High School Art Teacher LaSara Kinser said her students loved getting to work with chalk."It's not a material that we've worked with yet this year," she said. "And so they were so stoked, very excited." Kinser said her students drew portraits using chalk during a workshop led by Krell.The portraits from DCPS students hung inside the County Office Building for the duration of the festival so attendees could look at them.One of those DCPS high school students, Zye Pinder, also attended and performed in the festival. Pinder and her friend Jade Bryant both performed with New Creation Marching Unit.Pinder and Bryant enjoyed the live music at the event. Bryant said she also loved the face paint.Chalk artist Randy Segura traveled from the suburbs of Denver, Colorado to attend the festival this year.For his first year at the festival, Segura said it was a fun time and the weather was nice."Not as big of a turnout as we imagined but for its second year, I think it's growing," he said. "And I think it'll just continue growing." After creating a 3D paintbrush, Segura began a portrait."I figured if I had time, I would do a portrait of my father-in-law who just passed away last Tuesday," he said.Atkiss said the weather made the event even better."I think the unseasonably lovely weather has been a real treat," she said, laughing.

Daniela Kirby puts chalk to the pavement at the Chalk Arts Festival outside the Dorchester County Office Building in Cambridge Oct. 29.

title: 'Better sense of what's inside': Wildlife sculptors apply taxidermy experiences to art
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
'Better sense of what's inside': Wildlife sculptors apply taxidermy experiences to art

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 487
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Standing near his cast bronze birds in the Waterfowl Festival's PNC Pavilion on Harrison Street, wildlife sculptor Paul Rhymer talked about a skill that has aided his trade: taxidermy."A lot of wildlife sculptors started out as taxidermists," he said, adding that it's a common enough practice that a whole article could be written on it.
Although Rhymer took up taxidermy as a kid because his father did it, painting and drawing were Rhymer's first true loves. In the '80s, while working as an entry-level illustrator at the Smithsonian, Rhymer discovered an opening there for an entry-level model maker and taxidermist.
"I had the experience as a taxidermist with my dad," he said. "And so that taxidermy experience, messing around the basement with my dad, led to this career."
Rhymer fell in love with his new career. In the late '90s, he traded in his paints for clay and took up sculpting. And after a 25 years, he retired from the Smithsonian, giving him more time to sculpt.
For Rhymer, understanding an animal and its anatomy is helpful when it comes to sculpting.
"When you skin an animal out because you're mounting it, then you really know the anatomy," he said.
And Rhymer isn't alone. Sculptor Don Rambadt, who creates mixed metal welded sculptures, said taxidermy experience can give "a better sense of what's inside."
"Because I was actually looking at how the bones are articulated," said Rambadt, who did bird taxidermy as a volunteer at the Milwaukee Public Museum for a few years.
Both Rhymer and Rambadt consider these outside experiences important in their art careers.
Rambadt, who grew up loving nature, animals and art, started his college career studying natural resource management. After getting kicked out of college and taking a few years to work, he went back to college on a general biology track. At that time, he took a few art classes and was introduced to welding as an art form.
"By the end of that semester I had changed my major, transferred schools and was showing in galleries by the time I graduated," he said. Rambadt's knowledge of science has helped inform his art.
He said his career combines his two loves: science and art.
For Rhymer, who is a Marylander, a lifetime of outdoor activities — from hunting to birdwatching to fishing — has contributed to his work.
"You can watch the mannerisms of how things move, and what they do and their behavior," he said.
Rhymer, who started showing his art at the Waterfowl Festival in 2004, appreciates the tradition of it all.
"It's the granddaddy of wildlife art festivals," he said. "Because it's the Waterfowl Festival and I started out as a duck hunter, I love those roots that it started out as a waterfowl show. ... And I love the hook of art and conservation."
Both Rhymer and Rambadt's art can be found in the PNC Pavilion during the festival. Their work can also be found on their websites, rhymerstudio.com and donrambadt.com.

title: Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County

 September 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — The Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians' annual Native American Festival has had many locations in its 33-year history.It began on Elliott Island, then moved to Andrews, then Cambridge before settling at its current location on the baseball fields in Vienna 21 years ago.
"We've been all over the county," Chief Donna Abbott said. "But the entire county is our ancestral homelands, so it's worked out well for us."
That history was at the forefront of the event Saturday, Abbott said. As she surveyed the field shortly before the Grand Entry, she reflected on how the festival has helped support one of the Nause-Waiwash's most important goals — education.
The festival was designed to celebrate Nause-Waiwash history, culture and traditions and share these with the public.
"And definitely, after 33 years, it has become a tradition," Abbott said.
Since its beginnings, the festival has evolved, incorporating more Indigenous heritages.
At the event Saturday, Abbott highlighted performers from throughout the Americas, including Aztec fire dancers from near Mexico City and hula dancers from Hawaii.
"We also celebrate other nations," Abbott said. "We celebrate the South Americans, we celebrate the Mexicans, the Canadians, the Alaskans. We're all about all Native Americans."
The festival features vendors, demonstrations, food and dancing that aim to educate attendees.
In a shady spot near the back of the baseball field, Leigh Hunteman and her pack of dogs provided information about dog sledding, which finds its origins in Indigenous communities from what is now Canada and Alaska, according to an encyclopedia of Indigenous culture and history produced by the University of Saskatchewan.
Hunteman, a longtime Eastern Shore resident, said she has been coming to the festival since it was located in Cambridge and has been bringing her dogs to Vienna for several years.
The event is a good opportunity for Hunteman to teach people about competitive dog sled racing, which isn't commonly practiced in Maryland, she said. And the dogs are always excited to meet new people, she added.
Abbott said that longtime vendors like Hunteman, along with newer sponsors and vendors, have helped shape the festival into an evolving event that showcases more aspects of Indigenous cultures with each year.
Growing the event is important, she said, because of a shared goal between the festival's participants.
"We're all striving for the same thing," Abbott said. "We're all striving for the same goal, and that is to keep our history alive. There's so much of it that's been lost, and not just ours, but all the Indigenous history."
Abbott said preparations are already underway for next year's festival, which will be held Sept. 19 in Vienna.

title: Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NECK DISTRICT — Bernie Dryden perused an auction in late August, viewing every item. An old tattered Bible that sat on the very last table caught his eye. Dryden purchased it for $12.50 as the very last item sold at the auction.He figured he would give the Bible to his grandson, who is currently studying theology, but upon thumbing through the pages, he found extensive records from a singular family dating back to the Civil War Era. While analyzing the text, he realized one of the final names listed in the birth records was his friend, Alan Wright.
"This is a family Bible, and I recognized the surname as being prominent down in the Neck District, where I live. So I kept looking, and there was an entry there documenting a birth, and I knew the guy," Dryden said.
Dryden's grandson didn't accept the gift, saying it was more Christian to return it to the original family.
Wright was unaware the family Bible even existed before its return.
"When I got to look at it after Bernie gave it to me, my sister's name was in there, my brother's name was in there, and my father's," Wright said. This is the fourth family Bible in the Wright lineage.
Wright said his sister Ellen Paul is the family's historian, having compiled a detailed family tree and collected all the obituaries she can find.
Paul has spent the past 10 years compiling family records and has found the Historical Society and the Maryland room at the library particularly helpful. She has been able to trace the lineage of her family back to the early 1800s.
For Paul, the Bible was the missing piece of multiple family documents, helping verify important family dates and lineage. It even contained a marriage certificate from six generations back, providing a marriage date previously unknown.
A majority of the surnames in the Bible are Marshall until Paul and Wright's great grandmother, Lydia Marshall, married a Wright. "It's a Marshall Bible. Most of it is Marshalls, but it does have him (their father) and us three kids in there," Paul said.
The return of the Bible comes at an interesting time when another religious relic in Dorchester County that was purchased at the same auction was also returned to its original home.
A decades-old decommissioned sign from Old Trinity Church in Church Creek was sold at the same auction for $400. Members of the congregation were upset that someone was profiting off the church's name and expressed these feelings online.
The following Sunday, the sign showed up in the vesting room of St. John's Chapel, where The Rev. Dan Dunlap, rector of Old Trinity, serves as Vicar. A friend of Dunlap's purchased the sign back and gave it to Dunlap as a personal gift. He said it brought a tear to his eye, and he was deeply touched and humbled.
This time, a religious family relic has found its way home in an extremely similar nature — same auction, same seller, and also returned by a friend.
Wright said it felt fantastic to get the Bible, which was auctioned by Gage Thomas, a relative of Wright and Paul's, and to have it returned by a friend.
The religious relics finding their way back home are seen as somewhat of a parable to the Old Trinity Church congregation and to Wright and Paul.
"I mean, it's come full circle, right back to us, you know?" Paul said.

title: Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News
content:
Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News | Section: News 
 
 1144
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Saturday after Saturday small groups come and gather outside the booth of Fresca Frankie at the Chestertown Farmers' Market because, especially on a sunny day, her colorful and subtly shiny wares catch the light in just the right way that it attracts the eye and draws the marketgoer in for a closer look."Oh, they're bottle caps!" one curious patron said. "That's so cool!"
And that is usually followed up by a lot of "oohs" and "aahs" as they get the opportunity to see what's inside each small circumference of metal— a metal that was saved from the scrap bin at one time or another and now enjoys a second life as a sweet little canvas of Frankie's making. When you consider that the size of that canvas is approximately just one-inch, you become keenly aware that there must be something truly special going on in each one.
Lisa "Frankie" Ford, a Centreville resident, has been gracing the maker's row of the Chestertown Farmers' Market with those eye-catching bottle cap designs for more than a decade now, after spending most of her professional career in health care as an occupational therapist. In that role, she leaned heavily into the part of her personality that enjoys communicating with and helping others, and she said she relished the aspects of the work that enabled her to help patients heal through crafting, which became a vital part of their physical and emotional recovery.
"When I first started there was a lot more emphasis on utilizing crafts as a form of therapy," she said.
She recalled a stroke patient in particular, who really struggled with her fine motor skills.
"The craft was basket weaving," she noted. "And she had a lot of trouble getting the weave [to lay] right, or the material would break off in her hand."
As frustrating as the process was, she said, the patient persevered, eventually completing the project and placing the misshapen vessel on her mantel at home. The patient told Ford her kids would later ask why it was on the mantel when it was less than perfect, and the patient replied, "Because that's my recovery. It represents my recovery. It's the story of it."
Those stories and moments still resonate with Ford. However, there would be less and less of them as the health care industry began to change over the years. There came a point, Ford said, when she realized that she would need to change, as well. With the support and encouragement of her husband, Ford left health care to pursue crafting in various forms.
"My husband told me that he never saw me smile more than when I was at the farmers market," she said, and so her full-throttle adventure into full-time crafting began.
Around that time, she said, someone happened to gift a book of bottle cap art to her.
"I would be the first to tell you that I did not invent this idea," she said. She did, however, improve upon it and lend her own imagination to the task. Working with the caps would prove frustrating at first, she explained, as the glues suggested for the practice did not stand up to real-time wear.
"They were non-toxic and water-soluble; which I thought was a good thing."
And then she said she remembered a little piece of advice that her father had relayed to her often when she was growing up.
"'There's nothing that a good two-part epoxy can't fix.'"
Taking her dad's wisdom to heart she perfected her process of application and the concepts for bottle cap charms came fast and furiously. Each reimagined bottle cap artwork is designed to either be worn on a chain as a necklace or attached to a loop so it can be used as a key chain.
To help her mom present her designs in their best light, Ford said her daughter, Abigail, who was modeling at the time, suggested having the charms professionally styled for a photoshoot.
It is clear when visiting Ford's booth that her daughter had a great idea as this imagery and all the other enhancements that Ford adds to create a unique shopping experience is working. Trays of charms are labeled to convey varying areas of interest and styles, areas like sports, celestial, Maryland-centric, and hobbies. Marketgoers tend to linger and browse longer because there is so much to see; from details that are pinhead-sized to the overall aspect of the experience of shopping there and chatting with Ford, which she said is what she loves most about what she does.
And all that chatter results in a nice return customer base for Ford. In fact, if you're already wearing a Fresca Frankie when you visit the booth, her customer loyalty program kicks in automatically, offering a great discount on any pair from her up-cycled earring line.
In addition to her bottle cap charms, Ford displays her unique earring designs that she creates from recycled vintage jewelry. This aspect of her business has proven to be popular as legions of vintage jewelry lovers who wish to purge their troves, regularly contribute to the cause, so there is no shortage of resource material. And everyone wins because Ford provides discounts off of future purchases to those who donate their costume jewelry.
Rounding out her fashionable offerings are the bright and pretty displays of necklaces and bracelets she makes from soda can beads that she rolls herself by hand. She has a "secret-sauce" process for creating this line of lightweight and stackable accessories, which she admits discovering as a happy accident while trying to solve a design challenge.
Frustrated while trying to make a bracelet from a colorful strip of metal from an Arizona iced tea can, her subconscious fidgety fingers rolled the metal into a cylindrical bead, and eureka, the soda-can bead necklace was born. And you can literally see thousands of these shiny elements in containers catching that sun around her booth, where Ford continues to answer her customers' questions.
"Where do you get your ideas from?"
"Do people save their bottle caps for you?" The quick answer to that one is —"yes!"
And Ford is super grateful to those who do reach out and provide her with resources that would normally just get tossed.
Another customer comes by to take a closer look at a specific design and says, "How clever!" — and then asks about how the charm can be worn. Ford explains about the option to wear it as a necklace and tags her comment with something she explained she often tells a potential customer.
"Get used to people getting a little bit closer to you than they normally would when you're wearing it."
Fresca Frankie's booth will be open at the Chestertown Farmers' Market through the end of the year, and then returning for the spring market. You can check her out at her online Etsy shop and on Facebook. Those interested in donating vintage costume jewelry, can contact her via email at frescafrankie@yahoo.com

title: Caroline County is without director for arts council
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County is without director for arts council

 September 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 306
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The one thing that is clear about the former executive director of Caroline County Arts Council, Nicholas Tindall, is that he does not work there anymore. After multiple calls to board members on the council and staff members, the most that was revealed was that, "It was spelled out not to say anything." Not long ago, Tindall was seen at every major Caroline County event advocating for the arts in the community. He put up a massive canvas at Caroline Pride and people of all ages delighted in putting on their mark.He helped coordinate a broadly embraced arts district banner project that brought artists of all ages together.It was a public arts project that made the whole town shine. He worked with tattoo artist Sean Parker to create a vibrant botanical mural on the side of Pizza Empire.A bright future is still seen for the arts council."We raised close to $2,000 when we were selling ice cream at the Summerfest.We will continue to support the Summerfest.There is still good programming that is happening.The volunteer board of directors still has staff and volunteers and artists that are engaged and involved in the good stuff. The Caroline County Arts Council is going to continue to serve the community in exciting ways and is continuing to make grants," said Sue Simmons past president of Caroline County Arts Council.Tindall looks toward his future as well."I have some flexibility now to do what I want to do. I want to get back into the studio. Or try and put some more bids on public art projects. It is a positive having a little bit more freedom right now. I am also looking for a more serious full time gig," Tindall said. 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT

title: Medieval Europe was far from democratic, but that didn't mean tyrants got a free pass
author: Joelle Rollo-Koster The Conversation
content:
Medieval Europe was far from democratic, but that didn't mean tyrants got a free pass

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Joelle Rollo-Koster The Conversation | Section: News 
 
 1157
 Words 

 Read News Document

 My students tend to imagine the Middle Ages as something like the "Kingdom Come" or "Total War" video games: an age of utter political chaos, when swords and daggers ruled, and masculinity and physical strength mattered more than governance.As a historian of the Middle Ages, I believe this turbulent image has less to do with reality than with medievalism – a term for how modern people have reimagined life during Europe's Middle Ages, from roughly 400-1400.
Medieval Europe may have been violent, and its standards for governance would not win praise today. But people could certainly recognize dysfunctional politics, whether in a royal court or in the church, and proposed solutions.
At a time of rising authoritarianism, and when U.S. politics seem mired in chaos, it's worth looking back at how societies centuries ago defined bad governance.
Tyrants, kings and bad bishops
Authors in the Middle Ages thought about politics in terms of leadership and often called bad politics "tyranny," whether they were criticizing one leader or a whole system. In any case, tyranny – or autocracy, as it's often called today – is a concept great thinkers had been discussing since antiquity.
For ancient Greeks, tyranny meant ruling single-handedly for the benefit of one. Aristotle, the foundational thinker on the topic, defined tyranny as the antithesis of perfect rulership, which he believed was kingship: a single ruler ruling for the general interest of all. In his view, a tyrant was controlled by desire for "power, pleasure and wealth," while a king was driven by honor.
Modern political theorist Roger Boesche observed that tyrants tend to decrease the population's leisure time. According to Aristotle, free time allowed people to think and "do" politics – that is, to be citizens.
During the Roman Republic, political thinkers compared tyranny to a diseased limb that needed to be cut off the body politic. Ironically, certain Romans eliminated Julius Ceasar for fear he was becoming a tyrant – only to get Augustus, who eventually became an emperor.
Types of despots
In late antiquity, political writers began to think about tyranny in religious leadership, as well.
In his "Sententiae," a set of books on theology, the seventh century archbishop Isidore of Seville broached the subject of bad bishops. These men conducted themselves like "proud pastors," he wrote, who "tyrannically oppress the common people, they do not guide them, and they demand of their subjects not the glory of God but their own." In general, Isidore criticized political incompetence grounded in the leader's anger, pride, cruelty and greed.
Centuries later, European leaders and writers were still debating the nature of tyranny – and what do to about it.
John of Salisbury, a bishop and philosopher in 12th century England, proposed quite a radical solution: tyrannicide. In "Policraticus," writings about political theory, he wrote that it was a duty to redress the order of things and kill a tyrant who was evil, violent and oppressive.
In John's organic conception of tyranny, however, a tyrant (the body) could exist only with the support of society (its limbs). He was one of the earliest authors to argue that tyranny survived not simply by the whim of the tyrant but with the support of his followers.
By the 14th century, the leading legal thinker of the time, Bartolus de Sassoferrato, differentiated between two types of tyranny. Despots came to power through legal means but acted unlawfully. He defined usurpers, on the other hand, as rulers who assumed power illegitimately, wallowed in pride and did not follow the law.
Taking down a tyrant
At times, disliked or "inconvenient" leaders were deposed, such as England's Richard II. The record of his deposition itemized almost three dozen charges against the dethroned king: from rejecting council, defaulting on loans and exhorting religious authorities to murdering, disinheriting and impeaching rivals. We know that he did not end well: He died during imprisonment in 1400, though exactly how is a mystery.
In Germany, King Wenceslaus of the house of Luxembourg was deposed on Aug. 20, 1400, on grounds of being a "useless, indolent, careless divider and unworthy owner of the empire." The German newspaper Die Welt ranks him as the worst king of Germany – fond of drink and his hunting dogs, and possessed by fits of rage.
Violent disposals of supposed "tyrants" were not always done in the shadows. In 1407, Louis of Orléans, brother of King Charles VI of France, rode unknowingly into a deadly trap. He was assaulted by a large group of men who escaped and chased onlookers away.
Louis was not only brother to Charles "the Mad," but a political rival of John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, with both men vying for control during the king's bouts of mental illness. John assumed responsibility for ordering the murder.
He and the lawyer he hired, a theologian named Jean Petit, argued that Burgundy had acted in the interest of the nation by ordering the death of a treasonous and greedy tyrant, and that Louis' killing was therefore justified.
Men of the cloth
Medieval politics did not differentiate much between the secular and religious worlds. Popes were political leaders and could be considered tyrants, too.
During the Great Western Schism of 1378-1417, a split in the Catholic Church when multiple popes competed for the throne, all parties insulted each other with claims of illegitimacy and usurpation.
Enemies of Pope Urban VI, for example, argued a telltale sign of tyranny was his uncontrollable anger, which disqualified him for leadership. Dietrich of Nieheim, who worked at the papal chancery, noted in his chronicle, "The more he spoke, the more Lord Urban became angry, and his face finally became like a burning lamp or fiery flame from anger, and his throat was filled with hoarseness." French cardinals deposed Urban in 1378 on grounds of illegitimacy and tyranny.
He was not the only pope unseated for being tyrannical, even if that exact word was not used. The Council of Constance, a council of European clergymen convened to end the schism, deposed Pope John XXIII in 1415 on grounds ranging from disobedience and corruption to poor administration, dishonesty and obstinacy. Two years later, the same council deposed Pope Benedict XIII, accusing him of persecution, disturbing the peace, fostering division, promoting scandal and schism, and unworthiness.
Medieval bishops and kings are hardly role models for democracies today, but their political world was not so chaotic as we often imagine. Even a world ignorant of democracy attempted to define what bad leadership was and set limits on the authority of the ones they considered irresponsible. Rules of adequate political conduct were established, though the law did not always take precedence over violence.
But it's worthwhile to remember the ways people have viewed bad leadership, hundreds of years before our own era's fractured politics. Today, however, we have a big advantage: We vote our leaders in and out.

title: Kent Island Heritage Society marks 50 years of preservation
author: REBECCA PLACEK
content:
Kent Island Heritage Society marks 50 years of preservation

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA PLACEK | Section: Life 
 
 273
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The Kent Island Heritage Society celebrated its 50th anniversary on March 25, highlighting five decades of preserving local history and acquiring significant historical sites.Founded in May 1975 by five local women — Marian Stewart, Mary White, Emily Denny, Mildred Schoch and Annie May Price — the society has become a cornerstone of Kent Island's historical preservation efforts. During the anniversary event at Historic Christ Church, four key speakers reviewed the organization's achievements and the island's rich history.
The society's journey began with William Claiborne mapping and claiming Kent Island in 1631. Over the years, KIHS has acquired several important historical properties, including:
- The Cray House (1809), renovated and opened in 1977
- Stevensville Train Station (1902), donated in 1987
- Kirwan House (1879) and Museum Store (1889), willed to the society in the 1990s
- Historic Stevensville Post Office (1877), purchased in 1997
- Historic Stevensville Bank (1809), obtained in 2000 through a $1 annual lease from owner Bill Hufnell
- Kent Island Heritage Center Museum (formerly "School House #2"), acquired in 2023 through a bequest from former treasurer Lynne Riley Coleman
Upcoming events include the Maryland House and Garden Pilgrimage on May 3, featuring tours of the Historic Bank, Train Station/Caboose, Cray House and Historic Christ Church. The society's annual Kent Island Day celebration will take place May 17, featuring a parade, entertainment, food, vendors and exhibitors in Historic Stevensville. The new Kent Island Heritage Center Museum is scheduled to open during this event.
Kent Island Heritage Society historic sites are open to visitors the first Saturday of each month from April through November, on Kent Island Day and during special group tours.
For more information, visit https://kentislandheritagesociety.org/

title: Labor Day — cooking for end of summer celebrations
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Labor Day — cooking for end of summer celebrations

 August 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Labor Day is the last official summer holiday to be celebrated.The kids are ready for the return to school, the last-minute vacations are planned, and it is time to plan that Labor Day party.
Today we will explore some tasty dishes for that special day that does not require a lot of labor. Cooking outside is done year round now, and the grill awaits the food. Hot dogs and hamburgers are some of the favorite grill foods.
The 2024-25 school year does not start until after Labor Day this year for most schools, which is great for the kids who work in the summer. An extra paycheck helps pay for the school fees, shoes, clothes, classroom supplies and tuition.
Mason, my oldest grandson, has been going to college part time as well as working full time this summer. Colin, his little brother, also started working this summer in the food service industry. I tell both of them how lucky they are to be able to work in the air conditioning while others aren't so lucky.
That first day of school is always exciting and emotional for the first-time student and parents. In 1970 and 1971, when my two oldest boys started school, I played the strong parent role — walking them down the hallways of Buckingham Elementary, leaving them in the care of the teacher, walking bravely out to my car.
Turning around, I got out of the car and walked across the lawn to the back of the school and peered in the windows. How embarrassing when the teacher and students waved at me — including my own boys.
Thank you, American workers, for working to support your families, the young children, the elderly, the disabled, and those who supported you as long as they could. You are the backbone of America, and we support you. And just know it comes from the bottom of our hearts.
Here are some recipes for the grill to savor the ast days of summer.
DIJON GRILLED CHICKEN BREAST
1 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1 tbsp mayonaise, 1 tsp vinegar, 1 tsp black pepper, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 garlic clove (minced), cooking spray, chicken breasts (boneless, skinless).
In a small bowl, mix together Dijon mustard, mayonnaise, vinegar, black pepper, salt and garlic clove. Lightly coat the grill with cooking spray and preheat for 4 to 5 minutes. Place 4 chicken breast halves on the grill. Spoon the sauce over the chicken and grill for 5 to 7 minutes. Make sure you use all of the sauce. Double this recipe for a crowd.
GRILLED ITALIAN SAUSAGE AND PEPPERS
2 lbs Italian sausage, green peppers (seeded, thinly sliced), 1 onion (thinly sliced), 1 tsp black pepper, 1/2 tsp salt.
Cut Italian sausage into 4 portions. Lightly spray the grill with cooking spray and preheat for 3 minutes. Place the sausage on the grill. On top of the sausages place green peppers, onion, black pepper and salt. I sometimes sprinkle Old Bay seasoning. Double this recipe to fill the grill.
How about some great side dishes?
GERMAN POTATO SALAD
My friend Hannah always brings this great dish to cookouts, luncheons and dinners.
10 medium potatoes (peeled), 6 slices bacon, 3/4 cup sliced onions, 2 tbsps flour, 2 tbsps sugar, 2 tsp salt, black pepper, 1 tbsp celery seed, 3/4 cup water, 1/3 cup vinegar.
Cook potatoes until just done — do not overcook. When cool, cut into slices and set aside. Fry bacon, remove bacon from pan. Cook sliced onion in the bacon drippings. Add flour, sugar, salt, dash of black pepper, and celery seed. Cook until just bubbly. Add water and vinegar and stir until slightly thickened. Pour this mixture over the potatoes. Crumble the bacon over the top. Serve warm.
JELLO COOKIES
4 cups flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/2 cup butter, 1 cup sugar, 1 3-oz package of dry Jello (flavor of your choice).
Sift flour with baking powder. Cream butter and gradually add sugar and package of dry Jello. Cream well. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Drop batter by heaping tablespoons on a greased baking sheet. Bake for 12 to 13 minutes. Makes about five dozen.
STEAMED CORN
6 ears corn (husked), 2 tbsps granulated sugar, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp salt.
Fill a pot full of water and bring it to boil. Stir in the sugar, lemon juice and salt. Place the corn into the boiling water. Let the water return to a boil. Once boiling again, cover with a lid and turn off the heat. Cook the corn for 8-10 minutes or until tender.
SWEET CORN RELISH
10 fresh ears of sweet yellow corn (husks and silk removed, slice kernels off the cob with a sharp knife), 2 large red bell peppers (cored, and finely chopped), 2 large green bell peppers (cored and finely chopped), 8 ribs celery (finely chopped), 1 large yellow or sweet onion (finely chopped), 4 cups apple cider vinegar, 2 cups sugar, 1 tbsp ground mustard, 3 tsps salt.
Combine all the ingredients in a pot and bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar is dissolved. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer uncovered for about 20 minutes until the vegetables are tender. Ladle the relish into hot sterilized jars and seal with lids. Process the jars in a water bath for 10 minutes. Keep stored in a dark, cool place. Will keep at least one year. Once opened, store in the fridge for up to two months. Makes approximately eight pints. Wait a week or two before eating the relish to allow time for the vinegar to mellow out. Use it on hamburgers, hot dogs, sandwiches, fish, serve it with roasted chicken or mix with tomatoes/onions/cilantro for a Summer salad.
MEXICAN SALAD
1 onion, 4 tomatoes, 1 head lettuce, 4 oz grated cheddar cheese, 1 8-oz bottle French dressing, 2 cups Dorito chips, 1 lb ground beef, 1 15-oz can red kidney beans.
Chop onion with tomatoes and lettuce and put in a large bowl. Toss in cheddar cheese and French dressing. Crunch and add Dorito chips. Brown one pound of ground beef and add kidney beans when beef is browned. Simmer for 10 minutes. Mix into the salad and serve.
GRAHAM FROZEN STREET
Cool Whip (8 oz. container), box of graham crackers, container of color sprinkles or toppings such as nuts and cookie crumbles.
Lay out a cookie sheet to place your graham cracker sandwiches on. Pour sprinkles on a paper plate. You can separate if you have different varieties of patriotic sprinkles. Break sheet of graham cracker in half. Scoop Cool Whip with a tablespoon and place 2 tbsps on one half of the graham cracker. Close the sandwich gently and smooth sides with your finger or spoon. Dip each side of the sandwich in sprinkles. Place the finished sandwich on a cookie sheet. When the cookie sheet is full, cover with foil and place in the freezer for a few hours.
PINEAPPLE UPSIDE DOWN CAKE
Topping: 1/4 cup butter (melted), 1/2 cup brown sugar, 20-oz can pineapple slices (or 20 fresh pineapple rings), 1 jar of pitted maraschino cherries. Cake: 1/2 cup butter (softened), 3/4 cup sugar, 2 eggs, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour (sifted), 1 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/2 cup milk.
Preheat the oven to 350-degrees. Grease a 8-by-8-inch baking dish. Topping: Add the brown sugar to the bottom of the pan. Melt butter, pour over the top of the brown sugar, mix together, and spread over the entire dish. Place the pineapples and cherries on top of the brown sugar, place cherries in the center of each pineapple slice.
Cake: Start by adding the butter to a large bowl and cream for one minute. Add the sugar and cream again for one more minute. Add the eggs, one at a time, and mix together. Add the vanilla and mix together. Combine flour, salt, and baking powder. Sift into the bowl and mix. Add the milk, mix together, and gently pour cake batter over pineapple. Bake for 40-45 minutes or until a cake tester comes out clean. Let the cake cool to room temperature and turn the cake upside down onto a cake plate. If you used canned pineapple, be sure to drain pineapple juice before removing the pineapple slices.

title: 'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: Community 
 
 932
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Academy Art Museum Director Sarah Jesse is moving on to the University of Rochester in March after a three-year stint in Talbot County.Although this institute is orders of magnitude bigger, she will continue her focus on community engagement with the arts.
Feb. 23 is her last day before she moves on to be director of the Memorial Art Gallery. She said she has enjoyed living and working in Easton. There is a search committee for the next candidate.
"I love this place. I love the people. I love the staff and the people who support this place. I love how important this place is to the area and how beloved it is," Jesse said. "That has made this job feel very rewarding. This has been a total professional highlight for me coming here. I have learned so much, and it has been excellent training for my next step. It has been so fun. I will miss it a lot." She feels she is leaving the Academy in excellent hands, and it is in excellent shape. Looking forward, her next post is in a larger city and connected to a university.
"It is a bigger institution.
The operating budget is $9 million, and the operating budget of this (The Academy) is $1.6 million.
So with that comes more resources, more bandwidth, more opportunity to do more ambitious projects.
It is bigger. It is a very large museum," Jesse said.
She worked at the museum at her undergraduate alma matter Oberlin College in Ohio, and the experience touched her.
She was first generation to go to college.
The Oberlin museum gave prized artworks, like those by Robert Rauschenberg, to students to live with in their dorm rooms. She wants to give that kind of radical outreach to the students at the University of Rochester.
"I have worked in museums for over 20 years.
Ultimately it comes from my working class background and growing up in a rural part of Michigan.
My parents worked in the automotive industry, and my parents did a lot to expose us outside of our rural isolated world. We did not have much access to art and culture," Jesse said.
But something from the arts hit her deeply, and she was hooked.
"When I did have a seminal experience at the Detroit Institute of Arts, it spurred this desire to want to have art in my life," she said.
She wanted to work at art institutes that reflected her passion for sharing art with all kinds of people.
"That has always been the motivation for working in the museum field.
Not just to serve the traditional audience, but to serve the nontraditional museum goer," she said.
"I would have considered myself nontraditional.
Seeing how museums have completely transformed my life makes me want to give other people the opportunity to have a relationship to art and to museums." This desire to break down barriers has been a guiding core principle in each of her museum jobs in the last 20 years. She worked with the Academy Art Museum board to get rid of the entrance fee.
They agreed. She called this a home run.
Elitism is a stigma that all museums bear, she said.
"We have more than made up the loss in revenue from the donation box next to the front desk.
And people say to me, 'I feel compelled to support this institution.' My mentor told me, 'Be compelling and the money will come.'" This follows through in her belief of what an art institution could be.
"My unapologetic path is to take this thing designed for the public good and make it for the public good. It has been a total collective effort and total partnership for donors, members, staff.
Everyone is on the same page and that makes it so easy," she said.
She wants to tout the current civil rights photography exhibit that came from the collection at the High Museum in Atlanta.
"The show uses contemporary artists who are using their work to talk about race in the United States. The title of the exhibition is 'A Fire That No Water Could Put Out.' It is taken from Martin Luther King's last speech before he was assassinated," she said. "It is a fitting title for the show because that fire still burns today in terms of we have made progress on civil rights, but there is obviously so much more this country needs to go to overcome the legacy of slavery." "It is an easy case to make for the value of art having this exhibition.
This work helped spur the civil rights movement and it not only documented it, it helped shape it," she said.
Like a librarian, Jesse's role as director is to have art speak to people.
"If you spend the time, if it is good artwork, it will reveal itself to you, it's meaning. It does require discipline and the ability to read images. I love doing in gallery programming where we are in front of a work of art or talking about a work of art with a group of people. Art of itself doesn't always speak to people. Having a facilitator and hearing people's observations can help you find meaning in it," Jesse said.
Speaking of her fondness of the Academy, could also mark her direction forward.
"I want to thank the community. Anything we have accomplished here has been because of collective effort. It takes the whole community of people to make this place live up to its public spirited mission," she said. 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT

 Sarah Jesse, director of the Academy Art Museum, will be working in Easton until Feb 23. She is taking a new job as the Memorial Art Gallery director at Rochester University.

title: Temple B’nai Israel presents 'a joyous evening of klezmer music'
author: Staff Writer
content:
Temple B’nai Israel presents 'a joyous evening of klezmer music'

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Music 
 
 313
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Have you ever danced the Hora?If you've ever attended a reception for a bar or bat mitzvah or danced at a Jewish wedding, you probably have. This popular dance is perhaps the best known example of klezmer music, a style of instrumental music that dates back centuries.
At 7 p.m. on Thursday, March 6, at Temple B'nal Israel, the Satell Center for Jewish Life on the Eastern Shore, The Seth Kibel Trio will entertain with a program of klezmer music (Eastern European Jewish folk music).
The trio will also take some musical detours into Yiddish theater, Yiddish folksong, as well as jazz and swing.
"Historical commentary and anecdotes from Kibel will provide an insightful context for their selections. A pre-concert lecture presentation from Kibel will make this a true evening of "edutainment," according to an announcement from the Easton synagogue.
"This program is presented as part of the Susan and Barry Koh Music Series. Klezmer, which literally means 'tool of song' in Yiddish, is the secular folk music of Jews of Central and Eastern Europe. In the first decades of the 1900s, this music flourished not only in the Old World but also in the New, in the immigrant community of New York City," the announcement reads. "The result was a quintessentially American sound."
"Seth Kibel is one of the Mid-Atlantic's premier woodwind specialists, working with klezmer, jazz, swing, and other bands. Wowing audiences on clarinet, flute, and saxophone, Seth has made a name for himself in the Washington/Baltimore region, and beyond. He is the featured performer with The Kleztet, Bay Jazz Project, Music Pilgrim Trio, The Natty Beaux, and more," according to the announcement. "His most recent recording, "Clown With A Stick," was released in May 2023 on the Azalea City Recordings record label. www.sethkibel.com."
Everyone is welcome, admission is free. Register at bnaiisraeleaston.org/event/Klezmer or call 410-822-0553.
Temple B'nai Israel is located at 7199 Tristan Drive in Easton.

title: Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work
author: Post staff report
content:
Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Post staff report | Section: News 
 
 637
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The letterpress studio of Lead Graffiti was voted Newark's favorite artist of 2024 in a recent citizen poll by the Newark Post. That inspired the Newark Arts Alliance to dedicate its January exhibition to an overview of Lead Graffiti's work over the past two decades and its dedication to "printing slowly & patiently via letterpress in Newark, Delaware."The solo exhibition, "Lead Graffiti: An Exhibition of Letterpress and Book Arts" runs through Jan. 17 at the Newark Arts Alliance Gallery, located in the Shoppes at Louviers on Paper Mill Road. A public reception will be held on Jan. 10 from 6 to 8 p.m. The gallery is open to the public Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 4 p.m. daily and noon to 8 p.m. on Fridays.
Lead Graffiti was formed in 2008 by Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher as an experimental letterpress laboratory. The husband-and-wife team of artists/designers focused on public causes, a love of words and typography, passing historical and technical information forward, and a playful disregard for the usual design rules.
Located in a 2,200-square-foot space in Newark's Sandy Brae Industrial Park, Lead Graffiti is packed with cases of wood and metal type, printing presses of all kinds, a working hot-metal Intertype linecaster, and all the gear that Gutenberg would have known.
The studio's letterpress work is included in more than 75 significant collections of libraries and institutions, along with solo exhibitions at The British Library in London, the Hamilton Wood Type Museum in Two Rivers, Wisconsin, and the American Institute of Graphic Arts in Philadelphia. Lead Graffiti has been written up in Sports Illustrated Magazine and makes a grand entry in printer/author Chris Fritton's book The Itinerant Printer, where he wrote, "Lead Graffiti is the incorrigible, unpredictable, and uncompromising brainchild of Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher — a shop where the only rule is there are no design rules, and the thing you learn every day is that there's always more to learn."
Nichols and Cypher have given dozens of talks and tours to various organizations and student groups and conducted numerous in-house and online workshops related to letterpress and bookmaking. One of the studio's major projects was an endurance letterpress series of 115+ broadsides produced over five years (2011 — 2015), visually documenting the daily events of the Tour de France in handset type and ink on paper.
For three decades as a professor and director of the visual communications program at the University of Delaware, Nichols helped lead the program to an international reputation. He was also co-director with his teaching colleague Bill Deering of the program's summer study abroad to London.
Beginning in 2001, the trips were for students in advertising and graphic design to visit design studios, advertising agencies, filmmakers, and museums to provide experiences with design creativity, typography and historical perspectives. A pair of early visits to the letterpress studio of Alan Kitching and the St. Bride Printing Library unexpectedly provided Nichols and Cypher with two life-altering experiences. Their creative focus switched from blink-of-the-eye advertising design to the slow and patient world of letterpress printing and book arts for the next two decades.
In 2002, Nichols, Cypher and Deering founded Raven Press at the University of Delaware. Over the next four years, it became a new teaching tool. Cypher's interests in typography, colorful paste paper painting and exploring various forms of bookmaking also benefited Raven Press externally. Upon Nichols' retirement from teaching in 2006, the couple formed Lead Graffiti, collecting presses and cases of type to continue their creative work.
In 2006, their first major post-teaching project solidified their intellectual connection to Newark. As volunteers, Nichols and Cypher were tasked with designing, photographing and producing the 300-page hardback book "Histories of Newark: 1758 — 2008." The design is highlighted by their photography of a citizen's band of about 4,000 Newark residents that runs through the book.

title: 'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films

 August 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Newark Independent Film Festival is returning for its second year next week.The Delaware event is set for Aug. 14, 15 and 16 at Chapel Street Players on Creek View Road.
"We're offering audiences something completely different, something that was made with love," organizer Kazy Tauginas said. "Regardless of genre, the filmmakers that made these films, they put their souls into them, and you can feel it on the screen. I think that people will be very pleasantly surprised at the quality of the films that they're going to be watching."
The festival will feature 58 short films spanning many genres, including horror, drama, comedy, documentaries and art-house films. Filmmakers are coming from all over the United States and from as far away as Germany.
"Just hearing the stories and what people went through just to tell something that they felt was really important to them at that time, that separates us from what studio films are all made for," Tauginas said. "They're all profit-driven. Indies are a lot of times just driven by the heart."
There are also a number of films that were shot right here in Delaware, including "Return to Hockessin No. 107C," which is about the history of the Hockessin Colored School, and "Unseen American Dream," a documentary about a blind couple from Wilmington raising sighted children.
"Delaware locals have their own category at my festival," Tauginas said. "And then, of course, we have filmmakers from Los Angeles and New York and everywhere in between."
Tauginas is an actor, director and writer who has written and starred in more than 20 independent films. His acting career also has included guest spots in major television shows, and he has appeared in several movies, including "The Equalizer 2," starring Denzel Washington.
He lives in Newark and also works as a real estate agent and serves on the Newark Planning Commission.
The film festival will include the premier of the feature film "Mirror Life," which Tauginas wrote, directed and starred in. The movie is about a woman who's searching for her cousin who disappeared after entering an illegal human clinical trial.
Tauginas said that major film studios are moving more and more of their productions overseas, leading to fewer opportunities for actors here. That's part of what inspired him to start the film festival, to provide an opportunity to showcase more independent films.
"Filmmakers are going to be able to see their film on screen, in front of an audience, on the big screen with a dynamic sound system in a proper venue, so that it can get the attention that it deserves," he said. "I think it's a really important thing, especially for independent artists."
He added that he hopes the festival is an economic boost for Newark as the filmmakers from out of town arrive in Newark, stay at the Hyatt Place hotel on Main Street and patronize local restaurants and shops.
Tauginas, who used to own the Korner Diner on Main Street, said he knows that the summer is a slow time for Newark businesses. With a location right off Interstate 95 and a walkable downtown, Newark is a great place for the festival, he said.
"I can't think of a better place that you would want a film festival," he said.
The Newark Independent Film Festival will show 58 films in seven blocks spread over three days. Tickets for each block are $15. For more information and to buy tickets, visit newarkindependentfilmfestival.com.

title: Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences
author: Tom McCall
content:
Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Copper timpani, sliding trombones, heraldic trumpets and a focused baton are just some of the instruments making up the 45-member Mid-Shore Community Band. Band Leader Matt Fullerton keeps all the moving pieces in order.The band brought its music to Thompson Park on Nov. 9 during the Waterfowl Festival, and band members commanded a range from flutes to thundering drums.
But the most significant diversity the band exhibits is not in its musical abilities, but in the ages of its members.
Members of the band range from high schoolers to those in their upper 70s. There are people from all different walks of life who come together to make music.
"We do this because we love music. If nothing else it is therapy. No, it is a lot of fun," Fullerton said.
Fullerton has been conducting since 1975 and has a masters in music. He taught the band at Easton Middle school for 30 years. He said he can play most of the instruments in the band.
Tracie Thomas, who plays clarinet, has been in the band since its founding in 2009.
"One of the best parts is getting to play with my old musical director from middle school, Matt Fullerton," she said. "Just being able to play is the best part. We generally have a season, and we will have a repertoire for the season that we select for each concert. Of course we already have Christmas music out. We have started rehearsing for that."
She said they have everything from jazzy Christmas to sleigh ride Christmas music.
"We really try hard to be a part of the community. Our band is here to serve other nonprofits like we are today. Every concert we have played is no charge and often raising money for another organization. Everybody here is volunteering their time," Thomas said.
There was also a vast expanse of musical choices on display at the Nov. 9 concert, including a theme from the Disney film Fantasia "Night On Bald Mountain," a medley of computer gaming songs, a march and a hoedown.
"It includes themes from Assassin 33, 'Bratja' from Full Metal Alchemist, 'Dragon Born' from Skyrims, 'Sadness and Sorrow' from Naruto and 'Baba Yetu' from Civilization 4," Fullerton said of the gaming medley.
He noted that Hollywood used to produce most music, but the successful gaming industry is paying composers to make the digital worlds come alive.
"The same backing that creates that, as they do for themes for movies. It is possible that more people hear these than some of the pieces more than some of the movie themes," Fullerton said.
Of course the band also played a crisp "Star Spangled Banner" and got the crowd on their feet.
They practice at the Easton High band room every Tuesday at 7 p.m. They always looking for new players, even if they haven't dusted off their tuba in 10 years. To learn more, visit mscb.org.

title: Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved Wells Cove as the site for a proposed Black watermen's monument Aug. 26, further representing the history and legacy of the county's iconic industry.Tilghman Hemsley, a Queenstown artist and director of American Patriotic Monuments Inc., who created the original Kent Narrows watermen's monument 20 years ago, said he had been approached about the lack of Black representation in that project.
Seeking commissioner approval to establish the new monument on county property at Wells Cove, Hemsley presented mock-ups of the detailed sculptures.
Symbolizing the rich heritage of Black watermen, the monument will depict life-size bronze sculptures featuring a conversation between a head boat captain and an oyster boat worker, according to Hemsley. The piece will also feature other important aspects of the industry, including a man working with clams, a woman picking crabs, another cleaning fish, as well as a young boy with a fishing pole along for the experience.
"It's a sculpture that leans into the whole industry," Hemsley said.
"The piece is designed for the public to be able to come through and be part of the sculpture," he said.
With the history of the Black watermen engraved into the side of the pieces, "it's all about education," he said.
The monument is slated for a location between Bridges Restaurant and the Jetty restaurant. Hemsley emphasized the interactive nature of the work, allowing visitors the opportunity to pass between the pieces and engage with the sculptures as they visit the local area.
The watermen will be life-size bronze sculptures while the boat pieces will be stainless steel and powder-coated, he said.
Hemsley said the design of the pieces should make the monument low maintenance.
The project has already received approval from the Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation Department and a letter of recommendation from the Kent Narrows Foundation, he said.
The commissioners unanimously approved Wells Cove as the site for the proposed monument. Commissioner Jim Moran noted he would have preferred a competition among artists to design a tribute to Black watermen but supported the plan.
Hemsley noted time is of the essence if the statue is to be ready by July 4, 2026, in celebration of the country's 250th anniversary.
Serving as director of the project, Hemsley said various other artists will be involved in the sculpture work. The proposed monument has an advisory committee that includes watermen, he said.
With commissioner approval, the next steps include seeking funding grants, according to Hemsley.
Although highly appreciated, just like the original watermen's monument, the project would not be solely dependent on county support, he said.
The total cost for the project is estimated at about $475,000. The previous watermen's monument cost about $300,000, he said.
Statues typically take about three years to complete, but Hemsley was confident as long as funding came through.
"It's aggressive, but we can do it," he said.
A fundraising event with auctions, games and music will be held at the Kent Island American Legion Nov. 8 starting at 7 p.m., he said.
Hemsley is also working with the Centreville Veterans Information Committee to create a life-size statue honoring the more than 400 Black soldiers of Queen Anne's County who fought for the Union during the Civil War.
Working with Chesapeake Charities, the veteran statue committee has been hard at work establishing itself as a nonprofit, according to John Wright, statue committee chair.
Wright credited the enthusiasm of the committee in working to establish a historic monument.
"I'm glad I am in a position to help," he said.
With the sculpture to be completed in stages, the committee foresees about a year and a half before a statue stands in front of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center.
Donations can be sent to United States Colored Troops Memorial Fund, P.O. Box 42, Centreville, MD 21617.
As a Maryland nonprofit, American Patriotic Monuments Inc. seeks to lead public arts projects and monuments that celebrate American legacies.
More information, including sponsorship opportunities, can be found at apmiart.org.
Information about Hemsley's work can be found at tilghmanhemsleyfinearts.com.

title: Easton artists fair offers handmade treasures
author: SUBMITTED
content:
Easton artists fair offers handmade treasures

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED | Section: Life 
 
 281
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The annual Autumn Artists & Crafters Fair, offering an impressive display of original creations, will take place Saturday, Nov. 1, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the community center of Easton Club East at 29600 Lyons Drive in Easton.Visitors are invited to start their holiday shopping early while exploring handmade work in a diverse range of categories — jewelry, embroidery, greeting cards, crochet clothing, sea glass art, original photography and more. This show offers something for everyone — whether it's a thoughtful gift, unusual home accent or useful kitchen accessory.
"We promote crafting and artistic expression in our community," said Kathy Chroniger, the show organizer and lifestyle director at Easton Club East. "We hope shoppers will enjoy these handmade treasures as much as our artists enjoyed making them."
New exhibitors this year include Richard Roney-Dougal, a designer goldsmith who retired to Easton two years ago after working in art and jewelry on multiple continents and many U.S. states. He has exhibited in many of America's most elite shows, including the Philadelphia Museum of Art Contemporary Craft Show and American Craft Council's prestigious American Craft Made Show in Baltimore.
On Nov. 1, Roney-Dougal will be showing a series of small repoussé plaques made with copper and gold leaf. He calls them "fragments," with the "of what" left to the imagination of viewers.
Other exhibitors include pastel artist Donna Finley, jeweler Norma Lynch, crochet designer Reba Kushner, nature photographer Cal Jackson, embroidery artist Nancy Mocarsky and others.
Easton Club East is a large subdivision located off Dutchman's Lane in Easton. It hosts the annual show in its community center next to the subdivision entrance. In addition to free admission, the show offers plenty of free parking.
