Mid-Shore Calendar

 June 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Angela Price | Section: Calendar 
 
 2884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Those seeking to have an event published in the Star Democrat's calendar are asked to email details to community@stardem.com.YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 1 p.m. Yoga for advanced beginners with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
FIRST RESPONDERS CELEBRATION, 11 to 11:30 a.m., Service Memorial, corner of Dover and West Streets, Easton. Sen. Ben Cardin will join the Prager family and Bluepoint Hospitality in the celebration, recognizing Talbot County's finest. Following the ceremony, attendees are invited to enjoy a complimentary slice of authentic Roman-style pizza at nearby Bluepoint Hospitality eatery, Roma Alla Pala.
CLASSIC MOTOR MUSEUM TOUR, 10 a.m. to noon, Class Motor Museum, 102 Morengo, St Michaels. Embark on a fun journey through time and horsepower with our exclusive "Car Talk" tour of the Classic Motor Museum of St. Michaels. This immersive experience offers a unique opportunity to delve into the captivating world of automotive history, featuring a curated collection of vintage cars spanning from the iconic Model T to the sleek Mustang and Stingray. $35. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
YOGA ON NAVY POINT, 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, St. Michaels. Instructor Colleen Morrison will lead participants through an all-levels class on CBMM's waterfront campus. Registration is required and open now at bit.ly/CBMMYoga2024. The cost is $20 for a single session or $70 for all four sessions in May or June, with a 20% discount for CBMM members on all pricing.
YARN AND NEEDLE GROUP, 12:30 to 3 p.m., Brookletts Place Talbot County Senior Center, Easton. Every Tuesday. Some help may be available for knitting and crocheting. Open to anyone 60 years of age or older at no cost. Info: 410-822-2869.
NATIVE PLANTS FOR LANDSCAPED SPACES, 1 to 2:30 p.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Mikaela Boley, from the University of Maryland extension office here in Talbot County, as she walks us through the building blocks of creating a sustainable landscape that can provide us with years of enjoyment without negative impact on the environment. Three sessions, Tuesdays May 28, June 4 and 11, plus a field trip by car, Friday June 7. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.

Facebook: wednesdaymorningartists. Email is: wednesdaymorningartists@gmail.com
PLANNING FOR OUR FUTURE BEFORE IT REACHES US, 1 to 2:30 p.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join experts Gordan Fronk and Elena Sallitto as they demystify estate and elder planning, ensuring that you are well-prepared for the future. "Planning for Our Future Before It Reaches Us," delves into the intricate world of estate and elder law to safeguard your assets, make informed decisions, and prioritize the well-being of your loved ones. Two sessions, May 29 and June 5. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
POPLAR ISLAND TALK, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Learn about Poplar Island's unique story and continuing habitat successes in this talk given by Kristina Motley from Maryland Environmental Service. Poplar Island is an environmental restoration project located in the Chesapeake Bay of Talbot County, Maryland. The beneficial use project, started in the 1990's, relies on dredged material collected from the approach channels to the Baltimore Harbor to restore lost remote island habitat within the Chesapeake Bay. Two sessions, Wednesday June 5, and a field trip Monday, June 10, to Poplar Island from 9 a.m. to noon. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Raymond Vergne, M.D., as he turns his focus on the intriguing lives and careers of selected vice presidents from the 20th century. This course is the final chapter in his comprehensive series, offering a deep dive into the often overlooked but fascinating world of Vice Presidents. Three sessions, May 23, 30 and June 6. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
WATERFOWL FESTIVAL OPEN HOUSE, 2 to 7 p.m., 40 S. Harrison St., Easton. Ribbon cutting, book signing and more. The re-introduction of the Waterfowl Building to the community.
FIRST FRIDAY GALLERY WALK, downtown Easton. On First Friday, the art galleries of downtown Easton extend their hours and invite visitors on a tour of artistic adventure — openings, lectures, book signings and more.
CHESAPEAKE CHAMBER MUSIC FESTIVAL, Historic Ebenezer Theater, 17 South Washington Street, Easton. Chesapeake Music's 39th annual Chamber Music Festival will present six extraordinary concerts. For complete program listings and to purchase tickets, go to chesapeakemusic.org.

title: Country Cooking: Fresh fish for supper
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Fresh fish for supper

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1276
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An Eastern Shore tradition is certainly fresh caught fish from the local waters being served tonight in the local restaurants or Mom's kitchen. I have great memories of a fish for supper on West Line Road — near the Bay, the river and the ocean.My family were recreational fishermen and only fished on weekends or vacation days. Down the road from our farm, the late Mr. Frankie Savage spent his retirement years fishing locally and was known as "the fish man" by all in our area.
Mr. Frankie came in the yard in his old "fish pickup" with the back full of tubs of ice covering fresh caught fish — it was always in the afternoon, as his mornings were spent fishing. Mom would come with her "fish basin" ready to get her desired amount.
I will never forget Mr. Frankie's routine — pull up, uncover the iced fish, hang the scale on the sturdy pole and tell the kinds of fish he had caught. Mom would get "her desired amount of fish," better known in the country as "a mess of fish."
After weighing them, the fish were poured into Mom's basin, and she brought out her change purse to pay. Before Mom turned to return to the outside kitchen to clean them, Mr. Frankie would throw in some more fish and say, "Ms. Laurie, the wife and I loved that cornbread you sent down."
Mom would smile and say, "I'll be making more" as she walked over to the fish she was about to scale, clean and slice for pan-fried fish supper.
In the summertime, Mom always had freshly cooked collard or turnip greens, fresh garden picked homemade stewed tomatoes and a pan of cornbread. Did I mention the gallon jug of iced tea and/or lemonade?
I never heard Mom complain about these delicious meals that required a lot of work or about how it was too hot to cook. Mom always said her joy came from her family coming in the door saying, "Supper smells good, Mom" or "Hurry and wash up 'cause I'm hungry."
SHAD FISH ROE AND EGGS
2 eggs, 1 tsp milk, 1 sac of shad roe, 1 tsp butter, salt and pepper, green onions (chopped) — optional.
Scrape shad roe into the bowl. Mix eggs, salt, pepper and milk in a different bowl. Add roe and mix again. Melt butter in a medium size skillet. Cook the mixture just like you would be cooking scrambled eggs.
BAKED CATFISH
1 lb blue catfish fillets, 1/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup milk, Canola oil for frying, 1 cup ground yellow cornmeal, 2 eggs, 2-3 tsps Old Bay or J.O. Crab Seasoning (or to taste), salt.
Whip the eggs and milk together and add Old Bay or J.O. Crab Seasoning. Mix the cornmeal and flour together and place on a plate. Dip fillets in the seasoned egg mixture and place on the cornmeal/flour mixture, sprinkling the top of the filet with the dry mixture and pressing it in with your hand. Place prepared fillets on a baking sheet and let stand for 15 minutes. Preheat oil to 350 degrees on medium heat in a heavy cast iron skillet and carefully place fillets in oil when it is hot (to avoid crowding you may have to cook fish in batches). Fry until golden brown and crispy, about 2-3 minutes per side. Fish is done when it can be easily flaked with a fork. Place cooked fish on a plate lined with a paper towel and season with salt.
OVEN BAKED FISH
2 lbs fish (cleaned and filleted), 1 tbsp salt, 1 cup milk, 1 cup dried bread crumbs.
Cut fish into serving size portions. Add salt to milk. Dip fillets in milk and roll into dried bread crumbs. Place in a well greased baking pan. Sprinkle each piece of fish with minced or chopped butter pieces. Bake in a preheated 500-degree oven for 10 to 12 minutes or until fish flakes easily when touched with a fork. Serve with fresh vegetables and macaroni and cheese.
SALMON CAKES
1 lb. fresh salmon meat, 2 beaten eggs, 4 tbsps bread crumbs, 3-4 tbsps milk.
Combine salmon meat with eggs, bread crumbs and milk. Add one tablespoon of milk at a time to determine consistency. Mix and form into cakes. Fry in hot oil until golden brown on both sides.
BAKED FISH WITH TOMATOES
1 1/2 lbs fresh fish fillets, 2 tsps mustard, 3/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp Old Bay, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 2 fresh tomatoes, 1 cup grated parmesan cheese, 1/4 cup butter or margarine.
Cut fish fillets into serving sizes and single layer fish in a well greased two quart casserole dish. Spread mustard over the fish. Sprinkle salt, Old Bay seasoning and black pepper on top of mustard. Peel and slice tomatoes over top of mustard mixture. Mix together Parmesan cheese with butter or margarine and spread over the fish mixture. Cover and bake in a preheated 325-degree oven for 30 minutes.
GRILLED MARYLAND BLUEFISH
2 lbs Maryland bluefish fillets, 2 cups Italian salad dressing, 2 lemons (cut in wedges).
Place bluefish fillets in a baking dish. Pour dressing over fillets, cover and refrigerate for 2 hours. Place fillets on a hot, oiled grill. Baste fillets frequently with dressing and cook for about 10 minutes. Turn and baste again. Fillets are done when they just begin to flake when tested with a fork. Serve with lemon wedges. For convenient cooking on charcoal grill, cover grill with foil and poke holes in foil to circulate heat.
MARYLAND BAKED PERCH
3 lbs perch (dressed), 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 3 medium sliced mushrooms, 1/2 cup sliced onion, 1/4 cup chopped green pepper, 1 cup orange juice, 3 tbsps 1 tsp grated lemon rind, 1 tbsp flour.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Season fish with salt and pepper. Place fish in a baking dish. In a bowl, combine mushrooms, onions and green pepper. Spread vegetable mixture over fish. Combine remaining ingredients in a saucepan. Cook over moderate heat, stirring frequently until mixture thickens. Pour sauce over fish and vegetables. Bake for 6 to 8 minutes or until the fish flakes easily with a fork.
SIMPLE FRIED BLUEFISH
4 bluefish fillets, 1 bowl of milk, 2 eggs (beaten), 2 cups flour, 1/2 inch olive oil in a large skillet, 3 tbsps parsley (chopped), 1 tsp paprika, 1 tsp lemon pepper, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 lemon (cut into wedges).
Place all of the fillets in a bowl of milk and let soak for several minutes. Dip fillet in a bowl of well beaten eggs. Season flour with parsley, paprika, lemon pepper and salt. Roll each fillet in flour. Heat oil to medium-high. Place fillets in hot oil. Fry to a golden brown, turning once. Remove fillet from pan and layer over paper towels. Serve hot or cold with wedges of lemon.
GRILLED MARLIN STEAKS
2 large marlin steaks (about 3/4-inch thick), 1/3 cup pineapple juice, 2 tbsps grapeseed oil, 2 tbsps sesame oil, 1/2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce, 1 large clove garlic (minced), 1/2 tsp fresh ginger (minced), freshly ground black pepper to taste.
In a small bowl, combine pineapple juice, grapeseed oil, sesame oil, soy sauce, garlic, ginger and black pepper. Whisk all the ingredients until well blended. Put marlin steaks in a large resealable bag and pour the marinade over. Close the bag and massage/flip it until the steaks are well coated. Transfer to the refrigerator for 1 to 1 ½ hours, turning and massaging steaks once or twice. Preheat barbecue to 500-550 degrees. Place the marlin steaks on a plate and discard the marinade. Transfer the steaks on the hot grill, close the lid and grill for 3 minutes on one side. Flip them and cook for another 2 minutes with the lid closed.

title: Local students win top honors at state art contest
author: Staff Writer
content:
Local students win top honors at state art contest

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kent Island High School senior Mark Monroe and sophomore Aubrey Kline earned 2nd and 3rd place in The Arc of Maryland's "Together We're Better" Art Contest — marking the third consecutive year that Kent Island students have claimed top awards in the statewide competition.Their winning artwork will be published in The Arc of Maryland's annual coloring book, which will be on display at ArtScene 2025 at KIHS on May 1.
Kent Island art teacher Andrea Schulte was honored in spring 2024 with The Arc of Maryland's Statewide School Inclusion Award for her championing of students with disabilities and fostering a culture of empathy and accessibility in the arts.
For Schulte, this mission has become deeply personal. After suffering profound hearing loss this past year, she has become a member of the disability community herself—an experience that has only strengthened her passion for making art education more inclusive, while inspiring students to embrace their varied abilities. Her leadership in The Arc's "Together We're Better" initiative has not only provided students with intellectual and developmental disabilities greater opportunities in the arts but has also helped all students develop greater compassion, understanding, and inclusivity.
School district Fine Arts Supervisor Michael Bell accompanied Schulte to awards in support of her and her students. He said Schulte has gained momentum as a state arts leader, presenting at numerous conferences on empowering student voice. "Andrea's dedication — while navigating her own hearing loss journey — is nothing short of inspiring. She leads by example, showing students that their voices, stories, and creativity matter," said Bell.
Monetary prizes presented to the school have been used by Schulte's National Art Honor Society to host an annual art party for students with developmental disabilities — further reinforcing dedication to inclusive arts education.
"Mark and Aubrey have used their artistic talent to make a real impact, advocating for students with developmental disabilities through their work. We're proud of their accomplishments and excited to see them recognized at the state level," Principal Dan Harding said.

title: Learning the story of Harriet Tubman
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Learning the story of Harriet Tubman

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 History was brought to life with a performance telling the story of Harriet Tubman, an Eastern Shore native and one of the most significant abolitionists of her era.The Friends of Maxwell Hall, a group dedicated to preserving and bringing to light the history of the hall, put on a performance Feb. 15 featuring Shemika Renee, a first-person historical performer,
Mike Callahan, a member of the Friends of Maxwell Hall, shared a little bit of the property's history with Southern Maryland News.
The historic property was built by George Maxwell, a Scottish immigrant, approximately 255 years ago. Maxwell was a merchant and sold goods to local people and had grown tobacco on his property.
The house, situated on the Star Spangled Banner Trail, was in despair by the 1980s with holes in the ceiling and was purchased and remodeled to become the landmark it is today.
While Maxwell enslaved people, the story told at the house was one of triumph.
Renee delivered a riveting telling of Tubman's life through her perspective.
Renee started her performance by detailing the early years of Tubman, including her life-changing traumatic head injury that caused severe headaches throughout her life and narcolepsy.
She detailed how Tubman actually became "Harriet Tubman" as it was not her given birth name. Tubman was born Araminta Ross and had the nickname "Minty."
When she was older, she took her mother's name — Harriet — and her husband's last name of "Tubman" and became Harriet Tubman.
"I wanted to be free," Renee said while in character. "I will never forget that first sunrise when I knew I had crossed the border. … It was like the sun was gleaming down through the leaves, and the gold was just shining on my hands."
Echoing Tubman's actions of constantly going back to help family, friends and others find freedom, Tubman said, "I feel that I could have saved so many more people if they had even known that they was in bondage."
The Friends of Maxwell Hall hosts an annual colonial fair the third weekend of October every year, spirit investigations and a variety of other events. To find out more, go to www.friendsofmh.com/events.

title: Country Cooking: The other side of the barnyard
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The other side of the barnyard

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1187
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Driving down the country road to the farm, I realized that you always see one side of the barnyard as you turn into the driveway.This is the side where the water trough sits, and the feed containers are placed on metal tracks. The cows and hogs hang out here waiting to be fed. The corn cribs and the smokehouse are nearby.
On the other side of the barn is the area where the pony and goats hang out. At one time, we had a small lamb that we cared for while its owner was away. The goats would constantly get out and wander down to neighboring farms — eating everything in sight. They soon found new homes.
The Easter holiday is over, but I have some ham and lamb recipes I want to share with you. What was on your table for Easter dinner last week? For most, ham rates number one, with lamb, beef, seafood, turkey and chicken as other choices.
I know many families opt for lamb, but even though I know it is a very healthy choice, I just can't cook or eat lamb. Lamb meat comes from the young lambs and is a very rich source of iron, high quality of protein, zinc and vitamin B12.
I will include a lamb recipe today for those who like lamb. My mom always prepared the tastiest hams but only once or twice ever cooked lamb — probably because the children refused to eat it.
This past week I purchased a small ham — on sale — and decided to cook it instead of freezing it. It was delicious.
Ham and lamb can be eaten at any time of the year.
BONE IN BAKED HAM
This ham recipe comes from my kitchen. I have used it for many years. I purchase one whole bone-in ham, about 15 pounds and trim off any excess fat.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a mixing bowl combine one-pound brown sugar and 1/2 cup yellow mustard, mixing until you have a thick paste. Line a baking pan with foil, making sure the foil is long enough to fold over covering ham completely. Spray foil with cooking spray just in case the brown sugar mixture escapes from the foil. Place the ham on the foil and spread with sugar-mustard paste on top. Fold and seal foil. Keep ham sealed until cooking is complete — Bake for 4 hours. Check for doneness and let sit, covered, for another hour. Carve and serve.
NOTE: the ham bone will be great after Easter for seasoning in a pot of bean soup or ham and cabbage.
PINEAPPLE HAM
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Use a 8 to 10-pound ham and score the top in a diamond-shape, making the cuts half an inch deep. Place ham in a roasting pan. Mix together 3 cups brown sugar with 3 tablespoons yellow mustard, mixing until smooth and spooning onto top of ham. Mix together the juice from an 8-ounce can of pineapple rings and 1 cup honey. Drizzle this mixture over the ham and brown sugar paste. Place the pineapple rings on top of the ham and secure with wooden toothpicks. Cover and place in the preheated oven. After 15 minutes, remove the cover (foil or a lid) and baste with pan drippings, doing this several times until the scouring marks have opened, letting the juices seep into the meat. Continue baking until ham is well done according to size of ham (see package directions).
LEG OF LAMB
4 to 5-pound leg of lamb (bone-in, fat trimmed), salt and pepper, extra virgin olive oil, 5 garlic cloves (peeled and sliced), 2 cups water, 8 gold potatoes (peeled and cut into wedges), 1 yellow onion (peeled and cut into wedges), 1 teaspoon paprika,1 teaspoon all-natural garlic powder, fresh parsley for garnish (optional). For the rub: 15 garlic cloves (peeled), 2 tablespoons dried oregano, 2 tablespoons dried mint flakes, 1 tablespoon paprika, 1/2 tablespoons nutmeg, 1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil, juice of 2 lemons.
Take the leg of lamb out of the refrigerator and leave in room temperature for about 1 hour. In the meantime, prepare the remaining ingredients and make the lamb rub. Prepare the seasoning.
To make the rub or seasoning, in a food processor, combine the rub ingredients. Blend until smooth. Set aside (or in the fridge, if preparing in advance). Salt the meat. When ready, pat the lamb dry and make a few slits on both sides. Season with salt and pepper. Sear the Lamb. Turn the oven on broil. Place the leg of lamb on a wire rack and put it directly on the top rack so that it's only a few inches away from the broiler element. Broil for 5 to 7 minutes on each side or until the leg of lamb is nicely seared. Remove from the oven, then adjust the oven temperature to 325 degrees. Apply the seasoning or rub. When the lamb is cool enough to handle, insert the garlic slices in the slits you made earlier. Now cover the leg of lamb on all sides with the wet rub and place it in the middle of a roasting pan with an inside rack. Add two cups of water to the bottom of the roasting pan. Season the potato and onion wedges with paprika, garlic powder and a little salt, then add them to the pan on either side of the lamb. Cover and roast. Tent a large piece of foil over the roasting pan (make sure it does not touch the lamb) then place the pan on the middle rack of the 325-degree oven. Roasted for about 1 hour. Remove the foil and return the roasting pan to the oven for another 15 to 20 minutes or until the lamb temperature registers 125 degrees. Let rest. Remove the pan from the oven and let the leg of lamb rest for about 15 to 20 minutes before serving (the lamb will continue to cook, and its internal temperature will continue to rise to around 130 degrees).Place the roast lamb and potatoes in a large serving platter over a bed of rice, you like. Garnish with parsley. Or you may carve the lamb first, then arrange the sliced lamb with the potatoes over the rice.
BAKED PINEAPPLE
Multiple generations love this side dish. My son John will eat this even as a dessert or breakfast dish. It goes perfect with any of these recipes today.
One 20-ounce can of crushed pineapple including juice, ¾ cup granulated sugar, 2 large eggs, 2 tablespoons cornstarch, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, 1 ½ tablespoons butter (divided into small pats), 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon.
Preheat your oven to 350 degrees. Lightly grease a 9-by-9-inch baking pan to prevent sticking. In a mixing bowl, add the crushed pineapple (with its juice), granulated sugar, eggs, cornstarch and vanilla extract. Stir until the mixture is smooth. Transfer the pineapple mixture into a greased baking pan. Evenly distribute the small pats of butter across the surface of the mixture, then sprinkle with ground cinnamon to enhance flavor. Bake for 45 minutes, or until the mixture begins to exhibit a golden hue perfectly caramelized. Let cool and serve.

title: You are what you read at the Talbot County Free Library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
You are what you read at the Talbot County Free Library

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 729
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Ralph Waldo Emerson famously claimed, "A man is what he thinks about all day long." Modern-day foodies have come up with something similar, if slightly more prosaic: "You are what you eat."Both maxims are, I suppose, to one degree or another, true.
In my own case, two streams seem to have moved through my life, building and eroding as they went. The first of these has been, of course, life itself, the experiences of love and rejection, success and failure, learning and loss that, in toto, affect and effect a life.
But in my case, and surely that of any lover of the written word, there is that second, somewhat less obvious current: one's reading material.
I'll never forget the uneasiness I experienced when, upon entering sixth grade, I detected an unexpected shift in the behavior of my peers. Boys I had known and played hide-'n-seek with since first grade were suddenly putting Brylcream in their hair, flirting with girls and talking about cars.
When I compared the great loves of my life (sandlot baseball, fishing, games of kick-the-can and ghost-at-midnight) with these new pursuits, I found the latter decidedly wanting. Why would anyone want to worry about what their hair looked like when they could go outside and climb a tree?
Looking back on it now I realize I was, at ten years of age, just old enough and smart enough to suspect what was being asked of me: that I turn my back on the joys of boyhood and march blindly into what looked to me like a minefield of grown-up responsibility. Peter Pan could not have asked for a better recruit.
And so it was that, in my last year of elementary school, I consciously rebelled against my fellow students' desire to grow up before their time. Taking Huck Finn as my model of the boyhood I wished to preserve, I began wearing a straw hat and took to bicycling through the neighborhood with a cane-pole slung across my handle bars.
I was too young to realize that, even in this, I was showing the first signs of growing up. Instead of imitating, as I had for years, TV cowboys and WW2 combat soldiers, I was imitating a character out of a book.
It was a formula that would serve, and sometimes disserve, me all my life.
As a teen I read Hemingway, took up hunting and, to my shame, began to speak disparagingly of men I deemed unmanly. As a young adult, I read Henry Miller, rented a room in a flophouse and adopted a bohemian lifestyle.
It was probably a combination of both authors' influence that drove me, at 24, to Santa Fe. In those days, before Ralph Lauren discovered it, New Mexico's capital still had a sleepy foreign air to it … and I couldn't afford a flight to Paris.
It was during my second spring in the Land of Enchantment that — thanks to the paperback copy of Joyce Cary's "The Horse's Mouth" I saw protruding from her purse — I was able to work up the courage to approach the most beautiful girl in town. I give Cary's protagonist, Gulley Jimson, another of my literary alter egos, full credit for introducing me to the woman who would become my wife.
Melissa, in turn, introduced me to Virginia Woolf and, for the first time in my life, I found myself trying not so much to imitate a character from fiction as to imitate the fiction itself, to write descriptions true enough to life that a character like Mrs. Ramsey might (I prayed) emerge from my scribblings.
There have been other writers whose talents I have emulated and envied — Alice McDermott, Wendell Berry, Arundhati Roy and Graham Swift, to name a few — and I still come across characters worthy of imitation as well (Berry's Burley Coulter always springs to mind), so that now, at 72 years of age, I can even wonder how much of my life has been of my own making, and how much a mere product of literature.
Which leads me to the following conclusion: If we must be careful about what we think about all day, as it presages what we will become, then we must be equally careful about what we read.
The Talbot County Free Library is many things — archive, lending library, refuge, incubator, lecture hall, community hub. But it is also, fundamentally, a forging-place of the soul.

title: Artists dazzle at second annual Plein Air Adkins
author: Contributed
content:
Artists dazzle at second annual Plein Air Adkins

 November 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 345
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Saturday, Nov. 4, Adkins Arboretum continued its mission to provide an exceptional experience in nature with free admission to its second annual Plein Air Adkins paint out, exhibit and sale.This event gave both artists and the public a memorable and immersive encounter with the native landscape on a perfect autumn day.Forty-one artists painted the Arboretum's wetlands, meadows and woodlands while observers watched, walked and soaked in the warm fall colors.As blank canvases and panels became works of art, the public could see nature as interpreted through each artist's eyes. Live music and food trucks complemented the festivities.Artists painted from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., then framed their works and exhibited them on their easels at the edge of the South Meadow behind the Visitor's Center. The public browsed and made purchases as judge Alison Barry reviewed the work and chose the award winners.Barry, the grand prize winner of last year's inaugural event, said the quality of the work was outstanding, and she could have given even more awards.In her judging, she looked for excellent handling of the artist's medium and good use of composition, color and values. Barry also sought paintings that were not just journalism dutifully recording the scene but instead revealed the character of the artists and a poetic interpretation of the landscape.The award winners were:■Grand Prize: Christine Rapa■Second: Amanda Milliner■Third: Pamela Chase■Honorable Mention: Nancy Fine, Rhonda Ford, Richard Fritz, Jose Ramirez and Maureen Wheatley■Artist's Choice: Homer Proctor."Don't miss the experience of seeing nature through a painter's eyes at the 3rdAnnual Plein Air Adkins on Saturday, Nov. 2,2024," the arboretum said in a press release. "There's none other like it!"Plein Air Adkins is sponsored in part by the Caroline County Council of Art, Choptank Electric Cooperative and Unity Landscape Design/Build.Adkins Arboretum is a 400-acre native garden and preserve at the headwaters of the Tuckahoe Creek in Caroline County.For more information, visit adkinsarboretum.org.

title: A spectacular choral performance at Temple B'Nai Israel
author: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat
content:
A spectacular choral performance at Temple B'Nai Israel

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Music 
 
 388
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The house was absolutely full on Saturday, July 27, as people gathered at Temple B'Nai Israel to see this year's Allegro Academy Summer Choir Festival.The audience ranged from children in arms to senior citizens, with some folks even standing, waiting for the promise of a rich program of Gospel music, featuring a Choral Mass by Robert Ray.
The choir of almost 70 was led and conducted by Amy Morgan, the founder and artistic director of the Allegro Academy. In just three weeks of intensive practice and rehearsals, Morgan nurtured the choir into a wonderful powerhouse of symphonic harmony, which reverberated through the Temple.
Accompanying the choir were some highly distinguished musicians, who also supported the solo vocalists Ta'vea Roberts, an Easton High School student, and John Wesley Wright, a professor of music at Salisbury University.
The concert erupted into action with the upbeat traditional Spiritual "Great Day," followed by "Music Down In My Soul" by Moses Hogan. "Ascribe to the Lord" by Rosephanye Powell completed the first triad of songs by the full choir. The Allegro Singers, an all female group of the full choir, then lowered the tempo with a haunting Stacey Gibbs arrangement of "Swing Low," followed by an upbeat number, "Still I rise" by Rosephanye Powell featuring Roberts singing the most stunning, soaring high notes.
The full choir then delivered the main feature, Robert Ray's "Gospel Mass," through the six sections of the Mass from the "Kyrie"….Lord Have Mercy" to the final "Agnus Dei" featuring Wright. This slow tempo song, with its unforgettable and moving melody and lyrics, had many a damp eye in both audience and choir.
The finale of the evening was the song "Total Praise" by Richard Smallwood, which featured the whole choir and instrumentalists including drums, bass, piano, keyboards and guitar. The final "Amen" sent a soundwave a bit like a choral version of Phil Spector's "wall of sound" echoing through the rafters, and the audience exploded in a standing ovation.
This was a great production, driven by the highly talented Morgan, whose disciplined and motivating teaching style coached out accurate multipart harmonies that delivered a beautiful, rich, balanced choir sound that will be long remembered by both audience and performers.
The wonderful coincidence of a Christian-based Choral Mass in a Jewish Temple reminds us all that great music binds us together, whatever our color or creed.

title: Dancers bring Hispanic culture to Chestertown - Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge highlights program
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Dancers bring Hispanic culture to Chestertown - Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge highlights program

 October 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News

 Words

 CHESTERTOWN - Stunning costumes, festive dancing, and heartfelt songs were joyfully celebrated at the Kent County Alliance's final event celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month at the Raimond Cultural Center last weekend.Events throughout the month included an exhibit for art and poetry featuring paintings by Granillo, poems by Iris Figueroa, and textiles of Latin America; an outdoor festival with Talavera painting workshops for children, a dance party, and food trucks with Latino offerings; along with Saturday's music events. All were supported by the Kent Cultural Alliance, the Kent County Local Management Board, and E(Ñ)E: Alliance for Hispanic Culture and Community founded by Granillo.Highlighting Saturday's program were performers from the Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge who performed popular dancing styles from Mexico, while the second dance group led by Maria Lopez from Delaware were based on Guatemalan dances.Lopez said the colorful costumes and masks were the typical, long-standing costumes used by Guatemalans even at the time of the Conquest. The second dance's music was from a marimba, which, Lopez said, pays homage to their forefathers that began this rhythm.Originally from Argentina, vocalist Sergio Cilla shared with the audience three tangos and three folklore songs from different parts of his country. "When you think of Latin music, you think of something fun and colorful," Cilla said. "Tangos, which began in the 1920s, are generally melancholy, with lyrics that usually have something about loss." His first two pieces were titled "Nothing" and "The Simple Things." Next came the sambas, with the first "Samba to Forget" with a typical melody that comes from the northwest part of Argentina.He also performed a more festive "Ballad for a Crazy Man" that represented the freedom that can come from letting go of one's inhibitions.His final number was titled "Song with Everyone" and was shared in the different countries of Argentina, Chile, Peru, and Brazil."It was meant for all voices to sing as one," said Cilla.At the end of the evening, Granillo who learned to play at the age of 14, took up his acoustic guitar.The first piece he learned, he recalled, was a song he kept hearing again and again.Not knowing any English, he imagined what it could mean, and tried to make the same sounds he heard in recordings.He began playing the song for the evening's audience and everyone recognized it at once - "Let it Be" by the Beatles.Granillo also shared one of the first songs he had written."When I reached out to my colleagues in the community about possibly doing these events, they were ready to start work," said Fredy Granillo, local artist and musician and the coordinator for the programs in September."I believe we all need to learn from each other." "In all that we do at the Alliance, we maintain a sharp focus the role arts and culture plan in connecting people," said Kent Cultural Alliance Director John Schratwieser."By allying the arts and humanities together, we can build stronger communities through those things which connect us."

title: The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist
author: Tom McCall
content:
The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Ronnie Wells has been coming to the Waterfowl Festival for 28 years. But this year is a little different — he has been chosen as the featured poster artist.When this Texan got the call for this monumental honor, he realized he had to make the art. He was asked to create a sculpture and a painting to be made into the 2024 poster. The two works are of canvasback ducks landing in water only to discover that there is a stiff-looking decoy they have come to.
"They asked me would you be willing to do the poster as well as the sculpture. I said I would be honored," Wells said.
Wells based the works on a Ward Brothers 1936 canvasback duck decoy. Wells thinks 1936 was decoy carvers' peak year of expertise and creativity.
"I have always admired the Ward Brothers and their contribution to the art of decoy carving. I recently collected a 1936 model Canvasback Drake, which I used in the sculpture and the poster. They were artists and didn't even know it," Wells said.
Wells calls the canvasback the king of ducks. He loves the distinct noise their shorter wings make when they fly.
Wells is a hunter, and he said there are canvasbacks that make it to Texas.
"I have never killed a canvasback. I actually knocked one down and never found it and it bugs me to this day," he said. "It is one of my favorite ducks to paint and sculpt. They are such a magnificent looking ducks. They have a wide body and a Roman nose as far as a beak. Thick neck, they call them bull necks."
His inspiration for the poster and the sculpture was clear to him.
"When they called, I first thought of ducks as kind of my forte, and then I thought canvasbacks. The third thing I thought about was the Ward Brothers," he said.
After he got the call from the festival to create the poster, he started making thumbnail sketches of ducks. He sent that pencil sketch in for approval. Ultimately he created the final image in oil.
Wells has had a long career in the arts. He got an art degree and made a living as a medical illustrator. At the hospital where he worked, young doctors kept buying the miniature bronzes that he brought in to the office and put on his desk.
Wells will have an exhibit set up in the clear-roofed tent across from the Waterfowl Building during the festival. While still getting ready, he and his wife Patricia are unloading the art to be displayed. She handles all the driving and cleaning the sculpture with a Swiffer.
"He sculpts while I drive the box truck," she said.
Wells made three big sculptures for the festival. One has already sold.
The official festival sculpture was taken to the Tidewater Inns Crystal Room for the unveiling Thursday night. He made copies, and each one sells for $35,000.
As a market, a cultural event and a community of friends, the festival, "is such a fun thing to do. I have two of my old duck hunting buddies that we hunted in East Texas for 30 years. They came just for this event. I was shocked when they said they are going to be there. They are staying at the Tidewater. That is an honor in itself,' said Wells.
"This is kind of my swan song," he said, "even though it is a canvasback."

title: Local chef nominated for James Beard Award
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Local chef nominated for James Beard Award

 February 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although Bas Rouge is getting national attention, it is a local restaurant at its core.On its menu, passion for the Chesapeake takes center stage, says Executive Chef Harley Peet. His efforts to celebrate the Eastern Shore's people and ecology have helped land him on the shortlist for one of the culinary industry's most prestigious awards.
The James Beard Foundation has named Peet as a semifinalist for best chef in the Mid-Atlantic region. Just getting considered is a "huge deal" for the team at Bas Rouge, the executive chef said.
"I have never pursued it because I was so intimidated by it. But then I built this amazing team, and Mr. (Paul) Prager, the owner, helped me build this amazing team and put this amazing restaurant together," Peet said. "... Then we started getting the influx. Going for the James Beard built a lot of confidence in myself and in my team."
Established in 1990 and first awarded in 1991, the James Beard Foundation's Restaurant and Chef Awards recognize exceptional talent and achievement in the culinary arts, hospitality, media and broader food system, as well as a demonstrated commitment to racial and gender equity, community, sustainability and a culture where all can thrive, according to the James Beard website.
Nominees for the award will be announced on Wednesday, April 3, and winners will be announced at the James Beard Restaurant and Chef Awards Ceremony on Monday, June 10.
The Bas Rouge team draws inspiration from the endless bounty of the Chesapeake to inform its menu, which offers European-style dishes made with local ingredients.
"Every year, every turn of the season it absolutely floors me with something that tastes even better," Peet said. "The natural shift of final products that are coming out of the Bay or coming out of the fields in the summer, they continuously always get better. The purveyors, and the growers and the foragers that we deal with are constantly trying to find something better, something more mind blowing."
"This is a miraculous thing about this area. It never disappoints," he said.
These local ingredients are transformed into elegant dishes in Bas Rouge's kitchen, including the restaurant's lunchtime favorite wiener schnitzel, an array of oysters and, when the chefs have it in, a Dover sole that Peet says draws diners from as far as D.C.
"It is food that we love and have a passion to cook and eat," Peet said. "I think the idea of taking a raw ingredient from the Chesapeake Bay or from a field delivered to the back door by a forager. What do you do in these small towns? You fish, you hunt, you gather because it is fun. It is part of the lifestyle here. So as far as what the food is about and has to say, the food is about myself and my team taking as much local (as we can), accented with fine imported ingredients because of course you have to have some diversity."
"We have a hyper focus on what we have right here," he said.
But beyond the Chesapeake's flora and fauna, Peet said that he has decades of lived experiences on the Eastern Shore from which he draws inspiration.
He recalled one time 20 years ago when he was just out of culinary school and his first assignment was on Tilghman Island. He was using oysters in a dish, but he wanted to know where the ingredients came from.
There was a bus boy who also worked as a waterman. Peet got an invitation to go oystering.
"So I am up there in my sailing gear. And these watermen are laughing at me. They are in white rubber boots and Grundens, and I am out there in Haley Hansen and Patagonia. They said, 'You know we are about to get dirty?' And I said, 'Alright, let's do it.'"
He learned by doing. He learned how oyster tonging works, how dredging works and how patent tonging works. He even learned how certain boats are rigged.
"If you don't understand that, then preparing (the ingredient) and serving it lacks a little passion. We have a round-about 360-degree connection with that. Terroir is a number one," said Peet.

 The Wye Parish Bazaar will mark its 60th anniversary on Saturday, Nov. 1, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Parish Hall and on the grounds of Old Wye Church on Route 662 in Wye Mills.The Christmas Shoppe will feature decorations, many handmade by the church ladies. Winter blooming plants including amaryllis, Christmas cactus and paper whites will be available. Trinkets and Treasures will offer jewelry and other items, while Handmades will include mittens.
The Sweet and Savory Shoppe will sell homemade cakes, cookies and pies, as well as brandied cranberries, fruitcake, jams and jellies, bread-and-butter pickles, basil paste and herbed olive oil.
New this year is the Emporium, located under a tent by the church, offering bargain-priced items. The Christmas Book Cottage in the Vestry House will sell books at 80 percent off, including adult and children's titles, holiday-themed books, cookbooks, puzzles and stocking-stuffers.
The Bazaar Cafe will serve vegetable crab soup, sausage and potato soup, Italian wedding soup, country ham biscuits and Smith Island cake.
At 11 a.m., the Wye Parish town crier will announce a performance by the Queen Anne's Chorale of Christmas music in Old Wye Church. Church tours will be offered throughout the morning. The church has been restored to its original 1721 condition.
The bazaar is a fundraising activity of the Episcopal Church Women of Wye Parish. Proceeds will be donated to Haven Ministries, Compass Regional Hospice and Tides of Grace.

 DENTON — Artsway Banners are back in Denton for the third year in a row.In partnership with 12 artist, the Caroline County Council of the Arts placed the banners around town, with this years theme highlighting "Everyday Magic."
According to the Council of Arts website, the theme represents "the magic you experience on a everyday basis in Denton, showcasing the beauty, unity, and positivity that define our community."
The program is important for showcasing the county's arts scene, organizers said.
"It facilitates the presence of art in the community," said George K. Karos, executive director of Caroline County Council of Arts. "There's a wonderful opportunity for Caroline County artists countywide to take the banner and create what they want...

The banners well be hung up for a couple of months and will be auctioned off after they are taken down.

title: 'Friendship set to music': Club aims to keep square dancing alive on the Eastern Shore
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Friendship set to music': Club aims to keep square dancing alive on the Eastern Shore

 October 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester Square Dance Club is a lively bunch who enjoy each other's company just as much as they enjoy dancing.Some members joined a few months ago. Others have been a part of the club for over 15 years.
According to longtime member Roger Parks, there used to be around 17 square dancing clubs on the Eastern Shore.
Now, there are only two.
To keep the Dorchester Square Dance Club alive, Parks went to caller school and called for free to sustain the club through pandemic-era challenges. The caller plays a critical role in square dancing, directing dancers through the steps.
The group's current caller, Dennis O'Neale, began calling in 2006.
"Calling is a matter of me telling people what to do. We split it up into two parts, what we call the patter part, which I move people around and get them used to whatever calls I tend to work with," O'Neale said.
The second part is a singing call, during which O'Neale gives the instructions taught during the patter part through song. He changes the words of the songs to fit the calls, which is melodic and smooth.
"Square dancing is one of the most unique things because you can go all around the world and its the same. There's square dancing in Japan, Germany, China, Russia, and every caller in those countries calls in English," O'Neale said.
According to the club's head Bill Mocarsky, this is because all of the training for calling is done in English.
O'Neale described square dancing as "friendship set to music," emphasizing community and family over competition. While watching the members dance, their smiles were noticeable and if someone missed a call or messed up, everyone giggled and kept it moving.
The club is not only fun, but O'Neale and Parks are grateful that it offers mental and physical engagement while still being affordable at $10 a night. The members sometimes mix it up by doing round dances, easy line dances and other family-friendly dances like the Virginia Reel and Bingo Waltz.
Square Dancing is generally correlated with country music, but the club dances to a diverse range of genres and artists. Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell and Fleetwood Mac were among the artists O'Neale called to on Tuesday night. He said Patti LaBelle's "New Attitude" is his favorite song to call to.
"We're having a good time socializing. We don't smoke in our dance area, we don't drink in our dance area and we could be a church group or not, but the key is, we're making a family," O'Neale said. "Anywhere you go, if you're a square dancer, or you go to a square dance club, you instantly have a new family."
The Dorchester Square Dance Club is always accepting new members of all ages and backgrounds. They meet every Tuesday at Maple Elementary School in Cambridge at 5:30 p.m.

title: A New-Englander brings her poetry to the Eastern Shore
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A New-Englander brings her poetry to the Eastern Shore

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Columns 
 
 731
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Poetry is a funny thing. Really, it's a shape-shifter.I'm a little slow when it comes to poems. I can only read one at a time and can only do that when I have the time to really give the poem the attention it deserves — which sadly, even in retirement, seems to happen less and less often these days.
That "shape-shifter" remark is the result of Sue Ellen Thompson's poem "The Nest," published in her most recent book, "Sea Nettles" (811.54 Thom).
I read "The Nest" for the first time, I don't know, maybe a week or two ago. Sitting by the fire, a glass of bourbon on the table beside me, I made my way through its three simple verses and was pleased.
The first and third verses were spot on, but I sort of slid over the second. On the whole, I thought it a good poem, if perhaps not one of Sue Ellen's best. I am a big Sue Ellen Thompson fan. She is far and away one of my favorite poets.
But I also know myself well enough not to trust a first reading. Even mid-poem, my mind can wander and miss something important. Maybe it's the bourbon.
Anyway, last night I gave "The Nest" a second chance. And I thank the nine muses that I did.
The poem concerns something with which I am all too familiar these days: aging — a pair of older friends, husband and wife. He is just out of the hospital and visibly reduced by his illness. She is worried, attentive. That second verse I blew over in my first reading ends with a sentence describing the wife:
Her features still have their fine,
flared edge, but fear of losing him
has made their beauty more difficult
to admire, like the silver serving dish,
its surface battered by knives.
My brain's voice-over tends toward exclamation, and this line elicited an unqualified "Oh my God!"
I mean, where do poets come up with analogies like that? Who would ever think to compare the damage fear can effect upon a well-preserved beauty to a silver serving dish? But isn't it perfect? Think about the women you've known who have lived long enough and loved well enough to know what losing the love of their life will cost them. For that matter, think about the men.
A silver serving dish battered by knives. I'd give my left arm to come up with a simile like that, and I coasted right over it on my first reading, missed it entirely. Shape-shifters indeed.
Though I suspect Sue Ellen will always be a New Englander at heart (and there is, I believe, something austere and flinty about her writing that, to my Southern ear, smacks of the Northeast), she has now lived in Talbot County for almost 20 years.
Anyone who's ever swum in the Chesapeake will recognize in the title of her latest book the influence our region now holds upon her as well. What a gift it is to have a poet of her accomplishments living here. Her readings at the Avalon, her lectures at the Talbot County Free Library, the classes she teaches — she has enriched our lives.
Not too long ago, I shot Sue Ellen an email extolling Jane Hirshfield's poetry and thanking her for introducing me to that wonderful writer. Sue Ellen, ever generous, replied that Hirshfield is, in her opinion, an "essential poet." I love that phrase, that idea, that there are poets out there that are essential, necessary, like oxygen or water.
In her anthology, "The Autumn House Anthology of Contemporary American Poetry" (811.508 AUTU), Sue Ellen has introduced me to any number of "essential poets" — Doug Anderson, Hayden Carruth, Robert Hass, Maxine Kumin, Sharon Olds and Jane Kenyon come immediately to mind.
But there is of course another. The Eastern Shore holds many treasures, but surely one of them is Sue Ellen Thompson.
On Monday, April 14, at 6 p.m. in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, Sue Ellen will present a combination lecture/reading she's entitled "Writing About Family." If you know her poetry, I'm sure you have been struck, as I have been, by how candidly and unflinchingly Sue Ellen writes about those she loves.
I am very much looking forward to hearing how she manages to handle such volatile material without damaging the very relationships she seeks to honor.
Oh, and don't forget: April is National Poetry Month. See you in the 800s.

title: REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 890
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GILPIN POINT - Descendants and dignitaries gathered Sunday, Nov. 5, to commemorate the valor and patriotism of a local Revolutionary War hero.Members of the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution honored the memory of Col.William Richardson by placing a bronze marker on his grave at 1 p.m. on the unseasonably warm and calm day.Richardson's descendants gathered to unveil the marker and place a wreath on his grave. About 100 people attended and participated in the ceremony at Gilpin Point Park near Harmony, on a tiny parcel of his former plantation.Born in 1735 in Talbot County, Richardson was colonel of the Fifth Regiment of the Maryland Line and the Eastern Shore Battalion of the Flying Camp. He fought at the Battle of Harlem Heights. He died in 1825 at Gilpin Point.Colonel Richardson Middle and High schools in Federalsburg are named for him.Colonel Richardson High School alumnus and band director Thomas Cheezum led the school's marching band in a selection of patriotic songs and armed forces hymns."I love it," Cheezum said. "I mean, this is something that I live for because I'm a part time historian, and I am a big believer in truth, justice and the American way." Chapter Regent Jerry Seiler served as mistress of ceremonies and introduced as the first speaker Elizabeth Deering, state vice regent of the Maryland State Society, Daughters of the American Revolution."We are one of the largest women's organizations in the world, with over 3,000 chapters in all 50 states, Washington D.C. and overseas," Deering said. "The placement of markers is a tangible way to honor and connect with Revolutionary War ancestors and to also raise public awareness of their service." "Today we honor a revolutionary war patriot, Col. William Richardson, who served our nation as a Continental Army officer, and later in life as a politician," Deering said. "He helped to decide whether Maryland should ratify the proposed Constitution of the United States." Also participating in the ceremony were other leaders of the Maryland State Societies of the Daughters and Sons of the American Revolution.Speakers included State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R - 37) and Caroline County Commissioner Frank Bartz.On behalf of the Commission, Bartz said the marker is a "symbol of our collective gratitude and a pledge to uphold the memory of those who laid the foundation for our nation" as well as "a lasting reminder of the courage, sacrifice and unwavering spirit that shaped the history of our great nation." Mautz presented a citation on behalf of the Maryland General Assembly."The most significant aspect of today is to have our students and our youth and our next generation here to understand how we got to where we are," he said."Thank you for allowing me to relive fond memories and create new memories today," Richardson descendant Kristen Dukes said. "By mere chance, my family and I have fallen into this honored lineage of a true patriot.We owe much to his great achievements, such as the establishment of Caroline County, his leadership at the Battle of Harlem Heights and his direct involvement in electing George Washington as the first President of the United States." Another descendant, Petty Utermohle, told the crowd her mother "loved to say that he was known as the 'Fighting Quaker.'" "He was a Quaker until he was removed or, as she put it, kicked out of the meeting house because he was a soldier, and they were peaceful people," she said. "Thankfully, he made that decision." Seiler credited Caroline County Parks and Recreation employees for sprucing up the area around the grave, which had become overgrown.Following the marker dedication by Elizabeth Hinson and Suzanne O'Donnell, the descendants gathered at the end of the grave to unveil the marker and lay a wreath.A 3-volley musket salute was followed by a CRHS band member playing Taps.The Rev. Daniel Gedman, pastor of St. Luke's Global Methodist Church in Denton, who prayed the invocation, also concluded the ceremony with a benediction.

title: Eastern Shore photographer wants people to know what happens in Delmarva communities
author: Tom McCall
content:
Eastern Shore photographer wants people to know what happens in Delmarva communities

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At a gallery show opening at ShoreToBeFun Photography on Aug 22, Steve Atkinson laid out cheese, crackers and tea next to his array of prints, which adorned a variety of canvases. From coffee mugs, to cotton bags to coasters, to greeting cards, to big framed prints, he has found many ways of presenting his work.Atkinson, a photographer, can be seen at nearly every Caroline County Chamber of Commerce Event with his Pentax camera, his signature gray beard, and his gentle demeanor. It's these moments he loves to capture.
"The heart of Caroline County is the community. There is a good sense of community in, especially in Denton. People are trying to help each other," Atkinson said.
He got his start because he wanted people to know about what was going on in the area.
"In 2006, I started an online calendar of events. It was called Shoretobefun. It was the only calendar I knew of that had events from every county on the Delmarva peninsula. I started going to events, sometimes I was reporting. And I figured, 'Why don't I start taking photos of the event,'" he said.
Atkinson lives in Kent County and gives the same dedicated coverage to that county too.
"I enjoy taking photos at events and sharing them with the people there," he said.
But his work captures more than just the happenings on the Eastern Shore. Atkinson is also interested in pursuing his own unique vision. Clouds really grab his attention.
"I enjoy shooting clouds and anything to do with the history and heritage of the area. I am reestablishing a site called Explore Chesapeake Country through my photos. Once a week, I was doing a photo of those highway historical signs that you zoom by at 100 miles an hour. The big white metal ones," he said.
He loves the marker across from the Caroline County Courthouse, which commemorates a 1938 speech by then-President Franklin D. Roosevelt at that site.
His fine artwork takes in sunsets, blue herons, tall ships with fireworks and watermen, which he shares with others through his shop.
"Mostly I am retired. I get retirement income. This store has been open two years. I have been calling it an eclectic gift shop. Tracey Snyder was looking at this building as a great incubator site. So she brought me and the landlord together. That is how this store happened," he said.
"I don't think I am good at photography. People tell me I am good and I say, 'OK if you say so.' I think I have an eye for some uniqueness. I want the pictures that I produce to be something that if you happen to go by that location, it looks like that. The camera sees things differently than we do," he said.
Although he uses a camera in his work, he thinks he offers more than that.
"I am a creator. I can create unique gifts through a process called sublimation," he said. "I can put photos on slate, cutting boards, mugs. Those are created in house. I made them."

 RIDGELY - As bluegrass musicians picked and strummed, members and friends of St. Benedict - St. Elizabeth Catholic churches enjoyed the music, along with fellowship, good food and drink at the parish's second annual Bluegrass Festival Saturday, July 22, in Ridgely.Headlining the festival was local bluegrass favorite Flatland Drive. title: Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — From iconic Hispanic icons like Frida Khalo, to colorfully rich portraits of Guatemala landscapes, to a tree with all the Hispanic flags hanging from its branches, the Academy Art Museum was filled with a variety of portraits.In celebration of Hispanic cultural heritage, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center hosted a poster competition and invited community members to rejoice in the submissions.
Every year, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center asks the Hispanic community to participate in choosing a theme for the annual celebration. Victoria Gomez Lozano, deputy director for Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said the theme for this year is "Ser Hispano, es Ser Valiente," which translates to "Being Hispanic is Being Brave."
The top three posters win prizes, and the first place poster will be used as the official poster for the 2025 Hispanic Heritage Month in Easton.
Roxana Tapia, judge of the competition, said the first, second and third place winners this year came from various ages and ethnicities. But they all had the common goal of celebrating Hispanic heritage.
"You don't even have to be a Latina in order to participate," Tapia said. "What I liked about this year is that we have people from all ethnicities. So if for any kids, I invite them to come over and participate, it's always fun. (Artists) should be proud of their work."
The winners of this year's competition were Piper Hambleton and Ellis Williams for their collaborative work. Their poster portrayed a large tree with flags from every Latin American and Hispanic country attached to its branches.
Alberto Gamez, a judge and ChesMRC board member, called the colorful art piece "The Tree of the Nations."
"I love that it was like a tree of life, but each branch had a different nation, and they covered a lot of them. So I love that it included everybody," Gamez said.
Gamez said he enjoyed all the art submitted this year and the various stories attached to the works, including third place winner Ahias Murillo, whose portrait "I Paint My Own Reality" showed Frida Khalo with an array of Latin American flags behind her. According to Gamez, the piece spoke on the identity and growth of Latinos.
The second place winner Majo Arrivillaga, whose portrait of two faceless individuals was meant to depict the different faces migrants have while traveling to the United States, also included a colorful landscape of Guatemala.
Arrivillaga said she loves drawing because it allows her to show people the beauty within the Latino community and encourages Latino artists of all ages to take the leap and share their work with their community.
"Being Hispanic, for me, is being a person who works, studies and centers their family," Arrivillaga said. "We are multifaceted and we can do it all. That's what makes us brave."

title: Empty Bowls event feeds body and soul
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Empty Bowls event feeds body and soul

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot Empty Bowls raised around $30,000 for Talbot County food pantries on Saturday at St. Mark's United Methodist Church by combining the community's good will with handmade bowls and local restaurants' soup making abilities.There, guests, each of whom paid $30 for admission, were able to select one of about 400 painted bowls, all created by members of the community. The bowls were made in a variety of places, including Kiln Born Creations, high school art classes and The Academy Art Museum's pottery studio.
With their selected bowls, guests were then treated to a variety of soup options, all provided by local restaurants.
Around 250 people attended the event, and it brought different parts of the community together for a good cause. People from Tilghman to Easton to Bellevue filled a bowl.
"It was amazing. We had a really great event. The turnout was wonderful. The soups were amazing and were donated by local restaurants. We had music by The Royal Oak Musicians, and it was a festive upbeat event for the community," said volunteer Amy Jacobs.
"It is a glimpse into what I think our community should be like. It was a lot of different people from the community that are all coming together and they are all sharing a meal and just getting to know each other, talk and support a great cause," Jacobs said.
The soups were donated by The Ivy Cafe, Piazza, Garden and Garnish, Hambleton House, Pope's, Tea at the General Store, Bluepoint Hospitality and the Bistro. Bread was donated by Panera.
Some of the soups included chicken dumpling, venison chili, vegetable barley with tomato, cream of mushroom, white bean winter vegetable and cured duck legs, pasta fagioli and butternut squash.
The food pantries that received support include Care Packs, the Neighborhood Service Center, Harvest of Hope Church of God, Royal Oak United Methodist, The Scott's United Methodist Church, St. Michaels Community Center and the Tilghman Food Pantry. A new food pantry has been established at Chesapeake College, and it too benefited from this event.
There was a crew of 20 volunteers, many who came from local high schools and churches.
Qlarant provided a grant to allow groups like BAAM and The Multicultural Center to paint bowls at no cost.
Sponsors included Bette Kenzie and Ellen C. Evans.
Since 2009, when the event began, Talbot Empty Bowls has distributed $320,613, Jacobs said.

title: Hundreds compete in Quick Draw
author: Tom McCall
content:
Hundreds compete in Quick Draw

 July 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 485
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Downtown was filled with art and people Saturday for the Plein Air Easton's quickest event.The annual Quick Draw, in which around 200 artists were given two hours to create a painting of a scene around downtown Easton, has become a fan-favorite event of Plein Air since it was first held 20 years ago. Tourists flocked with their dogs to get a look at the creative process.
Neil Hughes, an artists from Medford, New Jersey, said he prefers having more time to work on his paintings but that "it's a great event, hard not to have fun."
Kaitlyn Hay an artist form Washington, D.C., said the event gave her the opportunity to appreciate work by many of the event's talented participants. "The quick draw is so fun. You just get into the zone. I am certainly nowhere near the level of some of these fellow painters, but it is just fun to participate."
One of the youngest painters at the event was 7-year-old Isabel Tilley. "I have been painting basically all my life," she said. "I painted a cream-colored fence. I am inspired by art."
Not only were there a lot of easels and paints moving around downtown, but there were art lovers waiting to find pieces that spoke to them.
"I have come for probably 15 years, and for 10 of those years, I have bought something," said Stephanie Saunders. "I usually come to the Quick Draw and see what is around."
Nancy Tankersley, the judge of the Quick Draw event, cruised through the work with a clipboard, looking for the best.
There were many volunteers moving art, handing out water and keeping time.
Nancy Espenhorst, a volunteer, said, "I have numerous jobs. I drive a golf cart. I sell art. I am at the information table, and I blow the horn. I like to stay active, and you get to see lots of people."
The event is organized by the Avalon Foundation.
Bill Witowski, the Avalon Foundation's chair, said art sales from the Quick Draw and other Plein Air events support the organization's efforts in the community yearound.
"Just look how many people have come out. It is just a magic time, and look at all the art sales," Witowski said. "That really helps the foundation, which feeds back into the community."
The quick draw is an award-driven paint off. Up to $1,500 is in the offering.
"There are only nine awards so sorry to those of you who didn't make the final list. I really like a strong sense of place," Tankersley said.
The grand prize for the quick draw with an invitation to compete in Plein Air Easton 2025 was given to David Orrin Smith from Seattle.
"That format of paint something from life in two hours at the scale that I work in, which is 30x42 and watercolor, that is what I do all year long all the time," Smith said. He was grateful to all the volunteers who made the event happen.

title: A 'one of a kind' exhibit in Cambridge shows Tubmans strength, softness, humanity
author: Lily Tierney
content:
A 'one of a kind' exhibit in Cambridge shows Tubmans strength, softness, humanity

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The walls of the Harriet Tubman Freedom Center look a bit different these days.Currently, they are covered by a "one of a kind" art exhibit depicting Tubman in various artistic mediums through the lens of 40 artists from all over the globe.
"Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" was curated by Maryland-based artist Larry Poncho Brown and will be featured at the center through Sept. 30. The exhibit is free and open to the public.
"It gives a different twist here in Dorchester County with Harriet Tubman and people to engage in a modern view in some type of atmosphere with art expression," Harriet Tubman Freedom Center President Alex Green said. "It's a really cool exhibit."
The walls emphasize Tubman's strength through her serious and intentional facial expressions, show her softness through depictions of her as a child, and allow her humanity by representing her in such a multifaceted way.
For Green, inspiring people to learn and understand history, particularly Tubman's character of unselfishness and community support, and adopt community-minded values can help prevent communities from repeating past wrongs. It is particularly important for the younger generations, which is why the center provides youth programming, Green said.
"We want to understand how history pretty much played out, with information, not partisanship. We just want to understand," Green said.
Green said the exhibit is a great opportunity to inspire youth to learn the history of Tubman and Dorchester County.
"The younger generation can carry the torch further with understanding. The lack of it is going to cause us to repeat the things that have happened," Green said. "So I think it's very important that children get a chance to engage. Get Harriet introduced, let them make a decision on how they want to process it," he said.
There is an emphasis that everyone is welcome at the freedom center, as long as they believe freedom is the ultimate goal. That is why the door says, "Turn into freedom," Green said.
"In here, we want you to feel free with your opinions as long as it's in the context of freedom," Green said.
The different styles of the gorgeous depictions of Tubman are true representations of freedom. Green said it was difficult for some of the artists to give them away because they've grown so attached.
The Harriet Tubman Freedom Center is located at 3030 Center Drive in Cambridge, and "Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" is open from Tuesday to Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturday from 9 a.m to 3 p.m. It will run until Sept. 30, with the potential of the exhibit being extended through Dec.
"That way we give people more of a chance to be engaged with it, because you come out, look, walk around, you can leave a donation, or you don't have to. You can sign your name, or you don't have to. It's not a requirement. It's not like $5 at the door. But you just can come and take in this amazing exhibit," Green said.

title: Best way to honor legacy of Anne Frank is simple
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Best way to honor legacy of Anne Frank is simple

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A recent chain of events led me to think about another chain of events during World War II for a young girl who once aspired to be a famous writer.She ultimately achieved that goal, but not in a way that she had ever dreamed about or ever aspired to do.
Her name is Anne Frank.
Anne died at age 15 along with most of her family in a Nazi concentration camp.
Before she and her family were sent to the concentration camp, they spent two years hiding from the Nazis in a secret sealed apartment in Amsterdam. During that time, Anne kept a written diary now known as "The Diary of Anne Frank."
Her diary was published posthumously in 1947. Translated into almost 70 languages, it is one of the most widely read accounts of the Holocaust.
I had largely forgotten about Anne Frank and her diary until a series of unexpected events unfolded during a recent weekend.
On a Saturday afternoon, my wife and I drove to St. Michaels to enjoy a beautiful early spring day. It was a by all measures a perfect day.
The next morning was far from perfect.
It started when my wife launched a frantic search for her wallet. Like most wallets it contained her driver's license, credit cards and health insurance cards. It also included a substantial amount of cash for a Monday bank deposit to be used to pay for long-planned and much needed home improvement project.
After retracing all her Saturday steps, we concluded her wallet likely fell out of her back pocket while we were sitting on a park bench in St. Michaels.
I called the St. Michaels police to ask if anyone had turned in a lost wallet. The answer was no, not yet. The officer volunteered to go to the park and search for it. When he called back, he told us there was no trace of it. He also told us some who find lost wallets take the cash and throw the wallet into a trash can. He was kind enough to search the trash can in the park, but with no success.
Once we accepted that reality, I started to write a list of all the onerous tasks that follow the loss of a wallet.
Angry and frustrated, I said to my wife, "This is what the world has come to. No one cares anymore except about themselves. You lose a wallet, and no one turns it in. Worse yet, they probably took your cash and credit cards with no remorse telling themselves it was an unexpected stroke of 'good luck.'"
Minutes later, there was knock at our front door. A couple from Washington, D.C., whom we had never seen before told us they were also visiting St. Michaels on Saturday. They discovered her wallet. Using the address on my wife's driver's license they drove to our house on their return to Washington and delivered it.
They refused any reward other than accepting a heartfelt thank you.
As I reflected upon that unexpected random act of honesty and kindness my thoughts turned to Anne Frank and words she wrote in her diary.
With a wisdom and eloquence well beyond her years she penned, "It's difficult in times like these: ideals, dreams and cherished hopes rise within us, only to be crushed by grim reality. It's a wonder I haven't abandoned all my ideals, they seem so absurd and impractical. Yet I cling to them because I still believe, in spite of everything, that people are truly good at heart."
With all due respect to the memory of Anne, I cannot fully embrace her thinking that people are truly good at heart. Many are, but some are not and never will be. This was confirmed by her death, the deaths of most of her family (all but her father who saved her diary) and at least six million other innocent people who perished in concentration camps during the holocaust.
That said, our experience with a lost wallet was a reminder the best way to honor the legacy of Anne Frank is simple. Not always easy but a most meaningful way.
In difficult times like these when dreams and cherished hopes rise within us, only to be crushed by grim reality, we can and we should strive very day to be people who are "truly good at heart."
David Reel is a public relations and public affairs consultant who lives in Easton.
