title: Interim executive director named for Chesapeake Music
content:
Interim executive director named for Chesapeake Music

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 291
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In early September, career nonprofit professional and consultant Margaret Enloe-North assumed the leadership at one of Talbot County's premiere organizations for bringing amazing artists and performances to the Mid-Shore."We are very pleased to welcome Margaret as part of the Chesapeake Music team!" says Board President Barry Koh. "I know that her nonprofit experience will prove to be invaluable as we move forward and ultimately search for a new, permanent Executive Director in the spring."Enloe-North has spent her 30-year career entirely in the nonprofit sector.Having launched her new business, the Firebird Coaching & Consulting in 2021, she now serves as a coach for individual clients and small businesses and provides nonprofit clients with expert support in the areas of leadership, master planning, strategic communications, programming and fundraising."I really love serving as an Interim ED for organizations that are doing great work! My role allows a Board of Directors the opportunity to deeply reflect on the organization's future while also knowing that daily operations will continue to work smoothly," explains Enloe-North. "And I am really looking forward to working alongside the Board as we envision and lead Chesapeake Music into a new era. I have always appreciated both jazz and classical music and am delighted to help them bring renowned and up-and-coming musicians to the Mid-Shore that delight and surprise our audiences."Based in Easton, Chesapeake Music is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to bring renowned jazz and classical musicians to delight, engage and surprise today's audiences, and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's. They have been doing it for more than 35 years. To learn more about Chesapeake Music or to purchase tickets to this concert, visit their website at chesapeakemusic.org. 
 
 Caption: Pictured is Margaret Enloe-North, new interim Executive Director of Chesapeake Music.

title: Annmarie Gardens to host annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival
author: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Annmarie Gardens to host annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival

 September 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com | Page: 8A | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Both this Saturday and Sunday the Annmarie Sculpture Garden & Arts Center in Solomons will host the 31st annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival when dozens of vendors and performers along with lots of activities for kids will once again be set against the backdrop of the spacious 30-acre sculpture garden.Heading into her third year of coordinating the event this weekend, Helen Lindsey is both enthusiastic about its prospects and optimistic for a stellar turnout among participants and patrons to make for a memorable occasion for those who arrive for either day or both."This year we're hosting over 180 artists and over 40 performers from as far south as Florida and as far north as Massachusetts," Lindsey said. "I hope many people can join us in Solomons on Saturday and Sunday for our 31st annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival. Those who attend will enjoy a fabulous weekend of both the visual and performing arts, activities for kids, great food, wine, beer and so much more." Lindsey noted that the scenery of the Annmarie Sculpture Garden is usually one of its main appeals to visitors, but this weekend during the two days of what has developed into its signature event has countless things to offer guests who arrive for one day or both.This year tickets covering both days at a cost of $15 per person are being offered for the first time for those interested in attending Saturday and Sunday."Set amidst the spectacular backdrop of the 30-acre sculpture garden, Artsfest is truly a unique arts experience," Lindsey said. "Explore the excitement of the Tent Circle and the Arts Building, then wander the shady Wooded Path to find artists, performers and family activities like the Discovery Tent and Zany Zone nestled in the beautiful woods at Annmarie Garden." "Every year I look forward to this signature event," Lindsey added. "Because it is a perfect example of our mission here at Annmarie - connecting people to art and nature. See it for yourself and don't miss out on all the fun." IF YOU GO The 31st annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival will take place this Saturday, Sept. 16 and Sunday, Sept. 17 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Annmarie Garden & Sculpture Center, located at 13470 Dowell Road in Solomons.The event will feature numerous exhibits throughout the 30-acre sculpture garden including those in the Tent Circle and Arts Building and the shady Wooded Path.A one-day pass can be purchased online in advance for $10 or for $12 at the gate.This year a weekend, two-day pass is being offered online at $15 per person, while kids 11-under and AMG members get in free.For more information, go to www.annmariegarden.org.

In addition to the various arts and entertainment, music and food and beverages being offered at the Annmarie Garden Artsfest Art & Music Festival, face painters will be on hand to provide an added touch to the festivities.
 
MICHAEL REID/SOUTHERN MARYLAND NEWS
 
La Plata's Sophia Joyce kicks an oversized ball toward her sister, Fiona at Artsfest in 2021 at Annmarie Sculpture Garden & Arts Center Dowell.
 
COURTESY ANNMARIE GARDENS
 
This Saturday and Sunday at the Annmarie Garden & Sculpture Center's 31st annual Artsfest Art & Music Festival guests will have the chance to listen to over 40 performers over the two-day event.

title: Making pumpkin puree
author: Mary Hunt
content:
Making pumpkin puree

 October 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 327
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hello, fall baking! I can't think of a better way to do that than with fresh, homemade pumpkin puree - the star of the show in so many fall recipes.HOMEMADE PUMPKIN PUREE RECIPEIngredients:2 whole small pumpkins Directions:With a sharp knife, cut off the tops of the pumpkins, right below the stem, and throw that top part into the garbage.Next, cut the pumpkins in half. Scrape the seeds and stringy insides using a big spoon or even an ice cream scoop. Place the seeds in a bowl to roast later (yum!), and toss the pulp and strings into the garbage. Repeat until all the pumpkin halves are cleaned out.Cut each of the halves into a couple of wedges.Lay a piece of parchment paper on a large sheet pan (cookie sheet). Spread out the pumpkin wedges on the pan, skin up or skin down - it doesn't matter. Place the pan in the oven and set to 350 F. Roast for about 45 minutes, or until the pumpkin pieces are fork-tender (very soft). Remove from the oven.Allow the pumpkin pieces to cool sufficiently so that you can handle them safely. Pull or scrape the skin from the pumpkin meat using a knife. Toss the skins into the garbage.Place a few chunks of roasted, skinned pumpkin into a food processor. Pulse small batches of pumpkin until totally smooth. (Add a tablespoon of water if it seems too dry to get it smooth. Too watery? Strain it through a fine mesh strainer to get rid of some of it.) As you complete a batch, pour it into a bowl, then continue until all the pumpkin has been pureed.A blender will work, too, but you may need to add a bit ofwater to produce a smooth puree. No food processor or blender? No worries. You can mash it up with a potato masher, or force it through a potato ricer or even a food mill.Mary Hunt is thefounder ofEverydayCheapskate.com, afrugal living blog, and the author of the book "Debt-Proof Living. title: Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE —Rescue Fire Company Train Garden Chairman Gary Hickman's father was visiting the train garden on Gay Street the day of the Pearl Harbor attack in 1941."He was just here that day as a child," Hickman said.
Eighty-three years later, the RFC Train Garden — the longest continually running train garden in the country — is celebrating its 90th anniversary.
Hickman said this milestone is so important because "the gentlemen back in 1934 had the forethought to be able to put this together for the community and the children of the community."
Hickman remembers coming to the train garden as a kid. He said he loved trains as a child.
"I used to come here as many times as I could during the Christmas season when it was open," he said.
That love never drifted for Hickman, who plans to continue on with his role as chairman for as long as he can.
On a Monday evening, families slowly made their way in and out of the old City Hall on Gay Street, where the train garden is located. Quaid Windsor, 4, walked around the train garden with his parents as he snacked on popcorn. He said he liked the trains the most.
Hickman said support from the local business community makes it possible for the train garden to keep chugging along.
"When I was growing up as a kid, it was a hobby, and it was an affordable hobby," Hickman said. "And now things are so expensive. ... And all of these sponsors re-sponsor us every year and they give us money so we can continually change and add things and buy new engines and upgrade things as we go along."
Hickman said that with continued volunteer support from the fire company, he sees the train garden making it to the 100-year mark in another decade.
"As long as I'm around, we're going to continue," he said.

Mid-Shore Calendar

 September 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Calendar 
 
 2078
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Those seeking to have an event published in the Star Democrat's calendar are asked to email details to community@stardem.com.YARN AND NEEDLE GROUP, 12:30 to 3 p.m., Brookletts Place Talbot County Senior Center, Easton. Every Tuesday. Some help may be available for knitting and crocheting. Open to anyone 60 years of age or older at no cost. Info: 410-822-2869.
CONSTITUTION DAY, noon to 1:30 p.m., Academy Art Museum, 106 South St., Easton. Ceremony and performance by reenactors of Thomas Jefferson and Frederick Douglass. Free admission and Constitutions.

Group shares our artwork at meetings and collaborates with many different forms of media. Artists' work displayed in the window of Vintage Venue on Race Street in Cambridge. Facebook: wednesdaymorningartists. Email is: wednesdaymorningartists@gmail.com.
'AGING IN PLACE', 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., Oxford Community Center. Speaker Maggie Black. An informative health presentation about "Aging in Place" — setting the stage with discussions about what is typical aging and when one needs to be concerned. Free. Bring your lunch. Limited seating. RSVP at oxfordcc.org.
'DANCING IN COLOR,' 7 p.m., Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover St., Easton. In this collaboration between the folk-pop band Bombadil and contemporary dancer Madison Rivis, Rivis has choreographed movements for herself and the band using their latest album "In Color" as inspiration. Bombadil in turn taught Rivis how to play and sing the songs.
THIRD THURSDAY, 5 to 7 p.m., downtown Denton. Businesses extend their hours and offer specials. Info: DowntownDenton.com.
COMMUNITY TALK, 5:30 p.m., Oxford Community Center. Lifetime Wells International President and Co-founder David Powell will talk about Project Africa. This is brought to you by Oxford's Dick and Zoe Schramm. Free. RSVP at oxfordcc.org.
WINE EDUCATION SERIES, 6 to 8 p.m., The Ebenezer Theater at Prager Family Center for the Arts, 17 S. Washington St., Easton. Presentation and Tasting; Questions & Answers; Wine Market to shop glassware, books, accessories and art. Pre-orders available for wine & cheese. Led by Wardroom Wine Director, Anthony Austin, guests will sample five wines as they learn about regional details.
CAMBRIDGE FARMERS MARKET, 3 to 6 p.m., Long Wharf, High and Water Streets, Cambridge. Find local produce, meats, cheeses, crafts, and more at the weekly, waterfront Cambridge Farmers Market. Info: office@downtowncambridge.org.
THURSDAY DECK PARTY, 5 to 7 p.m., Blue Point Provision Co., Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay, 100 Heron Blvd., Cambridge. Music, delicious dining specials, and drink specials including our signature Choptank Crush cocktail.
FOUR ELEVEN KITCHEN RIBBON CUTTING, 5:30 to 7 p.m., 411 Kitchen, The Packing House, 411A Dorchester Ave., Cambridge. Business after hours featuring ribbon cutting. Register: info@dorchesterchamber.org or 410-228-3575.
FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
MARYLAND OUTDOORS FESTIVAL, Molly's Place, Kennedyville. The Maryland Outdoors Festival is a celebration of outdoor activities, from hunting and fishing to hiking and camping.

Info: carolinehistory.org or 410-479-2055 and leave a message.
DANCING WITH THE STARS, 7 p.m., Oxford Community Center. Local celebrities participate in a dance competition. This is a fundraiser in partnership with Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center. Doors open at 6:30 p.m. Tickets cost $25 per person and includes dinner, one cocktail and dancing after the competition. Tickets and voting: oxfordcc.org.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
GLENN MILLER ORCHESTRA, 7 p.m., Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover St., Easton. The legendary Glenn Miller was one of the most successful of all dance bandleaders back in the Swing Era of the 1930s and '40s. A matchless string of hit records, the constant impact of radio broadcasts and the drawing power at theatres, hotels, and dance pavilion, built and sustained the momentum of popularity.
KHATIA BUNIATISHVILI LABYRINTH, 7:30 p.m., The Ebenezer Theater at Prager Family Center for the Arts, 17 South Washington Street, Easton. From Bach to Liszi, a journey from the Baroque to the Classical with one of the most prominent pianists of our time. 720-560-6358.
MUSIC ON THE NANTICOKE, 4 to 7 p.m., River Pavilion, 114 Water St., Vienna. Free concert with Randy Lee Ashcraft & The Saltwater Cowboys.
SUICIDE BRIDGE BOAT DOCKING CONTEST, noon to 5 p.m., Suicide Bridge Restaurant, 6304 Suicide Bridge Rd., Hurlock. Workboats and charter boats compete to "dock" their boats. They compete for cash, prizes, trophies and of course, bragging rights.
MARYLAND OUTDOORS FESTIVAL, Molly's Place, Kennedyville. The Maryland Outdoors Festival is a celebration of outdoor activities, from hunting and fishing to hiking and camping.
EDDA GLASS AND MAX HATT BOSSA NOVA AND JAZZ, 7 p.m., Stoltz Listening Room, Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover St., Easton. Max Hatt / Edda Glass's music has taken them far and wide, by airwave in numerous NPR and PBS specials, and on the road with stops including New York City's Lincoln Center, D.C.'s Kennedy Center, the Sundance Film Festival, and Wilco's Solid Sound Festival.

Dan Small, the associate director of natural land stewardship at the Center for Environment and Society at Washington College, will talk about the plans for expanding the Oxford Conservation Park and how it fits with the goals of the Natural Lands Project. Free. RSVP at oxfordcc.org.
PAWS FOR READING, 3:40 to 4:25 p.m., every fourth Thursday, Central Branch library, Denton. Children ages 5 to 12 can proactice reading to a trained service dog. One registrant per session. Register: carolib.libcal.com.
CAMBRIDGE FARMERS MARKET, 3 to 6 p.m., Long Wharf, High and Water Streets, Cambridge. Find local produce, meats, cheeses, crafts, and more at the weekly, waterfront Cambridge Farmers Market. Info: office@downtowncambridge.org.
'ROOTED WISDOM' PODCAST LAUNCH, 7 to 9 p.m., Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover St., Easton. In this new podcast series, Anthony Cohen, historian, Menare Foundation president and explorer of the American past, sets out to find the stories of the Underground Railroad. Register: adkins.donorshops.com/product/RW-podcast-launch/rooted-wisdom-podcast-launch-september-26.
'VIOLIN VIRTUOSO,' 7:30 p.m., Easton Church of God, 1009 N. Washington St., Easton. The Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra proudly opens its 27th season as the Delmarva Peninsula's only professional symphony orchestra with a concert series titled "Violin Virtuoso." Tickets: midatlanticsymphony.org.
FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
FEDERALSBURG HERITAGE DAY, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., Heritage Museum, 100 Covey-Williams Alley. Special exhibit of images and artifacts from the Caroline County Minutemen. Former Federalsburg Town Manager and State Senator Rich Colburn will be speak at 1 p.m. Raffle, dinner at Exeter House, bake sale, light refreshments.
EASTON FARMERS MARKET, 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., 100 Block North Washington Street, Easton. Open rain or shine. Live music at 10:30 a.m.
ST. MICHAELS FARMERS MARKET, 8:30 to 11 a.m., 206 S. Talbot Street, St. Michaels. Open rain or shine.
CAR SHOW, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., Preston Carnival Grounds, 114 Williamson St., Preston. Proceeds go to Bardet Biedl Syndrome Foundation and Preston Elementary special needs program. $20 registration. Info: 410-924-0042.
BEER GARDEN, 1 to 4 p.m., Adkins Arboretum, 12610 Eveland Rd., Ridgely. Kick off fall with an afternoon of live music, great beer, and tasty food in one of the Eastern Shore's most beautiful outdoor spaces. Tickets: adkins.donorshops.com/product/2024-BEERGARDEN/beer-garden.
JOUSTING CHAMPIONSHIP, 1 p.m., Tuckahoe Equestrian Center, 619 Crouse Mill Road, Queen Anne. Jousting is Maryland's official state sport. Open to the public to watch. Please bring your own chairs. Info: 410-310-7945.
BIRDING AND BOATING THE HARRIET TUBMAN BYWAY, 2 to 6 p.m., Linchester Mill, Preston. Join Harriet Tubman Tours and Delmarva Birding Weekends as they go birding along the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway. During the guided, self-driven tour, attendees 'learn about the many daring escapes led by the famed freedom seeker and human rights activist know as "The Moses of Her People." Contact dmvbirds@gmail.com to reserve your space.

FAIRYFEST, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., Adkins Arboretum, 12610 Eveland Rd., Ridgely. Maypole dancing, magical potions, elven archery, artisan fairy houses, a meadow pirate ship and more. Register: adkins.donorshops.com/product/FAIRYFEST2024/fairyfest-2024.

Tickets $20 at oxfordcc.org.

title: Meet the maker: Charm Tree Jewelry Studio welcomes steel metalsmith and author
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Meet the maker: Charm Tree Jewelry Studio welcomes steel metalsmith and author

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 375
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — As part of its regular Meet the Maker series bringing in experts highlighting their craft, metalsmith school Charm Tree Studios recently welcomed celebrated steelsmith and new author Bette Barnett, of California.Renowned for her work combining steel, gold and silver in her unique jewelry-making process, Barnett taught several studio classes about various aspects of metal working, including etching steel plates and powdered metals. Barnett also demonstrated Keum Boo, an ancient Korean art form of applying gold to metal through heat and pressure, on steel that she has perfected over the years.
Following her corporate career retirement in 2013, Barnett was drawn to crafting and beading workshops, and after learning how to solder necklace clasps, she fell in love with steelwork in particular.
"And I never looked back," she said.
Taking every class and workshop she could get her soldering mitts on and receiving fantastic mentorship, Barnett continued to experiment with different styles.
Steel is a cost effective material with a high melting point, she said, and she soon found it offered itself to mixing and playing well with other materials.
To pass on her late instructor's techniques, Barnett began teaching and writing a research paper that eventually morphed into her book.
Barnett's new book "Creating Steel Jewelry: Etching, Fusing, Keum Boo, Enameling, Stainless and More" delves into the fundamentals of metalsmithing while also exploring her own techniques and explorations into the world of smithing.
Charm Tree Jewelry studio owner and metalsmith instructor Melissa Kay-Steves is always eager to ever expand the repertoire. Since opening its doors more than five years ago, the goal of the studio has been to bring skilled and unique experts to teach and showcase new styles.
Learning the basics, "will take you anywhere you want to go," she said.
Within the metalsmith school's state-of-the-art studio and workshops, Kay-Steves lays fundamental ground work and it is often visiting masters who showcase how to perfect and hone skills, leading students through a gateway of possibilities, she said.
Charm Tree Jewelry Studio regularly hosts Meet the Maker events open to all curious jewelry lovers and craftspeople.
"There's nothing else like it in the area," Kay-Steves said.
More information about Barnett's studio can be found at studiomigoto.com. More information about Charm Tree Jewelry including year round classes and guest instructors, can be found at charmtreejewelry.com.

title: Joe Hickey: a classic rock veteran in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Joe Hickey: a classic rock veteran in St. Michaels

 August 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — For Joe Hickey, local musician and seasoned guitarist, rock was not only a genre of music. It was his life.From the Bee Gees to Led Zeppelin to Otis Redding, Hickey has played with them all and assisted in the movement that we now know as "classic rock."
After a 35 year hiatus, Hickey has re-devoted himself to music. A love that he has shared since boyhood. Hickey plays solo throughout the Eastern Shore and teaches guitar to new musicians of all ages.
Hickey, originally from Scotland, said when he was 12, his older brother who was serving in the Navy came back with a guitar and started playing. Hickey was hooked after that.
His interest turned to lessons, those lessons turned to passion and that passion took him on tour with countless classic rock bands throughout the '70s and '80s.
"There was so much great music out there," Hickey said. "There were so many bands around that everybody was trying to make it. Even in the early days of the Bee Gees or Led Zeppelin, they didn't think they wouldn't make it as big as they are today."
He moved to Chicago with his then wife and band Salvation. In Chicago he played with other bands and groups, but soon the life of a musician took a toll on his family and he got divorced in 1985. He said as a single parent of two children he had to change his career, and for over 30 years he took a hiatus from the music industry.
Over the decades, he remarried, had a successful career in marketing and raised his children. Though he stopped performing publicly, he never stopped playing for his family and friends.
Then in 2019, after he had moved to St. Michaels, a local group hired him to play a gig with them at Foxy's Harbor Grill, and it snowballed from there. Now he is playing throughout Maryland as a solo act and has recorded and released a CD.
Patti Foy, a friend of Hickey's, said she met Hickey at one of his shows. She said she enjoys the music he plays since it was music she grew up on. After Foy's father passed away, she inherited his guitar, and Hickey has been teaching her to play it.
Foy said Hickey is a patient teacher and encourages her to continue her lessons and improve. For Foy, Hickey is a lifelong friend and someone she trusts.
"He was a friend from day one," Foy said. "So every time, we'd always talk and see how he was doing … Even though he's going through his own personal stuff, he always takes time for other people. So I think it is amazing. He doesn't let that stop him. It doesn't define him."
Hickey said he enjoys playing, teaching music and pushing himself as a musician to learn more challenging songs. Hickey guarantees attendees of his shows will recognize 95% of the songs he plays.
"I'm enjoying doing it by myself," Hickey said. "I can pick and choose what I want to do and how often I want to play. ... I want to enjoy it. It's a job, and I've got to perform the best way possible so that people can enjoy what I'm doing and play songs that they like to hear."

title: A Caroline County witch finds peace, community
author: Tom McCall
content:
A Caroline County witch finds peace, community

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Witch James, a Caroline County witch, has a philosophy that informs their practices."Everything is push or pull," Witch James said. "By pushing and pulling, you complete the circuit. It is energy for me."
"People ask me all the time, 'Are you a good witch or a bad witch?' I don't believe in good and bad," they said. "I am electric."
Its a philosophy James, who lives outside of Greensboro, shares with a community of witches who call the Eastern Shore home. They have gatherings of up to 20 people of lots of different faith traditions. Christians, Muslims, Wiccans and atheists have all been a part of this circle, James said.
Coming from West Virginia, James was searching for community when he got to Caroline County. Struggling to find people with whom they aligned, James thought, "If you don't have community, build it." They started a Facebook group.
"I started taking full moon classes. I started advertising that I did readings and cleansings. I posted on Denton Happenings that there are over 400 energy workers, witches, shamans, whatever you call us."
This time of year, James' found community is preparing for celebrations of Samhain, an ancient holiday. James said it is the most sacred time of year for them personally.
"The Catholic Church created Halloween off of Samhain," James said. "... Witch's holidays do not go by the Gregorian calendar. They go by the lunar calendar. This year it falls on Nov. 1.
"The new moon is the weakest point in the veil between the living and the dead throughout the whole year. That is what Samhain is," he said.
These practices are not always well received by people outside the witch community, James said.
"In Caroline County, most people don't feel safe to be out. I had six death threats last year," they said.
James knows of six covens in Caroline County and is part of four of them. "They are all closed groups. Mine is an open group because there needs to be an open group," they said.
But Witch James said the witches' non-violent belief system is accessible to people who are not part of the witch community. They are open to sharing.
"Sometimes I have people out here to do readings for them. I do tarot readings. I do pendulum readings. I do aura readings," James said. "Some people can see or feel the electromagnetic fields of other people. We are all electro-bio machines, and that is what an aura is."
James' family has deep tradition of healing as well.
"My family have been herbalists and healers for generations — the last 14 that I could find through my mother's side. My mother talks to the dead. My grandmother talked to the dead. My great grandmother talked to the dead," they said.
Asked what is great about the witch's path, James said, "The biggest take away is finding peace."

title: An ancient manuscript up for sale gives a glimpse into the history of early Christianity
author: Ian N. Mills The Conversation
content:
An ancient manuscript up for sale gives a glimpse into the history of early Christianity

 May 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ian N. Mills The Conversation | Section: Entertainment 
 
 962
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An important piece of early Christian history, the Crosby-Schøyen Codex, is up for auction at Christie's in London. This codex is a mid-fourth century book from Egypt containing a combination of biblical and other early Christian texts.The Crosby-Schøyen Codex was discovered alongside more than 20 other codices near Dishna, Egypt, in 1952. These manuscripts are collectively known as "the Dishna Papers" or "the Bodmer Papyri," after the Swiss collector Martin Bodmer.
Though often overshadowed by other 20th century discoveries, this trove of ancient manuscripts represents one of the most significant finds for understanding the history of early Christianity. As an expert on early Christian reading practices, I consider the Dishna Papers an invaluable witness to the formation of the Christian Bible. This ancient library shows how, before the consolidation of the Bible, early Christians read canonical and non-canonical scriptures — as well as pagan classics — side by side.
An overshadowed discovery
The middle decades of the 20th century were exciting years for scholars of early Christianity.
In 1945, a collection of 13 ancient codices was discovered near Nag Hammadi, Egypt. These contained dozens of otherwise unknown works, mostly associated with minority and marginalized forms of early Christianity. With titles like "The Gospel of Thomas" and "The Secret Revelation of John," this cache of non-canonical scriptures captured the public's imagination and inspired a bestseller.
The very next year, Bedouin shepherds discovered ancient Hebrew scrolls hidden in a cave at Qumran on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea.
The "Dead Sea Scrolls" found in this and a dozen subsequently discovered caves constituted a massive library of Jewish texts, including biblical works and hitherto unknown texts with remarkable parallels to the writings of the New Testament. This find was celebrated in news stories, documentaries and other publications as among the greatest discoveries of the 20th century.
At the very same time, the Dishna Papers were discovered, smuggled out of Egypt and sold to European collectors with considerably less fanfare. No headline hailed the discovery of the Dishna Papers. Instead, pieces of this collection were sold to the highest bidders, scattering the ancient library across the globe.
The Dishna Papers
Though less exotic than Nag Hammadi or Qumran, the contents of the Crosby-Schøyen Codex and the 20-some additional codices discovered near Dishna have proved every bit as important for our understanding of early Christianity.
Two manuscripts of the canonical gospels, Luke and John, belonging to this ancient library predate almost every other surviving copy of these gospels. Scholars used these new manuscripts to revise the text of the New Testament.
For instance, the vast majority of manuscripts of the Gospel of John describe Jesus as "the only-begotten Son" (1:18). But the early manuscripts discovered at Dishna read "the only-begotten God." Here and elsewhere, English translations of the Bible were changed to reflect the contents of the Dishna Papers.
But the library discovered near Dishna did not consist entirely of texts that ended up in the Christian Bible. Scriptures that were not included in the Christian canon, like Paul's "Third Letter to the Corinthians" and "The Shepherd of Hermas," were also found among the Dishna Papers.
One codex from Dishna contains the "Acts of Paul," an extra-Biblical account of Paul's travels and martyrdom. Another contains the "Infancy Gospel of James," a non-canonical story about the life of Mary, Jesus' mother. The discoveries at Dishna provide evidence that these writings, though unfamiliar to modern readers of the Bible, spent centuries on the periphery of Christian scripture.
The Dishna Papers included a few additional literary texts. One codex in this mostly Christian library contains several comedies by the Hellenistic playwright Menander. Another codex binds together a chapter of Thucydides' "History of the Peloponnesian War" with a Greek version of the biblical Book of Daniel.
Evidently, the owner of this Christian library had no aversion to the arts and sciences of pre-Christian Hellenism. In this library, pagan classics and Christian scripture stood side by side.
But whose library was this?
The Crosby-Schøyen Codex, which is now up for sale, actually supplies several important clues to the origin of the Dishna Papers with which it was found.
Thanks to recent radiocarbon dating of this codex and the contents of a closely related manuscript, the Crosby-Schøyen Codex can be dated with some measure of confidence to the middle of the fourth century — roughly 325 to 350 C.E.
The Crosby-Schøyen Codex itself contains five texts in Sahidic Coptic, a dialect of the ancient Egyptian language. Three texts are Biblical: Jonah, Second Maccabees 5:27-7:41, and 1 Peter. The rest of the codex contains part of a well-known Easter homily and a brief otherwise unknown exhortation.
These texts, argue scholars Albert Pietersma and Susan Comstock, may have been collected into a single codex for use as an Easter lectionary. A lectionary is a collection of readings used in Christian worship services. Such lectionaries were used in Pachomian monasteries, like the one located only a few miles west of Dishna.
This monastery was established in the mid-330s by Pachomius, the reputed founder of communal monasticism. His Pachomian Rule, by which the monks would have ordered their communal life, makes frequent reference to the public and private use of books. Pachomius' monasteries even taught illiterate monks to read.
It seems likely that this eclectic library of canonical and non-canonical scriptures, early Christian writings and pagan classics belonged to these book-loving monks in central Egypt. One of the Pachomian rules allowed monks to borrow books from the monastic library for up to one week.
Today, for a few million dollars, one such book can be yours forever. On June 11, 2024, the Crosby-Schøyen Codex will go to the highest bidder.
Ian N. Mills is a professor of of classics and religious studies at Hamilton College.

title: Cambridge veteran, photographer is behind new journal looking back at Vietnam War
author: Konner Metz
content:
Cambridge veteran, photographer is behind new journal looking back at Vietnam War

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Lon Holmberg was in Charlottesville, Virginia, seeing college friends in 1969 after he received his draft notice, when novelist and University of Virginia professor George Garrett gave him some advice."Make lemonade out of lemons," Holmberg recalls Garrett telling him, encouraging him to write a book on his soon-to-be life-changing experience in Vietnam.
More than 50 years later, Holmberg did just that.
Holmberg, a U.S. Army photographer during the war, brought thousands of negatives back from Vietnam. Now 80 and residing in Cambridge, Holmberg is the author of a new journal, "Crossing the Pass of Clouds." It includes written vignettes and black-and-white photos depicting what life was like in Vietnam.
"It's really hard to take in," Holmberg said of how it feels to have the book published after decades of trying. "Like all that time put into it. It's wonderful to be able to do it. I'm very proud of it."
The journal includes photos of U.S. Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird, then-national security advisor (and later Secretary of State) Henry Kissinger and then-South Vietnamese President Nguyen Van Thieu.
But for Holmberg, the book's purpose extends far beyond the historical figures. It captures soldiers working and enjoying downtime. It captures the culture and landscape of South Vietnam itself — especially the city of Saigon.
"It really was some sense of what it was like to be in Vietnam, to see the life of the indigenous people and farming communities," Holmberg said.
He compares it to a hologram. Like a 3D image, his memoir showcases a full perspective of Vietnam through the lens of one person.
"This is not just a collection of Vietnam pictures," Holmberg said. "These are a collection from one person, from one point of view."
"You kind of have a way of looking through the book into getting a feel of what Vietnam really was like in 1971," he said.
HALF-CENTURY LATER
The book's journey didn't come without hardships; Holmberg said he was rejected 31 times. It was never an option to give up.
"After you've been doing this for years and years, you're not just going to stop," Holmberg said.
By considering a university press and learning to write concise proposals, Holmberg found his publisher, The University Press of Mississippi, a few years ago.
His journal published in March, just days before the 50th anniversary of the Vietnam War's end on March 29.
Sandy Stillwell, Holmberg's wife, said he's been "steady" and has carried himself with a sense of humor during the arduous process of finding a publisher.
"While the process itself was challenging and the rejections disheartening, Lon is an optimist at heart," Stillwell wrote in an email.
The couple has settled on the Eastern Shore, and Holmberg credits his wife with being his rock as he completed the memoir.
Holmberg, a documentary photographer and longtime English professor, says he's working on two other projects, including one from his time exploring the prison system in New Mexico as a documentary producer.
'HUMANE'
The book's 196 pages are stocked full of written reflections about life before, during and after the war. Holmberg writes on return visits to Vietnam in 1996, a quarter-century after his time in the Army, and in 2010, as the teacher of a one-month English course for Hue University students.
Photos capture moments ranging from early anti-war protests in Washington, D.C. to soldiers working on the largest U.S. military base in Vietnam, Long Binh.
The book doesn't depict brutal images of war, but that doesn't make it any less realistic or meaningful, Holmberg and others say.
"Holmberg does not show the human wreckage of war. Instead, he gives us humane, sympathetic, respectful images of civilians and soldiers, generals and government officials," reads a review on the memoir's back cover written by University of Virginia English professor Stephen Cushman.
Holmberg says he didn't have an agenda with the book. Rather, he hopes Vietnam veterans and families can reconnect with Vietnam in a candid way without it being traumatic.
"I've gotten just overwhelming feedback," he said. "People really, really love it. It brought Vietnam back."
"Crossing the Pass of Clouds" is available for purchase at Flying Cloud Booksellers in Easton, Maryland, and on the Barnes & Noble website.

"The Submersive Thread" features fiber and threadworks by Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber. The exhibit runs through March 30
Here is rundown of the artists and their work, according to the AAM announcement.
Han Cao infuses found photos with modern narratives, using needlework to add texture and depth. Each piece invites viewers to engage intimately, bridging past and present through stitches that connect distant figures to contemporary observers. Cao's sense of humor adds another layer of depth to her work: through subtle nuances and playful elements, she examines conventional perceptions and invites viewers to approach her artwork with curiosity and joy.i
Jennifer McBrien's striking Warrior Women series features a dramatic departure from the typical confines of embroidery hoops, with vintage toile curtain panels cascading freely from their frames. McBrien's hybrid figures, merging avian and female forms, symbolize the fragility of endangered species, evolving alongside the deteriorating fabric. Complementing the series is the poignant installation Hanging Them Out to Dry, a visceral commentary on the plight of endangered birds. Hung on a clothesline, embroidered vintage napkins evoke a sense of vulnerability, emphasizing the urgent need for conservation efforts to safeguard threatened species from extinction.
Michael-Birch Pierce explores identity through embroidery, blending traditional techniques with contemporary themes. At the heart of Pierce's practice lies an intimate exploration of the self and the narratives chosen to weave around it. Through the medium of embroidery, Pierce delves into the layers of identity, often cloaking their creations in the superficial trappings of high fashion and costume. Their work challenges notions of authenticity, inviting viewers to peel back layers of artifice and notice the essence beneath.
Stacey Lee Webber's choice of American currency as a medium is particularly poignant. By stitching directly onto artifacts of commerce, she forges a tangible connection between past and present, laborer and leader. Ultimately, the act of embroidering through dollar bills becomes an act of defiance — a subversion of the traditional notions of value and representation, making symbols of capitalism available for introspection and critique.
The exhibition is organized in conjunction with the Museum's 27th Annual Craft Show in October. "represents a pioneering initiative for AAM as it embarks on a new path to integrate exhibitions of contemporary craft into its well-established 3-day event. The Museum seeks to enrich the visitor's experience by showcasing examples of modern craft alongside traditional work."
This exhibition was made possible through Westobou Gallery in Augusta, Georgia.
There are a number of other upcoming events at the Easton museum. according to AAM.
AAM Film Series: Unraveling Narratives
Now through March, 2025
(Film pass: $25 members, $35 non-members, per film $10 members,$15 non-members, includes beer and popcorn for members, $5 non-members) .
Dive into the themes of The Subversive Thread exhibition through Unraveling Narratives, a curated monthly film series that brings fiber art's cultural intersections to the screen. Join us for thought-provoking documentaries and narrative features, followed by facilitated discussions connecting the films' stories to the exhibition's exploration of fiber, craft, and culture. From powerful documentaries like Yarn to artist profiles like Outsider: The Life and Art of Judith Scott, this series invites audiences to experience fiber art in an entirely new dimension. Screenings are open to all, with refreshments provided for post-film discussions.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories
Every Thursday through March 27, 5-7 pm
Explore the art of embroidery and its connection to storytelling, line drawing, and mark-making. Throughout the exhibition's run, this mobile art-making station will be available to invite visitors to experiment with embroidery techniques. Inspired by the work of fiber artists featured in The Subversive Thread, this drop-in program offers examples of stitches and materials for creating your own textile art. Whether you're a seasoned stitcher or new to fiber arts, this hands-on experience brings a tactile dimension to the exhibition's themes of identity, craft, and creativity.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories with Jennifer McBrien
Thursday, February 13, 4:30 - 7 pm
Don't miss the chance to stitch with The Subversive Thread artist Jennifer McBrien at the Art Cart! Whether you're new to embroidery or an experienced stitcher, Jennifer will guide you through basic techniques or help you bring your own design to life. Additionally, please feel free to bring a piece of fabric and a concept to work on. Jennifer will be in the gallery from 4:30 pm until the "Threads of Disruption" lecture.
Threads of Disruption: A Contemporary Craft Conversation
Thursday, February 13, 6 pm
The exhibition's featured artists—Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber—share their unique approaches to fiber and thread art. This dynamic event begins with four mini-presentations from each artist, offering personal insights into their creative processes and the themes driving their work. Following these presentations, a lively discussion, led by the exhibition's curator, will explore the thematic connections of identity, subversion, and value that unite the artists' practices while highlighting the unique perspectives that set each artist apart. The evening concludes with an open Q&A session, offering an opportunity for meaningful dialogue with the artists.
Threads of Sound: Improvisational Music Inspired by The Subversive Thread
Friday, March 28, 5:30–7:30 pm
Experience the intersection of art and music with musicians Robert Hitz and Felicia Harrington in a dynamic, live musical experience directly responding to the textures, narratives, and themes of the exhibition. Guided by the exhibition's curator, this performance will explore the dialogue between visual and auditory art forms, weaving together an evening of creativity, inspiration, and discovery.

The beauty of language

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Phillip Alder | Page: 13 | Section: News

 English is a difficult language, but one full of variety. I particularly enjoy the diverse ways one can play with the words: anagrams, puns, homophones, spoonerisms, malapropisms, and so on. In particular, I like malapropisms. Mrs.Malaprop was a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's "The Rivals." She had the habit of using a word close to the one she really should have employed. For example, "an allegory on the banks of the Nile." See how many malapropisms you can find in the rest of this column.Today's deal comes from a rubber bridge game in which the stakes were expansive, very extensive. North had just bid and made seven notrump.This was the second deal.West had a normal preeminent opening of five clubs. North cue-bid six clubs to show a stroganoff twosuiter, but not necessarily that shapely and sarong. The rest of the bidding contained three ill-advertised doubles.Declarer thumped the club ace lead in hand and dashed one round of trumps with dummy's king before twitching his attention to hearts. When West absconded on the first round and couldn't ruff, it was an easy job for South to ruff out East's heart queen. Declarer retrained to dummy with a diamond ruff, drew East's two trumps and claimed.North-South had won a 50-point rubber. (Don't forget both the 100 honors on this deal and that now you receive a 100-point bonus for making a redoubled contract.) They corrected so much money that they were suddenly effluent.

title: Stef Scaggiari to perform at St. Paul's in. Centreville
author: Staff Writer
content:
Stef Scaggiari to perform at St. Paul's in. Centreville

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 180
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Acclaimed classical and jazz pianist Stef Scaggiari will appear in concert on Sunday, April 27, at 4 p.m. at St. Paul's Episcopal Church, located a301 S. Liberty St. in Centreville.The program is entitled "Chopin and All That Jazz" and will feature a mix of classical and jazz music. The first half includes Chopin's "Ballade in G Minor." The second half of the program will feature Scaggiari singing classic songs accompanied on the church's restored Steinway "A" piano.
Scaggiari, a Queen Anne's County resident, has played with the U.S. Marine Band, including many concerts at the White House. He has also performed often on the Eastern Shore. In addition to his career as a concert artist, he is director of music at St. Paul's.
There are no tickets for the concert, but donations will be accepted, and the proceeds will go toward St. Paul's Friends of Music, which makes concerts such as this possible. A reception will follow in Donaldson Hall at St. Paul's. The church facilities are fully handicapped-accessible.
Additional information is available by calling the church office at 410-758-1553.

 Read News Document

 Indigenous sites in Maryland have been dated as early as 12,000 years ago by archaeologists. Many Indigenous people lived along the then Susquehanna River, using the resources provided by the land.As the Susquehanna's channel widened and the Chesapeake Bay began to form about 10,000 years ago, a majority of these settlements were inundated by water. The people who lived there moved, often following food resources such as oysters and fish.
"The Chesapeake Bay has long been a vital resource for people including Native Americans, especially as the Bay began to form," said Julia A. King, professor of Anthropology at St. Mary's College of Maryland. "It provides all sorts of seafood. The rising waters created marshlands that sort of acted as a refrigerator by providing animals and plant species that people could use. A lot of native settlements were located near riverine environments and marsh."
Thanks to state and federal grants, a growing relationship with today's Piscataway descendants, and a strong partnership with Maryland's Department of Natural Resources, King has been working with her students and colleague Travis Hanson, an archaeologist, to uncover the history of Indigenous peoples in Southern Maryland.
On a cloudy fall day earlier this year, Hanson joined park rangers and others at Chapel Point State Park to detail their ongoing work in the park as part of the Department of Natural Resources' annual Science Week. In pre-colonial times this area was home to the Potobacs, who were part of the Piscataway Chiefdom, which had emerged on the shores of the Potomac River around 1200 AD.
Hanson guided the small group through a narrow trail at Chapel Point State Park to an area next to a natural spring where paw paw trees were growing. The area was chosen for exploration due to the concentrations of oyster shell middens–basically dumping areas for discarded oyster shells, which indicate people had been gathering nearby and eating oysters. In 2023, Hanson, King and others dug several small test pits to search for artifacts and any structural remains.
Evidence indicates there was an extensive Indigenous settlement in the area that likely stretched to the other side of the Potomac.
"We found lots of projectile points, ceramics, and stone tools," said King. "We only scratched the surface and found hundreds of artifacts."
Through her work, King has developed a collaborative relationship with contemporary Piscataway descendants including Francis Gray, the tribal chairman of today's Piscataway Conoy Tribe, one of three state-recognized tribes in Maryland. Gray joined the group that had gathered at Chapel Point.
"We've come to understand that by having conversations with archaeologists and researchers we can help each other out," Gray said. He noted that through their collaborative work they've been able to confirm Native American community locations and find ways to protect those sites.
"It's important for researchers and others to understand that they're finding artifacts that belonged to a people who still exist," Gray said. "This whole river here was not one small concentrated community. Like the Nanticoke, Choptank, and Wicomico, these were all metropolises before colonization, people lived on both sides of the Potomac River."
King hopes that through further research the team can discover the location of the Jesuit mission where Father Andrew White operated. White led the first Catholic Mass in the English-speaking colonies after Maryland colonists first arrived in the new colony in 1634. His parish was set up around 1641 in Chapel Point, although the exact location is unknown. Finding the parish may help inform the history of how early colonists interacted with the Piscataway and other tribes in the area.
What is known–the arrival of the colonists caused feuds among the Piscataway, who had previously been attacked by colonists from Jamestown. Records uncovered from that time suggest that the Piscataway Tayac Kittamaquund–the tribe's chief–killed his brother to take power in an effort to normalize relations with the arriving colonists. Kittamaquund's older brother–Wannas–had mistrusted the English.
Despite some initial normalizing of relations, the English colonists expanded their reach and took over the land once foraged and farmed by the Piscataway and other Indigenous peoples during the next several decades.
Gray hopes that the history of the Piscataway can be more accurately told and preserved through respectful archaeology, signage in state parks and interpretive education about Indigenous Peoples throughout Maryland.
"This is just woods to most people, they don't see the history," Gray said, as he stood in the middle of the former dig site at Chapel Point State Park.
At the Department of Natural Resources, staff are working with Gray, King, and Hanson to better tell the story of the Piscataway. During the fall event, the department's Environmental Justice Officer Mariah Davis discussed opportunities with Gray and park staff to create interpretive programs, written in coordination with the tribal community, to educate visitors about the rich Indigenous heritage in Southern Maryland at the park.
Davis and Gray also discussed opportunities to collaborate with the Piscatoway Canoy Tribe to grow culturally important crops and plant species on park land.
Gray welcomed the idea and suggested that a red cedar be planted in a prominent position at Chapel Point.
The red cedar tree is a sacred plant for the Piscataway people. They consider the evergreen as full of life and believe its red center core represents the life-blood of all animals, including man.
"We don't want the footprint of our people to be erased," Gray said.

title: Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 707
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Dave Yearsley has put in the hard work and overcome challenges to continue on with his love for auctioneering.From winning a competition with a 103 degree fever that was so bad he could barely see the bidders to becoming the 2025 Maryland Bid Calling Champion after experiencing a truck accident that resulted in a brain injury, Yearsley has persevered for his passion.
Since his first auction at the Ward World Championship in the early 1970s — when he was just a preteen — Yearsley, a Dorchester County resident, has auctioneered all over, from Texas to Missouri to the United Arab Emirates.
It all started with a daring decision.
Yearsley was 11 years old when he entered "the ugliest duck you ever saw" into a competition at the Ward World Championship, he said. His parents took him to the event in Salisbury, which also had an antique decoy auction. Sitting in the stands as Walton P. Taylor auctioned off antique decoys, Yearsley noticed Taylor's rhythm and told himself, "Wow, that's something I gotta learn to do."
"So I went home and I practiced all year long," Yearsley said, "and was terrible."
The next year, Yearsley was back at the championship with his parents and another "ugly duck" he had carved.
"So I'm 12," he recalled. "I got away from my mom and dad on purpose because I knew what I was going to do."
Yearsley ducked under a roped off area where the auctioneer, Taylor, was. With security guards watching, he went up to Taylor and shook his hand. "And I said, 'Mr. Taylor, my name's Dave Yearsley, and I want to sell decoys with you today.'"
After what felt to Yearsley like "the longest minute," Taylor said, "Young man, anybody that's got the guts to stand in front of me, you're damn right you're going to sell ducks with me today."
At this point, Yearsley's parents were searching for their son. Yearsley's mom was not happy when she found him onstage.
"She came racing up in front of the stage," Yearsley recalled. "'David, you get down here right now!' (she said)."
When Yearsley asked Taylor what he should do, Taylor replied, "It's time for you to learn not to listen to your parents."
From there, Taylor took Yearsley under his wing.
"He was my mentor," Yearsley said.
It took Yearsley two years to "get somewhat competent" at auctioneering, he said. To improve his speed, he practiced over instrumental bluegrass music.
"Instrumental bluegrass music has a definite beat," he said, adding that he got every instrumental bluegrass album he could to practice over.
In auction school, Yearsley learned tongue twisters, like "Betty Botter bought some butter," to improve his craft.
AGAINST THE ODDS
In September 2018, Yearsley got into a serious truck accident. His vehicle rolled over and he came out of it with a brain injury. It was possible he would not be able to walk or talk again. Eventually, both abilities came back to him, although his speech would slur.
"I didn't have good tongue control," he said.
Yearsley was told he would probably never be able to auction again. He said his doctor told him to keep trying because practicing might help bring back the skill.
"And that's what happened," Yearsley said.
In January, Yearsley was named Maryland's Bid Calling Champion by the Auctioneers Association of Maryland.
Lynne Zink, a past president of the association and the chair of the contest, said the annual competition brings auctioneers from across the state to vie for the title.
"Once someone has won the championship, then they don't get to compete again," she said. "So David will always be our 2025 champion."
Yearsley didn't think he would win it.
"I don't cry much — and I didn't let anybody see me do it — but I cried," he said about his response to winning the award. "I said, 'My god, how could I ever do this?'"
Yearsley wasn't the only one to shed a tear after he won. Zink, who is also an auctioneer and has known Yearsley for years, was happy to see Yearsley win the Maryland title.
"Whenever you see something like that, it's encouraging because he can be a role model for others," she said. "So when the doctors give you a prognosis and then you beat the odds, gosh, it makes everybody happy. Some of us were teared up."

Health is a secondary theme due to his injury recovery, and Business/Economy is relevant but less central.

 The red carpet will be unfurled for a high-end women's fashion show and luncheon in Easton on Saturday, Nov. 4, to benefit those served by the St. Vincent de Paul Society.All the featured women's apparel, specifically selected for the fall, winter and holiday seasons, will be from the Boutique, operated by the St.Vincent de Paul Society on Canvasback Drive in Easton.All proceeds from the event will assist the St. Vincent de Paul Society in providing food and financial support to disadvantaged residents in Talbot County.The show will be narrated by Janet Schilling, an Easton-based certified image and color consultant who is helping to curate the collection for the runway spectacular. It will be held from noon to 4 p.m. at the Maria Mitchell Social Hall at Saints Peter and Paul Church on South Washington Street.Schilling will narrate the runway walk as the models showcase some trendy looks along with complementary accessories.In addition, she also will offer advice to women in the audience on a range of fashion topics, such as what colors and accessories work best for your skin tone, what profiles flatter specific body types and how to transform your cluttered closet into a wardrobe sanctuary that makes you look great in clothes that fit your lifestyle."My goal is to help women move in the right direction and wear colors and styles that suit their individual personalities," said Shilling."Women who feel good about what they're wearing are more confident." All the clothing at the show will be available for purchase afterward at the Boutique, said Nadine Hilghman, co-chair of the event."Anyone who has not visited our boutique will be surprised by the designer labels we carry, along with such accessories as gold and silver jewelry," she said.The fashion show will also feature two silent auctions, one for a basket of select wines from the Triple Creek Winery in Cordova and the other a gift certificate for a restorative spa treatment.In addition, a limited number of silent auction tickets will be sold for two exclusive social gatherings, which will take place in March 2024 and feature hors d'oeuvres and specially crafted beverages.One of the events will be hosted by Father James Nash, the pastor of Saints Peter and Paul Church, on church grounds. Tickets for previous events hosted by Pastor Nash have sold out in less than an hour.The other will be a Boston Tea Party-themed gathering featuring food and drinks from the "home of the bean and the cod." title: Renovating history: Point Lookout Lighthouse reopens
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Renovating history: Point Lookout Lighthouse reopens

 April 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It helped guide ships through the hazards in the Chesapeake Bay and has a rich history in St. Mary's and mariner history.And now the public will be able to learn about some of that history themselves following a ribbon-cutting ceremony Monday that reopened the 195-year-old Point Lookout Lighthouse.
The lighthouse at the southern tip of St. Mary's County had been closed since June 2018 for renovations.
"It's incredible and once you're in there and you see, it's worth it," Maryland Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said. "I think the thing that I'm really impressed by is … having the relationship with [former lighthouse keeper families] the Yeatmans and the Gattons and just what it was really like living [back then]."
The total cost of the renovations was $5 million.
"How fantastic that folks can actually visit the lighthouse after almost a decade?" said Dawn Letts, who is the park manager of the Point Lookout State Park Complex.
The lighthouse had been closed for almost seven years.
"Historic preservations are very complex and it changed hands so many times before it came to the [Maryland Park Service] so a lot of things were added, a lot of things were taken away," said Maryland Park Service Director of Planning Jonas Williams, who previously served as assistant park manager at Point Lookout State Park. "So I think with the contractors we were able to identify a best course forward for making any modern changes to it and making sure the historic character of the building was still there."
"There was also the complexity of the project because it had to have a design for the exterior renovations," Letts said. "Then there also had to be a design component for the exhibits so there was a design build for both portions of the project."
The inside of the lighthouse features informational panels, period furniture, appliances, toys, vintage photographs and a large floor map of the Chesapeake Bay.
"It's great to see it functioning again," said Lisa Kane of Mechanicsville, who is a member of the Point Lookout Lighthouse Preservation Society.
The adjoining two sheds were also renovated and feature informational panels.
"There are two things that make this lighthouse and this site significant," Letts said.
Point Lookout is the country's oldest standing integral lighthouse, meaning that the light tower and keeper's quarters are in the same building, she said. Also, the presence of the buoy and coal sheds next to the lighthouse add a unique element to the site.
Referring to the two large sheds, which were constructed in the 1880s, Letts said, "A lot of times when the lights were automated there was no use for those buildings, however the Navy having them and utilizing them for storage space actually kept them intact and used, and that just makes the site unbelievable."
The ceremony was held in conjunction with Maryland State Parks Week, which also featured the reopening of the park's fishing pier on April 19 following a 6-month closure, as well as a stop to view Newtowne Neck State Park.
The Point Lookout Lighthouse, which was illuminated from 1830 until it was decommissioned in 1966, had over two dozen lighthouse keepers and assistants over the years, according to the U.S. Lighthouse Society.
The lighthouse will officially open several days per week to the public beginning later in May.
"I think it's also just incredibly exciting to have this to get people down here and you can just learn so much," Kurtz said. "We have a lot of things ongoing here at the park but I think all [of them] just continue to make this a focal point for the whole state."
Park to open camping in the fall
Point Lookout State Park is planning to reopen some of its camping sites in the fall.
Camping at the popular waterfront park has not been available for the past two years due to water and sewer line projects encompassing the entire park, as well as renovations of all of the pump stations.
Letts said the delay was caused by various factors, including supply chain issues and site conditions.
She said the park is hoping to reopen a couple camping loops in October for about a month and then fully reopen the campground next spring.

title: National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to Washington D.C.
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to Washington D.C.

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian American Art Museum is collaborating for the 11th year in a row with the National Cherry Blossom Festival for a series of in-person and virtual cherry blossom-themed public programs. The museum's cherry blossom family activities and celebrations are part of its hands-on program series, designed to spark learning, creativity and appreciation for the arts.The museum's popular Cherry Blossom Celebration for children and families will be presented in person Saturday, March 23, from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Weather permitting, the event will begin on the museum's F Street plaza with a Japanese taiko performance by the drumming group Nen Daiko.
Other performances in the museum's courtyard include double-dutch jump rope and other jump roping displays with Kangaroo Kids, and an all-vinyl music set of Japanese soul, funk, boogie, pop and disco by Les The DJ.
More information is available on the museum's website at https://americanart.si.edu.
Attendees can create their own cherry blossom-themed crafts and a spring-themed scavenger hunt will be available so visitors can explore the American Art Museum's galleries. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase at the Courtyard Café. This program is free, but registration is encouraged.
A cherry blossom-themed in-person workshop, part of the museum's series "Beyond the Studio," is scheduled for Sunday, March 24, at 1 p.m. Nicolas Shi, the official artist of the National Cherry Blossom Festival, will lead participants through an activity inspired by Washington's beloved cherry blossoms. This program costs $15 and requires advance registration by March 10 at 7 p.m.
The Art & Me Preservation Family Workshop, a virtual hands-on, artmaking workshop designed for children ages 3 to 8 and their caretakers, will take place Saturday, April 6, at 11 a.m. Families will discover how delicate sakura have been depicted in landscapes, figure paintings and prints for centuries, and how Smithsonian conservators preserve these beautiful yet fragile artworks. Then participants will create their own cherry blossom-inspired creations. This program is cohosted by the museum and the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art. This program is free, but registration is required.
A temporary video projection, co-presented by the National Cherry Blossom Festival and the museum, will illuminate the museum's facade from Wednesday, March 20, to Saturday, March 23, 8–9 p.m. Cherry blossom-themed artworks from Washington artists Robin Bell, Matthew Curry, Jonathan Monaghan and Shi will be projected onto the northwest corner of the building (Ninth and G streets N.W.). Each night, Bell will create a new video tableau, building new visuals upon the previous nights' work and mixing them live. Support for this event is provided by the DowntownDC BID and Park West Gallery.
Additional family activities are available on the Smithsonian American Art Museum's Family Zone webpage, including seasonal crafts, coloring pages inspired by artworks from the museum's permanent collection, videos and more.
About the Smithsonian American Art Museum
The Smithsonian American Art Museum is the flagship museum in the United States for American art and craft. It is home to one of the most significant and inclusive collections of American art in the world. The museum's main building, located at Eighth and G streets N.W., is open daily from 11:30 a.m. to 7 p.m. The museum's Renwick Gallery, a branch museum dedicated to contemporary craft, is located on Pennsylvania Avenue at 17th Street N.W. and is closed temporarily.
Check online for current hours and admission information. Admission is free. Follow the museum on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. For more,, call 202-633-1000 or 202-633-7970 or visit americanart.si.edu.
About the National Cherry Blossom Festival
The National Cherry Blossom Festival is one of the world's great celebrations of spring. The 2024 festival runs from March 20 to April 14 and includes four weeks of events featuring diverse and creative programming promoting traditional and contemporary arts and culture, natural beauty and community spirit.
The public can add the 2024 festival dates and signature event dates to their calendar and visit NationalCherryBlossomFestival.org or call 877-44-BLOOM for more information.

author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Taste of Cambridge brings delectable treats to downtown Cambridge

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 297
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The weather was perfect Saturday, drawing a large crowd to the 16th Taste of Cambridge event."We were extremely thrilled with the turnout," said Christina Wingate-Spence, Cambridge Main Street executive director. More than 300 Taste of Cambridge tickets were sold and the overall crowd in downtown Cambridge was upwards of 800, Wingate-Spence said.
The event — the second hosted after a hiatus during the COVID-19 pandemic — featured 11 cook-off contest competing for best crab soup, best crab cake, best Eastern Shore fare and best desserts.
Winners were:
Crab soup: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Crab cake: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Eastern Shore fare: Vintage 414 wine bar.Dessert: Blackwater Bakery and Eats.
Ticket holders voted for the people's choice award, which went to Blue Ruin's crab cake.
The judges for the four awards were: Laurie Forster, an author and national expert on all things wine; Tami Weber, WBOC morning show host; and Gena Levy, owner of Bay Country Bakery in Cambridge.
In addition to the cook-off contestants there was a Kid Zone, featuring a face painter and bounce houses. A giant crab balloon archway created by Cabin Fever Play Centre was the backdrop for many selfies.
Two stages featured a variety of entertainment. On the main stage at the intersection of Race and Gay streets, the Soul Crackers, an 11-piece ensemble from the Washington, D.C., area, made a repeat performance. They were followed by the Radio Pilots, a rock cover band, which received an enthusiastic welcome from the crowd.
On the second stage, located at the intersection of Muir and Race streets, a variety of students performed; along with Inland Fusion featuring Nancy and Jody; and Jayme D., a solo artist.
The event drew people from across the Eastern Shore and Washington, D.C. Wingate-Spence said the downtown shops had a large influx of customers throughout the day.

title: Masquerades, mimosas and metalwork: Academy Art Museum Craft Show featuring new events, offerings
author: Staff Writer
content:
Masquerades, mimosas and metalwork: Academy Art Museum Craft Show featuring new events, offerings

 September 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum in Easton is holding its annual Craft Show Oct. 26 and Oct. 27.It is the 27th year for the AAM Craft Show with a special preview event Oct. 25.
"The show will feature a wide array of juried exhibitors, including established artists, returning favorites from years past and many more artists new to the show," AAM said in an announcement. "Participating artists create work in all media including Basketry, Ceramics, Fiber — Decorative, Fiber — Wearable, Glass, Jewelry, Leather, Metal, Mixed Media, Sculpture and Wood."
AAM said this year's featured artist is Laura Baring-Gould.
She "works with elemental ingredients including bronze, paper, salt, beeswax, fabric, and wood to create sculptures."
Baring-Gould. received the Award of Excellence in Metal from the Philadelphia Museum and her work has been exhibited at the Smithsonian Craft Show, Philadelphia Museum Contemporary Craft Show, the American Craft Exhibition, Boston Public Library and the Museum of Fine Arts Boston.
AAM is bringing some new twists to the popular event.
The weekend of shopping begins with the Masquerade Ball Craft Show Preview Event, which will be held from 5:30-9:00 pm on Friday, October 27. Tickets will go on sale October 1. Attendees are urged to attend dressed in costume. The event will feature a collection of bespoke masquerade masks created by local artists, available for purchase or as an exclusive ticket add-on. Guests will also enjoy a fashion show featuring jewelry and wearable fiber art pieces created by Craft Show artists. The ticket price for the evening is $125 for Museum members and $150 for non-members. For a ticket with a custom-painted mask, tickets are $155 for members and $175 for non-members. All Preview Event tickets include unlimited re-entry to the show on Saturday and Sunday.
"We are very excited about our masquerade preview event this year, which adds a new layer of heightened fun and enthusiasm for our patrons," said AAM Interim Director Jennifer Chrzanowski.
Returning this year is the Craft Show Marketplace on Saturday, Oct. 26. Additional artist booths will be featured outside on South Street between the two show venues
— the Academy Art Museum and the Waterfowl building. The street will be engaged with other activities including classes with Woodworks on Wheels, a hands-on, mobile woodworking studio, owned and operated by Mark Freibaum, and wine tasting and charcuterie board design classes with Piazza Italian Market. Patrons can register in advance for classes on the Academy website which includes entry into the Craft Show all weekend.
New this year is the Craft Show Sunday Brunch, offered on Oct. 27 from 10 a.m. to 1 pm. The brunch includes a Mimosa bar. Tickets are $40 for AAM Members and $50 for non-members and includes admission into the show.
Woodworks on Wheels will also be hosting the free Little Crafters session on Sunday, Oct. 27 at 1-3 pm. Kids will learn the basics of woodworking and how to use a variety of tools in an assembly line style class, and at the end, will graduate with a golden hammer.
Craft Show hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 26, and 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 27. Attendees will be able to vote for their favorite artist for the Craft Show People's Choice Award which will be given on Sunday morning to the artist with the most votes. Admission to the Craft Show is $10 per Museum member and $12 for non-members, which includes a Craft Show tote bag.
"It has been an honor to chair the Craft Show for the past four years. This year promises to be our most dynamic show yet with over 70 top artists featuring renowned sculptor Laura Baring Gould, an outdoor market place, great food by Piazza and interactive workshops. There is something for everyone, and we look forward to seeing our neighbors at this fun and inspiring community event," Craft Show Board Chair Diz Hormel said.
For sponsorship opportunities or to purchase tickets or register for classes, visit academyartmuseum.org.
