title: St. Michaels’ Gingerbread Competition is back to spice up holiday celebration
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels’ Gingerbread Competition is back to spice up holiday celebration

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Christmas 
 
 412
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Dozens of gingerbread designers are competing for one of several cash prizes and for the admiration of the community this weekend.The St. Michaels' gingerbread competition is back in full swing after a nearly five-year hiatus. An array of intricately built gingerbread houses will be on show this weekend at the St. Micheals Woman's Club for the Gingerbread "House" Competition and Display.
Proceeds from the sale of these creations support the beneficiaries of Christmas in St. Michaels, including family service organizations, education and child development programs, and community enhancement organizations and programs.
Michele Lowe and Andrea Robinson, co-chairs of the Gingerbread Committee, both said they were fairly new to the area and heard of a St. Michaels gingerbread competition but had never witnessed it themselves.
Lowe said the memory of the competition was incredibly strong among the community and Lowe and Robinson felt a need to step up and bring back the beloved tradition.
"Everybody has been wanting this back since (2019)," Lowe said. "I guess we finally got coerced, and it's been a great success. We had a lot of the donations from the St Michael's Community Center, Critchlow Adkins (Children's Centers), who are also both beneficiaries."
Lowe mentioned that a young girl in the area, who last competed in 2019, had been eagerly awaiting and planning new designs for when the competition came back.
The gingerbread entries are divided into seven categories with cash prize awards. The categories cater to different skill levels and ages, including Master with a $500 prize and Adult with $300 first prize.
Additionally, there are categories for younger participants including young adults with a $100 prize, and children with and without an adult with a $100 prize for the respective categories.
Finally, there are categories for nonprofit organizations, Candy Backus Award (best depiction of the Eastern Shore) and a People's Choice Award.
Judges for the gingerbread competition include Commissioners of St. Michaels President Alfred Mercier, President and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Kristen Greenaway and St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald.
Prizes will be awarded on Sunday at the Woman's Club of St. Michaels at 2 p.m.
Robinson said she is happy with the support they have received this year and encourages people to continue their support into the new year.
"Thank you for your support, and please make gingerbread at home next year," Robinson said. "In order for us to keep doing this we need everybody to be excited next year and participate and start planning their creation for next year."

title: New art exhibit critiques America's 'consumption culture'
content:
New art exhibit critiques America's 'consumption culture'

 September 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 245
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new atrium exhibit at the Academy Art Museum debuts Friday, Sept. 15, and runs through August 2024.The exhibition is from South Dakota-based Oglaia Lakota artist Marty Two Bulls Jr.The exhibition "Marty Two Bulls Jr.: Dominion" examines America's "consumption culture, using the metaphor of the American Bison," according to a release from the Easton art museum."We are looking forward to welcoming visitors to Two Bulls, Jr.'s Atrium commission, which serves as a layered acknowledgment of the oppression Native American people have endured in their homelands as well as a critique of consumer culture. The breadth of Two Bulls, Jr.'s practice is incredible: from the immersive, floor-to-ceiling hand-cut prints he amasses on top of one another for his wall-mounted work, to monumental sculptures made from found objects such as bottles and trash cans, Two Bulls, Jr. conjures a mimesis of a crucial sociopolitical reality. We are excited for the interactive dimension of the exhibition, which will allow visitors to scan QR codes to learn the histories of some of the elements Two Bulls, Jr. incorporates into his work, such as barbed wire and the American bison," said AAM Curator Mehves Lelic.AAM's 2022-2023 Atrium Commission is supported by Carol Gordean, Joe Minarick in memory of Carol Minarick, and Mary Ann Schindler.For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/

title: Younger generations pitch in to continue Waterfowl tradition
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Younger generations pitch in to continue Waterfowl tradition

 November 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 662
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With more than 25,000 people attending this year's Waterfowl Festival, organizers needed all hands on deck to pull off the three-day event, including contributions of Easton's younger generations.Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon said her largest takeaway from this year's festival was the involvement and participation of youth volunteers.
"That is like my number one success story, the engagement of the kids, helping the festival, learning about the artists, learning about what the festival does," Kilmon said. "That was an incredible part of the success for me, as well as the hundreds and hundreds of adult volunteers that help us every year. But just seeing all those kids was just joy."
Kilmon said more than 200 high school students volunteered during the festival. She added that the lead points of contact at the different venues included many younger volunteers this year.
Kilmon also noted that expanding the festival's offerings for families and younger adults were goals for this year.
Throughout the weekend, families could be found at every corner. The Bay Street area had a fishing derby for kids and a "beer wetlands" tent tailored for younger adults. The Phillip Wharf Environmental Center brought its Fishmobile to show off live animals and educate children on the creatures in the Chesapeake Bay.
Behind the Easton Elks Lodge, Sean Mann Outdoors, a Trappe sporting goods store, held duck and goose calling clinics for kids on Saturday and Sunday.
Instructors Sean Mann and Nick Michael taught children ages four through 14 the basics of calling, passing down the skills in hopes of cultivating a young generation of callers. After Saturday's calling clinic, Mann asked parents to let their children use the duck and goose calls they were given to take home.
"Parents, please encourage these youngsters to call," Mann said.
Across town at the Bay Street Ponds, EJ Milhollan, 22, served as chair of the beer wetlands area for the second consecutive year. He's the son of Eric Milhollan, president of Waterfowl's Board of Directors.
"I've always worked at Waterfowl, and it was an opportunity that was kind of thrown at me, and I said, 'Why not?'" EJ Milhollan said. "And they asked me to come back this year. It was a good time last year."
For the Milhollans, the festival has always been a family affair. While it was Eric Milhollan's first year as board president, he's been involved as a volunteer ever since he was a child. Now, his wife and four children — EJ and 20-year-old triplets — carry on that family Waterfowl tradition.
Eric Milhollan sees the festival's growth as not simply attracting a new group of people, but "attracting more groups with different likes."
"It's community, it's family, it's downtown," he said. "You just see everything changing. It's just a fun place to be."
"The backbone of the festival, for this weekend, is certainly art," he continued. "But it's certainly tickets as well. You see different age brackets that like different things. So if you've been over to sportsmans' (pavilion), that attracts a certain type of people. And whether it's music, whether it's beer, whether it's just hanging out and the food, there's something for everybody."
Kilmon noted that by putting an emphasis on outdoor activities like the fishing derby, beer wetlands and calling clinic, the younger generations learn of Waterfowl's conservation and preservation efforts.
"All those outdoor activities really worked well to get our kids outside, get our families outside, and (help) them understand why we do what we do," Kilmon said. "To preserve these wide-open spaces for these kids to have when they grow up. I think these kids that we attracted to us this fall, hopefully, will engage with us throughout the year."
Reflecting on how involved he and his family have become, Eric Milhollan said his four children are bringing their friends over to enjoy the festival and continue its momentum.
"Just passing that off to different generations is what keeps it going," Eric Milhollan said. "And you see a lot of that here. You see a lot of families."

 An art exhibit at the Academy Art Museum in Easton featuring the work of Hoesy Corona wraps up Sunday, Sept. 10."Corona's work highlights the complex relationship between humans and the environment by focusing on our changing climate and its impact on habitation and migration patterns. Using the archetype of the traveler, who is seen holding suitcases and voyaging through a wide array of landscapes towards a better place, Corona tackles the reality of the human aspect of climate change while celebrating the lushness and vibrancy of flora, bodies of water, and geographic forms, and bringing attention to the multitudinous powers of nature," according to AAM's summary of the exhibit."The artist transformed the Museum's Saul Atrium Gallery with site-specific vignettes that each picture a character journeying from a land made uninhabitable by global warming. title: 15-year-old Javion Jones a new minister at Union Baptist Church
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
15-year-old Javion Jones a new minister at Union Baptist Church

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Javion Jones, 15, is now officially a minister at Union Baptist Church after he passed his minister's training class in May.After multiple tests, Jones took his final test, his trial sermon in front of the church.
On May 18, Jones conducted his trial sermon, where he preached on Luke 18:35-43. The scripture highlights Jesus coming near Jericho encountering a blind man. Jesus then preformed a miracle granting the blind man his sight.
"I picked that because as a young boy, people would say you're called, and I could just say thank you not knowing what was going on because I was blind to my calling because I was just young, and other people who were unblind spiritually could see it," Jones said.
After a church council vote, Jones was voted in as a minster at Union Baptist Church.
"I'm just a minister right now," Jones said. "I do know that shortly, my pastor will be placing me over the prayer department."
Jones' mother, Taryn Bell, is excited for what God has in store for Jones' future.
"I was just extremely proud as any parent would be," Bell said. "When I look at him, I know that being a licensed minister comes with a big responsibility, but I also know that Javion has a heart for serving. I'm someone who believes that if God called you, it's no limit to your age. But as his parent, I do try to make sure that he stays a kid and not feel the pressure that he has to have it all together. I'm just excited to see how God will continue to use him, and how he'll grow, and his ministry and the word."
Jones' long-term goal is to be elevated to the office of a reverend. Then, a couple years after, he plans to apply at a church and become a pastor. Jones also plans to study mortuary science in Catonsville after he graduates in 2028.
Those interested in contacting Jones about his trial sermon can reach him at @Javionjonesministry@gmail.com.

title: Busy fall schedules call for quick, hearty meals - COUNTRY COOKING
content:
Busy fall schedules call for quick, hearty meals - COUNTRY COOKING

 September 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: B4 | Section: News 
 
 801
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Busy schedules have begun filling the calendars therefore mealtimes and menus are changing as well. One thing is certain - the appetites remain just as normal - starving. Today we will revisit some tried and true recipes and some new ones. Since Fall signals lots of outdoor and indoor activities, food preparation needs to be simple but filling. Fall or autumn - whichever you call it arrives Sept. 23. Fall has always been my favorite season. Not too hot and not too cool - just perfect for fall house cleaning and preparing for the upcoming holidays.Fall fruits and vegetables seem to taste so delicious or is that because local crops are coming to an end.My local produce stand had a few late green peppers, and I grabbed several to make a family favorite - stuffed pepper soup. The crock pot is perfect for making this soup. Place 1-pound uncooked hamburger in first followed by one large can of tomato soup, undiluted, one medium size can of beef broth, one medium size can of diced tomatoes, one large diced onion, one large green pepper - cleaned and diced, and two tablespoons brown sugar. Place the lid on and cook on low for 6 to 7 hours. The last hour of cooking, add one bag of Boil-in-a-Bag of rice and continue to cook another hour. Not only does it taste good, but the aroma is tantalizing.Serve with breadsticks or an assortment of crackers.These next few recipes were popular with sports parents so I will run them again.AIR FRYER FRENCH FRIES1 pound russet potatoes, salt and pepper to taste, cooking oil.Wash 1 pound of russet potatoes and cut into wedges, Season with salt and pepper, Spray basket lightly with cooking oil. Place wedges in the air fryer basket making sure not to crowd them so air can circulate.Spray tops of potato wedges lightly with cooking spray, Cook at 400 degrees F for 7 minutes and then flip over and cook for 7 minutes more.AIR FRYER CHICKEN NUGGETS1 boneless skinless chicken breast, 1/4 teaspoon salt, 1/8 teaspoon black pepper, 1/2 cup unsalted butter melted, 1/2 cup breadcrumbs, 2 tablespoons grated Parmesan optional.Preheat the air fryer to 390 degrees for 4 minutes. Trim any fat from chicken breast, Slice into 1/2-inch-thick slices, then each slice into 2 to 3 nuggets.Season chicken pieces with salt and pepper. Place melted butter in a small bowl and breadcrumbs (with Parmesan, if using) in another small bowl. Dip each piece of chicken in butter, then breadcrumbs. Place in a single layer in the air fryer basket.Depending on the size of your air fryer, you may need to bake in two batches or more. Set the timer to 8 minutes. When done, check if the internal temperature of chicken nuggets is at least 165 degrees F. Remove nuggets from the basket with tongs and set onto a plate to cool.AIR FRYER CINNAMON SUGAR DOUGHNUTSCooking spray, 1/2 c. milk, 1/4 c. plus 1 tsp. granulated sugar, divided, 1 (0.25-oz.) packet or 2 1/4 tsp. active-dry yeast, 2 c. all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp. kosher salt, 4 tbsp. butter, melted, 1 large egg, 1 tsp. pure vanilla extract. For CINNAM ON SUGAR. 1/2 c. granulated sugar, 2 tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 tbsp. melted butter. Grease a large bowl with cooking spray. In a small, microwave-safe bowl or glass measuring cup, add milk. Microwave until lukewarm, 40 seconds. Add a teaspoon of sugar and stir to dissolve, then sprinkle over yeast and let sit until frothy, about 8 minutes. In a medium bowl, whisk together flour and salt. In a large bowl, whisk together remaining ¼ cup sugar, butter, egg, and vanilla.Pour in yeast mixture, mix to combine, then add in dry ingredients, stirring with a wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms.SLOW COOKER CHICKEN PARMESAN SLIDERS1 1/2 - 2 pounds boneless, skinless chicken breasts, Salt and pepper, 1 jar (24-ounce) or 3 cups all-natural marinara sauce, 2 teaspoons fresh pre-minced garlic, 1 teaspoon Italian seasoning crushed in hand, 12 slider wheat buns or rolls, 3/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese, 6 slices of Provolone cheese, cut into fourths.Lightly season all sides of chicken with salt and pepper. Add the chicken breasts, marinara sauce, garlic, and Italian seasoning to a slow cooker. Cook on LOW for 2 1/2 - 3 hours. Chicken is done when it shreds easily and is white all the way through (or registers 165°F internally). Shred with two forks.Preheat the broiler. Open up the buns and place them on a sheet pan, insides facing up. Broil for 1-2 minutes, until toasted. Watch closely so they don't burn! To build a sandwich place some hot shredded chicken on a bun, sprinkle with 1 tablespoon Parmesan cheese, top with two little pieces of Provolone or Mozzarella cheese, and pop the top of the bun in place.Frozen chicken burritos are a nearly perfect freezer meal. They freeze and thaw well and can go straight from freezer to microwave or oven.

title: Middle-schooler is youngest to ever publish a fantasy novel
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Middle-schooler is youngest to ever publish a fantasy novel

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Monday afternoon, 12-year-old Evelyn Klotz finished her middle school finals. The previous day, Klotz spoke to a sold-out audience at the Flying Cloud Bookstore about her newly published fantasy novel "Hero of Draconis."Klotz, a Trappe resident, set the book store's record as the first person to sell every copy of her book and sell out an event. But that wasn't the only record she broke that day.
Klotz also became the youngest person ever to write and publish a fantasy novel, according to TCK Publishing.
She began working on "Hero of Draconis" at 10-years-old. After writing on her own for some time, her father Eric connected her with a manuscript headhunter who gave her guidance on the writing and publishing process.
Klotz took a college-level writing course and edited her novel with the headhunter line by line.
"It really helped to improve my understanding of plot and characters because let's just say some of the characters were not the best before I went through it and fixed them," she said.
Klotz found inspiration in her backyard, her younger brother (who she based the character Meep on), and other fantasy novels like the "Eragon" series by Christopher Paolini. "The author of that series was only 18 when he published his first book, and I wanted to be better than that," Klotz said.
Eric Klotz said it feels like one of those proud dad moments. "I'm also a little annoyed because I feel like she's out-accomplished me already," he said with a chuckle. "But no, she's fantastic, and I'm super happy and proud of her."
Evelyn Klotz described the book as "a 340-page novel that follows the quest of four characters journeying across the fantasy planet to save the known world from total obliteration."
She said her main motivation for writing the novel was to create a world that hadn't been tainted by machines or technology while highlighting her love of nature.
Without offering spoilers, Evelyn Klotz said the novel ends with a massive cliffhanger.
"It's a big cliffhanger, an annoying cliffhanger" Eric Klotz said. He will have to wait along with the rest of her readers for answers in the second installment of her series, which is already underway.

title: Locals collect historical items in an attempt to preserve Cordova's story
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Locals collect historical items in an attempt to preserve Cordova's story

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 698
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CORDOVA — Teresa and Dale Dawson, the owners of Tuckahoe Seafood, are collectors and storytellers.They document the history of Cordova along with steaming and selling crabs. Their collection of ephemera marking the ups and downs of life in an Eastern Shore town makes up the Cordova Community Historical Society, nestled in Tuckahoe Seafood.
"Cordova was big around 1900," Dale Dawson said. "It was bustling because of the railroad. It was originally called Thimbletown. They had the largest packing cannery in Talbot County for tomatoes, beans and corn. It was the Talbot Packing Company. Farming in general changed from truck farming, which was produce, to grain farming. It all switched and the canneries went down hill."
"Our main focus is collecting memorabilia and information just so it doesn't get lost. Cordova has been long overdue to have a historical society," said Teresa Dawson.
This team enjoys going down historical rabbit holes together.
"One of my favorite stories is about Doc James. His name was James Fair," Teresa said.
Getting excited, Dale started to finish her sentences.
"Doc James lived in a little shanty, and he was really old. He was born in 1876 because he got a certificate from the President for being born during the cenntenial," he said. "... People used to come from Philadelphia and New Jersey. They would line up to meet with this guy as a healer."
There was another alarming story from Cordova.
"Cordova had a bank, and it was robbed around 1930 or 1932," Teresa said. "They blew the safe with nitro and got like $1,500. It was looted again. They people came back another year. They blew the safe door, and the owner heard it. They ran away, but didn't get any cash."
These citizen historians do it mostly for fun.
"If we don't do this, it is going to be lost," Teresa said.
Of all the items in their store, Teresa said her favorite is a pastel painting of the Baptist church by Jenny Willis, who died in 1952.
"We were thrilled to get it. She was a suffragette and a local correspondent for Cordova for The Star Democrat. She was a renaissance woman. A writer, a painter, a gardener. Really interesting," she said.
Dale's favorite item is a wooden box that was used to hold baking soda called "Parrot Monkey."
"It has the original address. It came in on a steamboat from Coveys Landing. They would come to the ramp and transfer cargo. So that is my favorite. We have tried to find more information on the steam boat business. The railroad put that out of business and trucking put the railroad out of business," he said.
The seafood business and museum is housed in a building built by Dale's father in 1946. It was a mechanic's garage.
Tuckahoe Seafood has been selling crabs since 1987 and collecting historical pieces almost as long.
They have gotten so many donations that they are running out of room in the seafood store. Every available surface has some historical object.
"We need a permanent home, because this is not ideal. It needs to be stored in a climate controlled (environment). It needs to have some more care put into it," Teresa said.
The Dawsons have helped to create a the Cordova Historical Society. They started having meetings once a month. They have had fund raisers and sold calendars and stickers.
"We have a president, a vice president, a secretary and a treasurer. It is very loose. We would like this just to be fun. We love meeting and talking about history. Show and tell at the end of the meeting," Teresa said. "Our main focus was trying to get Ingram's gas station restored and buy it. That is what we were fundraising for. But he is not selling it to us."
"We thought that would be a perfect location for a little museum," Dale said.
The historical society host events like Cordova Day, which will take place on March 9 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Cordova firehouse.
"We are going to have other people in the community, not just ours, who have exhibits and memorabilia on Cordova. We will have quilters and Rhonda's Round Biscuits, who does the beaten biscuits. It is going to be a day to celebrate Cordova," Teresa said.

25th Denton parade draws hundreds - Lighting of the green, Christkindlmarkt also appeal to young and old

 DENTON - Hundreds of people lined Denton's Market Street for the town's 25th Holiday Parade 6 p.m. Thursday, Dec. 7.The mild evening was filled with the sights and sounds of an old-fashioned small-town parade.
Fire trucks blared sirens, horns and flashing lights; floats generated bubbles and confetti; some marchers threw candy and waved flags; and marching bands strutted and played holiday music.
On the grandstand was master of ceremonies Keith Shaffer and three judges: Caroline County Teacher of the Year Rob Honer, His Hope Ministries Director Stefanie Johnson and CASA of Caroline Director Amy Horne.
Trophy winners were Schaefer Farms and Greenhouses, first place float; Pure Country 4-H Club, second place float; Denton Volunteer Fire Company, best fire equipment; Lockerman Middle School, best marching band; Grace Upon Grace Dance Studio, best dance troupe; Maryland Rough Riders, best equestrian unit; Bill and Gail Towers' 1931 John Deere tractor, favorite automobile; Caroline-Dorchester County 4-H Fair Queen Skylar Blunt, favorite royalty; and Chesapeake Culinary Center, best use of lights.
The parade began at the Health and Public Services Building on South Seventh Street, and made its way down Market Street, past the Caroline County Courthouse, where the Rotary Club of Denton hosted the lighting of the historic green, along with the Caroline County Garden Club and Caroline County Recreation and Parks.
Rotary Club President Angel Perez welcomed the crowd, and members of the North Caroline High School chorus sang holiday songs and led the singing of "Silent Night." Shoppers lingered along Market Street and popped in and out of stores as they made their way along the shopping district.
For the first time, the outdoor Christkindlmarkt, sponsored by Downtown Denton Main Street Inc. was held in conjunction with the parade. Starting at 5 p.m. and ending at 8:30 p.m., the outdoor holiday market on the green at Third and Market streets featured a large lighted Christmas tree, craft vendors, food trucks, and Santa and Mrs. Claus.
Patti Wood of Patti's Petals welcomed the combined events. "The more the merrier," she said. "It helps to bring foot traffic in, and that's what we want."

title: Parade, performances to mark Frederick Douglass Day
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Parade, performances to mark Frederick Douglass Day

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The second annual Frederick Douglass Day is being planned for Feb. 17.There will be a parade, performances at the Avalon and a gala dinner at the Armory. This is being put on by Tarence Bailey Sr., Operation Frederick Douglass on The Hill and the Bailey-Groce Family Foundation.
The event is a fundraiser, and tickets for performances are $85 and $135 including dinner. The parade is free to the public.
Feb. 14 is the anniversary of Douglass' birth, and Feb. 20 is the anniversary of his death. So this week in February commemorates his life, organizers said. It would be Douglass' 206th birthday.
February is also Black History Month.
"The parade is going to start in front of the Easton Police Department at 9:30 (a.m.). We have invited the 54th Massachusetts. We are waiting on word from them. We invited the U.S. marshals. Frederick Douglass recruited for the Massachusetts State Militia and held a position in marshals. We will have the Maryland National Guard. I want it to be everything that Uncle Frederick deserves," said Bailey, who is Frederick Douglas' five-time great nephew.
After the parade, the Avalon portion starts at 3. It is a play called Frederick Douglass Lion of Thunder by the actor Phil Darius Wallace.
There is an art competition for graphic design and AI to create posters for the event. AI needs to be 30 seconds long with sound, and there is a $500 award. It has to have three elements — a lion, Frederick Douglass and the African God of Thunder Shango.
A former American Idol singer Ayla Dennis will perform at the Avalon. She is from Easton. John Coleman will sing the Black national anthem.
While Azu will play the saxophone at the Armory, DJ Push Play D.C. will keep the tunes flowing. Bailey described the food as "Eastern Shore" with fried chicken.
"We have Mrs. (Millicent) Sparks doing her Harriet Tubman experience," Bailey said.
"Our whole goal was to try to create a state holiday for Frederick Douglass that we could push forward for a federal holiday. Every year we want it to be bigger and bigger and bigger and eventually go statewide as a Civil Rights heroes holiday," he said.
According to the event's Facebook page, "All proceeds from the evening support Operation Frederick Douglass on The Hill and the work of The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation Inc., with the ultimate goal of building an African-American Cultural Center." For more information, visit fdhill.org.
Donations may be made to The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation at any Shore United Bank or can be mailed to P.O. Box 266, Newcomb, MD 21653.

title: Church Hill Theatre thrives after being saved
author: Tamara Forte
content:
Church Hill Theatre thrives after being saved

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 919
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL - Saved from a wrecking ball demolition in 1983, the Church Hill Theatre is a preserved piece of history and home to many.Since its inception, the theater has hosted over 140 shows on its stage. On Oct. 27, the CHT celebrated 40 years of being "saved from the wrecking ball" with celebratory ribbon cutting.With a DJ, hors devours, theatre memorabilia and a multitude of stories, members celebrated with a champagne toast the past 40 years and all those who helped to save, renovate and make the theatre the success it is today.Located on Walnut Street in the somewhat sleepy small town of Church Hill, built in 1929, the theater boasts a history of card parties, dances, films, and even organ playing - as it was a community building before it was a theater.In 1944, a fire damaged the building, and it was renovated in the Art Deco style that still exists today.Fast forward to 1983, the local bank wanted to knock down the building for a parking lot. Friends for Church Hill Preservation began with Howard and Jan Burns, Suzanne and John Gutting and Howard and Mary Wood through much fundraising - selling chair nameplates raised $13,000 - the team was able to buy the building on Feb. 26, 1985. A plaque with the original name plates is still on display in the lobby.Donations also came from the Church Hill High School, no longer in existence.Under the newly organized Friends group, Mary Wood wrote their first theater production "1787."To date, Church Hill Theatre is one of the few remaining theaters, self-owned and not renting space. With owning a historic building comes lots of upkeep and general maintenance.Over the years, many things have had to be fixed, replaced, or renovated including the stage curtains, the chairs (2021), the floors, and the boiler - to name a few.The rich emerald and gold wall fabric is also new, as it was replaced and recreated specially to mimic the original Art Deco with the same coloring and shapes - exaggerated in size to impress the guests. This past August 2023, the marquee outside was also replaced.Juanita Wieczoreck, CHT business manager, says the marquee is " beautiful now. It's just gorgeous."Currently, the theater has a six-year plan to replace the almost obsolete gel lighting with LED lighting, expand the light panel, add a dimmer pack and lighting strip and replace the lighting fixtures. "Upgrade, fix, replace: a historic building always needs something," Wieczoreck explains. Donations are needed to help make this plan become a reality.Decades later, the magic is still happening. Becca VanAken, former CHT board member, current volunteer, and founder of the Green Room Gang Jr., not only met her husband at the theatre but also got married on the CHT stage surrounded by cast, complete with all the props and details: poster, playbills, and given speeches. With tears in her eyes, VanAken explains that this theatre is a "special place with special people."During COVID, the theater remained open virtually for some online classes. VanAken shares that the theater's virtual classes and involvement helped with overall community mental health and was a "home and family for many."Throughout the year, theater activities are available for all ages. Some activities include two five-week summer camps for kids that are in the Green Room Gang and Green Room Gang Jr. Starting Feb. 5, the B.A.S.K. Basic Acting Skills for Kids classes will run for five Saturdays for age groups first through fifth grades and sixth through 12th. Adult acting classes (18+) and intern and staff programs for high school, college, and beyond are also available.As a nonprofit, every dollar helps. Board member and theater Director Sylvia Maloney explains "Since profits from the shows are not enough to run the theater, we rely on grants, donations, and fundraising also." The annual Giving Campaign runs from November 2023 to January 2024. The easiest ways to give to the CHT is to call the office with a credit card, send a check made out to Church Hill Theatre, or come see the shows! Maloney emphasizes the importance of theatre by saying, "It's a gift. The gift of theater.You don't outgrow it because you get older or you get aches and pains the way it is with sports. It's something you can do your entire lifetime.There's so much to do in theatre. You can act, be a director, be a stage manager.If you like running around and doing errands, you can do props. You can do lighting.If you like sewing, the big major thing is costuming.You can do carpentry and build wonderful sets. [Theater] is also introducing the public to so many thoughts, ideas, positions, and understanding of what this world is all about."One of the best ways to support CHT financially, is to come and see this historic playhouse in action. The new renovations bring both more comfort and elegance to the playhouse. The next 2023 show is Orson Welles' radio version of "A Christmas Carol" on stage Dec. 15, 16 and 17. CHT Director, Kathy Jones has rewritten it to be held "in the round," which means the action will surround the audience. Families are welcome with both matinees and evening shows available. Upcoming shows for 2024 include: Charley's Aunt, March 8-24; My Fair Lady, June 7-23; Osage County, Sept. 13-29 and Ride the Cyclone, Nov. 8-24.The theatre will go dark for more renovations in late December 2023 until Jan. 12, reopening with a fundraising Cabaret Night.

title: New podcast seeks to bring new perspectives, a sense of place to Underground Railroad
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
New podcast seeks to bring new perspectives, a sense of place to Underground Railroad

 December 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Rooted Wisdom Podcast is an extension of the film "Nature's Role in the Underground Railroad," but with a twist.The producers and host want to incorporate multiple different avenues of Underground Railroad history, expanding beyond the scope of the film to explore themes like criminal justice inequality, redlining and voter suppression, and to highlight local histories through guided experiences.
"The podcast itself goes into the legacy of the Underground Railroad and how it is still in the tapestry of our contemporary issues today that we feel," George Burroughs, one of the podcast's producers, said. "From teenage criminal justice, inequality, redlining, redistricting, voter suppression, and we also, in the podcast, wanted to be able to go to different locations. We wanted to take it a step further and let (podcast host) Tony (Anthony Cohen), as a historian, interpreter, interview other people and to really dive into these issues."
The podcast's first series was released in September, and it showed three different perspectives about the Underground Railroad.
"The first three episodes, Tony talks with a filmmaker, a nonprofit leader and a wildlife photographer," Lauren Giordano, a podcast producer, said. "So getting those perspectives on the history and how that shows up for them and their work, in their lives, I think was something that was kind of unique about that."
But the podcast is not completely divorced from the natural, geography-based perspective of the film it's based off of. The podcast has nature references as well.
The guests on the Rooted Wisdom podcast, along with the host, bring multiple perspectives on how nature played a part in the Underground Railroad from their professions or experiences.
Adkins Arboretum in Tuckahoe State Park hold a big focus the podcast, as they do in the film.
The producers and the host believe that locals can look around and find that there is so much history of the Underground Railroad in their community. Their way to learn this history, the producers said, is through Rooted Wisdom.
"My background is in the history of the Underground Railroad, and as a Marylander, starting 30 years ago, I came to realize how much of that history played out on the Eastern Shore," Cohen said. "Not only Tubman and Douglas, but many of the abolitionists of the 1830s and whatnot had Maryland roots, and so the history is really anchored there."
"So I was involved in the community, and of some of those efforts which led to the establishment of the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway, the 123-mile route through Dorchester and Caroline counties that roughly follows her route."
Although the Rooted Wisdom podcast is Maryland-based, the plan is to expand. The producers and host believe that the podcast can give everyone a perspective from their own personal community with the history of the Underground Railroad.
"I think all of the podcasts that we've done and that we're envisioning or planning are really partly focused on a sense of place," Cohen said. "So I think as we travel around the state and eventually around the country doing this story, we'll be bringing, or bringing to light, a story that itself is often underground, and I think that'll be powerful for people."
To listen to the podcast, visit rootedwisdom.org/podcast.

title: Crowd enjoys music, fireworks in St. Michaels
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Crowd enjoys music, fireworks in St. Michaels

 July 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 314
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Around 1,500 people packed the campus of Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum on Saturday night to enjoy live music and the town's annual fireworks show along the Miles River.The Shades of Blue Orchestra performed at the event for the ninth time, playing classic hits from jazz artists like Frank Sinatra and Count Basie. A dance floor in front of the Tolchester Beach Bandstand was often packed with couples, friends and families dancing.
Conductor and veteran Michael A. Walker led the 18-piece big band. Before dusk, Shades of Blue took time to honor all branches of the military.
"We see this as our most community-centered event," Shannon Mitchell, vice president of engagement for the museum, said. "It's our local community (and) local residents that come in and enjoy the evening."
She added that the museum keeps admission costs for the event lower than other festivals in order to encourage attendance. Members of the museum received discounted prices Saturday.
"We provide a dance floor and a great view of the fireworks," Mitchell said.
Pat and Laura Conolgue made the drive down from right outside of Philadelphia to enjoy the weekend's festivities with their two daughters, 9-year-old Emily and 5-year-old Natalie.
It was the third year the Conologue family came to Big Band Night.
"It's better than the big city of Philadelphia," Pat Conolgue said.
Emily was on the dance floor for much of the night, making friends with other children as she learned how to dance. She said her favorite part of the night was dancing and celebrating.
Mitchell pointed out that expanding the kids' activities at the event is a goal for future years. This year, there were inflatables for kids to enjoy as attendees entered.
"With our new welcome center that opened last year, we're hoping to expand the event to have more kids activities on that side," Mitchell said, "potentially have music on both sides of campus in the future."

title: National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to D.C.
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to D.C.

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 390
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian American Art Museum is collaborating for the 12th year in a row with the National Cherry Blossom Festival for a series of in-person cherry blossom-themed public programs. The museum's cherry blossom family activities and celebrations are part of its hands-on program series, designed to spark learning, creativity and appreciation for the arts.The museum's popular Cherry Blossom Celebration for children and families will be presented in person Saturday, March 22, from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Weather permitting, the event will begin on the museum's F Street plaza with a Japanese taiko performance by the drumming group Nen Daiko.
Other performances in the museum's courtyard include an all-vinyl music set of Japanese soul, funk, boogie, pop and disco by Les The DJ. More information is available on the museum's website.
Attendees can create their own cherry blossom-themed crafts and explore the museum's galleries during a spring-themed scavenger hunt. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase at the Courtyard Café. This program is free, but registration is encouraged.
Two cherry blossom-themed in-person workshops, presented as part of the museum's series "Beyond the Studio," are scheduled for Sunday, March 23, and Sunday, April 6, both at 1 p.m. Washington, D.C., maker Miri Artyukhina of Capitol Stich Co. will lead participants through embroidery basics and skills required to create a festive spring artwork inspired by cherry blossoms (cost $15); space is limited, and advance registration is required.
Additional family activities are available on the Family Zone webpage, including seasonal crafts, coloring pages inspired by artworks from the museum's permanent collection, videos and more.
During the National Cherry Blossom Festival, the museum is presenting "Pictures of Belonging: Miki Hayakawa, Hisako Hibi and Miné Okubo," which honors three trailblazing Japanese American women artists. The women were three of the most active and critically acclaimed American artists of Japanese descent in the years that had been underrecognized within 20th-century American art history. The exhibition is free and is on view through Aug. 17.
For more about the Smithsonian American Art Museum, visit americanart.si.edu.
About the National Cherry Blossom FestivalThe National Cherry Blossom Festival is one of the world's great celebrations of spring. The 2025 festival takes place March 20–April 13 and includes four weeks of events featuring diverse and creative programming promoting traditional and contemporary arts and culture, natural beauty and community spirit. Visit NationalCherryBlossomFestival.org or call 877-44-BLOOM for more information.

title: Gallery walk with Lee Glazer: new exhibits on display at Academy Art Museum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Gallery walk with Lee Glazer: new exhibits on display at Academy Art Museum

 May 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Arts 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Lee Glazer, senior curator, took time to walk through the three exhibits that are up at The Academy Art Museum. The offerings are wildly different in theme and materials, but all engage the mind with their stories.Glazer is versed in the movements and times that created these artists and loves to talk to about art.
"It is a diverse array of approaches to art making. We have the old master prints by Durer. And here is a locally based Baltimore painter Philip Koch, who you can tell if you are familiar with Edward Hopper's work," she said.
And Darlene Taylor has a gallery full of mixed-media portraits of Black women.
The first exhibit is "Light: Paintings by Philip Koch." There are landscapes and architectural paintings inspired by Edward Hopper. Koch discovered Hopper's lonely representational work in the 1970s and was so interested that he went to Hopper's coastal residence to work.
"He went to Oberlin in the 1960s, so minimalism and conceptualism are the dominant strains in art schools. Like grids, big blocky forms. Very pared down and purely abstract. Not representational," Glazer said. "But when he went to University of Indiana for his masters, the environment was more receptive to realism."
In the 1980s, Koch had an epiphany. He was invited to be a resident at Hopper's former studio on Cape Cod. He goes back every summer allured by the sea views that moved Hopper as well. Koch has also painted in Maine.
"These are sort of a heightened realism, filtered through imagination and memory," she said. The paintings have a magical realist approach to realism. You can see a boat, but it is on a river of dreams. This is not straight plein air painting.
His title of the painting "Voyage of Life" is an homage to spiritual American 19th century painter Thomas Cole, who has a famous series of paintings called "The Voyage of Life."
"I like the blending of art historical references with lived environment — both visually and through memory," she said.
She moved on to the next gallery. It contains the show Darlene R. Taylor "Heirlooms." There are large portraits of Black women made of mixed medium collage. These women seem to evoke lost memories. Almost all of the artisit's subjects' backs are to the audience.
Taylor echoes 19th century forms like the silhouette. History serves as a muse. Lost genealogy seems to fuel this art's search for belonging.
A lot of the pieces are big and look down on the gallery space. Looking closely, there is old fabric, burnt paper and buttons sewn in to make the story topographical, almost sculptural.
Taylor teaches English at Howard University and has a home on Tilghman Island.
"She talks of these heirlooms as being a reclamation and reconstruction of African American archives. We don't see the face but typically it is a young woman in her 20s or 30s. This evokes some of the gaps or things that are unknown when you do archival research, particularly when you do research about African American men and even more so women in this country," Glazer said.
That something missing informs this work.
Looking closely at Taylor's stitching work, there are blue x's that connote the signature of a domestic laborer.
In the last gallery is "Albrecht Durer: Master Prints (1471-1528)." He was an innovative printmaker and art theorist.
Trained as a goldsmith, this woodcut and copper plate engraving artist rubbed elbows with DaVinci and Michelangelo. His black-and-white prints have so much narrative density, often religious, that each one is like a little movie.
To say his technique is exacting would be an understatement. The Academy supplies magnifying glasses to look at the prints to ensure details are not missed.
On top of being a vaunted and celebrated artist, Durer had a marketer's instinct to move. He was one of the first artists to create his own logo.
"These are the complete 16 engravings from Durer's series — the engraved passion. That was a super popular subject for private devotion. It is a narrative of Christ's last days on Earth," Glazer said.
Durer was alive during the dawn of the early modern age in the 1600s.
"We have got the printing press and movable type, and we have got an upwardly mobile merchant class, who for the first time has money to spend on this art," Glazer said. "Art and commerce can go together."
The three shows run through July 14. Admission is free.

 Those seeking to have an event published in the Star Democrat's calendar are asked to email details to community@stardem.com.WEDNESDAY MORNING ARTISTS, weekly at 9:30 a.m., 900 Peachblossom Place, Cambridge. All are welcome, from beginners to pros. There is always opportunity and something interesting to learn and see. Group shares our artwork at meetings and collaborates with many different forms of media. Artists' work displayed in the window of Vintage Venue on Race Street in Cambridge. Facebook: wednesdaymorningartists. Email is: wednesdaymorningartists@gmail.com
THE TALBOT COUNTY OF FREDERICK DOUGLASS, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA. What can Frederick Douglass, Talbot County's most famous native son, teach us as America continues struggling with racial divisions, the legacy of enslavement, and the quest for a just, free, and embracing society? Join Jeff McGuiness and Lance Morris in a discussion of the eloquent words penned by Douglass himself, juxtaposed against the very landscape that bore witness to the genesis of his quest for a society that transcends differences and dismantles the constancy of hate. Two sessions, May 22 and 29. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
PLANNING FOR OUR FUTURE BEFORE IT REACHES US, 1 to 2:30 p.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join experts Gordan Fronk and Elena Sallitto as they demystify estate and elder planning, ensuring that you are well-prepared for the future. "Planning for Our Future Before It Reaches Us," delves into the intricate world of estate and elder law to safeguard your assets, make informed decisions, and prioritize the well-being of your loved ones. Two sessions, May 29 and June 5. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
OYSTER GARDENING 101, 4:30 to 6 p.m., Pickering Creek Audubon Center. Oyster gardening provides import nursery habitat as well as filtering the waters of the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries; oyster reefs are a vital part of conserving the Chesapeake Bay. Come learn about a new spat growing program, the challenges these bivalve face, and the research methods we use to analyze the success of oyster nurseries. Sign up at pickeringcreek.org/programs/upcoming-programs/.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Raymond Vergne, M.D., as he turns his focus on the intriguing lives and careers of selected vice presidents from the 20th century. This course is the final chapter in his comprehensive series, offering a deep dive into the often overlooked but fascinating world of Vice Presidents. Three sessions, May 23, 30 and June 6. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
NATURE AT NIGHT HIKE, 8:30 to 10:30 p.m., Pickering Creek Audubon Center. Explore Pickering Creek's Farm-to-Bay Loop at night and use special UV flashlights to reveal nocturnal wildlife and unique plants and fungi not usually visible to the human eye. By the main parking lot, stop by a mothing station with the opportunity to see Luna moths and other impressive early summer species. Sign up at pickeringcreek.org/programs/upcoming-programs/.
FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
A SENSE OF PLACE, 10 to 11:30 a.m., via Zoom. This course is a discussion and exploration of our perceived special places. It celebrates the individuality and mutability of places and times. Readings will be suggested. Participation is a requirement. Three sessions, May 17, 24 and 31. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
EASTON FARMERS MARKET, 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., 100 Block North Washington Street, Easton. Open rain or shine. Live music at 10:30 a.m.
ST. MICHAELS FARMERS MARKET, 8:30 to 11 a.m., 206 S. Talbot Street, St. Michaels. Open rain or shine.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
CARPOOL, 8 p.m., Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover Street, Easton. Carpool is a tribute band that recreates the sound, feel, look and vibe that made the Cars world famous. carpooltributeband.com.
RIDGELY TRAIN STATION, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Open the first Saturdays of the month through September. The Ridgely Historical Society will guide visitors through the history of the town. Info: 410-991-8225.

YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 1 p.m. Yoga for advanced beginners with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
FIRST RESPONDERS CELEBRATION, 11 to 11:30 a.m., Service Memorial, corner of Dover and West Streets, Easton. Sen. Ben Cardin will join the Prager family and Bluepoint Hospitality in the celebration, recognizing Talbot County's finest. Following the ceremony, attendees are invited to enjoy a complimentary slice of authentic Roman-style pizza at nearby Bluepoint Hospitality eatery, Roma Alla Pala.
CLASSIC MOTOR MUSEUM TOUR, 10 a.m. to noon, Class Motor Museum, 102 Morengo, St Michaels. Embark on a fun journey through time and horsepower with our exclusive "Car Talk" tour of the Classic Motor Museum of St. Michaels. This immersive experience offers a unique opportunity to delve into the captivating world of automotive history, featuring a curated collection of vintage cars spanning from the iconic Model T to the sleek Mustang and Stingray. $35. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.

Learn about Poplar Island's unique story and continuing habitat successes in this talk given by Kristina Motley from Maryland Environmental Service. Poplar Island is an environmental restoration project located in the Chesapeake Bay of Talbot County, Maryland. The beneficial use project, started in the 1990's, relies on dredged material collected from the approach channels to the Baltimore Harbor to restore lost remote island habitat within the Chesapeake Bay. Two sessions, Wednesday June 5, and a field trip Monday, June 10, to Poplar Island from 9 a.m. to noon. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.

title: Denton dancer achieves mastery
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Denton dancer achieves mastery

 March 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The nearly packed house in the auditorium had on beautiful silk as live musicians played Indian music. Rows of flowers and tea lights bedecked the stage as a local dancer struck poses that are 5,000 years old.Aspiring doctor Retu Domnic gave a dance performance at Saints Peter and Paul Performing Arts Center on March 16. She danced alone for around three hours.
She had bells on her ankles and her hands, fingertips and her feet were ceremonially painted red. This was a special dance for Domnic, as it marked her professional debut.
The dance form she performed was called Bharatanatyam, originally a temple dance in southern India. The recital included Domnic's arangetram, which marks a significant milestone in the dancer's training.
She can now teach and is considered a master of the form. She had family travel from Kansas, Salisbury and Toronto to witness this moment.
"It was very special. I don't think I have ever had an event this big that was just for me and my accomplishment," Domnic said. "Not only is this my debut as a professional dancer, but it is also dedicated to my mom, and it was really special to have her memory. Everyone that came knew her and were mostly crying. I felt her presence there and I think that is why I did so well."
The audience reacted with applause after her performance.
"I got a standing ovation at the end," she said. "I made a little speech, then we all had dinner. I thanked my mom, my dance teacher, my dad and everyone that came and helped. Then I made a big announcement that I was going to medical school in two weeks — St. George's University in Grenada," she said.
She wants to study pediatrics or maybe psychiatry. In this dance on this night, she felt empowered.
"When I was onstage this time, I didn't really think about the steps. I just knew everything," she said. "I was more focused on the emotions and trying to convey that. During the dances everyone was tearing up."
After leaving Bahrain, a small island country in the Middle East, as a child, Domnic moved to Caroline County.
"I went to Denton Elementary, then I went to Lockerman and then to North Caroline," she said.
She only moved away to go to college at University of Maryland and then to get her masters in New York at Hofstra University. And then she started working full time in New York.
Domnic's mom, who passed away, taught dance in Salisbury. It is Domnic's dream to teach future students in honor of her mom.
"It is my dream and also my mom's dream to start back up my mom's dance school and teach kids maybe on the side as I go through medical school."

title: Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah

 January 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Saturday, Temple B'Nai Israel and community members gathered together for a community Hanukkah candle lighting. The celebration and observance is continuing through sundown on Thursday.Rabbi Fred Scherlinder Dobb, interim rabbi for the temple and Satell Center for Jewish Life on the Eastern Shore, emphasized Saturday's candle lighting as a tradition that strengthens Easton and the surrounding community.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher were two of the community members who attended, Dobb said.
"This is an opportunity to unite the members of Temple B'Nai Israel with the broader community," he said. "Year to year, different area clergypeople, and elected officials and others are able to join us."
Barbara Spector, president of the Temple B'Nai Israel's Board of Trustees, said there was singing, lighting of Hanukkah menorahs and games.
Hanukkah is considered a festival of lights and lasts eight days, in which Jewish people gather to light a candle in a menorah each day. It stems from the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the second century B.C.
"This eight-day holiday falls around the new moon that is closest to the winter solstice," Dobb said. "So it comes at the time of greatest darkness, both daytime and nighttime. And in that darkness moment, we introduce light."
This year, Hanukkah began Dec. 25. Temple B'Nai Israel celebrates with latkes (fried potato pancakes), sufganiyah (jelly donuts) and a dreidel (a four-sided spinning top).
As the only full-service synagogue in Talbot and neighboring counties, Temple B'Nai Israel is a sacred place for many that practice Judaism. Since beginning his interim role in November, Dobb has come to appreciate the diversity of those that attend the temple's programs and services.
"I am consistently astounded by not only the depth of thought and positivity of the members of this temple community, but also of the region as a whole," Dobb said. "I have not met someone from Easton and Talbot County who I have not been impressed by in some way.
"Irrespective of faith, or political affiliation or race, folks are sharing a spirit of sorts. And the larger community is clearly stronger for that ethos."
Spector and Dobb admit that distance is a challenge for many, especially in the rural Eastern Shore compared to other parts of the region. Temple B'Nai Israel sees people often come from Centreville, Cambridge, Stevensville and Chestertown, among other areas.
Dobb welcomes the challenges that may come with accommodating a wide range of people and practices.
"People of all backgrounds and ideologies and levels of observance, as well as different comfort and knowledge with tradition and Hebrew, all come together for the same events and the same worship services," Dobb said. "So finding the range of sweet spots that will touch everyone in some way is both a challenge and an opportunity."
Dobb said the Hannukah celebration is about "hope and community."
The rabbi said the theme of Saturday was that "we are all in it together."
"That applies to the civic fabric of our region and the democracy of which we are a part," Dobb said. "It also applies to the natural world for which we are all responsible, and we have to work together to caretake one another, as well as to be good stewards of the land and the day. These things can only be done in unison, and blessingly, that spirit of unity in the broader community is strong and growing."

title: Community-painted mural installed in Greensboro
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Community-painted mural installed in Greensboro

 July 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 401
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — A new piece of community artwork is on display in Greensboro at the corner of Sunset Avenue and Main Street. On Saturday, a 4-by-24-foot painting was installed on the side of Tenchi Spanish American Kitchen.The Choptank Tolomato Legacy Project and its executive director Jimmy Reynolds spearheaded the project, ensuring that hundreds of locals in and near Greensboro could put their own touches on the mural.
"Our intention was to do the mural on panels, take them into the community," Reynolds said. " … Get the mural project to where the people live, work and play so that they can be involved."
Funded by the Maryland State Arts Commission's Public Arts Across Maryland program, the mural includes portraits of famed abolitionist Frederick Douglass and his wife Anna Murray Douglass, who was born in Denton.
There are underground railroad quilt patterns, a depiction of the old site of the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company Carnival and imagery honoring the town's Native American and Guatemalan roots.
"We're knitting all these local stories together," Reynolds said. "So we're hitting everybody in the community, so everybody's involved."
The mural was taken to Greensboro Elementary School and the Benedictine School, Reynolds said, along with the Whitsitt Center, an addiction treatment center in Chestertown. Residents also painted the mural onsite in Greensboro during select Saturdays.
Reynolds pointed to a lack of transportation that motivated Choptank Tolomato, a cultural literacy and arts nonprofit based in Sudlersville, to begin taking projects to "outer communities" around two years ago.
"It's not regular outside of towns, and it's really hard for parents to get their kids around," Reynolds said. "So that's why we're out in the communities."
Choptank Tolomato works on projects up and down the Eastern Shore, in areas such as Kent Narrows, Centreville and Chestertown. It strives to involve underserved communities and children with learning disabilities.
Audrey Copeland, a student at Kent County High School, worked as the mural project's intern this spring and summer. Reynolds said Copeland helped involve fellow students with the painting.
As an artist and educator, Reynolds hopes that he can continue to provide visual-based education for the youth. He noted that for children with autism, the act of painting teaches "how to go through procedures."
"Part of what I see is my mission, too, is a way to show kids on the Eastern Shore that there is a path for them to do what I'm doing as a job in our area," Reynolds said.

title: Cleaning up iconic statue - Day of Resilience planned for Saturday

 CAMBRIDGE - The Harriet Tubman statue in front of the Dorchester County Courthouse got a good cleaning Monday morning in preparation for the Day of Resilience planned for Saturday, Sept. 9.Sculptor Wesley Wofford and his wife, Odessey, were on hand to help the volunteers learn the process of cleaning the towering sculpture, which will be dedicated as part of the ceremonies on Saturday.Wesley Wofford gently caressed the sculpture that he brought to life and installed in Cambridge a year ago."She's aging nicely," he said. "She has changed a lot in a year." He pointed to the patina along the leg and foot of a slave reaching up to Tubman, the changing color caused by visitors touching the statue. That is exactly what Wofford pictured when he designed the long leg and foot at the base of the statue."It's transformed this space," the sculptor said.The cleaning process was simple. A leaf blower was used to clean off loose dirt and leaves and then soap was used to scrub the statue.The soap was rinsed off and then the leaf blowers were used to blow dry the statue. A couple of hours later, a fresh coat of wax was applied.The washing process took less than an hour.Among those helping clean the statue were Adrian Holmes and April Byrd.Holmes is the president of Alpha Genesis CDC, which led the drive to raise funds and commission the statue. Byrd is the vice president.The ceremony on Saturday will start at the courthouse at 10:30 a.m. and a procession will proceed to the Choptank River where there will be libations at 11 a.m.The procession will return to the courthouse at noon for the dedication of the statue.

 The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum in St.Michaels will host the Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival XL on Friday-Sunday, Oct. 6-8.The Talbot County Young Professionals will also bring another event, Paddle-Jam, to the waterfront museum on Sunday, Oct. 8. The kayaking event is a fundraiser supporting CBMM's Rising Tide after-school program.The Small Craft Festival is "one of the nation's largest gatherings of small boat enthusiasts and unique watercraft," according an announcement from CBMM."Hundreds of amateur and professional boatbuilders and enthusiasts will come from all over the region to display their one-of-a-kind kayaks, canoes, and other traditional small craft at the 40th edition of the annual festival, which runs 10 a.m.-5 p.m. all three days." CBMM Shipyard staff and Chesapeake Wooden Boat Builders School instructors will offer boatbuilding and maritime demonstrations that day, and Chesapeake Light Craft will be on site with a selection of vessels from its fleet for guests to demo. That afternoon, there will be a spirited small craft race on the Miles River. Guests are encouraged to watch all the action from CBMM's waterfront and docks." A weeklong workshop on traditional Japanese boatbuilding, led by author, boatbuilder, and educator Douglas Brooks, concludes with a traditional Shinto launching ceremony to celebrate the completion of a 21-foot Japanese river boat.That evening, Brooks will be the keynote speaker at the dinner for MASCF participants.Everyone on campus for MASCF will be able to vote for their favorite boat, with the People's Choice award.The Paddle-Jam fundraiser is back for the first time since 2019 with CBMM inviting attendees to participate and enjoy the event by kayak, canoe or standup paddleboard."Paddlers of all levels are invited to join this 4.5-mile paddle poker "fun run" along the Miles River, beginning at 10am. Since 2015, the program has taught local students the basics of boatbuilding and woodworking with the opportunity to learn new skills, work with hand and power tools and explore the environment and history of the Chesapeake Bay region.The Talbot County Young Professionals are a committee of the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce, "We are so pleased to bring this exciting paddling event back, and what better location than the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum in St. Michaels and the Miles River!" said Amy Kreiner, president of the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce. "Rising Tide is such a valuable program, teaching our kids about the rich history and skills of our watermen, boatbuilders and the surrounding waterways." This year, the Paddle-Jam course begins at CBMM's Fogg's Landing launch and takes participants past the iconic Hooper Strait Lighthouse, Inn at Perry Cabin, Miles River Yacht Club, and more while following the St. Michaels shoreline. title: Castelli shares salty tales at museum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Castelli shares salty tales at museum

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Over 100 people gathered on March 5 at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum to hear about Marc Castelli's year on the water.The Kent County watercolorist, who works from photographs of boats and watermen, had many salty tales to tell as he showed his slideshow. The show, which Castelli has presented at the museum almost annually for more than a decade, is a visual diary of his year embedded with watermen.
"We have been doing this since 2012," said Pete Lesher, chief historian at the Maritime Museum. "This is clearly something that a lot of people look forward to.
Lesher called it "Castelli's year-in-review out with the watermen."
Castelli goes further than just bearing witness. He is collecting material for his artwork.
"Every day he goes out with the watermen in all weather conditions, in various locations, in various fisheries," Lesher said. "He creates a certain empathy with the culture of the watermen by educating us on their world."
Castelli gets his information from those who work on the water. He gets on board their workboats with a camera to collect images for his paintings. He knows the Chesapeake by river, and he knows the different ways fish are harvested.
Castelli showed a picture of an invasive blue catfish. Watermen use hooks on long lines to catch them.
"They can get up to 60 pounds," Castelli said. "They eat almost anything that swims in the water — 70% of the biomass of the James River are blue cats."
He said the Bay needs more than one processing plant for blue catfish.
This processor, Nick Hargrove, sells his product to the Maryland Food Bank and government institutions, such as correctional facilities and schools.
Castelli argues that based on what he has observed, this is not enough to address the volume of blue catfish infiltrating the Chesapeake's ecosystem. During the event Tuesday, he argued for a change in the law to allow for grinding up blue catfish for uses like cat food and fertilizer.
Castelli shared his thoughts on oyster populations, dolphin habitat and other issues he observed alongside the Chesapeake's watermen.
He brings an eye trained by art history to see abstract patterns in the water, on a perch's shiny scales and in a basket full of writhing crabs. With this trained eye, Castelli said, he has the ability to show the extent of waterman culture and to bring attention to their issues.
"If you look for and read in the print media and on TV, you will get the idea that this culture is done," Castelli said. "It is not. That it is moving on."
He noted that the majority of the men working the water are in their 50s up to 70s and 80s.
"It is very hard to get young people to work that hard," Castelli said.
Castelli works as hard as the watermen.
His Nikon was so filled with aquatic detritus after his year on the water that the camera company refused to clean out his camera.
"I take very detailed pictures with a lot of attention to textures and the shades of the colors," Castelli said. "I hate painting crabs, and I hate painting flannel as much as I hate painting nets.
He said he is fascinated by light and water. He shoots thousands of pictures of water.
All this emphasis on shapes repeating and light reflecting is weighted in his paintings by a passionate defense of the watermen themselves.
"When you are out there you are in a totally different world without any political biases going on," Castelli said.

 RIDGELY - Toadstools, unicorns and pixies all passed by the fairy king and queen, who sat in thrones and held scepters.Adkins Arboretum had its annual Fairyfest in a light rain on Oct. 7. The soft rain dampened no one's spirits as live music filled the pavillion and crafts were made in the main building. Drawing inspiration from pre-Christian Great Britain and the Celts, the woods were alive with magic fairy houses.In past years Adkins has been overrun with fairy fans, so now they put a cap on how many can attend. Even with that they had over 500 people attend. There were food trucks including Scottish Highland Creamery. The musical talent included Ampersand and Allegra Choir, who gave some rich harmonic a cappella singing.There was even belly dancing put on by the Sammati Dance Troupe.Little children with unicorn hats got to ride horses with their grandparents and parents closely monitoring the journey. A lot of the festival is geared toward little girls. They are perfectly suited for this kind of magic.Jenny Houghton is the assistant director at Adkins, but today goes by "Queen Fairy." She has monarch butterfly wings to match her braided red hair.She said, "Fairfest was my brain child. I came up with it about eight years ago, and it has become our most well attended event.We are sold out today at over 400. Our first year we had over 700 but realized we didn't have enough parking." She focused on Adkins' mission and how it fits well with the event."It is just a fun day getting kids outside in nature and helping them realize how magical it is. We had a lot of 4 to 6 year olds, but that said we are seeing older kids. We have a lot of teen volunteers who enjoy it as much as the kids. It is with our mission, which is to create exceptional experiences outside," Houghton said.There is a bridge that serves as an entrance to Adkins. All along the walkway there were ornate floral structures built by sponsor Chesapeake Blooms.One aspect of the event is a collection of fairy houses that are placed along a woodland path.This year six people were recognized for their building efforts. They are: Cristina Swaine, Dawn Folmer, Sheri Lynch, Clara Terry, Connie Schroth and Nancy Bennington.Charlotte Reyes, 6, of Cambridge was getting face painting. Mom Deenie Reyes, said, "It is very whimsical. It is almost like you are in another world. It is very hands-on for the kids. It is creative and fulfills little girls' fantasies." One of the woman painting faces and dressed as a bumblebee was Nancy Reid from Trappe. She said, "We are sharing the magic right here. title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: LAURA TAYMAN
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LAURA TAYMAN | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said.
"Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it." "The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises." "My tenure at the museum was wonderful," Hooker said.
"Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me." Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering." "I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said.
"And we really want to downsize our housing situation." "It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."
