title: Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi

 July 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly nine months after the previous rabbi retired, a new permanent rabbi has stepped into the role at Temple B'nai Israel.Rabbi Jordan Goldson assumed the position on July 1, following the retirement of Rabbi Peter Hyman in October.
In the search for a new permanent rabbi, the temple's Board of Trustees created a list of potential candidates for interviews after establishing priorities, according to Barbara Spector, the board president during the selection process. Spector said the board was looking for a Reform rabbi with more experience to fit Temple B'nai Israel's established congregation.
Before coming to Easton, Goldson had extensive experience leading congregations. After being ordained at Hebrew Union College in 1987, Goldson became a full-time Reform rabbi at Temple B'nai Tikvah in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, where he served for 12 years. Upon leaving the temple, Goldson lived in Israel for some time before moving back to the U.S. to lead several congregations around the country. Most recently, Goldson served as the rabbi at Har Sinai Temple in Pennington, New Jersey.
"He has a very calm demeanor and a wonderful background with his experience in being part of an inclusive congregation," David Holtz said. Holtz took over the position of temple executive director after Goldson was selected.
Holtz described him as "one of those very nice people that you're grateful that you've been able to encounter, particularly in a role that will mean so much to the community and to the congregation."
Hyman described Goldson as very bright, engaging, warm, creative and people-focused.
As the former rabbi at the temple, Hyman said maintaining a presence in the community was always his first priority, and he has great confidence in Goldson building on that foundation.
"He's really terrific," Hyman said. "He's going to continue to grow the congregation, and I know he'll be successful."
Hyman's years of dedication and congregation building have not gone unnoticed. Goldson recognized Hyman for his "spectacular job" in expanding the congregation and said he will build on what Hyman has done to increase the temple's reach.
Focused on inclusivity, Goldson said his plans to grow the congregation, creating an environment where "people feel that they matter."
Temple B'nai Israel is the hub for Jewish life on the Eastern Shore and represents a vast community. Goldson said he will reach out to the community and welcome people who may not know about the congregation.
"We'll be doing a lot of different things that I think are going to attract people to the temple," Goldson said.
The temple offers a religious school for students in kindergarten through 12th grade. Spector said she expects Goldson will help attract more young families to the temple and expand the religious school.
"We're just hoping he can help us get ready for the next decade by helping us educate young Jewish children," Spector said.
To support this effort, Goldson plans to expand the temple's programs, including youth, community service and religious education initiatives.
As he becomes more comfortable in his new role, Goldson has enjoyed the positive energy and dynamics of the community, and he recognizes that it will take more than just him to grow the congregation's impact.
"I can see that this is a community that embraces each other," Goldson said. "It's a very tight-knit, religious community and I'm really looking forward to working with the larger community here to see what we can do to make Easton and the surrounding areas the most wonderful place it can be."

title: Waterfowl Festival soaring to new heights
author: Staff Writer
content:
Waterfowl Festival soaring to new heights

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Congratulations to the many people who made this year's Waterfowl Festival a success.The annual celebration of wildlife, art, music and history brought between 25,000 and 30,000 people to Easton last weekend.
Congratulations, too, go to Deena Kilmon in her first year as executive director of the festival. She is definitely at the top of the list for a rookie of the year award.
If there was any fear of a drop-off with new leadership, Kilmon put those fears to rest and set a high bar for success in coming years.
"We know we broke every record we've ever broken," Kilmon said on Monday.
"We had the highest attendance ever," Kilmon said. "It's hard for us to gauge because not everyone buys a ticket. But we do know that every parking space was full and every bus had about 45 minutes to an hourlong wait, and we had to add three buses on Saturday to accommodate the people."
Kilmon got a helping hand from Mother Nature who blessed the weekend with lovely weather and temperatures approaching 80 degrees under sunny skies for several of the days.
The executive director said multiple vendors — many of whom are already asking about next year — sold out or had record days at the festival.
If you have a 2025 calendar already, mark the weekend of Nov. 14-16 for the 54th Waterfowl Festival. We have no doubt that Kilmon will improve upon the tremendous success of this year's festival.
The success of the Waterfowl Festival is a success for the town of Easton and Talbot County too.
Downtown Easton shops were packed all three days of the festival, and restaurants had waiting lists for tables.
Kilmon called the relationship between the festival and local businesses "incredibly important."
"We're symbiotic," she said. "So if they succeed, we succeed and vice versa."
The three-day festival has an economic impact of more than $3 million each year, Kilmon said. It benefits hotels, restaurants, retailers and even local nonprofits.
"It's typically one of the biggest fundraising events of the year because a lot of the food vendors and people involved in the festival, they are nonprofits," Kilmon said. "And they're allowed to keep their proceeds, so it's extremely important to a lot of people."
At a breakfast Friday morning, Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism Director Cassadra Vanhooser extolled the virtues of the business community that makes the "wonderful things" that happen in the county possible.
"It's that private investment along with the public investment that builds the community," she said. "And it's the festivals like the Waterfowl Festival — the granddaddy of them all — that weaves that fabric of the quality of life that we all love so much."
The festival may have just celebrated its 53rd anniversary, but it continues to grow and evolve.
Throughout the festival venues music filled the air and complemented the many duck and geese calls typical of the festival. Overall there were 38 musical acts on multiple stages.
"That made the festival have a different vibe this year, I think," Kilmon said, "just made it more of a friendly family party on every corner."
Feedback has been "incredibly positive," and Kilmon is excited to begin work on continuing Easton's Waterfowl tradition.
"Fifty-three years of our community coming together just gets better every year," Kilmon said. "And we're already working on next year, believe it or not."
It is good that Kilmon and her team are already working on the 2025 show. This year's show will be tough to top. We have no doubt they will rise to the challenge.

title: Maryland map hooks artists together
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Maryland map hooks artists together

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's an interesting piece of art on the wall of the Cecil County Arts Council in Elkton that pays homage to each county in Maryland; made by fiber artists from other states.Colleen Tiefenthal connected with artists in Washington, Florida, Connecticut and New Jersey and each turned out a piece that represents one of the 23 counties for the projected entitled "The Maryland Counties Rug Hooking Project."
"It was a really fun project," Tiefenthal said. "It was my concept and design. Then I reached out to my fellow rug hookers."
The North East woman — an Ohio transplant — hasn't met any rug hookers in Cecil County yet so she's the only local connection to the project. Tiefenthal knew all but two of the 16 rug hookers who had a hand in the map.
"I thought, 'how cool would it be ... that we could do one thing together,'" she said.
She got a grant from the Maryland State Arts Council to fund the project. That $4,000 covered the cost of materials and postage. Tiefenthal said the project taught her how to use a new computer program: Canva.
Work began with her cutting all the pieces of linen for the backing and much of the wool that was used to create each county.
"I sent them kits. They did their parts and sent it back," she said. "One person, it was their first attempt at rug hooking but she's a fabric artist." Most received more than one county to complete. They held several virtual meetings before the rug hooking began.
A board Tiefenthal painted to mimic the Maryland flag in grey tones is the base and each piece is wired onto the board. Accompanying the map is a legend with numbers corresponding to each county. Tiefenthal also created a booklet about the project and added a rug hooked segment of the Maryland flag. Each county is represented by something central to its heritage. For Cecil County, it's the Turkey Point Lighthouse.
Admitting she was nervous waiting for the pieces to return, Tiefenthal said the fear dissolved as she opened each package.
"When the first five to six pieces came back and were wonderful, it gave me confidence," she said. She knew the pieces were going to fit together.
Tiefenthal said it was her husband, Jim, who suggested a separate panel on the bottom of the display.
"It was Jim's idea for the "Touch This" panel," she said. This way the curious can feel the texture of the work but not touch the map itself.
The map visited Salisbury, Md. last weekend and has already made a stop at the North East Library. It's on display at the Arts Council, 135 East Main St. in Elkton until Oct. 7 then it moves to the Elkton branch library Oct. 7 through Oct. 28.
In 2027, it travels to a fiber art show in Newport, R.I. held by the International Guild of Handhooking Rugmakers and to Sauder Village for a similar show in Archibald, Ohio.

title: Tour five regional museums through virtual reality - Washington College's Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnership's new exhibit in downtown Chestertown
content:
Tour five regional museums through virtual reality - Washington College's Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnership's new exhibit in downtown Chestertown

 November 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 625
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Washington College's Center for Environment & Society (CES) and the Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnerships (DSMP) project are proud to invite local and regional visitors to virtually "tour" the collections from several regional museums, all in one place.Housed in the community space at 210 South Cross Street in downtown Chestertown, the exhibit includes interactive exhibit banners from the DSMP's collaborations with Kent County museums over the last six years, including Betterton Heritage Museum, the Worton Point Schoolhouse, the Waterman's Museum, the Kent Museum, and Sumner Hall.With the goal of preserving and providing greater access to the local histories of our community, the exhibit offers digitized looks into each museum viewable through virtual reality with 360-degree virtual tours of the museums, a look at digitized collections from each site, oral history interviews, and more.The exhibit also features a new curved projection theatre which creates an immersive environment in which to experience the virtual tours.The panels were created by Washington College students participating in the DSMP project and serve as a continuation of their work which was curated under the guidance of Sara Clarke-De Reza, Associate Professor of Education and Director of the Museum, Community and Field Education Minor; Julie Markin, Professor of Anthropology and Director of Archaeology; and Raven Bishop, Assistant Director of Educational Technology and Lead of the Virtual/Augmented Reality Digital Imaging Studio at the Millier Library.After a successful one-day pop-up showcase of the project last fall, an opportunity to put the work on display for a longer period, and for a wider public audience, emerged at the Cross Street space."Working with these museums affords our students the opportunity to apply concepts and best practices learned in the classroom to a project that makes a real impact for the local community," said Bishop. "Students and community stakeholders are immediately able to see the real-world impact of this work as it improves access to the history and culture of Kent County within and beyond our community." Bishop added that community partners often report that their organizations feel reinvigorated by the energy and enthusiasm that DSMP students bring to the project. The reciprocal relationship advances the common purpose of providing greater access to the important cultural heritage of the Eastern Shore that is held in so many small, rural community museums."It would be easy to say that the technology is the most interesting part of this project," said Bishop. "But what is most exciting about this project is the way students are able to authentically contribute to a community-engaged digital scholarship project with real-world impact.Bringing students off of the Washington College campus and into meaningful partnership with community members is one of the most important goals of our work. Students benefit from feeling a stronger connection to place and feel-good knowing that they can contribute to Kent County in a small way." The exhibit is located at 210 South Cross Street and is open to the public through January on the First Fridays of each month from 5-8 p.m., as well as every Saturday from 9 to 11 a.m. The collections may also be viewed by appointment.Scanning the QR codes on the exhibit's exterior windows will allow access to digital versions of the exhibit even when the space is closed. Cultural Heritage organizations are encouraged to reserve time in the space to hold meetings.More information about the Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnerships Project can be found at dsmpproject.net/

title: Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Every Wednesday, a group of local artists from a diverse set of mediums and backgrounds comes together to share their latest creations. This segment of their meetings is called "brings and brags."Twenty years ago, the group began meeting at the Dorchester Center for the Arts when it was still in the historic home on High Street. They then relocated to a deli inside of a strip mall, which didn't survive the pandemic. The loyal members began meeting at a park until finding their spot at Peach Blossom Place.
"It's a beautiful building," the group's leader Susan Lester said. "We've had a wonderful experience being here."
The Wednesday Morning Artists are an eclectic group, who bring their unique skillsets together in mixed-media collaborative pieces, one of a kind oil paintings and an array of other media. On the fourth Wednesday of the month, there is a live art demonstration that often includes hands-on participation.
The group is led Lester with support from Robert Gladney and Nancy Hoffman. The members also showcase their work outside of "brings and brags" at the Hyatt Regency on Saturdays during the summer, at community events like Taste of Cambridge and at pop-up art events around town.
Lester said her favorite part about the Wednesday Morning Artists is learning and collaborating with the members. "The fact that we're so diverse, we have such a range of artists, I never even heard of some of the stuff they do," she said.
The wide range of art forms include weaving, pine needle coiling, jewelry designing, photography, sculpting, music, woodcarving and the more traditional forms of art like oil painting and pottery.
"We have pine needle weavers, who knew? I never heard of that," Lester said. "You know, when you think of art, you think of acrylics or oils or watercolors, and it's way beyond that."
The group has also created fellowship outside of Wednesday morning, enjoying monthly dinners and an annual fall picnic at Gerry Boyle Park.
Lester said they are always accepting new members. "And trust me, we don't judge based on level of experience," she said. "Pros, beginners, we want you all, and we'll help you learn how to do it or you can help us learn."
For more information on the artists, future events, and how to join, visit the Wednesday Morning Artists Facebook page.

 CHESTERTOWN — The Artists' Gallery will feature the work of one of its exhibiting artists, Carol McClees, on First Friday, July 4, in a body of work titled Colorful Visions. McClees' goal is to create a vibrant painting that conveys a sense of life, vibrancy and movement — in her words, "ALIVE WITH COLOR!"A contemporary artist and award-winning painter, McClees' self-directed education has included studying with some of the best national and regional artists. While she has worked in a variety of mediums, she favors painting in oil.
McClees has exhibited her paintings in many juried shows throughout the United States, including but not limited to Coos Art Museum (Oregon), American Society of Marine Artists East Regional Show hosted by Biggs Museum of American Art (Delaware), Washington County Museum of Fine Arts (Maryland), and Buffalo Naval Park Museum (New York), as well as Working Artists Forum's Local Color and the Waterfowl Festival (Easton). Her work is part of many private collections throughout the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, West Coast and New England. McClees is an active member of many art organizations, including the American Society of Marine Artists, Working Artists' Forum and Mid-Atlantic Plein Air Painters Association. Her degrees include an RN and an MBA in marketing.
Born and raised in New England, McClees is married to a native Marylander and lives in Baltimore. She enjoys sailing on the Chesapeake Bay aboard her 36-foot Skean Dhu, tennis, Nantucket basket weaving, embroidery and reading.
McClees' artistic inspiration comes from a maritime landscape, a beloved animal or an architectural delight, whether painting in plein air or in her home studio. "Striving to achieve a painterly realism one brush stroke at a time, using abundant color, and supporting textural tools is my artistic goal. I love to find and capture the unique moment in time when the subject matter comes to life — that fleeting moment when the magical effects of the sun cause dramatic play between lights and darks. When accomplished, I believe that artistic tension is at its best, revealing a painting Alive with Color, which evokes thoughtful emotion and allows the viewer to complete the story."
The public is invited to attend the Artists' Gallery's opening reception for McClees on First Friday, July 4, from 5 to 7:30 p.m. Her paintings will be featured in the gallery throughout the month of July. The Artists' Gallery is located at 239 High St. in Chestertown, and is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sundays from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. For more information, visit www.theartistsgalleryctown.com or call 410-778-2425.

Tred Avon Players announces its 2024 season

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - Tred Avon Players unveiled an exciting lineup for the coming year as it enters its 43rd season of providing live theater to the Eastern Shore.The shows will be performed in partnership with the Oxford Community Center at 200 Oxford Road.
Flex Passes and individual ticket sales are available for all four shows at www.tredavonplayers.org.
'YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO REMAIN DEAD'
By Pat Cook Directed by Rob Sanchez Feb. 15-25, 2024 In this hilarious audience-participation murder mystery, narrator Harnell Chesterton takes the audience to visit a small community theater group staging a play set in the Deep South. The play's characters are all in an uproar because Fat Daddy, the patriarch of the family, is about to change his will. Is Fat Daddy the target of the killer? Is his wife, Sweet Mamma, looking to do him in? Or is it his son Earl, daughter-in-law Savannah or daughter Hyacinth?
Maybe it's the hired hand Clete! But - is it really Fat Daddy who is dead? Just wait until local police sleuth Officer Bainbridge begins his investigation!
'THE BOYS FROM SYRACUSE'
By George Abbott Music & Lyrics by Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart Directed by Liz Clarke April 18-28, 2024 The Boys from Syracuse is a spirited adaptation of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors. Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio embark on a quest to find Antipholus' lost twin in the city of Ephesus, leading to a series of comical misadventures.
Against the backdrop of war between Ephesus and Syracuse, the travelers navigate chaos, encountering mistaken identities and humorous situations.
As Antipholus of Ephesus becomes entangled in debts and love interests, the narrative unfolds in a whirlwind of hilarity. Set in the 1930s, the musical features a fast-paced, funny script by George Abbott and a swinging score with timeless tunes like "Falling in Love With Love," "This Can't Be Love," and "Sing for Your Supper." "The Boys from Syracuse" is a delightful and tuneful tribute to Shakespeare's enduring comedic masterpiece.
'THE HALLELUJAH GIRLS'
By Jessie Jones, Nicholas Hope, Jamie Wooten Directed by Sammie Mooney Aug. 15-25, 2024 Hilarity ensues in the small town of Eden Falls, Georgia, as a group of spirited women decide to transform their lives at SPADEE-DAH!, an abandoned church-turned-day-spa.
Meeting every Friday, the friends, led by the high-spirited Sugar Lee, confront the realities of time and loss after the passing of a dear friend.
Each woman faces unique challenges - from romantic disillusionment and family troubles to stagnant marriages.
As they strive to pursue their dreams and embrace change, the women navigate comic twists involving unexpected ex-boyfriends, unlikely marriage proposals, and a determined rival threatening their beloved spa. Amidst the laughter and joy, this rollicking Southern comedy captures the women's journey overcoming obstacles, forging new paths and celebrating the bonds of friendship.
'BLITHE SPIRIT'
By Noel Coward Directed by Susan Patterson Oct. 24 to Nov. 3, 2024 Blithe Spirit unfolds in the home of writer Charles Condomine and his wife, Ruth.
Charles invites the eccentric medium Madame Arcati for a seance to gather inspiration for his book. Unexpectedly, the seance brings back Charles' first wife, Elvira, causing mischief that only he can witness.
Elvira accidentally causes Ruth's demise, resulting in Charles being haunted by both wives. The trio seeks Madame Arcati's help to send the spirits back, blending farce, emotion, and wit in this intensely funny and character-driven play.

title: Col. Tench Tilghman honored with wreath laying
content:
Col. Tench Tilghman honored with wreath laying

 September 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 235
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Friday, the Col. Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution inducted four new members, called compatriots, into the organization - Michael Olds from Queen Anne's County, Joseph Roy Smith from Caroline County and Paul Wesley Hagood and his year-old son, James Wesley Hagood, from Talbot County.After the meeting, the Sons of the American Revolution and Daughters of the American Revolution sponsored a wreath-laying ceremony at Tilghman's grave in Oxford that was hosted by the Oxford Cemetery to honor the memory and contributions of Col. Tilghman to the cause of American independence and freedom.Descendants of Tench Tilghman including Mrs. Cox, Elizabeth Montgomery Hinson and Timothy Tilghman, attended the ceremony.The National Society of the Sons of the American Revolution, founded in 1889, is a non-profit and non-partisan organization dedicated to promoting patriotism, preserving American History and promoting education to our future generations.The next meeting of the local chapter will be a social event to occur at the White Swan Tavern in Chestertown on Saturday, Dec. 16.Refreshments will be provided. To learn more, go to facebook.com/Col-TenchTilghman.
